datasets.label: hugging-face.rete — the whole Hugging Face Hub as one graph: 2.9M models, 1.4M spaces, 1.35M people, and what was finetuned from what (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The public [Hugging Face Hub](https://huggingface.co) — **85.1 M triples** covering **2,932,554 models**, **1,428,760 spaces**, **972,446 dataset repos**, **94,404 arXiv papers** and the **1,354,271 accounts** behind them (1,315,773 users + 38,498 organizations, harvested account-by-account from the Hub API over three days). **The point of this graph is the derivation fabric**: **842,649 base-model edges** typed by *how* a model derives (`hf:finetunedFrom`, `hf:quantizedFrom`, `hf:adapterFor`, `hf:mergedFrom` — all `⊑ prov:wasDerivedFrom`), so `hf:finetunedFrom+` walks a whole model genealogy: 19,543 descendants hang off Llama-3.1-8B, and distilbert-base-uncased is the most-finetuned node on the Hub with 12,052 direct children. Alongside it: **981,507 space→repo edges** from the Hub's own used-in index (`hf:usesModel`/`hf:usesDataset` — Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct powers 33,872 spaces), **350,688 model→training-dataset** links, and **766,758 repo→paper citations**. The **social layer is complete**: **2,905,301 follower edges**, 567,191 following edges and **457,195 org-membership edges** — so you can ask which lab's members are most followed, or which accounts bridge two organizations. Papers are minted at their **arXiv DataCite DOI** (`https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.{id}`) and `hf:doi ⊑ scholar:doi`, so with the 🧠 reasoner the Hub federates for free with DataCite, Crossref, OpenAIRE, OpenCitations and DBLP on the shared DOI — an ML model and the paper that describes it become one connected question. Accounts and repos sit at their real, clickable `huggingface.co` URLs. Vocabulary `hf:` = `w3id.org/rete/huggingface#` (8 classes, 56 properties, OWL 2 QL, aligned to the rete scholar hub: `hf:User ⊑ scholar:Person`, `hf:Model/DatasetRepo/Space/Paper ⊑ scholar:Work`) and the ontology travels inside the file. One curiosity the counters preserve: **23,855 storage buckets** exist across the Hub, but it has no public bucket-listing API — the counts are all anyone outside HF can see. Built from the daily [cfahlgren1/hub-stats](https://huggingface.co/datasets/cfahlgren1/hub-stats) Parquet backbone (Apache-2.0, pinned revision) plus a resumable Hub-API people harvest — data/hugging-face/scripts/{harvest_profiles,harvest_edges,harvest_spaces_links,to_parquet,build_nt}.py → rete build --pyramid-algo types --card. Snapshot 2026-07-23. 1.16 GB, remote-lazy on Cloudflare R2; the 11 Parquet companion tables travel beside it.
datasets.license: Apache-2.0 (cfahlgren1/hub-stats backbone) + public Hugging Face Hub metadata (factual profile/repo data; attribution: "Metadata from the Hugging Face Hub, huggingface.co")

The old encoders still dominate by count (distilbert-base-uncased ~12k children, bert-base-uncased ~6.8k) even though the headlines belong to the big LLMs; swap in hf:quantizedFrom or hf:mergedFrom to see a completely different leaderboard.

examples.tip: The Hub's own used-in index as graph edges (981,507 of them): count hf:usesModel per model to rank what actually runs in demos, not what merely gets downloaded. Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct leads with ~34k Spaces. Swap hf:usesModel → hf:usesDataset for the dataset side.

examples.tip: The social layer joined to the profile counters: members of one org (hf:memberOf) with their follower counts. Change the org IRI — try huggingface.co/google, /microsoft, /stability-ai. 457,195 membership edges and 2.9M follower edges are in the file.

examples.title: The papers the most models cite
examples.tip: repo → arXiv paper edges (766,758), grouped. The winner is a quiet one: 'Quantifying the Carbon Emissions of Machine Learning' is cited by 388,740 models — it's the paper behind the CO₂ line in the model-card template. These papers sit at their real arXiv DOIs, so turn on 🧠 and they federate with DataCite, Crossref and OpenAIRE.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX hf: <https://w3id.org/rete/huggingface#>
PREFIX schema: <https://schema.org/>
SELECT ?title (COUNT(?repo) AS ?citedBy) WHERE {
  ?repo hf:citesPaper ?paper .
  ?paper schema:name ?title .
}
GROUP BY ?title ORDER BY DESC(?citedBy) LIMIT 20

examples.tip: Builds a drawable star around Llama-3.1-8B — what it derives from, what derives from it, and the Spaces that run it. Switch Output → Graph. Any repo IRI works as the seed; keep LIMITs on popular models, their neighbourhoods are large.

examples.tip: hf:pipelineTag across 2.9M models — text-generation (389,726) is now nearly 3× text-classification, with text-to-image and reinforcement-learning close behind. A one-predicate scan that reads as a map of the field.

datasets.label: figshare.rete — figshare public research outputs as a DOI-linked scholarly graph, with downloadable file URLs (in progress, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The public [figshare](https://figshare.com) corpus (Digital Science) — research outputs from figshare.com + ~150 institutional/publisher portals — harvested via OAI-PMH (the `oai_datacite` DataCite-XML format) and modelled against the rete **DataCite ontology** (`dcite:`, https://w3id.org/rete/datacite#). **IN PROGRESS**: this preview is **444,230 resources / 16.0 M triples** from 24 of 28 item types (peer review, software, thesis, preprint, media, physical object, online resource, book, chapter, conference-contribution, report, poster, presentation, model, event…); the three giant types **figure, dataset and journal-contribution are still harvesting** and will be folded in. Each resource sits at its canonical DOI IRI (`https://doi.org/{doi}`) and carries `dcite:doi`/`prefix`, its DataCite type + figshare `dcite:resourceType` label, title, `dcite:creator` agents (with ORCID + affiliation when given), subjects, publisher, rights, dates and — distinctively — **downloadable file URLs** (`dcite:hasPart` → `ndownloader.figshare.com/files/…`, on 92% of resources). Because works are keyed by DOI, this AUTO-MERGES with the DataCite / Zenodo / OpenAIRE / OpenCitations / DBLP datasets on the shared DOI — figshare is the research-DATA-and-software vertex of the scholarly graph. DOI prefixes span main figshare (`10.6084`) plus publisher/institutional portals (ACS `10.1021`, arXiv `10.48550`, Frontiers `10.3389`, Taylor & Francis, universities…). Built by data/figshare/scripts/{harvest_oai,oai_datacite_to_nt}.py → rete build --pyramid-algo types --card, embedding the dcite: ontology. Metadata is open (figshare OAI-PMH); each item's own file license varies. Remote-lazy on Cloudflare R2.
datasets.license: figshare OAI metadata (open); per-item file licenses vary

figshare software outputs and their REAL download URL — dcite:hasPart points at ndownloader.figshare.com/files/… and is present on 92% of resources (the thing a plain DataCite dump lacks). The ?file column links straight to the bytes.
Swap "software" for "dataset", "thesis", "preprint", "media", "poster", "report"… to browse another output type.

examples.title: Outputs by figshare type
examples.tip: How many resources of each figshare item type are in the graph so far. This preview covers 24 of 28 types (figure, dataset and journal-contribution are still harvesting) — physical object, media, online resource, preprint and thesis lead the completed set.

examples.title: Top DOI prefixes (figshare + publisher/university portals)
examples.tip: figshare mints many DOI prefixes: 10.6084 is main figshare.com, while institutional and publisher portals get their own — 10.1021 is ACS, 10.48550 arXiv, 10.3389 Frontiers, plus dozens of universities. Because every resource sits at https://doi.org/{doi}, these federate with the DataCite / Zenodo / DBLP datasets on the shared DOI.

examples.title: Recent theses with their subjects
examples.tip:
figshare theses newest first, each with a keyword subject. dcite:publicationYear is the author-declared year; dcterms:subject holds the free-text keywords/categories figshare records.

datasets.label: proteinbase.rete — Adaptyv Bio's experimentally-validated protein designs, with ESMFold-predicted 3D structures rendered inline (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: [ProteinBase](https://proteinbase.com/download) by [Adaptyv Bio](https://adaptyvbio.com) — a database of experimentally-validated protein designs. **5,253 designs** (`pb:Design`), each with its amino-acid sequence, submitting lab and design method, plus **205,620 evaluations** (`pb:Evaluation`) split into computational (165k) and experimental (40k) measurements. The graph links **773 authors/labs** (`pb:Author` — MIT, bioLM, EPFL-LPDI…), **191 design methods** (`pb:DesignMethod` — boltzgen, BindCraft, RFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN…) and **24 interaction targets** (`pb:Target`; `pb:Design pb:evaluatedAgainst pb:Target`). Every design carries its design-level scalar metrics as direct properties — `pb:molecularWeight`, `pb:isoelectricPoint`, `pb:proteinmpnnScore` and the **Boltz-2** confidence family (`pb:boltz2Iptm`, `pb:boltz2Plddt`, `pb:boltz2Pdockq`…) — while the full long-form measurements (binding strength, expression, ESMFold pLDDT per target, SPR/BLI kinetics) sit on the evaluation nodes. **The predicted ESMFold 3D structures render INLINE in the results table**: `pb:structure` points at the `.cif` mirrored to CORS-open R2, so the playground's 3D structure cell (3Dmol.js) shows each design's fold — click ⛶ for the lightbox; `pb:image` is the stylized render. Vocabulary `pb:` = `w3id.org/rete/proteinbase#`. Built by data/proteinbase/scripts/{to_parquet.py → to_nt.py} → rete build --pyramid-algo types --card. 1.33 M triples, remote-lazy on Cloudflare R2. Open Data Commons Attribution (ODC-By): "This work used Proteinbase by Adaptyv Bio under ODC-BY license."

examples.title: Top binders (Boltz-2 iPTM) — inline 3D structure
examples.tip: Designs ranked by Boltz-2 interface pTM (iPTM 0–1, the model's confidence in the binding interface). The Structure column is the ESMFold-predicted fold and renders INLINE as a 3D cell — drag to rotate, click ⛶ to enlarge. iPTM ≳ 0.8 flags a confident predicted binder.

examples.title: Designs per design method
examples.tip: How many designs each pipeline produced. boltzgen, protpardelle-proteinmpnn, BindCraft and RFdiffusion lead; a handful of methods appear only a few times. Design method is the tool/protocol the submitter used to generate the sequence.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX pb: <https://w3id.org/rete/proteinbase#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?method (COUNT(?d) AS ?n) WHERE {
  ?d a pb:Design ; pb:designMethod [ rdfs:label ?method ] .
}
GROUP BY ?method
ORDER BY DESC(?n)
LIMIT 25

examples.title: Experimental binding measured against a target
examples.tip: Designs with an EXPERIMENTAL binding_strength readout and the interaction target they were tested against (e.g. nipah-glycoprotein-g). These are wet-lab results, not predictions — pb:evaluationType is "experimental".

datasets.label: ethz-research-collection.rete — the ETH Zürich institutional repository as a scholarly graph, DOI/ORCID-linked to the hub (306,835 works + a file manifest, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The [ETH Zürich Research Collection](https://www.research-collection.ethz.ch/) (DSpace 7.6) — the institutional repository of ETH Zürich — as one range-queried scholarly graph. **306,835 items** (293,270 live + 13,565 deleted-tombstone records): **289,592 publications** and **3,678 research-data** items, typed by publication type (`ethz:JournalArticle` 143k, `ethz:ConferencePaper` 39k, `ethz:DoctoralThesis` 32k, book chapters, reports, working papers, datasets…). Each work carries title, abstract, dates, publisher, licence, availability (**36% open access**) and external IDs — DOI, arXiv, Web of Science, Scopus, ISSN, ISBN. **434,635 author nodes** link via `ethz:creator`; the **6,402 ORCID-identified** ones are minted at `https://orcid.org/{orcid}` so they MERGE with the ORCID dataset, and the **122,711 works with a DOI** are minted at `https://doi.org/{doi}` so they federate for free with OpenAIRE, DataCite, Crossref and OpenCitations on the shared DOI. The ETH affiliation **Leitzahl tree** is a `org:Organization` hierarchy (1,881 units, `org:subOrganizationOf`) you walk with a property path to roll up a whole department's output. The DSpace **entity-relationship graph** is preserved — version chains, citations, has-part, supplements. And the **ORIGINAL-file MANIFEST is a first-class layer**: **158,339 deposited bitstreams** (`ethz:File`) with MIME, byte size, MD5 checksum and a download URL — cataloguing **10.23 TB WITHOUT storing any bytes**. Harvested via OAI-PMH (the xoai complete-dump format), modelled by data/ethz-research-collection/scripts/xoai_to_nt.py against the `ethz:` OWL 2 QL ontology and aligned to the rete scholar hub, then rete build --pyramid-algo types --card. 11.6 M triples, remote-lazy on Cloudflare R2. Per-class Parquet/DuckDB companions (works, persons, files, journals, grants, units) + JSON Schema + Croissant + the OWL ontology travel beside it. CC0 metadata harvest; each item's own dc:rights governs its files.
datasets.license: CC0-1.0 (metadata harvest); per-item object rights vary (In Copyright / CC BY / CC BY-NC-ND / …)

examples.title: Recent ETH doctoral theses
examples.tip:
ETH doctoral theses, newest first — each ?t is minted at its ETH DOI (10.3929/ethz-…). ethz:DoctoralThesis is one of ~18 per-type classes the graph is typed by, so the types pyramid groups them.
Swap ethz:DoctoralThesis for ethz:JournalArticle, ethz:ConferencePaper or ethz:Dataset to browse another output type.

examples.title: The file manifest of a publication
examples.tip:
The ORIGINAL-bundle files of one item — here handle 20.500.11850/715512 (the paper 'MathGAP'). Each ethz:File carries its MIME type, byte size, MD5 checksum and a resolvable download URL; the bytes themselves are NOT in the graph, only their manifest.
Change the handle to any item's to see its files; the ?url column links straight to ETH's bitstream endpoint.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX ethz: <https://w3id.org/rete/ethz#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
SELECT ?name ?mime ?bytes ?url WHERE {
  ?w ethz:handle "20.500.11850/715512" ; ethz:hasFile ?f .
  ?f rdfs:label ?name ; dcterms:format ?mime ; ethz:sizeBytes ?bytes ; ethz:downloadURL ?url .
}

examples.title: Most prolific ORCID-identified authors
examples.tip:
Authors with the most deposited works, restricted to those with an ORCID (ethz:orcid) so the count is per real person, not per name string. Each ?a is minted at https://orcid.org/{orcid} — the SAME IRI the ORCID dataset uses, so adding orcid as a second source merges these nodes.
Kay Axhausen (transport planning) tops the list; the ?name is the person's name.

examples.title: A whole department's journal output (affiliation tree)
examples.tip:
Walks the ETH Leitzahl org tree with a property path: org:subOrganizationOf* gathers unit 02150 (Dep. Informatik / Computer Science) AND every institute and chair beneath it, then pulls the journal articles affiliated to any of them.
Swap unit 02150 for another Leitzahl code to roll up a different department.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX ethz: <https://w3id.org/rete/ethz#>
PREFIX org: <http://www.w3.org/ns/org#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
SELECT ?title ?y WHERE {
  ?u org:subOrganizationOf* <https://w3id.org/rete/ethz/unit/02150> .
  ?w ethz:affiliation ?u ; a ethz:JournalArticle ; rdfs:label ?title ; dcterms:issued ?y .
} ORDER BY DESC(?y) LIMIT 50

examples.tip:
How ETH's outputs split by access status — Metadata only vs Open access vs Closed / Embargoed. Open-access items are the ones whose ethz:hasFile bitstreams are publicly downloadable.

datasets.label: swissubase.rete — the Swiss national social-sciences & humanities data catalogue (FORS/DaSCH/UNINE/UZH), DOI-linked to the scholarly hub (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The metadata graph of [SWISSUbase](https://www.swissubase.ch/) — the Swiss national repository for social-sciences & humanities research data, run by **FORS** with DaSCH, UNINE and UZH's Language Repository. **12,530 studies** and **1,435 citable datasets** over **1,772 published versions**, harvested from the catalogue's own public APIs (no auth) into a 4.5 M-triple graph. Each dataset carries its **DataCite DOI**, multilingual title & abstract (de/fr/en/it), files, DDI-coded survey metadata (data type, time method, informed consent) and its usage licence; its **1,079,488 files** are individual nodes. **The canonical DOI (10.48573) is a CONCEPT DOI shared across versions** — like Zenodo — so the graph separates a citable `su:Dataset` (minted at `https://doi.org/{doi}`) from its `su:DatasetVersion`s (each `dcterms:isVersionOf` it, holding that version's own files, dates and licence), so nothing collapses: e.g. `10.48573/pjmf-8s41` has 19 versions. **It joins the rete scholarly hub for free**: `su:Dataset ⊑ dcite:Resource, scholar:Work` and `su:Study ⊑ scholar:Project`, and both DOIs are `scholar:doi`, so with the 🧠 reasoner it federates with DataCite, Zenodo, OpenAIRE, Crossref and DBLP on the shared DOI. The catalogue's controlled vocabularies (discipline, geography, funding source, licence, schema) travel as **SKOS concept schemes** with multilingual labels and a broader/narrower hierarchy, and the SNSF & EU funding concepts carry `skos:exactMatch` to their Crossref Funder DOIs. Metadata-only: the data files themselves are mostly **Restricted** (a bilateral download contract with the responsible Data Service Unit), 151 versions are Open and 120 under a Creative Commons licence. The OWL 2 QL ontology and 11 example queries ship inside the file. Built by data/swissubase/scripts/{harvest.py → to_nt.py} → rete build --pyramid-algo types --text-index. TEXT_INDEX over titles/abstracts. Remote-lazy on Cloudflare R2.
datasets.license: Catalogue metadata: SWISSUbase terms of use (swissubase.ch/en/terms-of-use); per-dataset data licences vary — mostly Restricted, 151 Open, 120 Creative Commons

examples.title: Most-versioned datasets
examples.tip:
Each citable su:Dataset is minted at its canonical concept DOI (prefix 10.48573) and groups its su:DatasetVersion nodes.
The top hit, 10.48573/pjmf-8s41, has 19 versions — SWISSUbase reuses one concept DOI across every version, like Zenodo, so the graph keeps the versions distinct instead of collapsing them.

examples.title: Creative-Commons dataset versions
examples.tip:
dct:license carries the canonical Creative Commons licence URI, and only the openly-licensed versions have it.
Most SWISSUbase data is Restricted (needs a download contract) — these are the freely reusable ones.

examples.title: Studies → the datasets they produced
examples.tip:
su:hasDataset links a research study to the citable datasets it produced (from the catalogue hierarchy).
The dataset IRI is its DOI, so each row resolves to a real DataCite record at doi.org.

examples.title: Licence-type breakdown
examples.tip:
su:licenseIconCode is the licence per dataset version: 'restricted' vs the Creative Commons variants (by, by-sa, by-nc, …), 'public' and 'public-domain'.
Restricted dominates — SWISSUbase mediates most access through a bilateral contract with the responsible Data Service Unit.

examples.title: Discipline SKOS hierarchy
examples.tip:
The SNSF discipline classification is modelled as a SKOS concept scheme with skos:broader / narrower and multilingual labels.
This walks each sub-discipline up to its broader field, in English.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX su: <https://w3id.org/rete/swissubase#>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
SELECT ?field ?subDiscipline WHERE {
  ?narrow a su:Discipline ; skos:broader ?broad ; skos:prefLabel ?subDiscipline .
  ?broad skos:prefLabel ?field .
  FILTER(LANG(?subDiscipline) = "en" && LANG(?field) = "en")
} ORDER BY ?field LIMIT 40

examples.title: Survey data with informed consent
examples.tip:
DDI domain metadata is reified as su:DomainMetadata blocks; su:consentOfRespondents flags survey datasets that recorded participant consent.
The numeric DDI codes (data type, time method) are kept raw because their label vocabulary is member-gated on SWISSUbase.

examples.title: Hub join by DOI — turn on 🧠
examples.tip:
Turn on the 🧠 reasoner: su:canonicalDoi and su:forsDoi are sub-properties of scholar:doi, so this resolves SWISSUbase DOIs — and the SAME query spans DataCite, Zenodo, OpenAIRE, Crossref and DBLP in a federated graph.
Without reasoning it returns nothing, because scholar:doi is never asserted directly.

datasets.label: neuro-showcase.rete — 3D neuron & astrocyte morphology + a fly connectome, with inline 3D previews (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: A small demonstrator that puts two harvested neuroscience datasets in one range-queried graph and shows the split between a **lossless queryable graph** and **lossy 3D render previews**. Three **Blue Brain NGV astrocytes** reconstructed from FIB-SEM electron microscopy — each linked (schema:contentUrl) to a Draco-compressed **.glb surface mesh** that renders **inline in the results table** (click 🧊): astrocytes have a fine 'spongiform' morphology below light-microscopy resolution, so these EM meshes show detail a skeleton cannot. And a connected **Drosophila mushroom-body cluster of 27 hemibrain neurons** (Janelia FlyEM) with predicted neurotransmitter and **30 real weighted synaptic edges** — the edge weights carried via **RDF-star** (`<< ?a neuro:connectsTo ?b >> neuro:weight ?w`). The full-resolution OBJ meshes and SWC skeletons stay as the analytical source of truth; the .rete keeps 100% of the metadata + connectome losslessly while the GLB is a disposable preview. Licence is MIXED — CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for the NGV astrocytes (NonCommercial, ShareAlike), CC BY 4.0 for the hemibrain neurons — so treat the astrocyte assets as noncommercial. Cite Zisis et al. 2021 (doi:10.1093/cercor/bhab254) and the Janelia hemibrain (Scheffer et al. 2020). Built by data/neuro-showcase/build_graph.py → rete build --text-index --card. Remote-lazy on Cloudflare R2.
datasets.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (NGV astrocytes) / CC BY 4.0 (hemibrain neurons)

examples.title: 🧊 The astrocytes in 3D
examples.tip:
The three NGV astrocytes, each with the URL of its Draco-GLB surface mesh in the ?model column — the playground renders it inline, so click 🧊 to open the mesh and rotate it.
These are electron-microscopy reconstructions: the sponge-like leaflet processes you can see are exactly the fine morphology that light-microscopy skeletons (e.g. NeuroMorpho's astrocytes) cannot resolve. Triangle counts are the full-resolution figures; the preview GLB is decimated to 15%.

examples.title: Neurotransmitters, with ChEBI & Wikidata 🔗
examples.tip:
The predicted neurotransmitter is a real concept node, not a bare string: each carries skos:exactMatch links to the molecule in ChEBI and Wikidata, so the graph joins to chemistry databases (chebi-full federates on these).
Acetylcholine → CHEBI:15355 / wd:Q180623, GABA → CHEBI:16865, glutamate → CHEBI:16015, dopamine → CHEBI:18243, serotonin → CHEBI:28790, octopamine → CHEBI:17134 — the whole set verified against Wikidata.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX neuro: <https://w3id.org/rete/neuro#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
SELECT ?neuron ?nt ?chebi ?wikidata WHERE {
  ?c a neuro:Neuron ; rdfs:label ?neuron ; neuro:neurotransmitter ?ntr .
  ?ntr rdfs:label ?nt ; skos:exactMatch ?chebi , ?wikidata .
  FILTER(STRSTARTS(STR(?chebi), "http://purl.obolibrary.org"))
  FILTER(STRSTARTS(STR(?wikidata), "http://www.wikidata.org"))
} ORDER BY ?nt LIMIT 30

examples.title: Decrypt the cryptic cell types 📖
examples.tip:
The hemibrain type names (MBON09, PPL103, DPM…) are cryptic, so each rolls up (skos:broader) to an explained class in the neuro: ontology carrying a plain-language skos:definition — MBON = Mushroom Body Output Neuron, PPL1 = dopaminergic teaching neuron, DPM/APL = broad modulatory neurons.
?region is a neuprint ROI (a mushroom-body lobe, the calyx, the lateral horn…), one of the places the neuron makes most of its synapses.

examples.title: Where the heaviest synapses sit (µm)
examples.tip:
For the strongest connections the graph carries a neuro:Synapse node with the 3D location (µm) where the two arbors come closest — the closest-approach point between the pre- and post-synaptic skeletons.
The DPM_R↔APL_R pair (the two giant modulatory neurons) meet at ~(128, 245, 127) µm. The standalone viewer's 'Heaviest synapses' list frames the camera on exactly this contact volume.

examples.title: Heaviest synapses in the circuit (RDF-star weights)
examples.tip:
The synaptic connections are edges (neuro:connectsTo) and the number of synapses per connection is attached to the edge itself with RDF-star — << ?a neuro:connectsTo ?b >> neuro:weight ?w — so this reads an annotation on a triple, not a separate node.
The cluster is a Drosophila mushroom-body memory circuit: DPM_R and APL_R (the giant modulatory neurons) dominate, feeding the MBON output neurons; ?nt is the presynaptic cell's predicted neurotransmitter.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX neuro: <https://w3id.org/rete/neuro#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?pre ?nt ?post ?w WHERE {
  << ?a neuro:connectsTo ?b >> neuro:weight ?w .
  ?a rdfs:label ?pre ; neuro:neurotransmitter/rdfs:label ?nt .
  ?b rdfs:label ?post .
} ORDER BY DESC(?w) LIMIT 15

examples.title: Neurons by predicted neurotransmitter
examples.tip:
Every hemibrain neuron carries a predicted neurotransmitter (the FlyEM classifier's top class over GABA / acetylcholine / glutamate / dopamine / serotonin / octopamine).
In this mushroom-body cluster acetylcholine and GABA lead — the excitatory Kenyon-cell / feedback-inhibition balance the circuit is known for.

examples.title: The connectome cluster as a network
examples.tip:
Switch Output to Graph. Each neuron becomes a node and every synaptic connection an edge, so the mushroom-body wiring draws itself — the DPM/APL hubs sit in the middle with the MBON and projection neurons around them.
Edges here are the plain neuro:connectsTo shortcut (the per-edge synapse weight lives on the RDF-star annotation, see the synapse example).

datasets.label: imaging-plaza.rete — EPFL/SDSC catalogue of research imaging software, with the SHACL shapes that score its FAIR levels (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The catalogue of research **imaging software and code** kept by [Imaging Plaza](https://imaging-plaza.epfl.ch/) (EPFL & the Swiss Data Science Center) — **76 curated entries**, from DeepLabCut, StarDist, Cellpose and CEBRA to MRI reconstruction networks and radio-interferometric imaging. Every entry is described with the **Imaging Plaza ontology**, an alignment of schema.org + the **Software Description Ontology** (`sd:`, OKN) + **metadata4ing** + **bioschemas** + **SPHN**, and the **full ontology and its SHACL shapes travel inside the file** (1,107 of the 5,834 triples). **The point of this graph is that the SHACL shapes ARE the FAIR score**: Imaging Plaza computes each entry's FAIR level by validating it, and every constraint carries the level it gates as its `sh:message` — so running the SHACL tab in the browser re-derives the badges the website shows, and each violation tells you exactly what a project must add to level up. Levels here run 1 (4) · 2 (15) · 3 (55) · 4 (DeepLabCut) · 5 (lungs-segmentation). Beyond the software: **227 people** (58 distinct ORCID iDs), 37 funder organizations with their grant numbers (SNSF, ERC, Marie Curie, Horizon 2020), **95 screenshots** that render inline in the results table, 68 supporting datasets with their imaging modality and dimensionality, **33 executable notebooks** and **16 runnable examples** — 9 of them live Gradio apps you can open from a query result. **It federates without reconciliation**: software subjects are minted at the bare repository URL (`https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}`), the exact IRI `open-pulse`, `c4dt`, `oss-github-benchmark` and `enac-it4research` already use, so a union merges the same nodes. Because the source stores every IRI-ish value as a plain string (its own shapes declare `sh:datatype xsd:string`), the source triples are kept *verbatim* and a link layer is *added* under predicates the shapes do not constrain — `owl:sameAs` to 58 ORCID IRIs, `dcterms:references` to 72 DOIs, `dcterms:license` to SPDX, and `schema:funder` resolving the funding chain — so the file still validates against the upstream shapes while joining ORCID, Crossref and OpenCitations. Two upstream facts are recorded rather than hidden and are visible in the graph: **cellpose is catalogued twice** under two casings of its GitHub owner (`MouseLand` / `mouseland`) with two different DOIs — the Nature Methods paper and the bioRxiv preprint — and dates are stored as date-*times* where the shapes ask for `xsd:date`, which the SHACL tab duly flags. 554 blank nodes were skolemised to the `inst:` IRIs the source already uses for people and organizations. TEXT_INDEX over descriptions and READMEs.
datasets.license: Metadata: reuse permitted with attribution to the original source of code and data (imaging-plaza.epfl.ch/terms); ontology CC-BY-SA-4.0

examples.title: The catalogue by FAIR level
examples.tip:
Imaging Plaza scores every entry 1-5 for how Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable it is, and shows the number as a badge. That score is not a stored opinion — it is computed by validating the record against the SHACL shapes that ship inside this very file.
The distribution is top-heavy at level 3 (55 of 76). Only DeepLabCut reaches 4 and only lungs-segmentation reaches 5; open the SHACL tab to see exactly which missing field stops each of the others.

examples.title: 📸 The catalogue as a gallery
examples.tip:
Every one of the 76 entries carries at least one screenshot (95 schema:ImageObject nodes in total), and the playground renders the contentUrl inline — so this is the Imaging Plaza front page, rebuilt from the graph.
The pictures are hotlinked from wherever the authors put them (GitHub raw, readthedocs, GitLab), so a few may 404 when a project moves its README assets.

examples.title: Who writes imaging software here — with ORCIDs
examples.tip:
227 author nodes across the catalogue; Pascal Fua leads with 4 entries, then Daniel Sage, Edward Andò, Sabine Süsstrunk and Thanh-an Pham with 2 each.
The ORCID column is the DERIVED link layer: the source stores the iD as a plain string (and four of them with a http:// scheme or a stray leading space), so the build normalises them into 58 real owl:sameAs IRIs — which is what lets you join this graph to ORCID or to open-pulse. The OPTIONAL keeps the ~170 authors who never supplied one.

examples.title: Software you can run right now
examples.tip:
The two things Imaging Plaza adds on top of a plain software directory: 33 executable notebooks (25 projects) and 16 runnable examples (11 projects). Nine of the latter have hostType `plaza-gradio-application` — live Gradio demos hosted for the Plaza, e.g. StarDist at huggingface.co/spaces — and the other seven are `other`.
The UNION merges both into one list; `kind` says which is which, and the URLs open the notebook on GitHub/GitLab or the demo itself.

examples.title: Which imaging modalities are covered
examples.tip:
Modality is recorded in two places — on the software itself (imag:imagingModality) and on each of its 68 supporting datasets — so this UNIONs both. `Any` (7) and MRI (7) lead, then CT, SMLM and MRSI.
The long tail is the interesting part: single entries for Digital Holography Microscopy, Radio interferometer, Satellite and `natural images` show the vocabulary is a free-text enum the submitters fill in, not a closed list — spelling varies.

examples.title: The papers and licences behind the code 🔗
examples.tip:
71 of the 76 projects cite a paper, and the build turns those citation strings into 72 real https://doi.org/ IRIs (dcterms:references) and the licence strings into SPDX IRIs (dcterms:license) — the join keys for Crossref, OpenCitations and DataCite.
Note cellpose appears TWICE with two different DOIs: the source catalogues it under both MouseLand/cellpose and mouseland/cellpose, one pointing at the Nature Methods paper and one at the bioRxiv preprint. That duplicate is upstream and kept visible rather than silently merged.

examples.title: Who co-writes with whom, as a network
examples.tip:
Switch Output to Graph. Each project becomes a hub with its authors hanging off it, so the people who appear on several projects become the bridges between otherwise separate imaging communities — the EPFL Biomedical Imaging Group, CVLab and the MRI groups.
Authors are separate nodes per submission rather than one node per human, so the same person can appear twice under slightly different spellings; use the ORCID owl:sameAs links to collapse them properly.

shacl_shapes.title: The FAIR ladder — what each project still needs
shacl_shapes.tip:
This is how Imaging Plaza actually computes the FAIR badge on every listing: not a stored number, but a SHACL run whose violations each name the level they gate. Reading the report bottom-up gives each project its to-do list — add a README and you clear level 3, add executable instructions and a container image and you reach 5.
Expect a lot of violations, and that is the point: only 2 of 76 projects get past level 3. The last constraint catches a genuine upstream typing bug — dates are stored as date-TIMES ("2018-03-26T00:00:00.000Z") while the ontology's own shapes declare xsd:date, so all 76 fail it. The file also ships Imaging Plaza's complete official shapes inside itself; this is a readable distillation of them.

datasets.label: c4dt.rete — EPFL's Center for Digital Trust technology showcase (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The catalogue the **EPFL Center for Digital Trust (C4DT)** keeps of the research its affiliated labs produce — **315 projects across 36 labs**, built from the [c4dt/showcase_v2](https://github.com/c4dt/showcase_v2) repository (AGPL-3.0). Each project carries a plain-language AND a technical description, its research categories and application verticals, 64 technical tags, languages, license, code repository, maturity, and the papers, videos, demos and blog posts written about it (275 resources, 209 of them papers). C4DT's own incubation work is modelled too: 27 incubations with their status and the 19 products that came out of them (d-voting, Calypso, the Swiss e-ID demos), plus 81 internal staff interest ratings that the repository's own JSON Schema never documented. **The point of this graph is that it JOINS the `open-pulse` EPFL/SDSC research-software graph without any reconciliation**: repositories are minted at the IRI Open Pulse already uses (`https://github.com/{owner}/{repo}`, 271 of them), every lab is `org:unitOf` EPFL's ROR IRI, and `c4dt:developedBy` is a sub-property of `pulse:ownedBy` — so an unmodified Open Pulse query returns C4DT projects, and the 🧠 reasoner turns 272 answers into 587. Vocabulary is mostly alignment, not invention: schema.org + W3C Org + SKOS + Dublin Core + Open Pulse, with the OWL 2 QL ontology shipped inside the file. Two facts the source's own schema gets wrong and this graph does not: the slug `meditron` belongs to TWO different projects (labs MLO and NLP) pointing at one repository, and `type`/`language` are comma-separated multi-values. TEXT_INDEX on descriptions.

examples.title: The 36 labs, and how much each contributes
examples.tip:
One row per EPFL lab in the showcase, busiest first. HexHive (Mathias Payer, software security) leads with 38 projects; MLO and SPRING follow at 23.
The last column counts projects that actually link a code repository — 272 of the 315 do, which is what makes this graph joinable with the open-pulse research-software graph.

examples.title: Privacy research aimed at health
examples.tip:
Categories and application verticals are two SEPARATE SKOS schemes, so this crosses them: research pillar = Privacy, target domain = Health. It returns MedCo, Unlynx, Drynx, CRISP and the GAEN contact-tracing work.
The third column is the layman_desc the showcase authors write for every project — a plain-language summary that exists alongside a technical one. Swap Health for Gov, Finance, Infra or Info.

examples.title: What EPFL's trust research is written in
examples.tip:
Python dominates at 126 projects, then C (40) and C++ (33) — the systems-security half of the portfolio — with Go at 26, mostly the DEDIS blockchain work.
Languages are SKOS concepts here, not strings: the source stores "Rust, Typst, TypeScript" in one field, and the build splits it. C and C++ are deliberately distinct concepts, which a naive slugifier would have merged.

examples.title: What C4DT itself incubated, and what came out
examples.tip:
The centre's own track record: 27 incubations, each a reified c4dt:Incubation node so the work description, the lifecycle status and the resulting products stay attached to one another.
d-voting reached "Incubated, on the market"; Calypso and Drynx are "Retired and archived". The Swiss e-ID grant has the most products — a GitHub org, a blog, a taxonomy white paper and a PoC report.

examples.title: The Open Pulse join: ask in THEIR vocabulary 🧠
examples.tip:
Turn the 🧠 Reason toggle ON. This query uses ONLY Open Pulse terms — pulse:ownedBy and EPFL's ROR IRI — and never mentions the c4dt vocabulary, yet it answers over this file, because the two graphs deliberately share IRIs instead of being mapped onto each other.
With reasoning OFF it returns the 272 GitHub repositories, which are typed exactly as Open Pulse types them. With it ON, c4dt:developedBy ⊑ pulse:ownedBy also rolls the 315 projects in, for 587 rows. Load the `open-pulse` dataset beside this one and the same query spans both.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX pulse: <https://open-pulse.epfl.ch/ontology#>
PREFIX org: <http://www.w3.org/ns/org#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?what ?kind ?lab WHERE {
  ?x pulse:ownedBy ?l .
  ?l org:unitOf <https://ror.org/02s376052> ; schema:name ?lab .
  ?x rdfs:label ?what ; a ?t .
  BIND(STRAFTER(STR(?t), "#") AS ?kind)
  FILTER(?kind != "")
} ORDER BY ?lab ?what LIMIT 200

examples.title: Papers written about the showcased software
examples.tip:
209 of the 275 related resources are papers, and each is typed schema:ScholarlyArticle and attached with schema:citation — the standard terms, so a reader who knows nothing about the c4dt vocabulary still finds them.
The showcase's own convention is to link the CONFERENCE page rather than the arXiv preprint, so these URLs mostly resolve to ACM, IEEE and USENIX.

examples.title: Labs, projects and shared repositories as a network
examples.tip:
Switch Output to Graph. Draws every lab as a hub with its projects hanging off it, and each project linked to the GitHub repository it ships — so the shared repositories become visible as the places two labs meet.
The clearest example is epfLLM/meditron, reached from BOTH the MLO and the NLP project called meditron: one repository, two catalogue entries, which is exactly why projects here are keyed on (lab, slug) and not on the slug alone.

examples.title: Which projects C4DT staff rate most interesting
examples.tip:
An editorial signal the showcase repository's own JSON Schema does not document at all: 68 projects carry showcase_interest, a 1-5 score per C4DT staff member. It is modelled as a reified schema:Rating so each score keeps its author instead of collapsing into one number.
DebateGPT, HalluHard, PrivacyShield and Votegral are the only 5/5s. Raters are recorded by first name exactly as the source gives them — there is no identifier to resolve them to a person.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX c4dt: <https://w3id.org/rete/c4dt#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
SELECT ?title ?lab (AVG(?score) AS ?avg) (COUNT(?r) AS ?votes) WHERE {
  ?p c4dt:interestRating ?r ; schema:name ?title ; c4dt:developedBy ?l .
  ?r schema:ratingValue ?score .
  ?l schema:name ?lab .
} GROUP BY ?title ?lab ORDER BY DESC(?avg) DESC(?votes) LIMIT 40

shacl_shapes.title: SoftwareSourceCode nodes are labeled and correctly typed
shacl_shapes.tip:
Checks that every schema:SoftwareSourceCode node (585 repos spanning both the 310 fully-described c4dt:SoftwareProject entries and 275 secondary c4dt:Resource-typed repos) carries both schema:name and rdfs:label, since every project/repo card in the C4DT showcase is rendered from these two fields.
Also checks that, wherever a node IS tagged or classified, the c4dt:tag/c4dt:category/c4dt:applicationDomain/c4dt:projectType edges point at the right target classes (skos:Concept, c4dt:Category, c4dt:ApplicationDomain, c4dt:ProjectType respectively) rather than stray literals or the wrong vocabulary.

shacl_shapes.title: SoftwareProject core metadata is complete
shacl_shapes.tip:
Checks that every c4dt:SoftwareProject (the 310 showcased projects that actually ship code, a subset of the 315 c4dt:Project and 585 schema:SoftwareSourceCode nodes) has a developing lab/org (c4dt:developedBy, must be a schema:Organization) and a discipline classification (open-pulse:discipline, must be an open-pulse:DisciplineEnumeration), plus non-empty dateAdded, laymanDescription, technicalDescription and slug values.
In the source data all six of these properties are asserted on exactly the same 310 nodes, so any violation flags a showcased project that silently lost its lab attribution, its discipline tag, or its plain-language/technical write-up.

shacl_shapes.title: Organizations only develop software resources
shacl_shapes.tip:
Checks that wherever a schema:Organization (the 38 labs, units and institutes catalogued alongside the 36 c4dt:Lab entries) is linked via c4dt:develops, the target is really a schema:SoftwareSourceCode node, catching an accidental link to a Note, Tag, or other resource type.
c4dt:develops is the inverse of c4dt:developedBy (310 links from the software side), so this shape also guards the two directions of the same relation from drifting out of sync as the catalogue is edited.

datasets.label: enac-it4research.rete — EPFL ENAC open science: research software, open data, repositories and student projects (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The open-science output of **EPFL ENAC** (School of Architecture, Civil and Environmental Engineering), compiled from the school's own public pages: **52 showcase projects**, the **40-entry open research scripts & software directory**, **54 student data-project offers**, and the **90 units** of the school's laboratory registry. The point of the graph is the *links out*: 38 GitHub / GitLab / c4science **repositories**, 25 **code organizations**, 12 **datasets** (Zenodo DOIs, a Zenodo community, Renku, PANGAEA) and 20 cited **publications**. Repositories, organizations and people reuse the exact IRIs of **Open Pulse** — 18 of 22 GitHub repos and 15 of 18 orgs were *verified* to already exist there — so this graph merges with the C4DT showcase and Open Pulse with no reconciliation step. Only 17 of 52 project pages name their lab outright; the rest are inferred from lab-site links, the owning GitHub org, the lab's full name in the prose, the head professor, or a guarded acronym match, and every inference carries its **verbatim evidence** on a separate property so you can audit or reject it. People, labs and cited papers are reconciled against EPFL Infoscience for ORCIDs, SCIPERs, affiliations, journals and open-access PDFs. TEXT_INDEX on for full-text search over its literals.
datasets.license: CC-BY-4.0 (compilation); page text © EPFL, quoted with attribution

examples.title: What's in this ENAC graph
examples.tip:
The shape of the graph: 52 showcase projects from the school's open-science pages, the 40-entry research software directory, 53 student data-project offers, and the 88 laboratories of the ENAC lab registry.
"Code repositories" counts only what a project or tool actually points at on GitHub, GitLab or c4science — third-party repos merely cited as prior art are linked with enac:mentions instead and are not counted here.

examples.title: Every ENAC repository, by lab
examples.tip:
The question this dataset exists to answer: which ENAC lab publishes which tool, and where the code actually lives.
Lab codes are the school's own acronyms — CNPA is the Laboratory of Numeric Cultures for Architectural Projects, LSMS the Computational Solid Mechanics Laboratory, RESSLAB the Resilient Steel Structures Laboratory. Repository IRIs are bare platform URLs, the same nodes Open Pulse uses.

examples.title: Where ENAC's open data lives
examples.tip:
Every dataset location a project or tool points at — mostly Zenodo deposits, plus a Zenodo community, a Renku project and a PANGAEA record.
Zenodo deposits are keyed by DOI rather than by record URL, so the two link forms used across these pages (zenodo.org/record/N and doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.N) collapse to one node — and match the DOIs in the zenodo-records dataset.

examples.title: What ENAC-IT4Research actually built
examples.tip:
ENAC-IT4Research (ENAC-IT4R) is the school's research-IT group. These are the projects whose pages spell out what the group itself contributed, in their own words — web apps, data pipelines, front-ends, infrastructure.
It is the field that separates a project the group built from one merely listed on the open-science pages.

examples.title: Audit an inferred lab attribution
examples.tip:
Only 17 of 52 project pages name their lab outright. The rest are inferred — from a link to the lab's site, the GitHub org the code sits in, the lab's full name in the prose, the head professor, or an acronym — and every inference shows its verbatim evidence so you can reject it.
Inferences live on enac:inferredLab, never on enac:developedBy, so what a page stated stays separable from what the pipeline concluded. Filter conf = "high" to drop bare acronym matches.

examples.title: Papers behind the tools, with open-access PDFs
examples.tip:
The pages cite these papers as bare DOI or arXiv links whose anchor text is often just "link" or "Paper". Titles, journals, dates and the open-access PDF come from EPFL Infoscience.
The lab is derived from the authors' departments in the Infoscience record — which is how the Tamaas paper attaches to LSMS and the timber-drilling paper to IBOIS.

shacl_shapes.title: Lab & unit core fields
shacl_shapes.tip: Every org:OrganizationalUnit (all 90 ENAC labs/institutes/sections in the graph) carries schema:name, rdfs:label, skos:notation, an enac:sourcePage back-link and an enac:unitCode in 90-for-90 of the source rows, so those five are required. campus, headOfLab and the reverse org:unitOf link to a parent org:Organization are only populated for some units (78/78-ish subsets), so they stay optional but are still type-checked when present.

shacl_shapes.title: Software repository fields
shacl_shapes.tip: Every schema:SoftwareSourceCode record (all 72 in the ENAC scripts & software directory) has both schema:name and rdfs:label, plus an enac:codePlatform link to a real enac:CodePlatform instance (e.g. GitHub/GitLab/SwissGit) - the class_links show 72-for-72 on all three, so all three are required. A record failing this shape is a repository entry the harvester scraped without a name, label, or hosting platform.

shacl_shapes.title: Organization to unit membership
shacl_shapes.tip: When an org:Organization has an org:hasUnit edge (true for 63 of the 119 Organization nodes - the ones acting as parents in ENAC's org chart, e.g. School over Institute over Lab), that edge must point at a real org:OrganizationalUnit. The property itself stays optional since leaf organizations have no sub-units, but its range is pinned so the org:hasUnit / org:unitOf pair the data uses both ways stays internally consistent.

shacl_shapes.title: Open-data project categorization
shacl_shapes.tip: Every enac:OpenDataProject (ENAC's open student data-project offers) carries at least one enac:category edge to a real enac:Category instance - 73 category triples against 30 OpenDataProject instances means the tag is present on essentially all of them (often more than one tag each), so minCount 1 just guarantees the tagging was actually populated. This lets the graph be faceted by topic instead of falling back to free-text description matching.

datasets.label: lombardi.rete — Mark Lombardi's conspiracy network drawings, as one graph (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The network drawings of Mark Lombardi (1951-2000) — the artist who drew the financial and political scandals of the late 20th century as hand-drawn node-link diagrams — digitized node by node and arc by arc by **Robert Tolksdorf** (Freie Universität Berlin) and published as GraphML/JSON/XGMML at [lombardinetworks.net](https://lombardinetworks.net/), from which this graph is built. Licensed **CC BY-NC-SA 4.0**; please credit Tolksdorf's digitization and Lombardi's estate. 51 works, 2,934 nodes (2,715 people and institutions) and 4,205 arcs. **Node ids are global across the corpus**: the same actor keeps one id wherever Lombardi drew them, so 340 actors recur in more than one work and the 51 drawings query as ONE network — Bill Casey (director of the CIA), Farhad Azima, BCCI and George H.W. Bush bridge otherwise separate scandals. In Lombardi's notation the LINE STYLE carries the meaning, and Tolksdorf's lombardi.owl types every arc accordingly (dashed = financial connection, directed solid = influence/control, ending in a double line = a blocked or failed transaction), so the OWL 2 QL reasoner (🧠) is meaningful here rather than decorative: lom:Edge alone returns nothing, and 4,205 arcs once entailment is on. Also carries the outcome annotations Lombardi lettered at the end of his red arcs ("1991: seized; net worth -$14 bil") and the 42 dollar amounts he wrote along individual arcs, plus three DERIVED layers: 210 work↔work overlaps with a Jaccard score (whose top hits are exactly the different versions of the same drawing — a good sanity check), the narration span of each work read off its Year markers, and 306 same-name links between actor ids the digitization never merged. For the 17 drawings the Museum of Modern Art holds, it also carries MoMA's own CC0 catalogue record (date, medium, the real dimensions of the sheet, credit line, accession) plus a link to the photograph MoMA hosts — linked, never mirrored, and each one carrying a dcterms:rights statement, since the artwork is © The Estate of Mark Lombardi and is NOT covered by this dataset's licence. TEXT_INDEX on for full-text search. scripts/lombardi/{fetch_lombardi.sh,lombardi_to_nt.py} → rete build --pyramid-algo types --text-index --card. Remote-lazy on Cloudflare R2.
datasets.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — digitization © Robert Tolksdorf (FU Berlin), lombardinetworks.net

examples.title: The originals, as objects
examples.tip:
For the 17 drawings the Museum of Modern Art holds, the graph carries MoMA's own catalogue record (their collection data is CC0). This is the physical object behind the network: Banco Nazionale del Lavoro is coloured pencil and pencil on a sheet 50 by 120 INCHES — 127 x 305 cm of paper.
The first column is the photograph MoMA hosts, rendered inline. That image is NOT covered by this dataset's licence — the artwork is (c) The Estate of Mark Lombardi and the graph carries a dcterms:rights statement saying so beside every one.

examples.title: The 51 drawings, with what each one narrates
examples.tip:
One row per work, biggest first. The Banco Nazionale del Lavoro drawing (Reagan, Bush, Thatcher and the arming of Iraq) is the monster at 342 nodes and 428 arcs; most others sit under 100.
The two year columns are the span the drawing NARRATES, not when it was made — computed from the little two-digit year circles Lombardi drew along his timelines, so "84/3" becomes 1984.

examples.title: Who bridges separate scandals
examples.tip:
This is the query the pictures cannot answer. Tolksdorf gave every actor a GLOBAL id, so an actor drawn in four different works is one node here — and the last column names those works.
Bill Casey (director of the CIA) ties Cabazon Arms to Gerry Bull's supergun and to Keeny Meeny Services; Farhad Azima ties EATSCO, Global International Airways and the Harken Energy drawing where George W. Bush sits. Lower the FILTER to 2 to see all 340 recurring actors.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX lo: <https://w3id.org/rete/lombardi/>
PREFIX lom: <http://www.lombardinetworks.net/lombardi.owl#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?actor ?kind ?drawings (GROUP_CONCAT(?title; SEPARATOR=" · ") AS ?appearsIn) WHERE {
  ?a a ?t ; rdfs:label ?actor ; lo:workCount ?drawings ; lo:appearsIn ?w .
  ?t rdfs:label ?kind .
  ?w rdfs:label ?title .
  FILTER(?t IN (lom:Person, lom:Institution))
  FILTER(?drawings >= 3)
} GROUP BY ?actor ?kind ?drawings ORDER BY DESC(?drawings)

examples.title: Lombardi's visual vocabulary, counted
examples.tip:
In Lombardi's notation the LINE STYLE is the semantics, and this query reads that grammar straight out of the ontology: the middle column is the mark on the paper, the first is what it means.
Influence or control (a directed solid arc) dominates at 2,191; money moves along dashed arcs; and 46 arcs end in a double line — Lombardi's sign for a transaction that was blocked or failed.

examples.title: The money he wrote along the arcs
examples.tip:
The 42 arcs carrying a hand-lettered sum, exactly as Lombardi wrote it — "$ 848 k", "$ 129 mil 11/85-1/86". Almost all of them are dashed arcs, his mark for a financial transaction.
Some endpoints are not people but Lombardi's own annotations: "July 1990: Bush bails out with profit" is a FinalInfo node, the punchline he lettered at the end of a red arc.

examples.title: Which drawings share a cast
examples.tip:
A derived layer: for every pair of works, how many people and institutions they have in common. Counted over actors ONLY — Lombardi's year markers also share ids across works and would otherwise fake a resemblance.
It is its own sanity check: the top pairs are the different VERSIONS of one drawing (Gerry Bull 4th and 5th share 49 actors, the two Harken Energy versions 41). Further down are the real surprises — unrelated works that turn out to share a cast.

examples.title: Two steps out from George H.W. Bush
examples.tip:
Follow the arcs two hops from one man and watch the corpus behave like a single network: the hops are free to cross from one drawing into another, because a recurring actor is one node.
Swap the name in the FILTER for anyone in the graph — try 'Bill Casey dir CIA', 'BCCI' or 'Farhad Azima'. The third column keeps the notation visible: which kind of arc the first hop was.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX lo: <https://w3id.org/rete/lombardi/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?start ?via ?viaDrawnAs ?reached WHERE {
  ?a rdfs:label ?start .
  FILTER(?start = "George H.W. Bush")
  ?e1 lo:source ?a ; lo:target ?m ; lo:arcType ?t1 .
  ?m rdfs:label ?via .
  ?t1 lo:drawnAs ?viaDrawnAs .
  ?e2 lo:source ?m ; lo:target ?b .
  ?b rdfs:label ?reached .
} ORDER BY ?via ?reached LIMIT 100

examples.title: How the stories end
examples.tip:
Lombardi closed many arcs with a red terminal and a hand-lettered outcome. Those annotations are nodes in the graph (lom:FinalInfo), so his punchlines are queryable prose: "1991: seized; net worth -$14 bil", "1978: died after suspicious fall down staircase".
Add FILTER(CONTAINS(?outcome, "collapsed")) to read just the bank failures — or use the Search tab, since this dataset carries a TEXT_INDEX.

examples.title: Reasoning: every arc, via the class hierarchy 🧠
examples.tip:
Turn the 🧠 Reason toggle ON before running this. Nothing in the data is typed lom:Edge directly — each arc is an InfluenceControl, a FinancialTransaction and so on — so with reasoning OFF this returns 0 rows.
With it ON, the OWL 2 QL rewriter walks the rdfs:subClassOf hierarchy in Tolksdorf's ontology (shipped inside the .rete) and all 4,205 arcs appear, whatever style they were drawn in.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX lo: <https://w3id.org/rete/lombardi/>
PREFIX lom: <http://www.lombardinetworks.net/lombardi.owl#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT DISTINCT ?from ?to ?drawnAs ?drawing WHERE {
  ?e a lom:Edge ; lo:source ?s ; lo:target ?o ;
     lo:arcType ?t ; lo:inDrawing ?w .
  ?s rdfs:label ?from .
  ?o rdfs:label ?to .
  ?t lo:drawnAs ?drawnAs .
  ?w rdfs:label ?drawing .
} LIMIT 200

examples.title: One drawing, redrawn as a graph
examples.tip:
Switch Output to Graph. This rebuilds the Nugan Hand Bank drawing — the Sydney merchant bank tied to the CIA that collapsed in 1980 — as a node-link network, with each arc keeping its original type as the predicate.
Put any title from the first example into the rdfs:label line to redraw another work. The layout is the browser's, not Lombardi's: his elegant hand-drawn arcs are not in the data, only the topology and the typing.

shacl_shapes.title: Drawing has title + node/arc counts
shacl_shapes.tip: Every lo:Drawing (one of the 51 network diagrams Robert Tolksdorf digitized from Mark Lombardi's hand-drawn originals) must carry a human-readable title (rdfs:label) and its two headline statistics, lo:nodeCount and lo:edgeCount, as integers -- these three are asserted without OPTIONAL in the card's own 'narrates' query, so they are effectively universal on this class. Any lo:accession (museum accession number) present must be a literal, and any lo:hasArc link must point to a real lo:Arc resource -- accession itself stays optional since it only applies to drawings tied to a known extant physical original, not to all 51.

shacl_shapes.title: Arc has a drawing, two endpoints, a type
shacl_shapes.tip: Every lo:Arc (one reified drawn line/arrow, digitized arc by arc) must belong to exactly one lo:inDrawing (a real lo:Drawing) and must have a lo:source and lo:target endpoint -- an arc drawn on paper always connects two actors and lives in one drawing, so these are construction-time invariants, not incidental fields. lo:arcType is required too (example 4's vocabulary-counting query asserts it non-optionally), since Lombardi's line style IS the semantic content of the arc; lo:amount (a dollar figure written along some arcs) stays optional and untyped-literal since only a minority of arcs carry a monetary annotation.

shacl_shapes.title: Overlap connects two drawings via shared actors
shacl_shapes.tip: Every lo:Overlap (a derived resource capturing which actors two of Lombardi's drawings have in common, computed only over Person/Institution/MergedInstitution nodes so shared Year markers don't inflate it) must reference at least two lo:Drawing resources via lo:betweenDrawing and must carry at least one lo:sharedActor. Its two summary statistics, lo:sharedActorCount (an integer) and lo:jaccard (a decimal similarity score), must also be present, since an Overlap resource only exists in this graph because those stats were computed for it -- there is no meaningful partially-built Overlap.

datasets.label: davidrumsey.rete — the David Rumsey Map Collection: 150,017 maps with images, dates and places (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The COMPLETE online catalog of the David Rumsey Historical Map Collection — 150,017 items spanning the 1470s to the 2020s: 71,320 atlas maps, 15,668 city views, 6,765 separate maps, plus celestial charts, aerial photographs, pocket, wall and case maps (80 item types, each an rdf:type class under drm:Item, so the schema pyramid rolls the collection up by kind). Every item carries its full LUNA record (42 fields → dcterms + drm:), a thumbnail (edm:preview) and a ~768px JPEG (edm:isShownBy) linked from the collection's own image servers, a IIIF Image API base (drm:iiifImage — deep-zoom any map to full resolution live), its IIIF manifest, the full-res JP2 master URL (drm:jp2Master, ~100MB each), a MIRRORED manifest backup (drm:iiifManifestMirror — all 150,017 manifest JSONs re-served CORS-clean from our own public bucket, for when LUNA rate-limits bursts), the master's pixel dimensions (drm:pixelWidth/Height, 150,011 items — the largest composites exceed 100,000 px a side), and our own 4K image tier: drm:avif4k gives 149,298 maps as AVIF q60 at up to 3840px, re-encoded from the collection's IIIF renders and served straight from R2 (73 GB, Content-Type image/avif) — roughly 10x the resolution of the browsable JPEG tier at a fraction of its bytes. 10,772 drm:Publication nodes rebuild the atlases: pages link up via dcterms:isPartOf, so an atlas queries as one book. drm:year (xsd:integer) gives a clean timeline; TEXT_INDEX is on for full-text CONTAINS over titles and notes. GEOCODED: 70,187 items carry a wgs84 point + GeoSPARQL POINT (map view) derived from their City/Region/Country text against GeoNames (CC-BY) — city-level for 22,660, country-centroid fallback for the rest, honestly flagged via drm:geoPrecision (precise Georeferencer bboxes would be a future upgrade; LUNA's own Bounding Coordinates field is filled on exactly ONE item of 150k). The six place fields (drm:city/country/region/stateProvince/county/worldArea) are rdfs:subPropertyOf dcterms:spatial, so the OWL 2 QL reasoner (🧠) lets one ?x dct:spatial ?place pattern search all of them. Images and descriptive data copyright Cartography Associates, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 — attribute "David Rumsey Historical Map Collection, www.davidrumsey.com". Harvested via the LUNA JSON API + IIIF (data/davidrumsey-maps/scripts/) → rete build --pyramid-algo types --text-index --card. Remote-lazy on Cloudflare R2.

examples.title: 📍 Old maps around Lake Geneva
examples.tip: The OldMapsOnline experience over one .rete: a bounding-box FILTER on the geocoded points finds every map placed around Lake Geneva, oldest first — the 1493 Nuremberg Chronicle Geneva woodcut and Braun & Hogenberg's 1572 town plan lead. Images come from our own 4K AVIF tier on R2, not the collection's servers. Switch Output → Map, or pan the box anywhere on earth by editing the four numbers. docs/oldmaps.html is this query as a whole app.

examples.title: 🔭 The largest scans: 100,000+ pixel monsters
examples.tip: drm:pixelWidth/Height are the MASTER scan dimensions — the biggest composites (multi-sheet panoramas and railroad surveys stitched into one image) exceed 100,000 pixels a side. Three ways in, side by side: OUR OWN 4K AVIF derivative (drm:avif4k — 149,298 maps re-encoded at up to 3840px and served from R2, so the image loads without touching the collection's servers), the JP2 master download (~100MB+), and the IIIF manifest for deep zoom in Mirador/OpenSeadragon — the only sane way to actually look at these.

examples.title: 📖 Atlases: claimed map count vs what's in the graph
examples.tip: 10,772 drm:Publication nodes rebuild the books: every scanned sheet links to its parent via dct:isPartOf. The catalog's own Pub Maps field (?claimed) sits next to COUNT(?m), what the graph actually holds — scans include text pages, covers and indexes, so the graph usually counts MORE than the claimed map total.

examples.title: 🖼️ Wall maps over two meters wide
examples.tip: Physical size lives on every item as drm:objWidthCm/objHeightCm — these are the wall maps wider than 2 meters, images served from OUR OWN 4K AVIF tier on R2 (drm:avif4k), each with its IIIF manifest for deep zoom. The 80 LUNA item types are rdf:type classes: swap drm:WallMap for drm:PocketMap to flip from the largest format to the smallest.

examples.title: 🌌 Celestial maps, oldest first, with images
examples.tip: A whole genre is one triple pattern, rendered from our own 4K AVIF tier — 1,905 celestial charts from 16th-century star atlases onward, with the physical sheet size alongside the image. Correctly, almost none of these carry a geocoded point: a map of the sky has no place. Try drm:AerialPhotograph or drm:Globe instead.

examples.title: 🌐 The IIIF stack: manifest, mirror + an image URL built in SPARQL
examples.tip: Every item carries its IIIF Presentation manifest (drm:iiifManifest), its IIIF Image API base (drm:iiifImage, level 2 — any size/region is one URL away), AND drm:iiifManifestMirror: our own CORS-clean backup of all 150,017 manifest JSONs, for when LUNA rate-limits bursts. The rendered image is OUR 4K AVIF; alongside it, BIND + CONCAT constructs a live IIIF URL inside the query, so you can see both routes to the same map — Janssonius' 1648 globe gores. Feed ?man or ?mirror to any IIIF viewer (Mirador, OpenSeadragon, Allmaps).

examples.title: 🗄️ Provenance chain: what we hold vs what Rumsey holds
examples.tip: Every layer of the stack in one row. OURS: a 4K AVIF derivative (drm:avif4k, 149,298 maps / 73 GB on R2) and a mirrored IIIF manifest (drm:iiifManifestMirror, all 150,017) — both served from our own infrastructure, so a viewer never depends on LUNA being up. THEIRS: the live IIIF manifest and the full-resolution JP2 master (~100 MB), which stay authoritative — we deliberately do not mirror the masters, since the collection is the archival source of record.

examples.title: 🧠 One spatial pattern, six place fields (Japan)
examples.tip: drm:city, drm:county, drm:stateProvince, drm:region, drm:country and drm:worldArea are all rdfs:subPropertyOf dcterms:spatial — and dcterms:spatial itself is asserted on ZERO subjects in this file, so with 🧠 Reason OFF this query returns nothing at all. This example switches the toggle ON for you: the single dct:spatial pattern is then rewritten into the six-way union and finds 1,305 maps whose place text mentions Japan — 1,103 of them via drm:country, 367 via drm:city, 37 via drm:region and 9 via drm:stateProvince (drm:county and drm:worldArea witness none: on these sheets they say "Asia", not "Japan"). The six right-hand columns are the asserted fields themselves, GROUP_CONCATed one row per map, so you can see which field the entailed match actually came from. Query rewriting, not materialization — flip the toggle off and re-run to watch 50 rows become 0.

datasets.label: farmacos-es.rete — todos los medicamentos autorizados en España (CIMA/AEMPS, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: Grafo de conocimiento del catálogo completo de medicamentos autorizados en España, construido a partir de la API REST pública del CIMA (AEMPS) y el Nomenclátor de Prescripción. 25,485 medicamentos (fmc:Medicamento ⊑ schema:Drug) con su condición de prescripción, fecha de autorización y flags (genérico/EFG, huérfano, biosimilar, triángulo negro, receta); 33,184 ingredientes reificados con dosis y unidad; 42,283 presentaciones (código nacional); principios activos, laboratorios (⊑ schema:MedicalOrganization), excipientes de declaración obligatoria, vías y formas farmacéuticas como skos:Concept. La clasificación ATC de la OMS está modelada como jerarquía SKOS completa (skos:broader + skos:exactMatch a BioPortal + rdfs:seeAlso a WHOCC), y las sustancias enlazan a SNOMED CT (http://snomed.info/id/) por la VTM del medicamento y por los códigos DCSA/DCP/DCPF de la extensión española de fármacos. Extracción médica estructurada: 48,997 interacciones farmacológicas a nivel ATC (fmc:Interaccion con efecto, recomendación y gravedad derivada — contraindicada / no recomendada / precaución / informativa) tomadas del Nomenclátor, y 761,945 secciones de prospecto y ficha técnica troceadas según la plantilla QRD europea (indicaciones, posología, efectos adversos, contraindicaciones, conservación, composición) con el texto completo indexado (TEXT_INDEX → CONTAINS) y las bandas de frecuencia de efectos adversos etiquetadas. Incluye además los problemas de suministro activos (desabastecimientos, con tipo, fechas y motivo) y los materiales informativos de seguridad dirigidos a paciente o profesional. 9.5 M triples, pirámide por tipos y Dataset Card embebida. scripts/farmacos-es/harvest.py (API oficial, sin scraping) + to_rdf.py → rete build --pyramid-algo types --text-index --card. Reutilización de información del sector público (Ley 37/2007); datos de la AEMPS. Remote-lazy en Cloudflare R2.
datasets.license: Reutilización de información del sector público (Ley 37/2007); datos de la AEMPS · CIMA

examples.title: Composición: principio activo, dosis y laboratorio
examples.tip:
Cada fila es un ingrediente de un medicamento con su dosis exacta (fmc:ingrediente reifica principio activo + cantidad + unidad, así que un combinado aparece en varias filas).
fmc:Medicamento es subclase de schema:Drug y el laboratorio titular es una schema:MedicalOrganization; el principio activo es un skos:Concept del Nomenclátor de la AEMPS.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX fmc: <https://w3id.org/rete/farmacos#>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX schema: <https://schema.org/>
SELECT ?medicamento ?principioActivo ?cantidad ?unidad ?laboratorio WHERE {
  ?m a fmc:Medicamento ; rdfs:label ?medicamento ; fmc:ingrediente ?i ; fmc:laboratorioTitular ?l .
  ?i fmc:principioActivo ?p ; fmc:cantidad ?cantidad ; fmc:unidad ?unidad .
  ?p skos:prefLabel ?principioActivo .
  ?l schema:name ?laboratorio .
} LIMIT 100

examples.title: Interacciones CONTRAINDICADAS (efecto + recomendación)
examples.tip:
Interacciones farmacológicas que la AEMPS clasifica como asociación contraindicada — la gravedad más alta. Cada fmc:Interaccion enlaza el medicamento con un grupo ATC objetivo (fmc:atcObjetivo) y trae el efecto clínico y la recomendación oficial.
Cambia el IRI de gravedad por .../gravedad/no-recomendada, /precaucion o /informativa para ver los otros niveles (48.997 interacciones en total).

examples.title: Principios activos más frecuentes
examples.tip:
Cuántos medicamentos distintos contienen cada principio activo — el ranking del catálogo español (encabezado por Hidroclorotiazida, Amlodipino, Olmesartán, Paracetamol…).
Quita el ORDER BY DESC para ordenar alfabéticamente, o filtra por un ?principioActivo concreto para contar sus presentaciones.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX fmc: <https://w3id.org/rete/farmacos#>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
SELECT ?principioActivo (COUNT(DISTINCT ?m) AS ?medicamentos) WHERE {
  ?m a fmc:Medicamento ; fmc:ingrediente ?i .
  ?i fmc:principioActivo ?p .
  ?p skos:prefLabel ?principioActivo .
} GROUP BY ?principioActivo ORDER BY DESC(?medicamentos) LIMIT 50

examples.title: Buscar en el prospecto dentro de un grupo ATC
examples.tip:
Anticoagulantes (subárbol ATC B01, recorrido con skos:broader*) cuyo apartado 'Posibles efectos adversos' del prospecto menciona 'hemorragia'. El texto de cada sección QRD se guarda en fmc:texto (indexado a texto completo).
Cambia el IRI del grupo ATC (p.ej. .../atc/N02 analgésicos, .../atc/J01 antibióticos) o la palabra del FILTER CONTAINS. Para búsqueda libre en TODO el catálogo usa el buscador '--contains' (índice TEXT_INDEX), más rápido que escanear.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX fmc: <https://w3id.org/rete/farmacos#>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT DISTINCT ?medicamento WHERE {
  ?a skos:broader* <https://w3id.org/rete/farmacos/atc/B01> .
  ?m fmc:atc ?a ; rdfs:label ?medicamento ; fmc:seccionProspecto ?s .
  ?s a fmc:EfectosAdversos ; fmc:texto ?t .
  FILTER(CONTAINS(LCASE(?t), "hemorragia"))
} LIMIT 100

examples.title: Excipientes de declaración obligatoria (alérgenos)
examples.tip:
Excipientes de declaración obligatoria (lactosa, gluten, colorantes azoicos, etc.) ordenados por cuántos medicamentos los contienen — información clave para intolerancias y alergias. El excipiente cuelga de la presentación (código nacional), no del medicamento.
Añade FILTER(CONTAINS(UCASE(?excipiente),"LACTOSA")) para agrupar todas las variantes de un mismo excipiente.

examples.title: Problemas de suministro activos (desabastecimientos)
examples.tip:
Desabastecimientos vigentes: cada fila es una presentación (código nacional) con un problema de suministro activo, su motivo oficial y la fecha de inicio, ordenados del más reciente. Los datos vienen del listado de problemas de suministro de la AEMPS.
Quita el filtro fmc:activo true para ver también los resueltos, o agrupa por ?motivo (COUNT) para ver las causas más comunes de desabastecimiento.

examples.title: Prospecto y ficha técnica (enlaces al PDF/HTML)
examples.tip:
Cada medicamento enlaza sus documentos oficiales del CIMA como URLs clicables: el prospecto para el paciente (HTML navegable y PDF) y la ficha técnica para el profesional. El texto de estos documentos también está dentro del grafo, troceado por secciones QRD e indexado (fmc:seccionProspecto / fmc:texto).
Propiedades disponibles: fmc:urlProspecto y fmc:urlProspectoPdf, fmc:urlFichaTecnica y fmc:urlFichaTecnicaPdf. Cambia el patrón a un ?m concreto o filtra por principio activo/ATC para localizar un prospecto.

shacl_shapes.title: Medicamento: ficha técnica y presentación obligatorias
shacl_shapes.tip: Cada fmc:Medicamento (los 25,485 medicamentos autorizados por la AEMPS) debe tener al menos una sección de ficha técnica (fmc:seccionFichaTecnica → fmc:SeccionDocumento, el tipo genérico de sección documental) y al menos una presentación comercial/envase (fmc:presentacion → fmc:Presentacion), ambas obligatorias por normativa española para cualquier medicamento comercializado. La clasificación ATC (fmc:atc → fmc:ConceptoATC) se deja opcional porque no todos los productos (p.ej. homeopáticos o de uso hospitalario especial) tienen código ATC asignado en el Nomenclátor.

shacl_shapes.title: Interaccion: campos de seguridad completos
shacl_shapes.tip: Cada fmc:Interaccion (48,997 interacciones farmacológicas extraídas de fichas técnicas) debe declarar su gravedad (fmc:gravedad → fmc:GravedadInteraccion, el enum de 4 niveles incluyendo 'contraindicada'), el grupo ATC objetivo con el que interactúa (fmc:atcObjetivo → fmc:ConceptoATC) junto a su código (fmc:codigoAtcObjetivo), el texto del efecto (fmc:efecto) y una etiqueta (rdfs:label). Los 5 campos aparecen exactamente una vez en el 100% de las 48,997 interacciones, por lo que se marcan obligatorios (y de cardinalidad simple salvo fmc:efecto, cuyo texto podría en teoría describir más de un efecto).

shacl_shapes.title: Presentacion: nombre y medicamento único
shacl_shapes.tip: Cada fmc:Presentacion (69,982 formatos comerciales/envases del Nomenclátor) debe tener un nombre comercial (schema:name) y enlazar a exactamente un fmc:Medicamento (fmc:medicamento) — ambas relaciones se dan 1:1 en las 69,982 presentaciones, confirmando que cada presentación pertenece a un único medicamento y tiene un único nombre. Los excipientes de declaración obligatoria (fmc:excipiente → fmc:Excipiente) quedan opcionales porque solo una parte de las presentaciones (53,994 de 69,982) los declaran.

shacl_shapes.title: SeccionDocumento: tipos literales de sección
shacl_shapes.tip: fmc:SeccionDocumento es la clase paraguas (761,945 instancias) que agrupa tanto las secciones de ficha técnica (fmc:SeccionFichaTecnica, 600,682) como las de prospecto (fmc:SeccionProspecto, 161,263). Esta forma solo fija el tipo de los campos literales (rdfs:label, schema:text, fmc:texto, fmc:seccionTitulo, fmc:seccionNumero como xsd:string) y que el enlace de vuelta al medicamento (fmc:medicamento) sea como máximo uno; no exige mínimos porque, en los datos agregados, la cobertura de estos predicados difiere entre los dos subtipos de sección (los conteos disponibles cuadran con el subtipo ficha técnica, no con el total de la clase paraguas).

datasets.label: open-pulse.rete — EPFL/SDSC research-software knowledge graph (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The Open-Pulse graph of research software in and around EPFL and the Swiss Data Science Center. 40,574 crawled GitHub entities — 31,787 repositories (schema:SoftwareSourceCode), 7,819 people (schema:Person) and 968 organizations (org:Organization) — plus the edges between them: who contributed to what (pulse:Contribution, person→repo, with commit counts and first/last dates), who is affiliated with which institution (org:Membership, person→org), which org owns which repo (pulse:ownedBy), and the scholarly articles repositories cite (schema:ScholarlyArticle). Built by the Open-Pulse git-metadata-extractor and modelled with the Open-Pulse ontology: schema.org + the W3C Organization & Time vocabularies + the project's pulse: terms, with raw GitHub facts (stars, forks, primary language, topics, timestamps) under the gme: namespace and institutions reconciled to ROR (country, type). People carry both their GitHub handle and, where reconciled, an ORCID. 3.70 M triples, a types pyramid and embedded Dataset Card. Per source_url the latest complete extraction is kept; the extractor's double-prefixed GitHub IRIs are normalized so repos join their owning org, and institution country is flattened from ROR. scripts/open-pulse/*.py → rete build --pyramid-algo types --card. Remote-lazy on Cloudflare R2.
datasets.license: GitHub public metadata (facts); Open-Pulse ontology © SDSC-ORDES

examples.title: What's in the graph
examples.tip:
The six entity types of the Open-Pulse model and how many of each: repositories (schema:SoftwareSourceCode), people (schema:Person), organizations (org:Organization), plus the pulse:Contribution and org:Membership edges and the schema:ScholarlyArticle citations.
Open the Schema tab to see the same breakdown as a type pyramid.

examples.title: ⭐ Most-starred repositories
examples.tip:
The highest-starred repositories in the crawl, with their primary language — a mix of EPFL/SDSC projects and the big open-source libraries they build on.
Stars come from pulse:githubRepoStars; the OPTIONAL keeps repos that have no detected language.

examples.title: 🏛 Organizations with the most repositories
examples.tip:
Which GitHub organizations own the most crawled repositories — EPFL labs and course orgs (ADA, EPFL-SI, LASA …) rise to the top.
pulse:ownedBy links a repo to its owning org; an org can carry more than one schema:name, so we SAMPLE one.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX pulse: <https://open-pulse.epfl.ch/ontology#>
PREFIX org: <http://www.w3.org/ns/org#>
SELECT ?org (SAMPLE(?nm) AS ?name) (COUNT(?repo) AS ?repos) WHERE {
  ?repo a schema:SoftwareSourceCode ; pulse:ownedBy ?org .
  ?org a org:Organization ; schema:name ?nm .
} GROUP BY ?org ORDER BY DESC(?repos) LIMIT 40

examples.title: 👥 Who built CEBRA
examples.tip:
The contributors to CEBRA (the Mathis Lab / AdaptiveMotorControlLab neural-embedding library) ranked by commit count. Each row is a pulse:Contribution edge from a person to the repo, carrying pulse:contributionCount.
Some contributors are identified by ORCID, others by GitHub handle; swap the repo IRI for any repository.

examples.title: 🌍 Research software by institution country
examples.tip:
Count repositories by the country of their owning organization's parent institution — a repo's GitHub org links to a ROR institution (org:unitOf) that carries gme:ror_country. Switzerland dominates, as you'd expect for an EPFL/SDSC crawl.
The country was flattened from ROR's nested country object during the build.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX pulse: <https://open-pulse.epfl.ch/ontology#>
PREFIX org: <http://www.w3.org/ns/org#>
PREFIX gme: <https://openpulse.science/git-metadata-extractor#>
SELECT ?country (COUNT(DISTINCT ?repo) AS ?repos) WHERE {
  ?repo a schema:SoftwareSourceCode ; pulse:ownedBy ?ghorg .
  ?ghorg org:unitOf ?ror .
  ?ror gme:ror_country ?country .
