SELECT ?person ?occupation WHERE {
  ?p skos:exactMatch ?wd .
  ?p rdfs:label ?person .
  ?wd wdt:P106 ?occ . ?occ rdfs:label ?occupation .
  FILTER(LANG(?occupation) = "en")
} LIMIT 40

examples.title: Datable manuscripts over time
examples.tip: Switch Output -> Time. wdt:P571 'inception' is an xsd:gYear; each manuscript carries an earliest+latest year, so the heatmap shows the surviving corpus thickening through the 6th-10th centuries - the height of the Irish scribal achievement.

examples.title: The largest manuscripts
examples.tip: Page dimensions in cm: wdt:P2048 height x wdt:P2049 width. The grand display gospel-books at the top vs the tiny 'pocket gospels' Irish monks carried on their travels - the physical range of early Irish book production.

examples.title: Search the contents
examples.tip: Full-text search (a text index backs it) over what each manuscript actually contains. Here, the 32 books carrying gospels; change 'gospel' to 'psalm', 'Priscian', 'computus', 'Isidore'... to trace where a given text survives. ?script is the hand (e.g. 'Irish minuscule').

examples.title: What the catalogue describes
examples.tip: Instance-of (P31) breakdown, resolved to Wikidata labels: ~300 manuscripts, the libraries that hold them, the named people (with Wikidata links) and the literary works they carry - the whole shape of MIrA in one scan.

examples.title: Why each book is in the corpus
examples.tip: MIrA's inclusion criteria (mira:category, straight from the project's 'About' page), each with its manuscript count - the published figures: Script: Irish (148), Origin: Ireland (106), Vernacular Old-Irish content (84), Named Irish scribe (41), Exemplar: Irish, Text of Irish origin, and the tentative 'Insular (Irish?)' outline categories. The reason a book joins the corpus, as data.

examples.title: The Old Irish glossed books (with images)
examples.tip: Manuscripts carrying vernacular Old-Irish content (mira:category = 'Vernacular content') - the famous glossed books (Würzburg, Milan, St Gall...) where Irish scholars wrote their own language between the Latin lines. Joined to the IIIF image where digitised: click a folio to read the glosses.

datasets.label: bioexplora.rete - 207k natural-history specimens (Museu de Ciencies Naturals de Barcelona, Darwin Core, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The OPEN natural-history collections of the Museu de Ciencies Naturals de Barcelona (bioexplora.cat) as one queryable graph - 207,163 SPECIMENS in Darwin Core across the museum's six collections: arthropods (MCNB-Art, 82,900), molluscs (MCNB-Malac, 50,083), paleontology (MGB, 32,581), vertebrates (MCNB-Cord, 31,954), the tissue bank and general zoology. Every specimen carries its full taxonomy (kingdom -> species), catalogue number, collector, date, locality, georeference and type status, expressed with the REAL Darwin Core term IRIs (dwc:scientificName, dwc:family, dwc:decimalLatitude...) - i.e. the museum's own properties. 13,543 specimens are PHOTOGRAPHED: the IIIF images (museum server, CORS-open) render inline; 43,826 are GEOREFERENCED as GeoSPARQL points (switch Output -> Map); 672 are name-bearing TYPE specimens. Plus two media layers: 667 skull and bone 3D SCANS (the Atles osteologic) linking out to their Sketchfab viewers, and 173 nature SOUND recordings that play inline (CC BY-NC-ND, by Eloisa Matheu via Xeno-canto - NOT the MCNB). 7.89M triples, remote-lazy over HTTP range from the bucket. Harvested KEYLESS from GBIF (the museum publishes Darwin Core archives on ipt.gbif.es), the Sketchfab account laboratorinatura, and Xeno-canto, by scripts/bioexplora_to_nt.py. CC BY 4.0 - credit the Museu de Ciencies Naturals de Barcelona (the audio layer excepted). TEXT_INDEX on for full-text search over its literals.

examples.title: The collection at a glance
examples.tip: The museum's six collections by specimen count: arthropods (MCNB-Art, 82,900) and molluscs (MCNB-Malac, 50,083) dominate, then paleontology (MGB), vertebrates (MCNB-Cord), the tissue bank and general zoology. 207,163 Darwin Core specimens in all.

examples.title: Specimens you can SEE (photos)
examples.tip: ~9,000 specimens are photographed. The ?photo column renders INLINE — molluscs, crustaceans, insects, fossils. Photos are mirrored to the bucket as fast WebP (p:preview, ~10-40 KB; the museum's source link is p:image), and ?collector comes from the shared Agent node. CC BY 4.0, credit the Museu de Ciencies Naturals de Barcelona.

examples.title: See it, hear it, place it — photo + sound + map
examples.tip: One row, four media, joined THROUGH THE GRAPH: a photographed+georeferenced specimen and a Xeno-canto recording that hang off the SAME species Taxon node (?spec p:taxon ?t, ?rec p:taxon ?t) — no string matching. A bird like the Great Crested Grebe shows its specimen photo (WebP), its call (inline player) and where it was collected (click the map cell for a full zoomable map). Stay in Table view to see all four.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX p: <https://bioexplora.cat/prop/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
SELECT ?species ?photo ?sound ?location WHERE {
  ?t p:rank "species" ; rdfs:label ?species .
  ?spec p:taxon ?t ; p:preview ?photo ; geo:asWKT ?location .
  ?rec p:taxon ?t ; p:audio ?sound .
} LIMIT 24

examples.title: The taxonomic tree (family › genus › species)
examples.tip: The taxonomy is now a real GRAPH, not flat strings: every name is a Taxon node linked to its parent rank via p:parentTaxon. This walks species → its genus → its family, one row per species placed in the tree.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX p: <https://bioexplora.cat/prop/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?family ?genus ?species WHERE {
  ?sp p:rank "species" ; rdfs:label ?species ; p:parentTaxon ?g .
  ?g rdfs:label ?genus ; p:parentTaxon ?f .
  ?f p:rank "family" ; rdfs:label ?family .
} ORDER BY ?family ?genus LIMIT 40

examples.title: Walk a whole family down to its species
examples.tip: A TRANSITIVE traversal: p:parentTaxon+ collects every species under a family in one hop, however many ranks deep. Change 'Cerambycidae' (longhorn beetles) to Carabidae, Helicidae (snails), Muridae (rodents)… to walk any branch.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX p: <https://bioexplora.cat/prop/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?genus ?species WHERE {
  ?fam p:rank "family" ; rdfs:label "Cerambycidae" .
  ?sp p:parentTaxon+ ?fam ; p:rank "species" ; rdfs:label ?species ; p:parentTaxon ?g .
  ?g rdfs:label ?genus .
} ORDER BY ?genus LIMIT 40

examples.title: Who collected the most
examples.tip: Collectors are shared Agent nodes (dwc:recordedBy) you can count and traverse. José Fernández de Villalta leads with ~32,000 records, ahead of the malacologists Rius Dalmau and Gasull. 3,876 named collectors in all.

examples.title: A naturalist's collection (species + family + place + photo)
examples.tip: Everything one collector brought in, connected through the graph: the Agent node → each specimen → up the taxonomy to its family → out to the country it was found → its photo. Change the name to anyone from 'Who collected the most'.

examples.title: Map of the collection
examples.tip: 43,826 specimens are georeferenced (GeoSPARQL points). Switch Output -> Map to see where the holdings were collected across the world — Catalonia and Spain dominate, with material from Morocco, Mexico, France and beyond. Shows up to 3,000 points.

examples.title: ★ FEDERATED: specimen → its country's boundary polygon
examples.tip: A CROSS-SOURCE join, the whole point of federation: bioexplora has the specimens (dwc:countryCode), geoadmin (auto-added as a source) has the country polygons. The query routes each block of patterns to its own dataset and joins on the ISO code — so every specimen pulls in the boundary polygon of the country it was collected in. Output → Map plots them as areas; Table view shows each boundary as a clickable mini-map. This is how you 'get the geospatial column' from another graph.

PREFIX dwc: <http://rs.tdwg.org/dwc/terms/>
PREFIX g: <https://w3id.org/rete/geoadmin/prop/>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
SELECT ?species ?country ?boundary WHERE {
  ?s dwc:scientificName ?species ; dwc:countryCode ?code .
  ?a g:iso ?code ; schema:name ?country ; geo:asWKT ?boundary .
} LIMIT 20

datasets.label: tree-city-inventory.rete — every tree in Geneva: 239,116 georeferenced trees with species, height & crown (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: Every recorded street and park tree in the canton of **Geneva** — **239,116 individual trees**, each one georeferenced, identified to a taxon and measured. This is the first city of a deliberately **multi-city** inventory: taxon nodes are keyed on the latin name and **shared across cities**, so when a second city lands, its planes and limes merge with Geneva's and cross-city questions (which species dominate which climate, how crown diameter scales with age, which cities actually record tree health) work with no reconciliation. Each `tci:Tree` is a `geo:Feature` carrying a `geo:asWKT` POINT plus species (**3,078 taxa**), total height, crown and trunk diameter, circumference, survey status, postcode and its **municipality** (48 of them, from Genève-Petit-Saconnex's 20,293 trees down). **2,849 are flagged champion trees** and 206 remarkable — the tallest champion is a *Sequoiadendron giganteum* at 46 m, exactly the sort of thing a city tree register knows and nobody ever asks it. Source measurements are dirty and were cleaned at conversion rather than hidden: 3,892 implausible dimensions (the raw file claims a 914 m tree) and 2 out-of-range dates dropped, and **one duplicate source id** — `ID_ARBRE` 393253 is used by both a *Zelkova sicula* and a *Quercus castaneifolia* — disambiguated instead of silently merging two trees into one node. From SITG's `SIPV_ICA_WEB_PUBLIC_TOT` (updated weekly), paged out of its ArcGIS FeatureServer as GeoJSON. opendata.swiss **Open use** — free use including commercial, attribution not required. 3.15 M triples in 25 MB, remote-lazy over HTTP range: a species census over all 239k trees faults **1.4 MB in 20 range requests**, 5.7% of the file. TEXT_INDEX on for full-text search over its literals.
datasets.license: opendata.swiss Open use (free use incl. commercial, attribution not required); attribute SITG anyway — the services carry © 2026 SITG

examples.title: The commonest trees in Geneva
examples.tip: A census over all 239,116 trees, grouped by the shared taxon node. Birch and oak lead at ~12,100 each, then spruce and pine — a temperate-continental signature. Remote-lazy: this reads about 1.4 MB of the 25 MB file in ~20 range requests.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX tci: <https://data.graphplaza.com/tree-city-inventory/ns#>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
SELECT ?species (COUNT(?t) AS ?n) WHERE {
  ?t a tci:Tree ; tci:taxon ?tx .
  ?tx skos:prefLabel ?species
}
GROUP BY ?species ORDER BY DESC(?n) LIMIT 20

examples.title: Champion trees, and the tallest of each species
examples.tip: 2,849 trees carry the CHAMPION flag. Grouping them by species and taking MAX(height) surfaces the giants: a Sequoiadendron giganteum at 46 m tops the list, with Cedrus atlantica and the London planes at 40 m. Note champion is a real boolean here — in the source it is an integer 0/1.
examples.sparql:

PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
SELECT ?species (COUNT(?t) AS ?n) (MAX(?h) AS ?tallest) WHERE {
  ?t a tci:Tree ; tci:champion true ; tci:taxon ?tx ; tci:heightM ?h .
  ?tx skos:prefLabel ?species
}
GROUP BY ?species ORDER BY DESC(?n) LIMIT 15

examples.title: 📍 Map the giant sequoias

examples.title: Which municipality has the most species diversity

examples.sparql:

PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?muni (COUNT(?t) AS ?trees) (COUNT(DISTINCT ?tx) AS ?species) WHERE {

GROUP BY ?muni ORDER BY DESC(?species) LIMIT 20

datasets.label: geoadmin.rete - world admin boundaries (geoBoundaries/OSM, 52k polygons, GeoSPARQL, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: World administrative boundaries with GeoSPARQL geometries, built for FEDERATED geospatial joins — 52k OSM-derived polygons (simplified to ~1 km), a lean 40.3 MB range-queried lazily. 213 COUNTRIES (ADM0), 3,133 REGIONS/states (ADM1) and 48,362 DISTRICTS (ADM2) as POLYGONS from geoBoundaries (OSM-derived, CC-BY), plus 1,251 populated PLACES as POINTS (Natural Earth) — three admin levels, points and polygons. Built by scripts/geoboundaries_to_nt.py.

examples.title: ★ SPARQL SERVICE: capitals from live Wikidata
examples.tip: SPARQL 1.1 federated query, ENGINE-level: the SERVICE block is shipped verbatim to query.wikidata.org and its solutions JOIN the local rows on the shared ?code — geoadmin's ISO 3166-1 code (g:iso, e.g. "ES" for Spain) meets Wikidata's P297 value. No VALUES pinning needed: the block is naturally bounded (~250 countries carry an ISO code). The local file answers the country names; live Wikidata the capitals (P36 + English label): Spain → Madrid, Kenya → Nairobi… Unlike '+ Add source' federation (the playground splitting one pattern set across sources), SERVICE is written INTO the query, per the W3C spec — both now work.

datasets.label: geoadmin-tiles.rete - the admin-boundaries graph AND a PMTiles vector basemap in ONE file
datasets.description: The SAME world-admin graph as geoadmin, but with a PMTiles vector-tile archive EMBEDDED as a section inside the one .rete file (geo-LOD 'option C'). One immutable, content-hashed, HTTP-range-queryable file holds BOTH: run SPARQL on the RDF graph, then switch Output → Tiles and the map range-reads its vector tiles from a kind-7 section of the very same file (no separate .pmtiles, no second request target). The .rete reader ignores the unknown section, so the graph opens exactly as before; the browser parses the 1 KB header to find the tile section's byte offset and faults tiles from there. GeoSPARQL has no native tiling — this is the experiment of carrying pre-tiled vector geometry next to the graph in one range-served file. Tiles built with tippecanoe (z0-9, true per-zoom LOD) and embedded by scripts/embed_tiles.py.

The features the query returns light up in green — here Spain's regions. One immutable, content-hashed, range-queryable file = graph + map tiles.

examples.title: The graph still works (countries)
examples.tip:
Proof the embedded tiles don't disturb the graph: a normal SPARQL query over the same one file, 213 countries with their ISO code and boundary polygon. The .rete reader skips the unknown tile section, so quads, dictionary and pyramid open exactly as in plain geoadmin. Switch Output → Tiles to see the map come from the same bytes.
Note the namespace: THIS file uses https://geoadmin.rete/ (class/ and prop/), not the w3id.org form its sibling `geoadmin` uses, and the name is prop:name rather than schema:name — the version of this query written against the sibling returned nothing at all (#212).

shacl_shapes.title: District: label/name/level/geometry required
shacl_shapes.tip: Every District (48,362 instances, the finest admin-boundary level in this graph) must carry an rdfs:label, a prop:name, a numeric prop:adminLevel and a geo:asWKT boundary geometry, since all four relations cover the full 48,362-row class. Also checks that when prop:partOf is present it targets a real class:Country resource (an IRI, not a literal) - 53 districts (48,362-48,309) lack a country link, so this is left optional rather than required.

shacl_shapes.title: Region: label/name/level/geometry required, fine geometry optional
shacl_shapes.tip: Every Region (3,133 instances, the admin level between Country and District) must have rdfs:label, prop:name, prop:adminLevel and geo:asWKT populated, matching the class count exactly (3,133/3,133 for all four). Also checks prop:partOf, when present, points to a real class:Country IRI, and that prop:geomFine (the higher-resolution boundary used for close zoom in the embedded PMTiles layer) is a plain literal - both are optional since only 3,111 and 2,993 of the 3,133 regions carry them respectively.

shacl_shapes.title: Place: named point with optional population
shacl_shapes.tip: Every Place (1,251 instances - the city/town point layer) must carry rdfs:label, prop:name and a geo:asWKT geometry, since all three relations cover the full 1,251-row class exactly. prop:population and prop:country are left optional because 1 and 3 places respectively lack them (1,250/1,251 and 1,248/1,251) - a hard minCount there would falsely flag otherwise-valid rows.

datasets.label: z-anatomy.rete - the human body in 3D: ~4,900 anatomical structures with mesh geometry, 3D spatial relations & GeoSPARQL-in-3D (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The human body as a queryable 3D knowledge graph. 4,884 anatomical STRUCTURES - bones, muscles, nerves, arteries, veins, viscera, lymphoid organs, joints and body regions - each carrying its real mesh GEOMETRY in an anatomical Cartesian frame (millimetres; +X=left, +Y=anterior, +Z=superior), a full partonomy (anat:partOf / anat:hasPart), multilingual terminology (English, Latin, French, Spanish, Portuguese - from Terminologia Anatomica) and an English description. The novelty is SPATIAL: every structure's centroid and bounding box are published as GeoSPARQL geometry (geo:asWKT POINT Z plus a geo3:box BOX3D), and the graph MATERIALISES three kinds of relation computed from the 3D meshes - geo3:adjacent3D (surfaces in contact, cross-system: e.g. the sternum touches the internal thoracic artery behind it), anat:tissueContinuousWith (adjacent structures of the SAME tissue - 'connected because they are the same tissue'), and geo3:thermallyCoupledWith (an illustrative typed physical relation - heat conduction across a contact involving a perfused/metabolic tissue). It is a worked example of extending GeoSPARQL from 2D to 3D: the engine ships geo3 FUNCTIONS (geof3:distance3D, geo3:within3D, geo3:contains3D, geo3:adjacent3D) so you can FILTER by true 3D distance - 'every structure within 45 mm of the liver' returns the hepatic portal vein, caudate lobe, diaphragm and gallbladder. Each structure links to its body-system Draco .glb (anat:glbFile + anat:meshNode; click the 🧊 3D viewer; the dedicated explorer isolates and highlights a single structure and its neighbours). Cross-linked to two OBO ontologies: 518 HPO PHENOTYPE terms (anat:relatedPhenotype - 'Abnormality of the liver', 'Cerebellar hypoplasia') and 527 Disease Ontology DISEASES (anat:relatedDisease - 'polycystic liver disease', 'gallbladder carcinoma'), so you can ask which diseases and phenotypes are located in a given organ. 417k triples, remote-lazy over HTTP range. Built from the Z-Anatomy project (CC BY-SA 4.0, github.com/LluisV/Z-Anatomy) by scripts/z-anatomy/*: headless Blender extracts mesh geometry + hierarchy from the 9 per-system FBX, and the 3D relations, geometry and ontology bridge are emitted to RDF. CC BY-SA 4.0 - credit Z-Anatomy; HPO (CC BY 4.0) and the Human Disease Ontology (CC0). The conditions-by-body-system framing is inspired by humanome.co. TEXT_INDEX on for full-text search over its literals.

examples.title: The 3D body — systems you can open in the viewer
examples.tip: Each row is a body system; the ?model column is its Draco-compressed .glb — click 🧊 3D to rotate and zoom the whole system inline. Every structure in the graph carries anat:glbFile (its system model) + anat:meshNode (the node name to isolate it). The dedicated explorer isolates and highlights ONE structure and its 3D neighbours.

examples.title: GeoSPARQL in 3D — everything within 45 mm of the liver
examples.tip: The headline: GeoSPARQL extended to three dimensions. geof3:distance3D is a rete engine function that computes true 3D distance (mm) between two geometries' bounding boxes — here between the liver's POINT Z centroid and every other structure's. The result is anatomically correct: the hepatic portal vein (10 mm), caudate lobe, diaphragmatic fascia, gallbladder neck and false ribs — the liver's real neighbours, found by geometry alone across four different body systems. Change 45 to widen the shell, or "Liver" to "Spleen", "Stomach", "Heart".
examples.sparql:
PREFIX anat: <https://w3id.org/rete/anatomy#>
PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
PREFIX geo3: <https://w3id.org/rete/geo3#>
PREFIX geof3: <https://w3id.org/rete/geo3/function/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?structure (ROUND(geof3:distance3D(?lw, ?w)) AS ?mm) WHERE {
  ?liver rdfs:label "Liver"@en ; geo:hasGeometry/geo3:asWKT3D ?lw .
  ?s a anat:AnatomicalStructure ; rdfs:label ?structure ; geo:hasGeometry/geo3:asWKT3D ?w .
  FILTER(?s != ?liver && langMatches(lang(?structure), "en"))
  FILTER(geof3:distance3D(?lw, ?w) < 45)
} ORDER BY ?mm LIMIT 15

examples.title: What is in contact with the heart (3D adjacency, cross-system)
examples.tip: geo3:adjacent3D links structures whose surfaces meet in 3D (bounding boxes within 3 mm), computed from the meshes — the 'structures next to each other' relation. Here: things touching any part of the heart, drawn from OTHER body systems (skeletal, muscular, respiratory) — its true anatomical neighbours: the sternum, ribs, diaphragm, lung surfaces, oesophagus and great vessels.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX anat: <https://w3id.org/rete/anatomy#>
PREFIX geo3: <https://w3id.org/rete/geo3#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT DISTINCT ?neighbour ?system WHERE {
  ?heart rdfs:label "Heart"@en . ?part anat:partOf ?heart .
  ?part geo3:adjacent3D ?n .
  ?n rdfs:label ?neighbour ; anat:inSystem/rdfs:label ?system .
  FILTER(langMatches(lang(?neighbour), "en") && NOT EXISTS { ?n anat:partOf ?heart })
} LIMIT 25

examples.title: Same tissue vs. heat — around the left kidney
examples.tip: Two different relations layered on the same 3D adjacency substrate, exactly as the design intends. anat:tissueContinuousWith = neighbours of the SAME tissue class (the mesocolon, pancreas, renal pelvis, suprarenal gland — 'connected because they are the same kind of tissue'); geo3:thermallyCoupledWith = a typed PHYSICAL relation (heat conduction) asserted where a perfused/metabolic tissue is in contact (the renal and suprarenal arteries). The template for adding further physiological couplings on top of pure geometry.

examples.title: Diseases & phenotypes located in an organ (HPO + Disease Ontology)
examples.tip: The cross-ontology join, from the ontologies' OWN anatomy axioms: each structure is linked to Human Disease Ontology diseases (anat:relatedDisease) and HPO phenotypes (anat:relatedPhenotype) through their FORMAL UBERON location axioms (disease_has_location / EQ inheres_in), not string matching. Where the exact site is a fine part not meshed on its own (cardiac muscle, bronchiole, renal glomerulus) the link rolls UP the UBERON part_of hierarchy to the containing organ, and a leaf disease with no location of its own inherits it from its Disease-Ontology parent. Every disease also carries its clinical crosswalk codes — ICD-10-CM shown here (?icd10); ICD-9/11, SNOMED CT, MeSH and OMIM are in the graph too. For the liver: hepatitis C (B19.20), hepatocellular carcinoma (C22.0), Budd-Chiari syndrome (I82.0). Change "Liver" to "Heart", "Kidney", "Lungs", "Thyroid gland", "Stomach", "Brain".

examples.title: The heart and its parts (partonomy)
examples.tip: Switch Output → Graph. The heart's part hierarchy (anat:hasPart) as a node-link star: chambers, valves, surfaces, borders and septa. Partonomy is the 'same structure' backbone that complements the geometric adjacency relations — anat:partOf is a sub-property of the OBO Relation Ontology's part_of (BFO_0000050).

shacl_shapes.title: Every 3D geometry carries a full 3D placement
shacl_shapes.tip: Each geo3:Geometry3D node (the 3D shape of one of the 4,884 anatomical structures) must carry the complete 3D placement the viewer and GeoSPARQL-3D queries rely on: geosparql:asWKT (a 2D-projected WKT), geo3:asWKT3D (the true 3D geometry), geo3:box (bounding box), geo3:sizeMm (extent in mm) and the geo3:x / geo3:y / geo3:z centroid. All seven are on all 4,884 geometries, so a gap would break 3D distance/adjacency queries.

shacl_shapes.title: Every anatomical structure is named
shacl_shapes.tip: Each anat:AnatomicalStructure (a bone, muscle, nerve, artery, vein, organ, joint, …) must carry at least one rdfs:label. Labels are multilingual here (~4.9 per structure), and they are how a query names a target — e.g. finding the node for 'heart' or 'liver' before a 3D-proximity search.

datasets.label: fzk-haus.rete - a building (IFC/BIM) as a 3D knowledge graph: walls, doors, windows, slabs, stairs & rooms with BOT topology + geo3 3D geometry (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: A CAD/BIM building turned into a queryable 3D knowledge graph. The model is AC20-FZK-Haus, an openly-licensed IFC4 sample building (a small two-storey detached house) from KIT / the IBPSA Project 1. IFC (ISO 16739) is the open BIM exchange format and is already semantic - typed elements, a spatial breakdown, and relationships between them - so it lifts cleanly into RDF over three vocabularies. TOPOLOGY uses the W3C Building Topology Ontology (BOT): a bot:Site -> bot:Building -> bot:Storey -> bot:Space tree (bot:hasStorey / bot:hasSpace) with bot:Element instances placed by bot:containsElement, for 102 elements across 2 storeys (Erdgeschoss, Dachgeschoss) and 7 named rooms (Wohnen, Kueche, Bad, Buero, Schlafzimmer, Flur, Galerie). The IFC specifics are kept under cad: - cad:ifcClass (IfcWallStandardCase, IfcDoor, IfcWindow, IfcSlab, IfcStair, IfcBeam, IfcMember, IfcRailing...), cad:material, cad:boundsSpace (the 81 IfcRelSpaceBoundary), cad:adjacentSpace (which rooms share a boundary - the living room touches all six other rooms), cad:fillsWall and cad:connectsSpace. The novelty is SPATIAL and shared with z-anatomy: every element publishes GeoSPARQL geometry (geo:asWKT POINT Z) plus a geo3:box BOX3D in metres, and the engine's geo3 FUNCTIONS (geof3:distance3D, geo3:within3D, geo3:contains3D, geo3:adjacent3D) let you FILTER by true 3D distance - 'the ten elements nearest the staircase' is answered by geometry alone. A dedicated 3D explorer (docs/building.html) renders every element and highlights a picked element's enclosing walls and adjacent rooms. 2,273 triples, remote-lazy over HTTP range. Built from the IFC with IfcOpenShell by scripts/cad/ifc_to_nt.py. Model: KIT / IBPSA Project 1 (github.com/ibpsa/project1-wp-2-2-bim), openly available; BOT (W3C LBD-CG); geo3 by rete.

examples.title: 🧊 The whole building in 3D
examples.tip: The ?model column is the building's glTF/GLB — drag to rotate it right in the table, or click ⛶ for the full lightbox. cad:glbModel points from the bot:Building to its 3D model on the bucket; the same mesh backs the dedicated explorer (docs/building.html). Each element is a named node keyed by its IFC GlobalId.

examples.title: 🧊 Each floor as its own 3D model
examples.tip: A genuine 3D-preview COLUMN: one rotatable model per storey (cad:glbModel on each bot:Storey), so you can inspect the ground floor (Erdgeschoss) and the upper floor (Dachgeschoss) separately — the walls, slabs, stair and roof timbers of each level. Each floor's GLB is built from just the elements contained in that storey.

examples.title: The building's rooms, floor by floor
examples.tip: The IFC spatial breakdown as BOT topology: each storey (Erdgeschoss at 0 m, Dachgeschoss at +2.7 m) and the rooms it aggregates via bot:hasSpace. The ground floor holds the living room, kitchen, bath, office, bedroom and hall; the upper floor the gallery.

examples.title: Bill of parts — elements by IFC class
examples.tip: How many of each IFC element type the model contains, grouped by cad:ifcClass: 42 structural members (the roof timbers), 13 walls, 11 windows, 5 doors, 4 slabs and 4 beams, 2 railings and 1 stair. The building's whole inventory in one GROUP BY.

examples.title: Rooms next to the living room
examples.tip: Spatial topology derived from the 81 IFC space boundaries: cad:adjacentSpace links rooms that share a wall. The living room (Wohnen) is the hub of the house — it borders all six other rooms. Room labels are language-tagged, so match as "Wohnen"@en.

examples.title: Walls that enclose the kitchen
examples.tip: cad:boundsSpace is the IfcRelSpaceBoundary relation — which building elements physically bound a room. Filtered to walls, this returns the kitchen's (Küche) enclosing walls. Swap the class for "IfcWindow" or "IfcDoor" to see what else opens onto the room.

examples.title: GeoSPARQL in 3D — the 10 elements nearest the staircase
examples.tip: The headline, shared with z-anatomy: GeoSPARQL extended to three dimensions. geof3:distance3D computes true 3D distance (metres) between two geometries — here the stair's POINT Z centroid and every other element's — and ORDER BY + LIMIT returns its ten nearest neighbours: the upper-floor window and railing, then the interior and exterior walls that ring the stairwell. The SAME engine that finds the liver's neighbours in the body, now on a building. Openings (voids) are filtered out.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX bot: <https://w3id.org/bot#>
PREFIX cad: <https://w3id.org/rete/cad#>
PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
PREFIX geo3: <https://w3id.org/rete/geo3#>
PREFIX geof3: <https://w3id.org/rete/geo3/function/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?element ?type (ROUND(geof3:distance3D(?sw,?w)*100)/100 AS ?m) WHERE {
  ?stair cad:ifcClass "IfcStair" ; geo:hasGeometry/geo3:asWKT3D ?sw .
  ?e a bot:Element ; rdfs:label ?element ; cad:ifcClass ?type ;
     geo:hasGeometry/geo3:asWKT3D ?w .
  FILTER(?e != ?stair && ?type != "IfcOpeningElement")
} ORDER BY ?m LIMIT 10

examples.title: The kitchen and the walls that enclose it (graph)
examples.tip: Switch Output → Graph. The kitchen (Küche) as a node-link star of its bounding walls, straight from the space-boundary graph (cad:boundsSpace). This is the room-enclosure structure the 3D explorer lights up when you pick a room. cad:enclosedBy is synthesised by the CONSTRUCT for display.

examples.title: Every element — typed, placed, and positioned
examples.tip: A five-column inventory: each building element with its IFC class, the storey it sits on (cad:inStorey), and the x and z of its centroid in metres (geo3 geometry). Ordered by height, so you read the house bottom-up — the base slab, then the walls, then the Dachgeschoss roof timbers (Sparren) up near z = 4.6 m.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX bot: <https://w3id.org/bot#>
PREFIX cad: <https://w3id.org/rete/cad#>
PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
PREFIX geo3: <https://w3id.org/rete/geo3#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?element ?type ?floor ?x ?z WHERE {
  ?e a bot:Element ; rdfs:label ?element ; cad:ifcClass ?type ; cad:inStorey ?s ; geo:hasGeometry ?g .
  ?s rdfs:label ?floor . ?g geo3:x ?x ; geo3:z ?z .
} ORDER BY ?z LIMIT 60

examples.title: Walls, the rooms they enclose, and where they sit
examples.tip: Joins the space-boundary graph to geometry: every wall that bounds a room (cad:boundsSpace), with that room, its floor, and the wall's x/y centre in metres. An exterior wall like Wand-Ext-ERDG-1 appears several times — it encloses the office, hall and kitchen at once.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX cad: <https://w3id.org/rete/cad#>
PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
PREFIX geo3: <https://w3id.org/rete/geo3#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?wall ?room ?floor ?x ?y WHERE {
  ?e cad:boundsSpace ?r ; cad:ifcClass "IfcWallStandardCase" ; rdfs:label ?wall ; cad:inStorey ?s ; geo:hasGeometry ?g .
  ?r rdfs:label ?room . ?s rdfs:label ?floor . ?g geo3:x ?x ; geo3:y ?y .
} LIMIT 80

examples.title: 🧊 Rooms per floor — neighbours and the floor's 3D model
examples.tip: Four columns mixing data and 3D: each room, its floor, how many other rooms it borders (cad:adjacentSpace), and a rotatable model of the storey it belongs to (cad:glbModel — the same floor GLB in every row of that floor). The living room (Wohnen) and bedroom (Schlafzimmer) lead with six neighbours each.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX bot: <https://w3id.org/bot#>
PREFIX cad: <https://w3id.org/rete/cad#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?floor ?room (COUNT(?n) AS ?adjacentRooms) ?model WHERE {
  ?s a bot:Storey ; rdfs:label ?floor ; bot:hasSpace ?r ; cad:glbModel ?model .
  ?r rdfs:label ?room ; cad:adjacentSpace ?n .
} GROUP BY ?floor ?room ?model ORDER BY ?floor DESC(?adjacentRooms)

examples.title: Doors & windows, and the walls they fill
examples.tip: The opening-fills-wall relation as cad:fillsWall: every door and window, its IFC type, the host wall it fills a void in, its floor, and its x centre. The front door (Haustuer) and the ground-floor windows all fill the exterior walls — the building's envelope in one table.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX cad: <https://w3id.org/rete/cad#>
PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
PREFIX geo3: <https://w3id.org/rete/geo3#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?opening ?type ?hostWall ?floor ?x WHERE {
  ?e cad:fillsWall ?w ; cad:ifcClass ?type ; rdfs:label ?opening ; cad:inStorey ?s ; geo:hasGeometry ?g .
  ?w rdfs:label ?hostWall . ?s rdfs:label ?floor . ?g geo3:x ?x .
} ORDER BY ?floor ?opening LIMIT 60

examples.title: Nearest the staircase, across floors (geo3)
examples.tip: The geo3 distance ranking widened to five columns: the elements closest to the stair by true 3D distance (geof3:distance3D), each with its IFC type, the floor it sits on, the distance in metres, and its height z. It reaches across storeys — a Dachgeschoss beam (Pfette) and an Erdgeschoss window both sit within ~3 m of the central spiral stair.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX bot: <https://w3id.org/bot#>
PREFIX cad: <https://w3id.org/rete/cad#>
PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
PREFIX geo3: <https://w3id.org/rete/geo3#>

SELECT ?element ?type ?floor (ROUND(geof3:distance3D(?sw,?w)*100)/100 AS ?m) ?z WHERE {
  ?stair cad:ifcClass "IfcStair" ; geo:hasGeometry/geo3:asWKT3D ?sw .
  ?e a bot:Element ; rdfs:label ?element ; cad:ifcClass ?type ; cad:inStorey ?st ; geo:hasGeometry ?g .
  ?g geo3:asWKT3D ?w ; geo3:z ?z . ?st rdfs:label ?floor .
  FILTER(?e != ?stair && ?type != "IfcOpeningElement")
} ORDER BY ?m LIMIT 12

datasets.label: gni-bim.rete - 224 IFC building models profiled into one graph: the TUM GNI BIM corpus (subset, discipline, schema, per-class element tallies) (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: A whole CORPUS of BIM models as one queryable graph - the wide sibling to the single, deep fzk-haus building. 224 anonymized IFC building models from the TUM Georg Nemetschek Institute (GNI - AI for the Built World / Chair of Computing in Civil and Building Engineering), released CC BY 4.0, profiled into RDF: 208 single-discipline student models that all model the SAME building shape (the 'BIM Fundamentals' master course), plus 16 models from 9 teams of the 'BIM Project' course - 7 of them a PAIRED architectural + structural model of the same building. Each gnibim:Model carries its subset (fundamentals/project), discipline (architectural/structural/single), IFC schema (IFC4 or IFC2x3), element/storey/space counts, file size, and a per-IFC-class element TALLY (gnibim:tally -> gnibim:ifcClass + gnibim:count) - so you can interrogate the whole corpus at once: the distribution of the 42 IfcElement subclasses (structural framing IfcMember ~69k and IfcPlate ~49k dominate, ahead of openings, furniture and walls), how differently 208 people modelled ONE building (130 to 5,689 elements for the same shape, mean ~1,170), or architecture vs structure side by side (architectural models average 5,623 elements - walls, curtain walls, furniture; the structural skeletons average 415 - beams, columns, slabs). Paired models are linked with gnibim:pairedWith under a gnibim:Project. Profiled with IfcOpenShell by scripts/gni-bim/profile_to_nt.py (entity counts only, no geometry); one 536 MB architectural model was recorded from its STEP header alone. 16.3k triples, remote-lazy over HTTP range. CC BY 4.0 - cite Wang, Fuchs, Wu, Esser, Wrabel & Borrmann, GNI BIM Dataset (2026); github.com/ZijianWang-ZW/GNI-BIM-Dataset.

examples.title: The corpus at a glance
examples.tip: The shape of the 224-model corpus: 208 single-discipline student models (all of the SAME building shape, from the BIM Fundamentals course), plus 9 architectural and 7 structural models from the paired BIM Project teams. Grouped by subset and discipline.

examples.title: Which building components fill the corpus
examples.tip: Summing the per-model tallies across all 223 parsed models: structural framing dominates — IfcMember (~69k) and IfcPlate (~49k) lead, ahead of openings, furniture, proxies, walls and windows. The whole 42-class IfcElement distribution in one GROUP BY.

examples.title: How 208 people modelled the SAME building
examples.tip: The 208 BIM Fundamentals models are all of one building shape — yet the element count ranges from 130 to 5,689 (mean ~1,170). A vivid measure of how differently people model the same thing: level of detail, furnishing, structural framing and proxy components all vary wildly.

examples.title: Every same-building model, by size (5 columns)
examples.tip: A five-column profile of each BIM Fundamentals model — its IFC schema (IFC4 or IFC2x3) and its element / storey / space counts — ordered by richness. Same building, wildly different models: the top ones pack 5,000+ elements and 30+ spaces; the leanest barely a hundred.

examples.title: Architecture vs structure, side by side (5 columns)
examples.tip: The seven paired projects (gnibim:pairedWith): each team's architectural and structural model of the SAME building, compared. The architectural model is far denser — walls, curtain walls, furniture — than the structural skeleton of beams, columns and slabs; Project 1 has 34,231 architectural elements against just 310 structural.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX g: <https://w3id.org/rete/gnibim#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?project ?arcElements ?arcStoreys ?structElements ?structStoreys WHERE {
  ?p a g:Project ; rdfs:label ?project ; g:hasModel ?a , ?s .
  ?a g:discipline "architectural" ; g:elementCount ?arcElements ; g:storeyCount ?arcStoreys .
  ?s g:discipline "structural" ; g:elementCount ?structElements ; g:storeyCount ?structStoreys .
} ORDER BY ?project

examples.title: A structural skeleton — one model's element classes
examples.tip: The element make-up of a single structural model (Project 0's structural discipline): beams, slabs and columns — the load-bearing frame, with none of the walls, furniture or curtain walls of its architectural twin. CONTAINS matches the language-tagged label.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX g: <https://w3id.org/rete/gnibim#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?ifcClass ?count WHERE {
  ?m g:discipline "structural" ; rdfs:label ?model ; g:tally ?t .
  ?t g:ifcClass ?c ; g:count ?count . ?c rdfs:label ?ifcClass .
  FILTER(CONTAINS(STR(?model), "Project 0"))
} ORDER BY DESC(?count)

examples.title: Every model + its downloadable IFC (5 columns)
examples.tip: The graph as an index into the actual files: each model with its discipline, IFC schema, element count, and a link to the raw IFC on the bucket (gnibim:ifcFile) — click ?ifc to download the real model (6 MB to 536 MB each; all 224 are hosted). Ordered by size.

examples.title: 🧊 Projects in 3D — architecture vs structure
examples.tip: Each rendered model as a rotatable, Draco-compressed glTF (gnibim:glbModel) — the architectural envelope beside its structural skeleton, for projects 0, 3 and 7. Drag a ?model3d cell to rotate, or ⛶ for the lightbox; the paired viewer docs/bim-pair.html toggles and overlays them and lets you pick a project.

datasets.label: smithsonian3d.rete - 2,199 interactive 3D models (Smithsonian Open Access, CC0, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: 2,199 interactive 3D MODELS from the Smithsonian Open Access program (CC0, public domain) - every object streams a Draco-compressed .glb you can rotate, zoom and inspect right in the results table (the 🧊 3D viewer). The collection spans the Institution: the National Museum of Natural History dominates (primate and animal CRANIA, mandibles, fossils and zoological specimens - Hylobates, Pongo, fossil whales), alongside famous objects from the National Air and Space Museum (the Apollo Command Module Columbia, modelled inside and out), American History, the National Portrait Gallery (Abraham Lincoln's life masks), Cooper Hewitt, African American History and the Freer|Sackler. Each model carries its title, the holding museum unit, its catalogue number, and a link (?record) to the full Smithsonian record. Built KEYLESS from the public smithsonian-open-access S3 bucket (the 3d/ prefix - each model a Voyager scene.svx.json listing Low/Medium/High Draco .glb derivatives) by scripts/smithsonian3d_to_nt.py, taking the Medium-quality mesh for streaming; the .glb files are served with CORS from Amazon S3 so they render inline. 15k triples, remote-lazy from the bucket, with lossless Parquet / DuckDB / SQLite table companions beside it for the Explore tab (the Model3D table holds every object). CC0 1.0 - free to use, share and remix; credit the Smithsonian. TEXT_INDEX on for full-text search over its literals.

examples.title: 3D models you can rotate
examples.tip: Every row is an interactive 3D model. The ?model column is a Draco-compressed .glb streamed straight from the Smithsonian's S3 bucket — click 🧊 3D to open the inline viewer, then drag to rotate and scroll to zoom. All CC0 / public domain. 2,199 models in the collection; this shows the first 60.

examples.title: Spinning turntable previews
examples.tip: A lightweight alternative to the live 3D viewer: ?spin is a tiny pre-rendered turntable clip (a Blender Cycles render, ~20 KB webm) that loops automatically right in the cell — no WebGL needed. Shown beside the full ?model mesh so you can compare. About 200 of the 2,199 models have a pre-rendered spin.

examples.title: Models by museum
examples.tip: Which Smithsonian museum each model comes from. The National Museum of Natural History dominates (its mass-digitised skull and specimen collections), with Air and Space, American History, the National Portrait Gallery, Cooper Hewitt, African American History and the Freer|Sackler also represented.

examples.title: Search the collection
examples.tip: Full-text search over the model titles (a text index backs it), each result a rotatable 3D model. Here the crania; change 'cranium' to 'whale', 'mammoth', 'mask', 'Apollo', 'Lincoln', or a genus like 'Pongo' to pull a different slice of the 2,199 models.

examples.title: Apollo & Air and Space
examples.tip: The National Air and Space Museum's 3D scans — including the Apollo Command Module Columbia, modelled both inside and out. Open the 🧊 3D viewer to fly around the actual spacecraft that carried Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins to the Moon and back.

examples.title: Natural History specimens (with catalogue numbers)
examples.tip: Vertebrate-zoology specimens from the National Museum of Natural History, each with its USNM catalogue number and a rotatable 3D scan — a digitised reference collection of primate and animal crania, mandibles and bones used by researchers worldwide.

examples.tip: Each 3D model links back to its full catalogue record on si.edu (?record) — the museum metadata, provenance and rights — shown beside the inline 3D mesh. The bridge from the scan to everything else the Smithsonian knows about the object.

datasets.label: lineara.rete - the Linear A corpus (undeciphered Minoan script, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The complete surviving corpus of LINEAR A - the still-undeciphered script of Bronze-Age Minoan Crete (c. 1800-1450 BC), used for palace administration and religious dedications. 1,721 inscriptions (clay tablets, roundels, sealings, libation vessels) from Haghia Triada, Khania, Phaistos, Knossos, Zakros and beyond, each linked to its findspot, scribe, support type and Minoan period, with the Linear A Unicode transcription and the Latin transliteration. The analytical heart is the SIGN and WORD layer: every document is connected to the 375 distinct signs and 1,314 word-sequences it carries (6,039 sign-attestations, 4,100 word-attestations), so you can study sign frequencies, recurring sequences and sign co-occurrence - the main tools for probing an undeciphered script. KU-RO ('total') and KI-RO ('deficit'), the two Linear A words scholars do agree on, are right there at the bottom of the accounts. 67 of the artifacts also LINK (prop:model3d) to the ERC INSCRIBE project's high-resolution interactive 3D scans (3DHOP viewers, University of Bologna) - HT 29, the Khania (KH) and Phaistos (PH) tablets, plus nodules, roundels and a vessel - so you can rotate and measure the actual clay. A second archive, the PAITO Project (Sapienza, Prof. A. Greco; prop:paito), is linked for the Haghia Triada sealings (per-artifact) and the Phaistos corpus (catalogue). Text after the transcriptions of Louis Godart & Jean-Pierre Olivier (GORILA, Ecole Francaise d'Athenes) and the tabulation of George Douros; compiled by mwenge as the LinearA Explorer (github.com/mwenge/lineara.xyz). 38k triples, embedded (instant, offline). Built by scripts/lineara_to_nt.js + scripts/lineara_inscribe.js. Scholarly/educational derivative with full attribution - inscription IMAGES are (c) Ecole Francaise d'Athenes and the 3D MODELS are (c) INSCRIBE / Universita di Bologna (all rights reserved, non-profit scientific use); NEITHER is included here, only references/links; the source repo states no explicit license, so attribute GORILA / Douros / mwenge / INSCRIBE and treat as non-commercial research data. TEXT_INDEX on for full-text search over its literals.

examples.title: The shape of the corpus
examples.tip: The seven kinds of thing in the graph: 1,721 Inscriptions, 1,314 distinct word-sequences, 375 Signs, 102 Scribes, 52 Sites, plus Support and Period. Because Linear A is undeciphered, 'Word' and 'Sign' mean recurring graphic sequences, not known vocabulary.

examples.title: The most common signs
examples.tip: How often each sign is attested across the whole corpus. KA, KU, SI and A lead — the workhorse syllabograms of the Minoan script. Entries like *301 are Douros/GORILA catalogue numbers for signs that have no agreed phonetic value (the script is undeciphered).

examples.title: Where the tablets were found
examples.tip: Findspots, by document count. Haghia Triada — the great Minoan villa archive in south Crete — dominates with 1,110 inscriptions, followed by the Khania, Phaistos, Knossos and Zakros palaces. Most surviving Linear A is administrative clay from a handful of Cretan centres.

examples.title: Cross-referenced to the 3D & photo archives
examples.tip: The corpus links out to two scholarly digital archives. prop:model3d → the ERC INSCRIBE project's interactive 3D scans (67 artifacts, University of Bologna; rotate and measure the actual clay — e.g. HT 29). prop:paito → the PAITO Project (Sapienza, Prof. Alessandro Greco): per-artifact pages for the Haghia Triada sealings (HT Wa …) and the Phaistos catalogue (tablets / clay sealings / vases — individual pages forthcoming). Both columns are clickable; HT Wa 1561 has both. The scans/photos are © their projects — acknowledge them; the graph stores links, not media.

examples.title: The sequences that recur across the corpus
examples.tip: The word-sequences attested in the most documents — the recurring administrative vocabulary of Minoan accounting. KU heads it, and the famous KU-RO ('total', see the next example) and KI-RO ('deficit') are in the list. Fraction signs (¹⁄₂ …) appear because the accounts record measured quantities.

examples.title: KU-RO — the Minoan word for 'total'
examples.tip: Full-text search (a text index backs it) over the Latin transliteration. KU-RO is the one Linear A word almost everyone agrees on: it means 'total', and it closes an account the way a sum line does — here 34 tablets end with it. Its companion KI-RO means 'deficit / owed'. Change 'KU-RO' to 'KI-RO' or 'SA-RA₂' to follow a different term.

examples.title: Signs that travel with KU
examples.tip: Sign co-occurrence: which signs share a document with KU, and in how many. Since Linear A cannot be read, this distributional method — which signs cluster together — is one of the main tools for probing the script's structure. PA, RO, DA, NA and TA are KU's commonest companions.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX la: <https://lineara.xyz/prop/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?sign (COUNT(DISTINCT ?i) AS ?sharedDocs) WHERE {
  ?i la:sign ?ku . ?ku rdfs:label "KU" .
  ?i la:sign ?o . ?o rdfs:label ?sign .
  FILTER(?o != ?ku)
} GROUP BY ?sign ORDER BY DESC(?sharedDocs) LIMIT 20

examples.title: Documents sharing the term SA-RA₂
examples.tip: Switch Output → Graph. A star of the 20 documents that share the sequence SA-RA₂ — one of the most-discussed Linear A terms (a transaction heading or commodity, found across several sites). Linking documents by a shared sequence is how scholars hunt for genres, scribal habits and the hand of single administrators.

datasets.label: nomisma.rete - coinage of Alexander the Great (PELLA)
datasets.description: PELLA - Coinage of Alexander the Great and the Macedonian kingdom, from Nomisma.org. 7,228 ancient Greek coin TYPES struck under Philip II, Alexander III, Philip III Arrhidaeus and the Diadochi (Cassander, Lysimachus, Ptolemy I), spanning 359-65 BC. Each type links by real IRIs to its mint (~150 cities from Pella and Amphipolis to Babylon, Sardis, Sidon and Susa), issuing authority, material (silver/gold/bronze), denomination (tetradrachm, drachm, stater...), region, and start/end dates as xsd:gYear. Every mint/authority/material/denomination/region carries an English rdfs:label, so the graph is fully self-describing. ~53,535 triples, embeds to ~150 KB. ODbL 1.0 (PELLA coin data) + CC-BY 3.0 (Nomisma vocabulary); attribute the American Numismatic Society / Nomisma.org.

examples.title: Shape of the corpus
examples.tip: Predicate totals over the whole graph: ~7.2k coin types each carrying a label, dates, material, denomination, and (mostly) a mint and authority. 9 predicates.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?triples) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY DESC(?triples)

examples.title: Silver tetradrachms of Alexander the Great
examples.tip: Bound-authority + bound-material + bound-denomination star, joined to mint labels: the famous AR tetradrachms of Alexander III, by mint (Abydus, Aegae, Amphipolis...).

examples.title: Most prolific mints
examples.tip: GROUP BY mint: the Macedonian capital Pella (1501 types) and Amphipolis (1266) dominate, then the eastern conquests Babylon and Sardis.

examples.title: Coin types per issuing authority
examples.tip: The cast of the Macedonian story by output: Alexander III (1972), Philip III Arrhidaeus (1025), Philip II (480), then the Diadochi Cassander, Lysimachus and Ptolemy I.

examples.title: Mints used by 3+ successive rulers
examples.tip: Two-hop join through a shared mint reveals political continuity: Amphipolis was struck by FOUR rulers (Philip II -> Alexander III -> Philip III -> Cassander). HAVING + GROUP_CONCAT name them.

examples.title: Who else struck at Cassander's mints
examples.tip: Builds a compact succession star: every authority that minted at a city Cassander also used. Centres on Amphipolis, linking Philip II, Alexander III, Philip III and Cassander - the whole Macedonian dynastic line in one mint.

shacl_shapes.tip: Numismatic data quality: every coin type (nm:TypeSeriesItem) should record a denomination, a material and start/end dates. SHACL finds exactly one coin type missing its material.

datasets.label: mimotext.rete - French Enlightenment novels + stylometry
datasets.description: MiMoTextBase, a Wikibase of French Enlightenment novels (c. 1751-1800) from the Trier Center for Digital Humanities. A self-contained literary graph: 1,774 works linked to authors (956 people), publication dates and places, genres, languages, narrative form and location, and 375 thematic concepts (4,096 work->theme edges). Its distinctive layer is computational: 520 work-to-work STYLOMETRIC SIMILARITY edges (a Burrows-Delta neighbourhood of which novels read alike), plus 191 scholarship-mention edges. English labels for every entity. ~25,155 triples, ~828 KB Turtle -> embeds. A browsable network of who wrote what, which novels are thematically and stylistically close, and which scholarship discusses them together. CC0 (public domain).

examples.title: What is in this graph?
examples.tip: Counts the main entity kinds (literary works, people, themes, spatial concepts) so you see the shape of the literary network at a glance.

examples.title: Most common themes across the novels
examples.tip: Ranks thematic concepts (P36 'about') by how many distinct novels treat them - the dominant motifs of the Enlightenment novel (sentiment, sentimentalism, travel, love).

examples.title: Baculard d'Arnaud's novels, by year, with genre
examples.tip: Lists the works of the most prolific author in this subset - Baculard d'Arnaud (41 novels) - with publication year (from xsd:dateTime P9) and genre. Author names are stored 'SURNAME, Given', so the match uses CONTAINS on the family name.

examples.title: Novels that share the most themes
examples.tip: Finds the pair of novels with the largest overlap of shared thematic concepts - a thematic 'bridge' between two books.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX wdt: <http://data.mimotext.uni-trier.de/prop/direct/>
PREFIX rdfs:<http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?novelA ?novelB (COUNT(?t) AS ?sharedThemes) WHERE {
  ?a wdt:P36 ?t . ?b wdt:P36 ?t . FILTER(STR(?a) < STR(?b))
  ?a rdfs:label ?novelA FILTER(LANG(?novelA)="en")
  ?b rdfs:label ?novelB FILTER(LANG(?novelB)="en")
} GROUP BY ?novelA ?novelB ORDER BY DESC(?sharedThemes) LIMIT 10

examples.title: Stylometrically closest novels
examples.tip: The 520 computed P49 stylometric-similarity edges link novels close in writing style (a Burrows-Delta neighbourhood). This lists labelled novel - neighbour pairs. In this subset the similarity is a direct work-to-work edge; the distance value itself is not carried.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX wdt: <http://data.mimotext.uni-trier.de/prop/direct/>
PREFIX rdfs:<http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?novel ?stylisticNeighbour WHERE {
  ?a wdt:P49 ?b .
  ?a rdfs:label ?novel FILTER(LANG(?novel)="en")
  ?b rdfs:label ?stylisticNeighbour FILTER(LANG(?stylisticNeighbour)="en")
} LIMIT 20

examples.title: Author ego-network: Baculard d'Arnaud -> novels -> genre
examples.tip: Builds a small subgraph of one author (Baculard d'Arnaud), their novels, and each novel's genre - rendered as a node-link diagram.

shacl_shapes.title: Novels in the style network are complete
shacl_shapes.tip: MiMoText's distinctive layer is 520 stylometric-similarity edges. Every novel in that style network should carry a label and name its author. SHACL flags 48 nodes that don't.

shacl_shapes.title: Novels with an author carry a date
shacl_shapes.tip: Every work that names an author should also carry a publication date — a few are undated.

shacl_shapes.title: Themed works are labelled
shacl_shapes.tip: Every work that has a theme should carry a label.

shacl_shapes.title: Works with a genre are labelled
shacl_shapes.tip: Every work that records a genre should carry a label.

datasets.label: mmm.rete - the full Mapping Manuscript Migrations provenance graph (23.3M triples, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The ENTIRE Mapping Manuscript Migrations (MMM) graph as one range-queried .rete: 23,349,356 triples over CIDOC-CRM / FRBRoo, unifying the Schoenberg Database (SDBM), Bibale (IRHT) and Medieval Manuscripts in Oxford (Bodleian) into one provenance graph of medieval and Renaissance manuscripts. Each manuscript is an frbroo:F4_Manifestation_Singleton with its production event (E12, with time-span and place), former/current owners (crm:P51 -> E21 persons and E40 organisations), the works/expressions it carries (mmm:manuscript_work), physical detail (material, folios, lines), a shelfmark (mmm:catalog_or_lot_number) and the catalogue/source records that document it (crm:P70i). Places are TGN entities carrying WGS84 coordinates. The MMM metadata ontology is merged in (class/property labels for the Schema view) and a type pyramid + Dataset Card are embedded. Queried lazily over HTTP range - the browser fetches only the dictionary chunks and index tiles each query touches, never the 141 MB whole. Featured here: Cambridge, University Library, MS Gg.1.1 (SDBM entry 212926), the 14th-century trilingual compendium ('A large collection of poetry', parchment, 633 folios). CC BY-NC 4.0 - non-commercial, attribute MMM (seco.cs.aalto.fi). Pick SELECTIVE shapes (a bound manuscript, a bound owner/collection, a shelfmark) for snappy lazy reads; whole-predicate aggregates over 23M triples scan far more.

examples.title: MS Gg.1.1 - the trilingual compendium's full record
examples.tip: Every fact MMM holds about Cambridge, University Library, MS Gg.1.1 - the 14th-century trilingual compendium of texts (SDBM entry 212926). A bound subject is the most selective shape: SPO routing fetches only this manuscript's tiles, a few HTTP ranges of the 141 MB file. You'll see the work it carries, its owners, shelfmark, material (parchment), folio/line counts and the Cambridge catalogue that documents it.

examples.title: MS Gg.1.1 - the trilingual texts inside (Latin, French, English)
examples.tip: What the 'trilingual compendium' actually carries: the work 'A large collection of poetry' and the THREE languages SDBM records for its expression via crm:P72_has_language - Latin, French and English. That mix (Latin + Anglo-Norman French + Middle English) is exactly what makes Cambridge UL MS Gg.1.1 famous. All bound to one manuscript, so it stays a selective lazy read.

examples.title: MS Gg.1.1 - its journey across the world
examples.tip: The manuscript's migration - the very thing MMM maps. Made in 14th-century England (production 1300-1401), MS Gg.1.1's recorded owners span 'Cambridge, University' (England) and 'Washington' (United States), and its last-known location is back at Cambridge with WGS84 coordinates: a medieval book that crossed the Atlantic and seven centuries. UNION gathers the ownership stops and the final location into one result.

examples.title: MS Gg.1.1 - work, owners and shelfmark
examples.tip: The compendium's text ('A large collection of poetry', SDBM's terse title), its shelfmark 'Gg. 1. 1.' and its two recorded owners (Cambridge, University; Washington), resolved through skos:prefLabel. One row per owner. Everything is bound to one manuscript, so it stays a selective lazy read.

examples.title: MS Gg.1.1 - provenance ego-network
examples.tip: Switch Output -> Graph. A small star around MS Gg.1.1: the work it carries, its owners, its material (parchment) and its shelfmark. Each OPTIONAL lets an edge appear only if present, drawing one manuscript's provenance as a node-link card.

examples.title: Other trilingual manuscripts (Latin + French + English), and where they are now
examples.tip: Gg.1.1's exact language profile, generalised across the corpus: manuscripts whose text is recorded in ALL THREE of Latin, French and English. SDBM's language IRIs are shared, so this is a three-way intersection on crm:P72_has_language - 160 manuscripts qualify - paired with their last-known location (often London or Oxford). A real multi-join: carries -> expression -> three languages, then where each ended up.

examples.title: The rare company MS Gg.1.1 keeps - the 3 manuscripts owned by 'Washington'
examples.tip: Gg.1.1 has two recorded owners: the University of Cambridge (1,190 manuscripts) and an obscure 'Washington' (only 3). Follow the rarer one backwards (reverse crm:P51) to surface the unlikely trio it sits among - a book of English statutes (Statuta Angliae, Edward III & Richard II), a Bible, and Gg.1.1's own 'large collection of poetry'. A bound owner keeps this a selective lazy read.

examples.title: MS Gg.1.1's owner, the University of Cambridge, across the linked-data web
examples.tip: Follow Gg.1.1's owner outward. The University of Cambridge is reconciled (owl:sameAs) to SIX authority files - Wikidata (Q35794), VIAF, the BnF, the US Library of Congress, the German GND and the French IdRef. Each ?authority is a real web IRI, so the table links straight out to it. This is how MMM threads its actors into the wider linked-data web.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX crm: <http://erlangen-crm.org/current/>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
PREFIX owl: <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#>
SELECT ?owner ?authority WHERE {
  <http://ldf.fi/mmm/manifestation_singleton/sdbm_orphan_212926> crm:P51_has_former_or_current_owner ?o .
  ?o skos:prefLabel ?owner ; owl:sameAs ?authority .
}

examples.title: How typical are Gg.1.1's three languages? (Latin vs French vs English)
examples.tip: Begin at Gg.1.1's own three languages, then fan out across the WHOLE graph to count how many manuscripts carry each: Latin ~121,600 (the universal language of medieval learning), French ~12,500, and English just ~5,900 - the vernaculars, English the rarest of the three. The heaviest query here: it walks every manuscript in those languages, so run it to watch the engine work, not for a quick answer.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX crm: <http://erlangen-crm.org/current/>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
SELECT ?language (COUNT(DISTINCT ?ms) AS ?manuscripts) WHERE {
  <http://ldf.fi/mmm/manifestation_singleton/sdbm_orphan_212926> crm:P128_carries ?gg .
  ?gg crm:P72_has_language ?lang . ?lang skos:prefLabel ?language .
  ?other crm:P72_has_language ?lang . ?ms crm:P128_carries ?other .
} GROUP BY ?language ORDER BY DESC(?manuscripts)

examples.title: Cambridge University Library - the Gg manuscripts
examples.tip: Manuscripts documented in 'A Catalogue of the Manuscripts preserved in the University Library, Cambridge' (collection sdbm_33357), with their shelfmarks - the Gg.1.x series that MS Gg.1.1 sits in (Gg.1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.5, 1.6, 1.7 ...). A bound object on crm:P70i_is_documented_in routes to just that catalogue's tiles, so it stays a selective lazy read.

examples.title: Manuscripts produced in England
examples.tip: Bind the place 'England' by name, then walk the CIDOC-CRM production event backwards (P7_took_place_at <- E12_Production -> P108_has_produced) to the manuscripts made there. Many now live elsewhere - several here are in the BnF in Paris - which is exactly the migration MMM traces. England produced ~14,650 of the graph's manuscripts.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX crm: <http://erlangen-crm.org/current/>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
SELECT ?msLabel WHERE {
  ?place skos:prefLabel "England" .
  ?prod crm:P7_took_place_at ?place ; crm:P108_has_produced ?ms .
  ?ms skos:prefLabel ?msLabel .
} LIMIT 100

examples.title: Where were manuscripts produced?
examples.tip: Counts manuscripts by production place through the CIDOC-CRM production event (E12_Production -> P7_took_place_at): Italy ~16k, England ~15k, France ~11k, then cities like Paris, Florence and Venice. An aggregate over the whole production relation scans many tiles - heavier than the bound examples above, but still streamed lazily, never a full download.

examples.title: Predicate totals (the shape of the graph)
examples.tip: Which CIDOC-CRM / FRBRoo predicates carry the provenance across all 23.3M triples - ownership (P51), production (P108/P7), documentation (P70i), the works carried. This scans the whole graph, so it's the heaviest example: switch the strategy to Progressive to read it from the embedded pyramid instead of a full scan.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?triples) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY DESC(?triples) LIMIT 30

shacl_shapes.title: Manuscripts record their provenance
shacl_shapes.tip: Provenance completeness over CIDOC-CRM: every manuscript (F4_Manifestation_Singleton) should carry a label, a former-or-current owner (a person) and a production date. On the full 23.3M-triple graph this targets every manuscript, so it is heavy - use the lazy remote path (it fetches only the shapes' targets) or run it on a bound subset; real provenance is incomplete, so expect many violations.

shacl_shapes.title: Every person is named
shacl_shapes.tip: Every CIDOC-CRM E21_Person should carry a skos:prefLabel. The actor list conforms.

shacl_shapes.title: Manuscripts name a work
shacl_shapes.tip: Every manuscript (F4_Manifestation_Singleton) should record the work it manifests.

shacl_shapes.title: Places are geolocated
shacl_shapes.tip: Every CIDOC-CRM E53_Place should carry WGS84 lat/long coordinates.

datasets.label: openalex-astrocytes.rete - astrocyte research graph (OpenAlex)
datasets.description: The 500 most-cited works on astrocytes (the star-shaped glial cells of the brain) from OpenAlex (CC0), as a connected citation core: 4,113 cito:cites edges linking 500 papers to 2,074 authors, 537 institutions and 875 sub-topics. Explore the most-cited papers, the most prolific labs, and which fields astrocyte research bridges (reactive astrocytes, blood-brain barrier, neuroinflammation, stem cells).

examples.title: What's in the graph
examples.tip: Predicate totals: ex:author and ex:topic edges dominate, with 4,113 cito:cites citation links and the dct:title / ex:citationCount paper metadata.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?n) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY DESC(?n)

examples.title: Most-cited astrocyte papers
examples.tip: ex:citationCount is the global OpenAlex citation count; Liddelow 2017 'Neurotoxic reactive astrocytes' tops the field.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
PREFIX ex: <http://ex/>
SELECT ?title ?c WHERE { ?w a ex:Work ; dct:title ?title ; ex:citationCount ?c } ORDER BY DESC(?c) LIMIT 15

examples.title: Most prolific astrocyte authors
examples.tip: Count papers per author across the citation core - the researchers who define the field.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX ex: <http://ex/>
PREFIX foaf: <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/>
SELECT ?name (COUNT(?w) AS ?papers) WHERE { ?w ex:author ?a . ?a foaf:name ?name } GROUP BY ?name ORDER BY DESC(?papers) LIMIT 15

examples.title: Leading institutions
examples.tip: Join author -> ex:affiliation -> institution label; which labs/universities produce the most astrocyte research.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX ex: <http://ex/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?inst (COUNT(DISTINCT ?w) AS ?papers) WHERE { ?w ex:author ?a . ?a ex:affiliation ?i . ?i rdfs:label ?inst } GROUP BY ?inst ORDER BY DESC(?papers) LIMIT 15

examples.title: Adjacent sub-topics
examples.tip: The OpenAlex concepts co-tagged with these papers - the neighbouring fields astrocyte research bridges into.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX ex: <http://ex/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?topic (COUNT(?w) AS ?papers) WHERE { ?w ex:topic ?t . ?t rdfs:label ?topic } GROUP BY ?topic ORDER BY DESC(?papers) LIMIT 20

examples.title: Who cites the field's landmark paper
examples.tip: Reverse cito:cites against Liddelow 2017 (W2572710398): every paper in the core that cites the most-cited astrocyte study, newest first.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX cito: <http://purl.org/spar/cito/>
PREFIX dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
PREFIX ex: <http://ex/>
SELECT ?title ?year WHERE { ?citing cito:cites <https://openalex.org/W2572710398> ; dct:title ?title ; ex:year ?year } ORDER BY DESC(?year) LIMIT 50

examples.title: Citation network of the top papers
examples.tip: Draws cito:cites among the most-cited works (citationCount > 1500) - the backbone of the astrocyte literature.

shacl_shapes.title: Papers are well-formed
shacl_shapes.tip: Bibliographic integrity: every Work needs exactly one title, a year, at least one author (a Person) and at least one topic (a Concept). One paper in the set has no author - SHACL catches it.

shacl_shapes.title: Authors are named
shacl_shapes.tip: Every ex:Person (author) should carry a foaf:name. The author list conforms.

shacl_shapes.title: Concepts are named
shacl_shapes.tip: Every ex:Concept (research topic) should carry an rdfs:label.

shacl_shapes.title: Institutions are named
shacl_shapes.tip: Every ex:Institution should carry an rdfs:label.

datasets.label: antarctic-expeditions.rete - Heroic-Age expeditions, crews & ships
datasets.description: Heroic-Age Antarctic exploration as an explorable social graph: 6 landmark expeditions (Discovery, Nimrod, Terra Nova, Endurance, Australasian, Belgian, 1897-1917) linked by ex:participant to ~76 crew, by ex:vessel to their 5 ships, and by ex:leader to their commanders (Scott, Shackleton, Mawson, de Gerlache). Each expedition carries ex:startYear/ex:endYear. Because expeditions share personnel and ships, genuine multi-hop paths exist (shared-crew bridges, leaders who served on earlier voyages). IRIs stay as wikidata.org/entity so nodes round-trip to live Wikidata. CC0. Pairs with the atlas 'Heroic-Age Sites' overlay: the huts and deaths on the map are where these crews lived and died.

examples.title: Shape of the expedition graph
examples.tip: Predicate totals: ex:participant dominates (~76 crew edges), then ex:vessel / ex:leader, plus rdfs:label and ex:startYear/ex:endYear. Shows the 6-expedition / 5-ship / ~76-person skeleton at a glance.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?triples) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY DESC(?triples)

examples.title: The crew of the Endurance
examples.tip: Bound-subject star on Shackleton's Endurance (Q1162294): every ex:participant with their name. Includes Mrs. Chippy, the ship's cat, a genuine P710 participant.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX ex: <http://ex/>
PREFIX wd: <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?person ?name WHERE {
  wd:Q1162294 ex:participant ?person .
  ?person rdfs:label ?name .
} ORDER BY ?name

examples.title: Crew who served on more than one expedition
examples.tip: Self-join through a shared ex:participant: people linked to two different expeditions are the network bridges (men who sailed with both Scott and Shackleton). STR(?e1)<STR(?e2) dedups the pair.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX ex: <http://ex/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?name ?exp1 ?exp2 WHERE {
  ?e1 ex:participant ?p ; rdfs:label ?exp1 .
  ?e2 ex:participant ?p ; rdfs:label ?exp2 .
  FILTER(STR(?e1) < STR(?e2))
  ?p rdfs:label ?name .
} ORDER BY ?name

examples.title: Largest crews
examples.tip: GROUP BY expedition counting ex:participant edges, joined to label and years — ranks the voyages by recorded crew size.

examples.title: Expedition -> leader + ship + crew ego-network
examples.tip: Builds one drawable star around an expedition (Terra Nova, Q973919): its leader, its vessel, its crew, each re-labelled so the renderer shows real names instead of QIDs.

examples.title: Time: expeditions by start year
examples.tip: Switch Output -> Time. The six Heroic-Age expeditions plotted by ex:startYear (1897-1917); hover a cell for the expedition names.

shacl_shapes.title: Expeditions are fully described
shacl_shapes.tip: Structural completeness: every expedition should name a leader (a Person), a vessel (a Ship) and start/end years. SHACL flags 2 expeditions with no recorded leader.

shacl_shapes.title: Every person is named
shacl_shapes.tip: A simpler structural check: every ex:Person carries an rdfs:label. The roster conforms.

shacl_shapes.title: Ships are named
shacl_shapes.tip: Every ex:Ship should carry an rdfs:label.

shacl_shapes.title: Participants are people
shacl_shapes.tip: Every value of ex:participant must be a typed ex:Person.

datasets.label: factgrid-illuminati.rete - Order of the Illuminati prosopography (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The 18th-century secret society as a prosopographical graph from FactGrid (CC0), an independent historical Wikibase: ~1,300 members of the Order of the Illuminati (Q10677) with their FactGrid properties and English labels. Property and object labels are resolved so the opaque P-numbers read in plain language.

examples.title: What's in the graph
examples.tip: Predicate totals: P91 (member of), P2 (instance of) and the other FactGrid properties on each member.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?n) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY DESC(?n) LIMIT 20

examples.title: Members of the Illuminati
examples.tip: Everyone linked by P91 (member of) to the Order of the Illuminati (Q10677).
examples.sparql:
PREFIX wdt: <https://database.factgrid.de/prop/direct/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?name WHERE { ?m wdt:P91 <https://database.factgrid.de/entity/Q10677> ; rdfs:label ?name } ORDER BY ?name LIMIT 200

examples.title: Which properties describe members
examples.tip: Group every fact about the members by predicate and show the FactGrid property label - the schema in plain language.

SELECT ?plabel (COUNT(*) AS ?n) WHERE { ?m wdt:P91 <https://database.factgrid.de/entity/Q10677> . ?m ?p ?o . OPTIONAL { ?p rdfs:label ?plabel } } GROUP BY ?plabel ORDER BY DESC(?n)

shacl_shapes.title: Every member is named
shacl_shapes.tip: Data quality on an untyped Wikibase graph: every classified member — anything typed as an instance of a class — should carry a readable label. The graph conforms; the labels were resolved at build time.

shacl_shapes.title: Members are named
shacl_shapes.tip: A second target: every entity with a "Member of" link should carry a label, so the network reads in plain language.

shacl_shapes.title: Entities with a recorded gender are named
shacl_shapes.tip: Every entity that records a gender should carry a label.

shacl_shapes.title: People with a career statement are named
shacl_shapes.tip: Every entity that records a career statement (the densest relation) should carry a label.

datasets.label: theographic-graph.rete - biblical narrative graph
datasets.description: Theographic Bible (CC BY-SA) as a narrative/genealogy graph (distinct from the atlas geo-events layer): ~3,000 people linked by tg:father/mother/child/sibling/partner, born/died places, group memberships, and events with participants. Walk genealogies and event chains.

examples.title: What's in the graph
examples.tip: Predicate totals: tg:sibling/child/father kinship, foaf:gender, places with wgs84 coordinates, events.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?n) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY DESC(?n) LIMIT 20

examples.title: Descendants of Abraham

examples.title: Abraham's children
examples.tip: Child edges one hop from Abraham, relabelled to names for the graph view.

shacl_shapes.title: Places are geolocated
shacl_shapes.tip: Geospatial completeness: every Biblical Place should carry a label and lat/long coordinates. SHACL flags 49 places that aren't geolocated.

shacl_shapes.title: Events are dated and located
shacl_shapes.tip: Every theo:Event should carry a year and an occurredIn place — a few events are undated.

datasets.label: monarch.rete - disease/gene/phenotype graph
datasets.description: A bounded slice of the Monarch Initiative biomedical KG (CC-BY): a disease neighbourhood linking genes (biolink:Gene), phenotypes (biolink:has_phenotype), gene-gene interactions (biolink:interacts_with) and taxa, with rdfs:labels and skos:exactMatch cross-references.

examples.title: What's in the graph
examples.tip: Predicate totals across the biolink associations: has_phenotype, interacts_with, in_taxon, plus labels.

examples.title: Phenotypes in the graph

datasets.label: opencitations.rete — OpenCitations Meta: 135.4M scholarly works with their authors and venues (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The complete **OpenCitations Meta v13.1.0** corpus (CC0) as one range-queryable graph — **5,184,588,893 triples (33.4 GB)** covering **135.4 million bibliographic records**: journal articles, book chapters, proceedings papers, datasets, theses and reference entries, each with its title, publication year and date, type, volume/issue/pages, and its venue. Every work sits at its **canonical `https://doi.org/{doi}` IRI** when it has a DOI (else its native `w3id.org/oc/meta/{omid}`), and carries its other identifiers as literals — `oc:pmid`, `oc:openalex`, `oc:issn`, `oc:isbn`, `oc:omid`. **Authorship is reified**, not flattened: a work `oc:hasContributor` an `oc:AgentRole` that carries `oc:agentOrder` (first author, second author …) and `oc:withRole`, and `oc:isHeldBy` an `oc:Agent` with `oc:agentName` and, where OpenCitations knows it, `oc:orcidId` — so you can ask for a person’s papers *in author position*, which a flat creator string cannot answer. Venues are first-class nodes (`oc:partOf`) with their own titles and ISSNs, and publishers hang off `oc:publishedBy`. Because works key by DOI and people by ORCID, this graph **auto-merges** with crossref, datacite, dblp, openaire, zenodo and the 25M-researcher orcid graph — no `owl:sameAs` needed. Ontology `oc:` = `w3id.org/rete/opencitations#` travels inside the file. Built by `data/opencitations/scripts/parquet_to_nt.py` → `rete build --memory-budget-mb` (bounded-RAM external build) from the 14.7 GB Meta Parquet, which is **published beside it** for SQL comparison. **No pyramid at this scale** — keep queries SELECTIVE (one DOI, one ORCID, one venue; each reads a few MB over HTTP range); a whole-corpus aggregate scans 33 GB. CC0.

examples.title: One paper, fully unfolded — venue and every author in order
examples.tip: Authorship is REIFIED here, so every author arrives with the position they hold on the paper (oc:agentOrder) and, where OpenCitations knows it, an ORCID linking to that researcher's record — something a flat creator string cannot express. The seed DOI and each ORCID are clickable. Swap the DOI in VALUES for any of the 135.4M works; keeping one bound subject is what makes this read a few MB instead of scanning 33 GB.

examples.title: Everything one researcher published (by ORCID)
examples.tip: Start from a person, not a paper: bind the ORCID and walk back through the reified role to every work that person holds a contributor role on, with its title, year, type and venue. Swap in any ORCID (they are the same IRIs crossref, datacite, dblp and the 25M-researcher orcid graph use, so this query works unchanged against those files too).

examples.title: A journal's papers, with identifiers you can follow
examples.tip: Venues are first-class nodes here, not strings — so you can pin one and list what it published, each row carrying the DOI (clickable), the PubMed id and the OpenAlex id. That triple of identifiers is what makes this graph a join table for the rest of the scholarly constellation.

examples.title: What kinds of works are in the corpus
examples.tip: A GROUP BY over 135.4M records. Aggregation STREAMS through per-group accumulators, so this holds O(groups) memory — a handful of rows — no matter how many records it scans; it is the query that proved bounded-memory aggregation at billion-triple scale. It still reads a lot of the file over HTTP, so give it a moment.

shacl_shapes.title: Articles carry bibliographic metadata
