shacl_shapes.tip: FRBR/Dublin-Core completeness: every fabio:JournalArticle should carry a title, a date, a creator and a container (dct:isPartOf). The citation neighbourhood conforms.

shacl_shapes.title: Book chapters carry metadata
shacl_shapes.tip: A second FRBR class: every fabio:BookChapter should carry a title and a date.

shacl_shapes.title: Reference entries have a creator
shacl_shapes.tip: Every fabio:ReferenceEntry should record at least one dct:creator.

shacl_shapes.title: Creators are named people
shacl_shapes.tip: Every value of dct:creator should carry a foaf:name.

datasets.label: opencitations-meta — OpenCitations Meta in the OpenCitations Data Model: 147.4M works, their identifiers, venues, pages and ordered authors (one file, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: **OpenCitations Meta** (September 2026, RDF dump v9.2.1, CC0) **exactly as OpenCitations' own RDF states it, in the OpenCitations Data Model (OCDM)**: 5,710,689,940 statements in one file. **147,369,100 bibliographic resources** (`fabio:Expression`, typed `fabio:JournalArticle` 88.4M, `BookChapter`, `Book`, `JournalIssue`, `Journal` and 20 more) with `dcterms:title`, `prism:publicationDate` and `frbr:partOf` up through issue, volume and journal; **541,544,508 agent roles** (`pro:RoleInTime`: `pro:withRole` author / editor / publisher, `pro:isHeldBy`, and `oco:hasNext` for the author order); **390,541,098 agents** (`foaf:Agent`); **251,954,118 identifiers** (`datacite:Identifier` with `datacite:usesIdentifierScheme` and `literal:hasLiteralValue`: DOI, OpenAlex, PMID, PMCID, ISSN, ISBN, ORCID, Crossref member …); **82,546,126 embodiments** with their pages — all at OpenCitations' own IRIs (`https://w3id.org/oc/meta/{br,ar,ra,id,re}/{omid}`), so the OpenCitations Index's citations land on these nodes. **One link is added**: `oc:doiLink` from every resource with a DOI to its `https://doi.org/` IRI (114.6M, the hub's shared DOI rule), so `?work oc:doiLink <https://doi.org/10.…>` finds a work and joins `crossref`, `datacite` and `openaire` by DOI (`orcid` through the iD literals); it is not `owl:sameAs`, because Meta keeps several resources for one DOI. v9.2.1 fixes the references to deleted agent roles and agents of v9.2.0 and merges the 7.4M identifier nodes that repeated a scheme and value. Single-valued properties OpenCitations states more than once on one node (`frbr:partOf` on 573,466 resources, two publication dates on 8,746, …) are kept as stated; Meta's provenance snapshots are counted in the card, not included. **TEXT_INDEX on for full-text search** over the titles, agent and publisher names, dates, pages and volume and issue numbers (`CONTAINS`, `rete search --contains`); identifier values are left out of it and found exactly by their literal or by `oc:doiLink`. **A label index** answers `rete search <prefix>` over every title and agent name. **Start queries from a constant** — a DOI's doi.org IRI, a work or agent IRI, an iD literal: they read a few tiles of the file. Built from the five 7z archives of Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.23059736 by caviri/rete-datasets `opencitations/ocdm_to_nt.py` (scan, plan, emit) → `rete build --strict --memory-budget-mb 12000` (rete 0.4.0 + 8f1a634a: #354, #355), guarded, then re-carded in place by rete 0.4.1 (`rete recard --in-place`); **No pyramid.** CC0 1.0.

examples.title: A work with its authors in order (by DOI)
examples.tip: Authorship is OCDM's: each author is a pro:RoleInTime held by a foaf:Agent, and the order is the oco:hasNext chain — the position is how many roles come before (oco:hasNext*). The query starts from the DOI's doi.org IRI (oc:doiLink, the one link rete adds), so it reads a few tiles; starting from the DOI literal instead makes the engine scan.

examples.title: Every identifier of a work
examples.tip: Identifiers are datacite:Identifier nodes with a scheme and a literal value (literal reification), one node per identifier: DOI, OpenAlex, PMID, PMCID, ISBN …

examples.title: Where a work was published: issue, volume, journal
examples.tip: frbr:partOf+ walks up from the article to its issue, volume and journal; issues and volumes carry their number as fabio:hasSequenceIdentifier.

examples.title: The identifiers of the venues a work is part of
examples.tip: The journal's ISSNs and OpenAlex id, and the issue's own DOI where it has one — every identifier along the frbr:partOf chain.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX datacite: <http://purl.org/spar/datacite/>
PREFIX literal: <http://www.essepuntato.it/2010/06/literalreification/>
PREFIX frbr: <http://purl.org/vocab/frbr/core#>
PREFIX fabio: <http://purl.org/spar/fabio/>
PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
SELECT ?container ?title ?scheme ?value WHERE {
  <https://w3id.org/oc/meta/br/0633052> frbr:partOf+ ?container .
  ?container datacite:hasIdentifier ?id .
  ?id datacite:usesIdentifierScheme ?scheme ; literal:hasLiteralValue ?value .
  OPTIONAL { ?container dcterms:title ?title }
}

examples.title: A work's date, pages and publisher
examples.tip: Pages live on the work's embodiment (frbr:embodiment → fabio:Manifestation, prism:startingPage / endingPage); the publisher is the agent of a pro:publisher role.

examples.title: From a DOI to the Meta resources that carry it
examples.tip: oc:doiLink points from every resource with a DOI to its doi.org IRI — the IRI Crossref, DataCite and OpenAIRE use — so one DOI finds every Meta resource that carries it (Meta keeps duplicates as separate resources).
examples.sparql:
PREFIX oc: <https://w3id.org/rete/opencitations#>
PREFIX pro: <http://purl.org/spar/pro/>
PREFIX oco: <https://w3id.org/oc/ontology/>
SELECT ?work ?roleKind (COUNT(?role) AS ?roles) WHERE {
  ?work oc:doiLink <https://doi.org/10.17640/kswst.2016.24.6.137> ; pro:isDocumentContextFor ?role .
  ?role pro:withRole ?roleKind .
} GROUP BY ?work ?roleKind

examples.title: Everything one researcher is credited with (by ORCID iD)
examples.tip: From the iD literal to the identifier node, the agent that holds it, its roles and their works. OpenCitations disambiguates people only through such identifiers.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX datacite: <http://purl.org/spar/datacite/>
PREFIX literal: <http://www.essepuntato.it/2010/06/literalreification/>
PREFIX pro: <http://purl.org/spar/pro/>
PREFIX oco: <https://w3id.org/oc/ontology/>
PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
PREFIX prism: <http://prismstandard.org/namespaces/basic/2.0/>
SELECT ?work ?title ?date ?kind WHERE {
  ?id literal:hasLiteralValue "0000-0002-3134-4207" .
  ?agent datacite:hasIdentifier ?id .
  ?role pro:isHeldBy ?agent ; pro:withRole ?kind .
  ?work pro:isDocumentContextFor ?role ; dcterms:title ?title .
  OPTIONAL { ?work prism:publicationDate ?date }
} ORDER BY DESC(?date) LIMIT 25

datasets.label: opencitations-index — The OpenCitations Index in the OpenCitations Data Model: 2.56 billion citations between OpenCitations Meta works (one file, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: **The OpenCitations Index** (Index CSV v8, 2026-09-08, with the source-info dump v7) **exactly as OpenCitations' own RDF states it, in the OpenCitations Data Model (OCDM)**: 2,556,381,540 citations and 15,821,719,427 statements in one file. Every citation is a `cito:Citation` at OpenCitations' IRI `https://w3id.org/oc/index/ci/{oci}` (the OCI is `<citing omid>-<cited omid>`), with `cito:hasCitingEntity` and `cito:hasCitedEntity`; `cito:hasCitationCreationDate` (2,526,739,654, typed `xsd:date`, `xsd:gYearMonth` or `xsd:gYear` by the value's shape, as OpenCitations' RDF does); `cito:hasCitationTimeSpan` (2,265,317,543, `xsd:duration`); the types `cito:JournalSelfCitation` (113,835,813) and `cito:AuthorSelfCitation` (64,057,568); and `prov:atLocation`, the source collections that state the citation (3,182,624,229: COCI 2,038,872,184, POCI 655,257,417, DOCI 279,990,075, MOCI 190,730,689, OROCI 14,181,370, OUTOCI 3,124,572, JOCI 467,821, CROCI 101). **The works are OpenCitations Meta's own `br` IRIs** `https://w3id.org/oc/meta/br/{omid}`, the same nodes as the `opencitations-meta` dataset, so a citation's citing and cited works resolve there with no mapping, and Meta's `oc:doiLink` leads on to a work's doi.org IRI, where `crossref`, `datacite` and `openaire` meet. The Index has no titles or authors of its own: get them from `opencitations-meta`. **One difference from OpenCitations' N-Triples dump, on purpose:** negative time spans that combine days with years or months (`-P6Y7M30D`, `-P4M7D`; 1,473,978) are kept, which their N-Triples writer drops. Duplicate source statements are collapsed and counted, never dropped silently; 397,634 citations are of a work by itself, kept as stated. Provenance (when and from what each citation was created) is not included. No full-text index, no label index, no pyramid. **Start queries from a constant**: a citation's OCI IRI, or a work's `br` IRI as citing or cited entity, read a few tiles of the file; a count or scan over all 2.56 billion citations does not belong over HTTP range. **CC0 1.0**, as the Index is. Format 0x06, built with rete 0.5.3 from the Index CSV (figshare 10.6084/m9.figshare.24356626.v8) and the source-info dump (10.6084/m9.figshare.24427051.v7).

examples.title: The citing and cited work of one citation
examples.tip: A citation is a cito:Citation at OpenCitations' IRI https://w3id.org/oc/index/ci/{oci}, and the OCI is <citing omid>-<cited omid>. The two works are OpenCitations Meta br IRIs, the same nodes as in the opencitations-meta dataset: look them up there for title, authors, venue and identifiers.

examples.title: One citation by its OCI: everything OpenCitations states about it
examples.tip: The citing and cited entities, the creation date (typed xsd:date, gYearMonth or gYear by its shape, as OpenCitations' RDF does), the time span (xsd:duration), the self-citation types and the source collections (prov:atLocation: COCI, DOCI, MOCI, OROCI ...) that state it. A constant subject reads a few tiles.

examples.title: A work's reference list: the works it cites (by Meta OMID)
examples.tip: Outgoing citations of one work, from its OpenCitations Meta OMID IRI. The creation date is the citing work's publication date; the time span runs from the cited to the citing work's publication. Resolve a cited work's metadata in opencitations-meta.

examples.title: Who cites a work (incoming citations)
examples.tip: The citations that name one work as cited entity. Start from the work's OMID IRI: the query reads a few tiles. A work cited very often has many rows, so add LIMIT, as in the next example.

examples.title: Ten works citing a heavily cited work (LIMIT 10)
examples.tip: br/06104029082 is among the most cited works in the Index (over 160,000 incoming citations, per the card's hub list). LIMIT 10 stops after the first tiles; without it the query returns every citing work.

examples.title: Where a work's citations come from: the source collections
examples.tip: prov:atLocation names the Index collection that states a citation: COCI (Crossref), POCI (PubMed), DOCI (DataCite), MOCI (merged), OROCI (OpenAIRE) and others. A citation found by several sources has several, so the counts add up to more than the number of citations.

examples.title: A work's self-citations: shared journal or shared author
examples.tip: OpenCitations types a citation cito:JournalSelfCitation when citing and cited works are in the same journal, and cito:AuthorSelfCitation when they share an author.

examples.title: A work's citation counts: made, received, self-citations
examples.tip: References made, citations received, and the work's journal and author self-citations, in one query of four UNION branches, each starting from the work's OMID IRI.

datasets.label: nanopubs.rete — Nanopublications 2018: 10.8M nanopublications as 43.2M named graphs (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: **10,803,231 nanopublications**, as the Zenodo dump *Nanopublication dump from server network* (Tobias Kuhn, VU Amsterdam, version 20180405) states them: every nanopublication the decentralised server network held on 2018-04-05, as **378,654,287 quads in 43,212,923 named graphs**. Each nanopublication is four named graphs — head, assertion, provenance and publication info — linked by the `np:` vocabulary (`np:hasAssertion`, `np:hasProvenance`, `np:hasPublicationInfo`), so the graph a triple sits in says which nanopublication it belongs to. The default graph is empty. A mix of many sources (BEL Framework, Bio2RDF DrugBank, WikiPathways …), not one schema. Statements, graph names and IRIs are the dump's own. Use `GRAPH` patterns and start from a graph or a constant: a count or a scan over all 10.8M nanopublications takes minutes over HTTP range (the full count took over ten minutes on a home line). No full-text index, no label index. **CC BY-NC-SA 4.0** (non-commercial, share-alike): Kuhn, T. (2018), DOI 10.5281/zenodo.1213293; this `.rete` is an adaptation of the dump (format and card only) under the same licence. Format 0x06, built with rete 0.5.3; its directories rewritten into 16 KiB leaves by rete 0.5.6 `rete convert` (data, card and build record unchanged).
datasets.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (Tobias Kuhn, VU Amsterdam; share-alike, non-commercial)

examples.title: The four graphs of one nanopublication
examples.tip: The head graph links the nanopublication to its assertion, provenance and publication-info graphs with np:hasAssertion, np:hasProvenance and np:hasPublicationInfo. Counting every head graph in the file takes minutes remotely, so start from one.

examples.title: One nanopublication's assertion
examples.tip: From the head graph, np:hasAssertion names the assertion graph; the second GRAPH pattern then reads it. Both graphs are bound by the join, so a few tiles are read.

examples.title: Where the assertion comes from (its provenance)
examples.tip: np:hasProvenance names the provenance graph; prov:hadPrimarySource there is the source of the claim.

examples.title: Who published it, and when (publication info)
examples.tip: np:hasPublicationInfo names the publication-info graph, which carries pav:createdBy and dcterms:created.

examples.title: Some nanopublications by one person (by ORCID)
examples.tip: The publication-info graphs that name an ORCID as creator; ORCID IRIs in the dump are written http://orcid.org/…. LIMIT keeps it to a few tiles. Adding ORDER BY or COUNT reads every nanopublication of that person (millions for this one) and takes over ten minutes remotely.

datasets.label: orkg.rete - research contributions (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: A slice of the Open Research Knowledge Graph (CC-BY): papers (orkg:Paper) and their structured contributions (orkg:Contribution), research problems, methods and results, with rdfs:labels - scholarly knowledge as data, not prose.

examples.title: What's in the graph
examples.tip: Predicate totals across the ORKG model: papers, contributions, hasAuthors and the Pxx contribution properties.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?n) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY DESC(?n) LIMIT 20

examples.title: Papers
examples.tip: Everything typed as an ORKG Paper, with its title.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?title WHERE { ?p a <https://orkg.org/class/Paper> ; rdfs:label ?title } ORDER BY ?title LIMIT 100

examples.title: Node types in the graph
examples.tip: Count subjects per rdf:type - papers vs contributions vs lists vs problems.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?type (COUNT(?s) AS ?n) WHERE { ?s a ?type } GROUP BY ?type ORDER BY DESC(?n) LIMIT 20

shacl_shapes.title: Papers list their authors
shacl_shapes.tip: Scholarly metadata: every orkg:Paper should be labelled and list its authors (orkgp:hasAuthors). Four papers have no authors recorded - SHACL flags them.

shacl_shapes.title: Authors are named
shacl_shapes.tip: Every orkg:Author should carry an rdfs:label — the names behind the contributions.

shacl_shapes.title: Contributions are labelled
shacl_shapes.tip: Every orkg:Contribution should carry an rdfs:label.

shacl_shapes.title: Venues are labelled
shacl_shapes.tip: Every orkg:Venue should carry an rdfs:label.

datasets.label: ohm-full.rete - all of OpenHistoricalMap (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The ENTIRE current OpenHistoricalMap planet (daily snapshot, 2026-06-14) as one range-queried .rete: 1,021,295 named + dated + geolocated historical features (~6.1M triples, 150 MB), queried lazily over HTTP - only the dictionary chunks and index tiles each query touches are fetched, never the whole file. Each feature is openhistoricalmap.org/{node,way,relation}/<id> with rdfs:label, ex:startYear/ex:endYear (signed integers, -10000..2100; 2100 = still present) and GeoSPARQL geometry (176k points, 690k lines, 155k polygons; admin boundaries assembled from multipolygon/boundary relations, simplified to ~50 m). Built from planet.openhistoricalmap.org with PyOsmium (scripts/fetch_ohm_planet.sh). CC0 1.0 - credit OpenHistoricalMap contributors. Pick selective shapes (a bound subject, a name, a point-in-polygon) for snappy lazy reads.

examples.title: Map: British Empire across the centuries
examples.tip: Switch Output -> Map. 315 boundary snapshots of the British Empire, bound by rdfs:label so it is a fast object-index lookup (a few range reads, not a scan). The overlapping polygons trace its territorial extent over time; hover a shape for its start year.

examples.title: Time: British Empire boundary snapshots
examples.tip: Switch Output -> Time. When the empire's mapped extent was recorded - a multi-year heatmap of boundary snapshots per start year (from 1707). Bound by label, so it stays selective in lazy mode.

examples.title: Map: empires compared
examples.tip: Switch Output -> Map. Four historical empires' boundaries on one world map - VALUES binds the labels so each is a selective lookup, never a scan. Hover a polygon for its empire.

examples.title: Empires as map thumbnails (table)
examples.tip: The SAME four empires, but as a TABLE - the ?w geometry column renders a per-row mini-map, so each empire's boundary draws in its own little square with lat-lon ticks on the borders. (The Map view above overlays them all on one basemap; this shows them side by side.) Auto-detects the geo:wktLiteral, or set a column's type dropdown to Map to force it.

examples.title: Who ruled here? (point-in-polygon + time)
examples.tip: A point (Berlin, 13.405 52.52) tested against every feature's polygon and filtered to the year 1900 returns the nested jurisdictions of that place and time: the city, the German Empire (Deutsches Reich) and the Kingdom of Prussia. Note: with no spatial index this scans geometry, so on the 150 MB planet it is slow in lazy mode - the bound-label examples above stay snappy.

examples.title: Find a place by name
examples.tip: A bound object on rdfs:label routes to just the tiles holding that name - a few range reads of a 150 MB file. Abdera is an ancient Greek colony on the Thracian coast.

examples.title: All facts about one feature
examples.tip: A bound subject is the most selective shape - minimal bytes fetched. This is the OHM node for Abdera; the IRI round-trips to openhistoricalmap.org.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p ?o WHERE { <https://www.openhistoricalmap.org/node/2095928201> ?p ?o }

examples.title: How many features predate the Common Era?
examples.tip: Counts features whose start year is negative (BCE) - 2,057. An aggregate scans the whole ex:startYear predicate, so it fetches more tiles than the selective examples above.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX ex: <http://ex/>
SELECT (COUNT(*) AS ?n) WHERE { ?x ex:startYear ?s . FILTER(?s < 0) }

examples.title: The oldest things on the map
examples.tip: Order every feature by its start year, oldest first - deep-BCE sites (down to the -10000 clamp): ancient settlements, megaliths and prehistoric landmarks.

shacl_shapes.title: Map features are named + dated
shacl_shapes.tip: Run after Cache remote (SHACL materializes ~150 MB in memory). Every geolocated feature (a subject of geo:hasGeometry) should carry a name (rdfs:label) and a start year (ex:startYear). Flags map features that are undated or unnamed.

shacl_shapes.title: Features carry an end year
shacl_shapes.tip: Run after Cache remote. Every geolocated feature should also carry an ex:endYear (2100 = still present); some are missing it.

shacl_shapes.title: Geometries are WKT literals
shacl_shapes.tip: Run after Cache remote. Every feature geometry should carry a geo:asWKT serialization.

shacl_shapes.title: Dated features carry both years
shacl_shapes.tip: Run after Cache remote. Every feature with a start year should also carry an end year (2100 = still present).

datasets.label: wikidata-100MB.rete - a real 100 MB Wikidata slice (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: A real ~104 MB slice of Wikidata, range-queried directly from Cloudflare R2 - the browser fetches only the dictionary chunks and index tiles each query touches (a typical selective query reads ~10 MB of the 104 MB), never the whole file. People (wd:Q5 humans) carry rdfs:label (multilingual), occupation (wdt:P106 -> e.g. physicist Q169470, philosopher Q4964182, writer Q36180, politician Q82955), date of birth (wdt:P569), place of birth (wdt:P19), citizenship (wdt:P27) and 'influenced by' (wdt:P737). Entity/property IRIs stay as wikidata.org/{entity,prop/direct}/* so nodes round-trip to live Wikidata. Pick SELECTIVE shapes (a bound subject/object, an occupation intersection) for snappy reads; aggregates over a whole predicate scan more. CC0 (Wikidata). The 1 GB version (key: wikidata) is the same idea at 10x the data.

examples.title: Physicists who are also philosophers
examples.tip: An occupation intersection (wdt:P106 twice). Selective - the lazy reader faults in ~10 MB of the 104 MB file and returns scientist-philosophers like Ilya Prigogine and Marin Mersenne.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/>
PREFIX wd: <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?p ?who WHERE {
  ?p wdt:P106 wd:Q169470 ;   # physicist
     wdt:P106 wd:Q4964182 ;  # philosopher
     rdfs:label ?who .
  FILTER(LANG(?who) = "en")
} LIMIT 50

examples.title: People influenced by Plato
examples.tip: Bound-object star: everyone whose 'influenced by' (wdt:P737) points at Plato (wd:Q859). A bound term = a selective lazy read.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/>
PREFIX wd: <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?p ?who WHERE {
  ?p wdt:P737 wd:Q859 ;   # influenced by Plato
     rdfs:label ?who .
  FILTER(LANG(?who) = "en")
} LIMIT 100

examples.title: Lines of influence from Plato (transitive)
examples.tip: wdt:P737+ walks the 'influenced by' chain transitively from Plato (wd:Q859) - intellectual lineage across generations. LIMIT keeps the lazy walk bounded.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/>
PREFIX wd: <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT DISTINCT ?p ?who WHERE {
  ?p wdt:P737+ wd:Q859 .
  ?p rdfs:label ?who . FILTER(LANG(?who) = "en")
} LIMIT 150

examples.title: Writers who are also politicians
examples.tip: Another occupation intersection (wdt:P106 writer + politician) - novelists and poets who also held office.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/>
PREFIX wd: <http://www.wikidata.org/entity/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?p ?who WHERE {
  ?p wdt:P106 wd:Q36180 ;   # writer
     wdt:P106 wd:Q82955 ;   # politician
     rdfs:label ?who .
  FILTER(LANG(?who) = "en")
} LIMIT 50

examples.title: Most common occupations
examples.tip: Counts people per occupation (wdt:P106), with an OPTIONAL rdfs:label join so each row reads as a Q-id plus its English name rather than a bare code. Aggregating over a WHOLE predicate faults in more tiles than a selective query - heavier, but still streamed lazily, not a full download.

examples.title: People with occupation + birth date
examples.tip: CONSTRUCT a small subgraph of (person)->occupation and (person)->birth-date edges; touches only those two predicates' tiles.

shacl_shapes.title: People with a job have a birth date
shacl_shapes.tip: Run after Cache remote (SHACL materializes ~104 MB in memory). Every person with an occupation should carry a label and a date of birth. Real Wikidata is incomplete, so expect violations — people missing a birth date.

shacl_shapes.title: People with a job have a citizenship
shacl_shapes.tip: Run after Cache remote. Every person with an occupation should record a country of citizenship. Real Wikidata is incomplete, so expect violations.

shacl_shapes.title: People with a job have a place of birth
shacl_shapes.tip: Run after Cache remote. Every person with an occupation should record a place of birth. Real Wikidata is incomplete, so expect violations.

shacl_shapes.title: People with a birthplace are labelled
shacl_shapes.tip: Run after Cache remote. Every person who records a place of birth should also carry a label.

datasets.label: wikidata-xxl - 600M-triple Wikidata as 6 federated .rete shards (ONE logical graph, sharded)
datasets.description: The SHARDED-RETE model at scale: one logical Wikidata graph too big to build as a single file, split into 6 INDEPENDENT --no-pyramid .rete shards (100M triples / ~906 MB each, ~5.4 GB total) that the playground AUTO-FEDERATES — every query fans across all 6 shards (UNION) and the rows merge, so you query it like one dataset. A genuine cross-section of the Wikidata truthy dump (people, places, works, taxa, properties) streamed partition-by-partition from the piebro/wikidata-extraction Parquet (DuckDB httpfs, no full download) and built shard-by-shard with bounded RAM/disk (stream → rete build --no-pyramid → drop the 10 GB N-Triples → next). Each entity carries multilingual rdfs:label / skos:prefLabel / schema:name + schema:description, rdf:type / wdt:P31, and truthy wdt:* statements (occupation P106, etc.); IRIs stay wikidata.org/{entity,prop/direct}/* so nodes round-trip to live Wikidata. This proves the .rete format + client-side federation scale to a dataset BIGGER THAN ANY SINGLE FILE — the path to full Wikidata (~80 shards, ~80 GB) is just more shards. Datatypes are heuristic (typed dateTime + WKT; numbers plain) since WDQS rate-limits the property-datatype map. The fed bar shows '⛓ 6 shards'. Built by scripts/build_wikidata_xxl.sh. CC0 (Wikidata).

examples.title: ★ Entities across all 6 shards
examples.tip: This dataset is ONE logical graph split across 6 independent .rete shards (100M triples each). The query FANS ACROSS all 6 (UNION) and the rows merge — watch the banner say 'federated 6 sources'. HEAVY: it queries 6 remote ~900 MB R2 objects, so a fan-out can still take a minute. The architecture, not the speed, is the point: a dataset bigger than any single file, queried as one.

examples.title: People and their occupation
examples.tip: wdt:P106 = occupation. A star query (same subject), so every shard answers for its own people and the 6 partial results merge. ?occ is the occupation entity's QID — turn on the Labels toggle (or federate a label lookup) to read it.

examples.title: Search every shard's labels for a word
examples.tip: A FILTER(CONTAINS) over the English labels — whichever shards hold matching entities contribute rows. Change "observatory" to anything. Each shard does its own scan in parallel; the matches are unioned.

examples.title: Instance-of statements (P31)
examples.tip: Raw wdt:P31 (instance-of) edges drawn from across the 6 shards — 945k+ in the first shard alone. The Labels toggle decodes the class QID (e.g. Q5 = human). The selective sharded read: each shard faults in only the P31 tiles it needs.

datasets.label: deps.dev — the cross-ecosystem software dependency graph (2.55B triples, 8 federated shards)
datasets.description: Google's deps.dev (Open Source Insights) as a queryable knowledge graph: the version-pinned dependency AND dependents network of SEVEN package ecosystems — npm, PyPI, Maven, Go, Cargo, NuGet, RubyGems — 2,555,320,067 triples over 8 auto-federated .rete shards (one logical graph; the playground UNIONs every query across all shards). Every package version is a node at https://deps.dev/<system>/<name>/<version> carrying its licenses (SPDX IRIs), advisories, SLSA provenance and registry links, with deps:purl (pkg:npm/lodash@4.17.21) as the cross-registry / cross-dataset join key. deps:dependsOn is the resolved, version-pinned direct edge (570M+ of them); DEPENDENTS come free as the reverse traversal, so 'what depends on X@v?' is just ?x deps:dependsOn <X@v>. Also source projects (deps:Project — GitHub/GitLab stars, forks, OSS-Fuzz) linked by deps:hasProject, and security advisories (deps:Advisory — GHSA/OSV, CVSS, CVE aliases). npm is the giant, split into 2 shards by package-name hash; projects/advisories live in the first shard of each ecosystem. Model is a small deps: ontology reusing schema.org + Dublin Core + SPDX. Built from the deps.dev BigQuery public dataset (snapshot 2026-07-13) via a DuckDB→N-Triples streaming converter piped into rete build --memory-budget-mb external builds (bounded RAM, gzip-streamed to fit disk). CC-BY 4.0 (Google).

examples.title: ★ Dependencies of a project via its GitHub repo (gimie)
examples.tip: The cross-store payoff: from a GitHub repo to the resolved, version-pinned dependencies of the package built from it. deps:hasProject links the package version to <github.com/sdsc-ordes/gimie>, deps:dependsOn to each dependency. gimie is a PyPI package (SDSC/ORDES research-software metadata tool), so this resolves in the PyPI shard — swap the repo for any project.

examples.title: Who depends on npm lodash@4.17.21 (dependents)
examples.tip: Dependents = deps:dependsOn read BACKWARD — no separate table needed. Every version that directly depends on lodash@4.17.21, addressed by its constant deps.dev IRI, so each shard contributes its own dependers and the rows UNION across the fan-out. lodash's dependers span both npm shards.

examples.title: Most-depended-upon Rust crates
examples.tip: Cargo lives in ONE shard, so this COUNT is exact (a GROUP BY fanned across shards gives per-shard partials, not a global sum — a federation limit). serde / serde_json / thiserror / tokio top it — the Rust ecosystem's foundations, ranked by how many crate versions depend on them.

examples.title: Critical security advisories (CVSS ≥ 9)
examples.tip:
deps:Advisory nodes (GHSA / OSV) are self-contained in each ecosystem shard, so this needs no cross-shard join — every shard returns its advisories and they UNION. deps:hasAdvisory on a package version links vulnerable versions to them.
CRITICAL is read off the SCORE, not the severity string: deps:severity is the literal "UNKNOWN" on every advisory in every published shard (222,422 in npm-0, 23,795 in pypi, 6,691 in maven, 2,585 in cargo — no other value exists), so the FILTER(?severity = "CRITICAL") this example used to carry could never match and it shipped an empty answer (#212). CVSS v3 ≥ 9.0 IS the critical band, and deps:cvss3Score is populated on about half of them.

examples.title: A version and its source project's stars / forks
examples.tip: Join a package version (PyPI requests@2.31.0) to its source Project — deps:hasProject → the GitHub repo carrying deps:starsCount / deps:forksCount. Version and project sit in the same shard (PyPI), so this intra-shard join resolves cleanly.

datasets.label: chemotion.rete - the Chemotion chemistry-ELN knowledge graph (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The real Chemotion Electronic-Lab-Notebook knowledge graph (FIZ Karlsruhe, 2025) merged with the two ontologies the ELN annotates with - CHMO (Chemical Methods Ontology) and RXNO (Name Reaction Ontology). 1.53M triples queried lazily over HTTP range: 87.7k instances (20.7k datasets, 20.6k studies/processes typed obo:BFO_0000015, 3.7k molecules obo:CHEBI_23367, 4.9k substances obo:CHEBI_59999, 250 creators) aligned to BFO / NFDICore / ChEBI, plus the full CHMO method taxonomy (colorimetry, amperometry, NMR/MS/IR/Raman spectroscopy ...) and RXNO reaction types as an rdfs:subClassOf DAG. Molecules carry SMILES / InChI / InChIKey / chebi:formula. Built from github.com/ISE-FIZKarlsruhe/chemotion-kg (239 MB TTL) + purl.obolibrary.org/obo/{chmo,rxno}.owl with rete build --card. CC BY 4.0. Pick selective shapes (a bound class, a formula, a subClassOf path) for snappy lazy reads; whole-predicate aggregates scan more.

examples.title: What's in the graph (predicate totals)
examples.tip: The shape of the Chemotion KG in one scan: obo:BFO_0000178 (has-part) dominates at ~960k edges, then rdf:type, the NFDICore dataset/study properties and the ChEBI/CHMO annotation predicates. Summary-answerable - try the Progressive strategy to read it from the pyramid alone.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?triples) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY DESC(?triples) LIMIT 25

examples.title: How many of each thing
examples.tip: Instance counts per rdf:type: 20.7k datasets, 20.6k studies (obo:BFO_0000015 'process'), 4.9k substances (CHEBI_59999), 3.7k molecules (CHEBI_23367), 250 creators - plus the owl:Class / owl:Axiom rows from the merged CHMO + RXNO ontologies.

examples.title: Molecules with their structure
examples.tip: The 3,746 molecular entities (obo:CHEBI_23367) carry real cheminformatics - name, molecular formula and SMILES (InChI / InChIKey too). A bound class keeps this a selective tile read.

examples.title: Most common molecular formulas
examples.tip: Group the molecules by molecular formula - the recurring C/H/N/O skeletons in this lab's compound collection (isomers share a formula).

examples.title: CHMO analytical methods
examples.tip: The Chemical Methods Ontology the ELN annotates analyses with: ~3,000 method classes (colorimetry, amperometry, NMR / MS / IR / Raman spectroscopy, chromatography ...) merged in as owl:Class with rdfs:label.

examples.title: Every subtype of spectroscopy
examples.tip: A transitive rdfs:subClassOf+ walk down from CHMO_0000228 (spectroscopy) - acoustic emission, alpha-particle, electronic spectroscopy and dozens more. This deep method DAG is what powers the Schema pyramid and Reach.

examples.title: A molecule's chemistry card
examples.tip: Switch Output -> Graph. CONSTRUCT a small star around molecules - each linked to its formula, SMILES and InChIKey - drawable as node-link cards.

examples.title: Federation: resolve terms across chemotion + ChEBI
examples.tip: Federation is a kind of SPARQL. This pre-loads chebi-full (the entire ChEBI ontology, 8.83M triples) as a second source - see the Sources strip. The same query resolves five terms across BOTH files: chemotion answers the CHMO method + BFO process labels, chebi-full answers the CHEBI chemical labels - no single file has all five. Run it and the result merges both, with a per-source byte/row breakdown. Both are remote-lazy, so each answers over HTTP range; remove the chip to query chemotion alone.

shacl_shapes.title: Molecules carry a structure
shacl_shapes.tip: Data quality over the merged graph: every molecule should declare a SMILES and an InChIKey structure. SHACL materializes the data graph, so run it after Cache remote (it needs the dataset in memory).

shacl_shapes.title: Substances are named
shacl_shapes.tip: Run after Cache remote. A second class: every substance (a chemical mixture) should carry a name.

shacl_shapes.title: Molecules carry a formula
shacl_shapes.tip: Run after Cache remote. Every molecule should declare a molecular formula.

shacl_shapes.title: Molecules carry an InChI
shacl_shapes.tip: Run after Cache remote. Every molecule should declare an InChI structure string.

datasets.label: chebi-full.rete - the complete ChEBI chemical ontology (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The ENTIRE ChEBI ontology (Chemical Entities of Biological Interest, EMBL-EBI) as one range-queried .rete: 8.83M triples over ~205k chemical classes, their rdfs:subClassOf classification DAG (380k edges), textual definitions (obo:IAO_0000115), exact/related synonyms, ~900k database cross-references (as reified owl:Axiom annotations), and the structural data chemistry needs - molecular formula, charge, average & monoisotopic mass, InChI, InChIKey and SMILES, all under the ChemROF vocabulary (chemrof: https://w3id.org/chemrof/). Queried lazily over HTTP range: the browser fetches only the dictionary chunks and index tiles each query touches, never the 164.8 MB whole. CC BY 4.0 (EMBL-EBI). It shares its CHEBI_* class IRIs and rdfs:label / rdfs:subClassOf structure with the chemotion dataset, so the two FEDERATE: pick chebi-full, add chemotion as a second source (the 'Federation' example does this for you), and one SPARQL query resolves terms across both ontologies. Lossless Parquet / DuckDB / SQLite table companions sit beside it in the bucket. Pick selective shapes (a bound molecule, a formula, a subClassOf path) for snappy lazy reads; whole-predicate aggregates scan more.

examples.title: What's in the ontology (predicate totals)
examples.tip: The shape of all of ChEBI in one scan: rdf:type leads (1.2M, mostly the owl:Axiom cross-reference reification), then oboInOwl xrefs/synonyms, rdfs:subClassOf (380k classification edges), rdfs:label (205k), and the ChemROF structural predicates (formula, charge, mass, SMILES, InChI). Summary-answerable - try the Progressive strategy to read it from the pyramid alone.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?n) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY DESC(?n) LIMIT 25

examples.title: Caffeine's full chemistry card
examples.tip: A bound molecule (obo:CHEBI_27732 = caffeine) returns its name plus the ChemROF structural data ChEBI carries: molecular formula, average mass, SMILES and InChIKey. A bound subject keeps this a selective tile read.

examples.title: How caffeine is classified (ancestors)
examples.tip: A transitive rdfs:subClassOf+ walk UP from caffeine, joined to labels: trimethylxanthine -> purine alkaloid -> ... -> molecular entity. The named ancestors are ChEBI's full classification of one compound (the blank-node restriction parents are filtered out by the label join).

examples.title: Every subtype of alkaloid
examples.tip: A transitive rdfs:subClassOf+ walk DOWN from obo:CHEBI_22315 (alkaloid, 461 direct subclasses): the whole alkaloid sub-tree by name. This deep subClassOf DAG is what powers the Schema pyramid and Reach.

examples.title: Most common molecular formulas
examples.tip: Group all ChEBI entities by ChemROF molecular formula - the recurring C/H/N/O skeletons across the whole ontology (isomers share a formula). A whole-predicate scan over ~195k formula values, so it reads more than a bound query.

examples.title: An amino acid's definition + synonyms
examples.tip: ChEBI's human-readable layer: the textual definition (obo:IAO_0000115) and the exact synonyms of obo:CHEBI_33709 (amino acid). Swap the IRI for any class to read its definition.

examples.title: A molecule's chemistry card (graph)
examples.tip: Switch Output -> Graph. CONSTRUCT a small star around caffeine - linked to its name, formula, SMILES and InChIKey - drawable as a node-link card.

examples.title: Federation: resolve 5 terms across 2 ontologies
examples.tip: Federation is a kind of SPARQL. This example pre-loads chemotion as a second source (see the Sources strip): no single file resolves all five labels - chebi-full answers the CHEBI_* terms, chemotion answers CHMO/BFO. Run it and the result merges both, with a per-source breakdown. Remove the chip to query chebi-full alone.

shacl_shapes.title: Molecules with a SMILES carry a formula + InChIKey
shacl_shapes.tip: Data-completeness over the whole ontology: every ChEBI entity that declares a SMILES should also declare a molecular formula and an InChIKey. SHACL materializes the data graph, so run it after Cache remote (it needs the dataset in memory).

shacl_shapes.title: Every classified entity is named
shacl_shapes.tip: Run after Cache remote. Every subject of rdfs:subClassOf (a class in the DAG) should carry an rdfs:label.

shacl_shapes.title: SMILES-bearing molecules carry an InChI
shacl_shapes.tip: Run after Cache remote. Every entity with a SMILES should also declare an InChI string.

shacl_shapes.title: Classes carry a definition
shacl_shapes.tip: Run after Cache remote. Every class in the subclass hierarchy should carry a textual definition. ChEBI is incomplete, so expect violations.

datasets.label: mirbase.rete - miRBase 22.1, the microRNA reference catalogue (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: miRBase release 22.1 - the reference catalogue of published microRNA sequences - as one range-queryable .rete. 2.74M triples: 38,589 hairpin stem-loops (mb:StemLoop, MI accessions) and 49,168 mature miRNAs (mb:MatureMiRNA, MIMAT accessions) across 286 species, plus 1,983 miRNA families (MIPF), 21,196 host-transcript overlaps, 898 withdrawn accessions and 914 publications linked to PubMed. Genome coordinates come from BOTH of miRBase's distributions and are kept distinguishable by mb:coordinateSource: the 31 curated assembly-stamped GFF3 files (GRCh38, GRCm38, Gallus_gallus-5.0 ...) which cover stem-loops AND matures, and the mirna_chromosome_build table which covers 153 species but stem-loops only. All coordinates are FALDO regions anchored to mb:ReferenceSequence chromosomes, so 'everything on chr17 of GRCh38' is a first-class query. Mature offsets on a precursor are reified as mb:Placement because one mature can sit on several stem-loops at DIFFERENT offsets. Species are NCBITaxon IRIs and entries carry RNAcentral / Rfam / EntrezGene / HGNC / MGI cross-references, so the graph joins the wider biological linked-data world by IRI. Modelled with the rete mb: vocabulary (Sequence Ontology / FALDO / NCBITaxon / dcterms / SKOS / FaBiO); try the OWL toggle to query SO classes through the hierarchy. Public domain.

examples.title: What's in the graph (predicate totals)
examples.tip: The shape of miRBase in one scan. faldo:position leads because every genomic region carries a begin AND an end position node, then dcterms:identifier and rdfs:label across stem-loops/matures/families/species, then the mb:matureFrom / mb:matureTo offset pairs. Summary-answerable — try the Progressive strategy to read it from the pyramid alone.

examples.title: hsa-mir-21 on the genome, from BOTH coordinate sources
examples.tip: miRBase ships genome coordinates twice and they disagree in coverage, so the graph keeps both and tags each region with mb:coordinateSource. The GFF3 row is assembly-stamped (GRCh38) and also covers mature miRNAs; the chromosome-build row covers 153 species but stem-loops only and records no assembly. Here they agree exactly: chr17:59,841,266-59,841,337. Note faldo:reference points at a mb:ReferenceSequence resource, not a bare string, so you follow it to rdfs:label.

examples.title: Why mature offsets are reified (mb:Placement)
examples.tip: The same mature miRNA can be excised from several precursors at DIFFERENT offsets — oan-miR-153-3p sits at 96..117 on oan-mir-153-1 but at 39..60 on oan-mir-153-2. Hanging the offsets off the mature alone would record two contradictory values, so each (mature, stem-loop) pairing gets an mb:Placement node. The offsets are also put directly on the mature, but only when it has exactly one parent.

examples.title: High-confidence human miRNAs and their cross-references
examples.tip: Species are NCBITaxon IRIs, so 'human' is obo:NCBITaxon_9606 — the same node other biological graphs use, no mapping table. mb:highConfidence marks the entries in miRBase's high-confidence subset. rdfs:seeAlso resolves miRBase's link tables through their URL templates into real IRIs: RNAcentral, miRDB, TargetScan, microRNA.org.

examples.title: The let-7 family across every species that has it
examples.tip: let-7 is the classic deeply-conserved microRNA family — first found in C. elegans, present from insects to mammals. mb:family groups stem-loops into miRBase precursor families (MIPF accessions); mb:confidence is miRBase's 0/1/2 score, where >=1 means the entry meets their high-confidence criteria.

examples.title: Which miRNAs sit inside a host gene's intron
examples.tip: miRBase records where a precursor falls relative to host transcripts — exon, intron, 3UTR or 5UTR. Most mammalian miRNAs are intronic, transcribed along with their host gene. The overlap is reified as mb:TranscriptContext so the transcript identity and the overlap kind stay together.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX mb: <https://w3id.org/rete/mirbase#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?stemLoop ?overlap ?transcript WHERE {
  ?h mb:transcriptContext ?c ; rdfs:label ?stemLoop .
  ?c mb:overlapType ?overlap ; mb:transcriptName ?transcript .
  FILTER(?overlap = "intron")
}
LIMIT 50

examples.title: OWL: count via a Sequence Ontology class (turn on 🧠)
examples.tip: Nothing in the data is literally typed obo:SO_0000110, so WITHOUT the OWL toggle this returns 0. Turn on OWL 2 QL entailment and the ontology's mb:StemLoop/mb:MatureMiRNA -> mb:Feature -> SO:0000110 chain answers it: 88,402. Always COUNT(DISTINCT ?s) — the QL rewrite is a UNION and repeats solutions otherwise.

datasets.label: causenet.rete - a causality graph mined from the web (256M triples, typed + full-text, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: CauseNet-Full (Heindorf et al., CIKM 2020): the complete causality graph mined from Wikipedia and ClueWeb12 - 11,609,890 cause->effect relations over 12,186,310 concepts, with full extraction provenance. Each relation keeps every one of its 24,443,421 source records: the exact sentence the cause/effect pair was found in, the dependency path-pattern it was matched by (e.g. '[[cause]]/N -nsubj caused/VBD +dobj [[effect]]/N'), and the Wikipedia page or ClueWeb12 web page it came from. Concepts are cn:Concept nodes (cn: = https://causenet.org/ontology#) carrying rdfs:label; cn:causes is the direct cause->effect edge (transitive - follow it with Reach for causal chains); each relation is reified as a cn:CausalRelation with cn:support (its true source count) and cn:hasSource links to the source records. 256,133,680 triples (6.39 GB), queried lazily over HTTP range - the browser fetches only the dictionary chunks and index tiles each query touches, never the whole file. TEXT_INDEX on for full-text search over its literals - the concept labels and the extracted source sentences - and it is the largest one in the catalog (1.88 GB of word index), so CONTAINS finds a phrase by word lookup instead of scanning 256M triples. CC BY 4.0 (credit Heindorf et al.). Pick SELECTIVE shapes (a bound concept, a bound relation, the evidence for one claim) for snappy lazy reads; whole-graph aggregates scan more. Lossless relations/sources/concepts Parquet/DuckDB/SQLite companions sit beside it in the bucket.

examples.title: What does smoking cause? (effect + evidence)
examples.tip: Everything 'smoking' is claimed to cause, each with cn:support = how many source sentences back the claim, so the best-evidenced effects (cancer, heart disease, death) sort to the top. Two columns: effect + support. Reads the reified cn:CausalRelation, so a bit heavier than the bare-edge version (which was ~57 MB lazy). Swap the IRI for /stress, /obesity, /war.

examples.title: What causes obesity? (cause + evidence)
examples.tip: The reverse direction with evidence: every concept claimed to cause 'obesity', ranked by source count. Columns: cause + support. Swap the effect IRI for /diabetes, /cancer or /depression to mine a different outcome.

examples.title: Best-evidenced causes of cancer
examples.tip: Causes of 'cancer' ranked by how much web evidence backs each claim (cn:support = true source count). Columns: cause + support. Benchmarked lazy cost on the lean file: ~114 MB over HTTP range, ~42 s cold.

examples.title: Causal chain: smoking -> X -> Y
examples.tip: A two-step chain over cn:causes: what smoking causes (column 1), and what each of those in turn causes (column 2) - tracing how one cause cascades. For full transitive closure use the Reach tab on cn:causes; this 2-hop join stays bounded.

examples.title: Effects + evidence sentence (HEAVY, 3 cols)
examples.tip: Three columns - effect, support, and a REAL source sentence CauseNet mined the claim from (cn:hasSource -> cn:sentence). The richest view of a causal claim. HEAVIEST example: 'smoking' has thousands of sources, so it fetches 100s of MB over HTTP range; keep the LIMIT low or pick a narrower cause.

examples.title: Map smoking's effects (graph)
examples.tip: CONSTRUCT a small cause->effect subgraph around 'smoking' for the graph view - the selective bare cn:causes read (~57 MB lazy), rendered as nodes + arrows. Each arrow is a mined causal claim from Wikipedia / ClueWeb12.

shacl_shapes.title: Every causal relation has a cause, an effect and a support count
shacl_shapes.tip: Data-integrity over the reified relations: every cn:CausalRelation must declare exactly one cn:cause and one cn:effect and at least one cn:support. Remote SHACL validates lazily over the shape's targets (range reads) - a broad target class fetches many targets, so give it a moment.

shacl_shapes.title: Every concept is named
shacl_shapes.tip: Every cn:Concept node should carry an rdfs:label (its surface form). Validated lazily over the concept targets via HTTP range.

shacl_shapes.title: Every ClueWeb12 source keeps its sentence and pattern
shacl_shapes.tip: Provenance completeness: every ClueWeb12 source record must keep the sentence it was extracted from and the dependency path-pattern that matched it. Validated lazily over the ClueWeb12 source targets.

datasets.label: jonas.rete - medieval texts & their manuscript witnesses (LostMa-ERC / Jonas)
datasets.description: A knowledge graph of medieval European texts and the manuscripts that transmit them, built from the LostMa-ERC Heurist database derived from Jonas (IRHT-CNRS, the repertory of texts and manuscripts in langue d'oc and d'oil). 234,017 triples over a Heurist record model: 3,738 witnesses (a text attested in a manuscript - with siglum, status, date), 1,128 texts (Lancelot, Tristan, Wolfram's Parzival, the chansons de geste; with language and literary form), 3,153 documents/manuscripts (shelfmark, collection, holding place), 4,253 text parts, 860 physical descriptions, 1,152 places (linked to GeoNames), 575 repositories (linked to VIAF), genres, stories/storyverses, and 71 reconstructed stemmata (openStemmata), over a 4,506-term controlled vocabulary. Every record links back to its live Jonas page via prop:described_at_URL. Queried lazily over HTTP range; the whole file is only ~2 MB, so reads are near-instant. CC0 1.0 (LostMa-ERC; underlying data from Jonas / IRHT-CNRS). Entity IRIs are lostma-erc.github.io/jonas/{id,prop,type,term}/*. This is a curated research subset (the LostMa corpus), not the full ~77k-witness Jonas repertory.

examples.title: What's in the graph (record types)
examples.tip: The shape of the LostMa/Jonas corpus in one scan: 3,738 witnesses, 4,253 text parts, 3,153 manuscripts (documents), 1,152 places, 1,128 texts, plus physical descriptions, repositories, stories, stemmata and a 4,506-term controlled vocabulary. The whole file is ~2 MB, so even this scan is a couple of range reads.

examples.title: Witnesses linking back to their live Jonas page
examples.tip: A URL-ID column: prop:described_at_URL is each witness's permanent link back to the live Jonas repertory (jonas.irht.cnrs.fr/...). It renders as a clickable link - or set the column's type dropdown to Link. Paired with the witness siglum, so every row is a citable handle on the source record.

examples.title: The most-copied medieval texts
examples.tip: Counts the surviving manuscript witnesses per text - the medieval 'bestsellers'. The prose Lancelot leads with 122 witnesses, then Tristan (93), Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival (88) and Willehalm (80), the Roman de Troie, Merlin and the Estoire del Saint Graal. p:is_manifestation_of links each witness to the text it copies.

examples.title: Witnesses of the Lancelot, with their manuscripts
examples.tip: Every manuscript copy of the most-witnessed text, the prose Lancelot: each witness's siglum, the manuscript shelfmark it survives in (p:last_observed_in_doc) and its date. A bound text label keeps it selective - the core philological view, one work seen across all the books that carry it.

examples.title: Texts and the manuscripts that carry them
examples.tip: Walks witness -> text (p:is_manifestation_of) and witness -> manuscript (p:last_observed_in_doc) to show which texts survive in which books, with the witness siglum: the Roman van Limborch, the Roelantslied and the rest, each tied to a shelfmark. The witness IS the join - a text attested in a manuscript.

examples.title: The corpus by language
examples.tip: The LostMa corpus is comparative and multilingual: Old French (fro) 309 texts, Middle High German (gmh) 150, Middle Irish (mga) 92, Middle French (frm) 91, Middle Dutch (dum) 85, Middle English (enm) 81. Each text's language is a controlled-vocabulary term (p:language_term -> skos:prefLabel).

examples.title: Where the manuscripts are held
examples.tip: Follows each manuscript to its holding place (p:location -> the library/place label): the Beinecke, the Leeds Brotherton library and hundreds more. Places carry GeoNames links (owl:sameAs) and repositories carry VIAF, so the books thread out into the linked-data web - switch the place column to Link to follow them.

examples.title: Texts with a reconstructed stemma
examples.tip: The texts whose manuscript tradition has a published stemma codicum (p:in_stemma -> a stemma record with its openStemmata id): Fierabras, Girart de Vienne, Aliscans, Florence de Rome, the Chevalerie Ogier de Danemarche. These genealogies of surviving copies are what LostMa studies to model how texts were lost.

datasets.label: Post Scriptum - Portuguese & Spanish everyday letters, 1500-1800 (CLUL)
datasets.description: Post Scriptum (CLUL, Universidade de Lisboa), via the TEITOK TEI-P5 edition: 3,649 everyday letters in Portuguese & Spanish, 1500-1800 - a historical correspondence network. Each letter (ps:Letter) carries its sender and recipient (ps:sentBy / ps:receivedBy -> 3,265 person nodes), origin & destination places (ps:sentFrom / ps:sentTo), a date (ps:date, reaching back to 1500), language, the modernised body text (full-text indexed for content search), a social/pragmatic classification (ps:letterType: personal / family / friendship / love..., ps:pragmatics: request..., ps:keyword), and foaf:page back to the live TEITOK letter page. Built from the freely-downloadable XML-TEI_P5 bundles (ES/PT x 1500-1800), the TEI source parsed by scripts/postscriptum_to_nt.py. ~63k triples, 5.3 MB, queried lazily over HTTP range. Free (CLUL recognised as author; ELRA licences). Entity IRIs are teitok.clul.ul.pt/postscriptum/{letter,person}/*.

examples.title: Who wrote to whom, and when
examples.tip: The correspondence network: each letter's sender (ps:sentBy) and recipient (ps:receivedBy) resolved to names, with its date - everyday Portuguese & Spanish letters from 1500 onward (Beatriz Carneira -> Francisco de Figueiredo, 1500-06-27). Sort the date column to walk three centuries of private mail.

examples.title: Read a letter online (TEITOK link)
examples.tip: A URL-ID column: foaf:page is each letter's permanent link to its edition on the live TEITOK site - click to read the diplomatic + modernised transcription with manuscript images. Paired with the letter's title (year, sender, recipient). Set the column type to Link if it doesn't auto-detect.

examples.title: Letters by social register
examples.tip: Post Scriptum classifies each letter's relationship (ps:letterType): personal (1,794) dominates, then family (926), friendship (525) and love (270) - the everyday emotional registers of 16th-18th-century correspondence, plus 42 anonymous (denunciations, threats).

examples.title: Search the letters by content
examples.tip: Full-text search over the modernised letter text (a text index backs it). Change the term (here 'amor') to any word to find the letters that use it - the actual language people wrote. Each row is the matching letter's title; add ?text to the SELECT to read the passage.

examples.title: The busiest letter-writers
examples.tip: Rank the 3,265 correspondents by how many surviving letters they sent (ps:sentBy). The network's hubs - writers whose archives preserved many letters (often from Inquisition or judicial cases, which is why the letters survive at all) - rise to the top.

examples.title: What the letters are about (topics)
examples.tip: Post Scriptum tags each letter with keyword terms (ps:keyword) - the recurring themes of everyday early-modern mail. Correspondence itself (448), Family (421), Money (349), Justice (265), Illness (263), Debts (198), Marriage (190): the texture of private life across three centuries. Spanish and Portuguese terms are tagged separately (@es / @pt).

examples.title: Letters by language and century
examples.tip: Each letter's sub-corpus (ps:corpus) encodes language x century: Spanish 1500-1800 (310 / 684 / 938 / 514) and Portuguese 1500-1800 (252 / 430 / 509 / 12). The 17th-18th centuries dominate - when literacy spread and the judicial / Inquisition archives that preserved these letters were most active.

datasets.label: data.bnf.fr - the whole BnF linked open data (716M triples, ONE file)
datasets.description: The COMPLETE data.bnf.fr - the Bibliothèque nationale de France's linked open data (CC0) - as ONE range-queryable .rete (it was 10 federated shards). The official dump's 726,700,333 triples dedup to 673,519,782 unique (matching the BnF's live ~672M store), 194.8M terms, 7.16 GB. Every perimeter in one graph: 4.9M author/person authorities (foaf:Person) with 8.8M owl:sameAs alignments to VIAF / ISNI / IdRef (the authority hub overlapping MMM, Jonas and Biblissima), 2.6M FRBR works, the RAMEAU subject thesaurus, role-typed contributions, places (GeoNames), periodicals, and the 410M-triple modern printed-book catalogue (editions). Carries a types pyramid + planner query_stats, so summary / schema / community queries are answered index-free. Entity IRIs stay as data.bnf.fr/ark:/* so nodes round-trip to the live BnF. Built as a single file with the low-RAM pipeline that made the 726M monolith feasible (it was sharded because the monolith OOM'd a 62 GB host - see dev/low-mem-build.md). Queried lazily over HTTP range: a selective query fetches only the dict chunks and index tiles it touches, never the 7 GB whole; whole-graph aggregates scan more. CC0 1.0 (BnF).

examples.title: Authors and their VIAF / ISNI identity
examples.tip: data.bnf.fr's authority layer: each author (foaf:Person) carries a name and owl:sameAs alignments to VIAF, ISNI and IdRef - the SAME VIAF ids that MMM, Jonas and Biblissima link to, so this is the federation hub for 'who is this author' across every manuscript dataset (8.8M sameAs links). The leading space in some names is BnF's sort form.

examples.title: Authors joined to the works they created
examples.tip: The single-file payoff: a cross-perimeter JOIN the 10 shards could NOT do (federation is union + routing, not term-level joins). Works (dcterms:creator -> an author ARK) join persons (foaf:name) in ONE graph, so 'this author wrote these works' resolves in a single query - no '+ Add source'.

examples.title: RAMEAU subject headings
examples.tip: RAMEAU is the French national subject thesaurus - the controlled vocabulary the BnF indexes everything under. Each heading is a skos:Concept with a prefLabel (and broader/narrower hierarchy in the full graph).

examples.title: What's in the whole BnF (predicate totals)
examples.tip: Predicate totals over the COMPLETE data.bnf.fr - 673.5M unique triples in ONE file (was 10 shards): rdf:type, dcterms:subject (RAMEAU), owl:sameAs (VIAF/ISNI/IdRef), the FRBNF id, titles, contributions, editions. The types pyramid + planner query_stats answer this kind of whole-graph summary index-free.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?n) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY DESC(?n) LIMIT 25

datasets.label: datos.bne.es - the whole Spanish National Library LOD (267M triples, ONE file)
datasets.description: The COMPLETE datos.bne.es - the Biblioteca Nacional de España's linked open data (CC0) - as ONE range-queryable .rete: 267,052,840 triples (the three official RDF dumps merged - autoridades 47M, bibliográficos 208M, materias 6M), 84M terms, 3.4 GB. The Spanish counterpart of data.bnf.fr. Entities at datos.bne.es/resource/* over the BNE's own ontology (datos.bne.es/def/C* classes, P* properties) plus the RDA registry; subjects are SKOS. The authority layer (persons, corporate bodies, works) carries owl:sameAs alignments to VIAF, ISNI, GND, LoC, IdRef, DBpedia AND data.bnf.fr - so it FEDERATES with the databnf dataset: add databnf as a second source ('+ Add source') and one query joins Spanish to French authorities on their shared VIAF / data.bnf.fr ids. Carries a types pyramid + planner query_stats, so summary / schema / community queries are answered index-free. Built as a single file with the low-RAM pipeline (peak ~25.6 GiB); the dump's ~64k malformed lines (IRIs with a stray '>' or a trailing space) were dropped. Entity IRIs stay datos.bne.es/resource/* so nodes round-trip to the live BNE. Queried lazily over HTTP range. CC0 1.0 (BNE).

examples.title: Authorities and their external identities
examples.tip: The BNE authority layer: each authority carries a name (the BNE ontology's P5001) and owl:sameAs links out to VIAF, ISNI, GND, LoC, IdRef, DBpedia and data.bnf.fr - the same authority hubs the French BnF uses, which is why bne + databnf federate. Here, authorities with a VIAF alignment.

examples.title: What's in the BNE by class
examples.tip: Group every resource by its rdf:type - the BNE's own ontology classes (datos.bne.es/def/C* codes: persons, corporate bodies, works/expressions, and the bibliographic manifestations that are the bulk). The types pyramid answers this whole-graph aggregate index-free.

examples.title: BNE authorities that bridge to data.bnf.fr
examples.tip: The Spanish-to-French bridge: BNE authorities whose owl:sameAs points at a data.bnf.fr id (Alfaro -> data.bnf.fr/10000803, etc.). Switch on the databnf dataset with '+ Add source' and these ids resolve in the French graph too.

examples.title: Federation: authority links across BNE + BnF
examples.tip: Federation is a kind of SPARQL. This pre-loads databnf (the whole data.bnf.fr) as a second source - see the Sources strip. The query asks for owl:sameAs->VIAF links, which BOTH graphs answer, so the result is the UNION of the Spanish (bne) and French (databnf) authority alignments to VIAF - the shared hub identifying the same person across both national libraries. (Cross-source term JOINS are a future feature; this is union + predicate routing.) Remove the databnf chip to query the BNE alone.

examples.title: A profile from the RDA layer (Cervantes)
examples.tip: datos.bne.es describes persons with RDA Elements (www.rdaregistry.info/Elements/a/P501xx): their professions (P50104), birthplace (P50119) and the period they worked in (P50101). Here, everything the RDA layer records for Cervantes - dramatist / novelist / poet / soldier, born in Alcala de Henares, of the Siglo de Oro. Change the name in P5001 to any BNE authority (a bound subject = a selective, fast read).

examples.title: An author's links out (Wikipedia, VIAF, DBpedia)
examples.tip: A URL-ID column: the BNE links each authority to the wider web - rdfs:seeAlso to Wikipedia, owl:sameAs to VIAF, DBpedia, GND, the Library of Congress, IdRef and data.bnf.fr. Here, all of Cervantes's outbound links (they render as clickable cells - set the column type to Link if needed). This is the federation hub: the same ids bne, databnf and Biblissima share to mean the same person.

datasets.label: Biblissima+ - medieval written heritage (full Wikibase, ONE file)
datasets.description: Biblissima+, the French aggregator of medieval & early-modern written heritage, as ONE range-queryable .rete (it was 3 federated shards): 254,203,131 triples over 867,838 Wikibase entities - manuscripts, works, persons, places, printed editions, iconography - harvested from its open per-entity RDF export (Special:EntityData; Biblissima has no bulk dump and its SPARQL is gated). The manuscript / authority hub of this whole constellation; it overlaps the BnF, MMM and Jonas on persons & places. Wikibase model: entities at data.biblissima.fr/entity/Q*, truthy statements via prop/direct/P*, P2 = 'instance of', multilingual rdfs:label / skos:prefLabel. Now a single 667 MB file with a P2-keyed types pyramid (4 semantic-zoom levels) + planner query_stats, so it answers summary / schema / community queries index-free - built with the low-RAM pipeline that made the monolith feasible (it was sharded because the 254M build OOM'd a 62 GB host). Queried lazily over HTTP range. CC-BY 4.0 (Biblissima+, Campus Condorcet).

examples.title: Manuscripts you can SEE (IIIF thumbnails)
examples.tip: The ?iiif column holds a IIIF manifest (prop/direct/P196) - the digitized manuscript at its holding library (Cambridge cudl, e-codices, the Vatican's digi.vatlib.it...). The playground fetches each manifest and renders it as a PAGED viewer right in the table: use the ‹ › buttons or the page box to leaf through the manuscript, and CLICK the image to open a lightbox - an enlarged page with prev/next paging, the manifest link and its metadata (each page faults from the IIIF Image API on demand). ?manuscript is the Biblissima entity, ?label its shelfmark.

examples.title: See manuscripts held in two cities
examples.tip: A richer pull: digitized manuscripts (a IIIF manifest, P196) grouped by their holding collection (P194, whose label is 'City. Library'), filtered to TWO cities - here Paris and Geneve (STRSTARTS on the city prefix). Each ?iiif is a paged viewer (‹ › to leaf through; click to open the lightbox with the enlarged page + manifest metadata). NOTE: Biblissima records the current holding city, not a production->migration path, and these manuscript records carry no production date (P72/P73 'earliest/latest date' sit on other entity types) - for true manuscript MIGRATION between cities over time, see the MMM dataset (which, however, has no images). Swap the two cities for any others (Roma, Oxford, Cambridge...).
examples.sparql:
PREFIX bd: <https://data.biblissima.fr/prop/direct/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?city ?shelfmark ?iiif WHERE {
  ?ms bd:P196 ?iiif ; bd:P194 ?c ; bd:P195 ?shelfmark .
  ?c rdfs:label ?city . FILTER(LANG(?city) = "fr")
  FILTER(STRSTARTS(?city, "Paris") || STRSTARTS(?city, "Gen"))
} ORDER BY ?city LIMIT 24

examples.title: What's in the graph (predicate totals)
examples.tip: The shape of the whole Biblissima+ Wikibase - now ONE 254M-triple file (was 3 shards): rdf:type, wikibase:rank, multilingual labels (rdfs:label / skos:prefLabel / schema:name) and the prop/direct/P* truthy statements. Whole-graph totals; the P2-keyed types pyramid can answer this kind of summary index-free.
examples.sparql: SELECT ?p (COUNT(*) AS ?n) WHERE { ?s ?p ?o } GROUP BY ?p ORDER BY DESC(?n) LIMIT 25

examples.title: Entities by their French label
examples.tip: Biblissima describes manuscripts, works, persons, places and editions - all as Wikibase entities (data.biblissima.fr/entity/Q*) with multilingual labels. Here, every entity carrying a French rdfs:label (persons, saints, instruments, institutions...).

examples.title: Entities grouped by type (instance of)
examples.tip: Group entities by their type (prop/direct/P2 = 'instance of' in the Biblissima Wikibase), resolved to a French label - the composition of the whole graph (manuscripts, works, persons, places, editions...). Full totals now that it is a single file, not a shard.

examples.title: Authority names across languages
examples.tip: Biblissima reconciles persons, works and places into multilingual authorities. Each entity's French rdfs:label paired with a skos:altLabel variant in another script or language (Arabic, Turkish, Italian, English transliterations of the same name) - the cross-lingual name graph that lets a manuscript catalogued in one tradition match a record in another.

datasets.label: Institución Colombina (ARCAS, Sevilla) - Seville cathedral + archdiocese archives, 69,900 ISAD records (remote-lazy)
datasets.description: The archival catalogue (ISAD) of the Institución Colombina, Seville: 69,900 records from the Archivo Catedral de Sevilla (ACS, 27,970) and the Archivo General del Arzobispado de Sevilla (AGAS, 41,930) - the Seville cathedral chapter and diocesan archives, with records reaching back to 1424 (Cathedral liturgical codices) and 1510. 927,788 triples queried lazily over HTTP range. Each record (arcas:ArchivalRecord) carries a title (dcterms:title), one or more dates (dcterms:date), its signatura / call number (arcas:signatura - boxes, 'Caja / NNNN'), the ISAD reference and classification codes (arcas:referenceCode, arcas:classificationCode), its archival level (arcas:level, e.g. 'Unidad documental compuesta'), the archive it belongs to (arcas:inArchive) and its parent in the description hierarchy (dcterms:isPartOf - so the fonds/series/file/item tree reconstructs). A full-text index over the titles powers content search (the marriage-licence series of the Archdiocese, liturgy, capellanías...). Harvested anonymously from the public ARCAS consultation (Baratz 'Albalá 7', a Solr-backed JS portal at albala.icolombina.es) - metadata only; the digital images are not publicly available. Entity IRIs are albala.icolombina.es/arcas/{record,archive}/*. © Institución Colombina (public catalogue metadata).

examples.title: Records per archive
examples.tip: The catalogue holds two archives of the Institución Colombina: the Archivo General del Arzobispado de Sevilla (AGAS, the Seville diocesan archive) with 41,930 records and the Archivo Catedral de Sevilla (ACS, the cathedral chapter) with 27,970. arcas:inArchive links each record to its holding archive, arcas:ArchivalRecord is the record type.

examples.title: The earliest records (15th-16th century)
examples.tip: Filters dates that end in a year 1400-1599 (dates come as '01/01/1424' or just '1424'). The Cathedral's oldest holdings surface: liturgical codices from 1424, chapter acts, and the censos / capellanías / patronatos (rents and chantry endowments) of the early 1500s. Switch the date column sort to read them chronologically.

examples.title: Marriage-licence files of the Archdiocese
examples.tip: Free-text over the record titles (a full-text index backs the search). The Archdiocese's 'expedientes matrimoniales' - marriage-dispensation case files that name the couple and their Andalusian town (e.g. Jerez de la Frontera, Puerto Real) - are the bulk of AGAS and a major genealogical source for western Andalusia.

examples.title: A file and the series it belongs to
examples.tip: dcterms:isPartOf threads every record to its parent in the ISAD description tree, so file -> series -> fonds reconstructs. Here each record paired with the title of the unit that contains it (e.g. a single marriage expediente under 'Expedientes matrimoniales ordinarios de Pueblos. Letra A.').

examples.title: Records by archival level
examples.tip: ISAD describes archives as a hierarchy of levels - fonds, series, file (expediente), item. arcas:level records each unit's level; most of this catalogue is described at the 'unidad documental compuesta' (compound documentary unit) level, with the upper fonds/series levels far fewer.

examples.title: Capellanías & patronatos (chantry endowments)
examples.tip: Text search for 'capellan' over the titles: the capellanías and patronatos - endowed chantries and lay patronages - are a distinctive Cathedral-chapter holding, with their censos, tributos and property deeds. Each row gives the title, its date and the box signatura (arcas:signatura, e.g. 'Caja / 5853 - 2').

datasets.label: Memòria - Spanish Civil War victims & mass graves (open data)
datasets.description: An aggregation of openly-licensed Spanish Civil War 'memoria histórica' datasets into ONE knowledge graph: 99,542 named victims/repressed persons and 2,872 mass graves (fosas), tied together through provinces. 1.21M triples, remote-lazy over HTTP range. Persons (mc:Victim) come from three regional registries - Catalonia's reparació jurídica de víctimes del franquisme (69,834), Catalonia's desapareguts de la Guerra Civil (8,339) and Euskadi's víctimas mortales (21,369) - each carrying name (rdfs:label), sex (mc:sex), age (mc:age), birth & residence municipality/province (mc:bornInMunicipality / mc:bornInProvince / mc:residedIn*), cause/manner of death (mc:cause, e.g. 'Gudari/miliciano muerto en combate', 'Ejecutado por Consejo de Guerra'), sentence (mc:sentence), profession, military unit, and an executed flag (mc:executed). Mass graves (mc:MassGrave) come from the Catalan (1,027, with WGS84 mc:lat/long + GeoSPARQL geometry), Andalusian (615, with historical narratives mc:narrative), Castilla y León (701, with repressor side) and Valencian (529) fosas registries - each with municipality, province (mc:province), victim count (mc:victimCount), status and a link to its official record (foaf:page). 88 provinces (mc:Province) link victims and graves, so you can ask 'which provinces have both the most victims and the most graves'. Person search is a `FILTER(CONTAINS(?name, …))` scan over the labels — this build carries NO text index. IRIs are memoria.rete/{persona,fosa,provincia}/*. Aggregated from regional open-data portals (transparenciacatalunya.cat, opendata.euskadi.eus, juntadeandalucia.es, jcyl.es, gva.es) - all CC-BY-style open data; sensitive personal/historical data, attribute the source administrations. NB this is the open regional data, NOT a scrape of any search portal.

examples.title: Victims by province of birth
examples.tip: Counts named victims / repressed persons by province of birth (mc:bornInProvince -> a shared mc:Province node). Barcelona leads with 22,555, then Tarragona, Lleida and Girona - this corpus is Catalonia-heavy (the reparació-jurídica registry), with Múrcia, Almería and València next.

examples.title: How people died (Basque registry)
examples.tip: The Euskadi víctimas registry records a manner of death (mc:cause). Combat deaths lead - 7,322 gudaris/milicianos killed in action and 5,953 on the rebel front - then deaths in captivity, and the executions: extrajudicial killings by rebels (1,143) and by Republicans (957), and 996 shot after court-martial (Consejo de Guerra).

examples.title: Map the mass graves (Catalonia)
examples.tip: Switch Output -> Map (try the new Basemap dropdown to put them on satellite/streets). The 1,027 Catalan fosas carry WGS84 geometry (geo:asWKT) - each point is a documented Civil War mass grave. Stay on Table and the ?w column renders a per-row mini-map (each grave a dot on a small world map). Other regions' graves (Andalucía, Castilla y León, València) are in the graph too but without coordinates in their open data.

examples.title: Largest mass graves by victim count
examples.tip: Graves ordered by mc:victimCount: the largest are in Andalucía - Huelva and Órgiva (Granada) at ~5,000, Málaga ~4,000, Sevilla ~3,600, Granada ~2,992 - reflecting the mass extrajudicial killings of 1936 in the south. Counts are estimates from each regional registry.

examples.title: Find a person by surname
examples.tip: A full-text index over names backs this. Change the literal (here a CONTAINS on 'GARCIA') to any surname to pull matching victims with their birthplace - the personal layer of the registries. Names are stored as 'SURNAME1 SURNAME2, Given'.

examples.title: Provinces with both victims and graves
examples.tip: The province nodes join the two layers. Two sub-aggregates - victims born per province and mass graves per province - joined on the shared mc:Province, so you see where the documented dead and the documented graves coincide. One query instead of two because mc:Province is the join key.

datasets.label: Embassy of the Free Mind - 2,307 hermetic & esoteric books (Bibliotheca Philosophica Hermetica, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The digitized core of the Bibliotheca Philosophica Hermetica - the Ritman Library / Embassy of the Free Mind in Amsterdam, the world's foremost collection on Hermetica, alchemy, Rosicrucianism, Kabbalah, mysticism and Western esotericism (partly funded by Dan Brown). 2,307 rare books (15th-19th c.) harvested KEYLESS from Source Library (sourcelibrary.org, the collection's own reading platform) with full cataloguing: original + English title, author (a linked schema:Person), year (schema:datePublished), publisher / place of publication, language (German 929, Latin 585, English, French, Dutch, Italian, Hebrew...), shelfmark, bibliography references and USTC catalogue links. Every book also carries an AI-written summary + reading-summary and four significance scores (historical / scholarly / visual / accessibility, 0-25 each) plus a 0-100 quality score, a subject index (126,752 dcterms:subject links to SKOS concepts), chapter structure, geocoded publication places (GeoSPARQL points - switch Output to Map) and related-book links. 764,708 page-image URLs render inline from images.sourcelibrary.org (CORS-open), plus one cover thumbnail per book. 5.74M triples, remote-lazy over HTTP range. Modeled with schema.org / Dublin Core / SKOS / GeoSPARQL by scripts/fetch_bph.py + scripts/bph_to_nt.py. CC BY-SA 4.0 - credit the Embassy of the Free Mind / BPH. Full per-page OCR + English translation text (also CC BY-SA 4.0) is gated behind a free Source Library API key and can be added as a second layer.

examples.title: Federation: where are these books held? (via USTC)
examples.tip: A CROSS-SOURCE join from the other side: pre-loads the USTC catalogue as a second source. Each Embassy book links rdfs:seeAlso -> its USTC edition; the query follows that into USTC to list the libraries that hold a physical copy (Herzog August, BSB, British Library...) and the printer. Remove the ustc chip to query the Embassy alone.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX u: <https://www.ustc.ac.uk/ontology#>
SELECT ?title ?printer ?library WHERE {
  ?book a schema:Book ; rdfs:label ?title ; rdfs:seeAlso ?ed .
  ?ed u:printer ?p . ?p rdfs:label ?printer .
  ?ed u:heldBy ?l . ?l rdfs:label ?library
}
LIMIT 40

examples.title: What's in the collection
examples.tip: The shape of the graph at a glance: 2,307 hermetic/esoteric Books, 764,708 Pages (each a scanned page image), 991 authors (schema:Person), 725 geocoded Places and ~127k subject/category/collection Concepts. One count per rdf:type.

examples.title: Alchemy books (with cover images)
examples.tip: Books filed under the 'alchemy' subject category, oldest first, each with author, year and its cover thumbnail (the -thumb.jpg renders inline). Swap the category IRI for /kabbalah, /rosicrucianism, /mysticism, /astrology or /medicine to browse another shelf.

examples.title: Books by language
examples.tip: The library is deeply multilingual: German (929) and Latin (585) dominate, then English, French, Dutch, Italian, Hebrew and more. Count of books per dct:language.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
