PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
PREFIX efmo: <https://data.embassyofthefreemind.com/ontology#>
SELECT ?language (COUNT(?b) AS ?books) WHERE {
  ?b a schema:Book ; dct:language ?language
}
GROUP BY ?language
ORDER BY DESC(?books)

examples.title: The oldest books in the library
examples.tip: Sorted by publication year ascending, so the incunabula and early-16th-century imprints surface first, each with its author and English title. schema:datePublished is a typed xsd:gYear.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
PREFIX efmo: <https://data.embassyofthefreemind.com/ontology#>
SELECT ?year ?title ?author WHERE {
  ?b a schema:Book ; schema:datePublished ?year ;
     rdfs:label ?title ; dct:creator ?author
}
ORDER BY ?year
LIMIT 30

examples.title: Most-represented authors
examples.tip: Which authors have the most books in the BPH? Books per schema:author, with the author's name. Beyond 'Anonymous'/'Unknown', the alchemical and Rosicrucian corpus (Paracelsus, Boehme, Fludd, Khunrath...) rises to the top.

PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>

}
GROUP BY ?author

Clusters over the great early-modern printing cities - Frankfurt, Nuremberg, Basel, Amsterdam, Paris, London. examples.title: Highest-rated books (AI quality score)

examples.sparql:
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>

SELECT ?title ?author ?score WHERE {

}
ORDER BY DESC(?score)

examples.title: A book's related-works network
examples.tip: The AI-inferred related-works links (efmo:relatedBook) as a node-link graph - each book joined to the titles it is connected to (citations, influences, same-work editions). A small influence neighbourhood of the collection.

datasets.label: USTC - Universal Short Title Catalogue (727 Embassy/BPH-cited editions, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: A bounded, federation-ready extract of the Universal Short Title Catalogue (ustc.ac.uk, University of St Andrews) - the authoritative bibliography of early-modern European print. Exactly the 727 editions the Embassy of the Free Mind / BPH collection cites (by USTC number), harvested from the public edition pages as a FAIR-USE research subset: USTC is a copyrighted scholarly database with no open licence and no bulk API, so this is 727 of ~1M records - NOT a copy of the catalogue (© USTC / University of St Andrews). Each edition (ustc:Edition, IRI = https://www.ustc.ac.uk/editions/{sn}) carries its standardized title, imprint, place/country/region, year, format (2°/4°/8°/12°...), pagination, authors (with roles) and printers (Lukas Jennis, Lazarus Zetzner's heirs and the other great alchemical presses), USTC classifications (Religious, Science, Medical, Philosophy, Witchcraft & Demonology...), language(s) (Latin, German, French, Dutch, English, Greek, Hebrew), 10,779 library HOLDINGS across 1,146 institutions (Herzog August Bibliothek Wolfenbüttel, British Library, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, SBB Berlin...) each with shelfmark, and 891 links to DIGITAL copies (Google Books, ProQuest EEB, Cervantes Virtual...). 88,452 triples, remote-lazy. Built to FEDERATE with the bph dataset - the edition IRI is exactly bph's rdfs:seeAlso target and every edition back-links u:embassyBook -> the Embassy book, so one cross-source query joins the Embassy's cover + AI summary to USTC's imprint, printers and library holdings. schema.org / Dublin Core / SKOS. Attribute USTC / University of St Andrews.
datasets.license: © USTC / Univ. of St Andrews (research subset)

examples.title: Digitised editions — where to read a copy
examples.tip:
USTC hosts no images itself, but 891 of these editions link out to a digitised copy (u:digitalCopy) and 713 name who digitised it (u:digitisationProvider — Google Books, MDZ, Gallica and the rest). Providers like ProQuest/EEBO are subscription-gated, so they stay as plain out-links.
ASK FOR WHAT THE FILE HAS. This example used to select schema:image and u:iiifManifest, and the published object carries NEITHER predicate — not once — so it answered nothing (#212). The four schema.org predicates in here are name, author, locationCreated and datePublished; the digitisation links are all in the u: namespace.

examples.title: What's in this USTC subset
examples.tip: The shape of the extract: 727 early-modern Editions, 10,779 library Copies (physical holdings), 1,146 Libraries, and ~1,226 Persons (authors + printers). One count per rdf:type. This is only the 727 editions the Embassy/BPH collection cites - a fair-use slice of USTC's ~1M records.

examples.title: Which libraries hold these books
examples.tip: Counts holdings per library (by institution + city, so same-named 'Universitätsbibliothek' entries stay distinct). The great early-modern collections surface: Herzog August Bibliothek (Wolfenbüttel), the British Library, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek (München), Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX u: <https://www.ustc.ac.uk/ontology#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?library ?city (COUNT(?e) AS ?editions) WHERE {
  ?e u:heldBy ?l . ?l rdfs:label ?library ; u:city ?city
}
GROUP BY ?l ?library ?city
ORDER BY DESC(?editions)
LIMIT 25

examples.title: Books by USTC classification
examples.tip: The subject make-up of the Embassy's cited editions in USTC's own classification scheme - Religious (313), Science, Medical Texts, Philosophy and Morality, and the tell-tale 'Witchcraft and Demonology'. Count of editions per dcterms:subject.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
SELECT ?classification (COUNT(?e) AS ?editions) WHERE {
  ?e dct:subject ?c . ?c skos:prefLabel ?classification
}
GROUP BY ?classification
ORDER BY DESC(?editions)

examples.title: Editions with a digital copy
examples.tip: USTC records where a digitisation is available online - the title plus the deep link (Google Books, ProQuest Early European Books, Cervantes Virtual...). 514 of the 727 editions have at least one. The URL column is clickable.

examples.title: The busiest printers
examples.tip: Editions per printer/press (skipping 's.n.' = sine nomine, printer unknown). This is a who's-who of the early-modern alchemical trade: Lukas Jennis and the heirs of Lazarus Zetzner (both Frankfurt/Strasbourg) printed much of the Rosicrucian and Hermetic corpus.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX u: <https://www.ustc.ac.uk/ontology#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?printer (COUNT(?e) AS ?editions) WHERE {
  ?e u:printer ?p . ?p rdfs:label ?printer
  FILTER(?printer != "s.n.")
}
GROUP BY ?printer
ORDER BY DESC(?editions)
LIMIT 25

examples.title: The oldest editions
examples.tip: Sorted by year ascending - the earliest imprints in the Embassy's cited set, each with its place of printing and format (2° folio, 4° quarto, 8° octavo...). schema:datePublished is a typed xsd:gYear.

examples.title: Federation: Embassy cover ⋈ USTC record
examples.tip: A CROSS-SOURCE join. This pre-loads the bph (Embassy of the Free Mind) graph as a second source (see the Sources strip). Each USTC edition back-links u:embassyBook -> the Embassy book; the query then pulls that book's cover image + AI summary from bph and shows them beside USTC's imprint and place - two catalogues describing the same physical book, joined on the shared identity. Remove the bph chip to query USTC alone.

datasets.label: Fuero Juzgo — the manuscript tradition: 52 witnesses, IIIF, Wikidata & Biblissima (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The manuscript tradition of the FUERO JUZGO — the 13th-century Romance (Castilian / Leonese / Asturian) translation of the Visigothic Liber Iudiciorum, made c. 1260 under Fernando III. Compiled from Mónica Castillo Lluch's Índice de fueros (UNIL) and PhiloBiblon (BETA, texid 1191): all 46 PhiloBiblon witnesses + the Galician López Ferreiro fragment + 3 BOOST-only manuscripts + 2 twelfth-century Catalan fragments of the Libre jutge = 52 testimonies, each with shelfmark (fjo:siglum), holding institution, dialect (leonés occidental/oriental, asturiano, castellano, agallegado…), an integer date range (fjo:notBefore/notAfter, so you can query 'all 13th-c. witnesses'), PhiloBiblon manid/anaid, and — where recorded — its incipit, prologue incipit, explicit and scribal colophon (the shared prologue 'Con cuidado del amor de Cristo… de don Sisnando' and the 'Pedro Martiz Gualego me scripso' colophon thread through the tradition). The manuscript STEMMA is modelled (fjo:copyOf links the 18th-c. antiquarian copies BNE 683 & 1681 back to their medieval exemplars — the Códice Murciano, Escorial d.III.18 & P.II.17). 12 EDITIONS (Villadiego 1600 → Llorente 1792 → Reguera 1798 → the RAE 1815[1817] academic edition promoted by Jovellanos → Orazi, Perona, Romero Cambrón…) link by fjo:editsWitness to the exact codices they establish; 11 STUDIES (Menéndez Pidal, Gessner, Fernández Llera, Castillo Lluch, García Martín…) link by fjo:studies. 12 DIGITIZED witnesses carry a IIIF manifest (fjo:iiifManifest) that renders as an in-table facsimile viewer — both Munich BSB codices, the BnF Espagnol 256 (Gallica), the Bodleian Holkham misc. 46 and all 8 Escorial codices (Real Biblioteca Digital); the flagship is BSB Cod.hisp. 28 (365 canvases, CC Public Domain Mark). Works, institutions, persons and places carry owl:sameAs to Wikidata (so the graph FEDERATES with the wikidata datasets and, via the cross-source join, with live Wikidata — see the map example), and two witnesses are owl:sameAs Biblissima+ entities (BnF Esp. 256 = Q44277, BSB Cod.hisp. 6 = Q264558), bridging to the `biblissima` dataset. A small purpose-built ontology (fjo:, Work/Witness/Edition/Study/Person/Institution/Place, aligned to Dublin Core, FOAF, SKOS, schema.org) travels inside the file. ~1.5k triples, remote-lazy over HTTP range (served from Cloudflare R2, data.graphplaza.com). Built by scripts/fuero_juzgo_to_nt.py from the two curated sources + verified IIIF/Wikidata/Biblissima lookups — no scraping. Scholarly compilation; credit Mónica Castillo Lluch (Índice de fueros, UNIL) and PhiloBiblon; BSB Cod.hisp. 28 images CC PDM 1.0. TEXT_INDEX on for full-text search over its literals.
datasets.license: Scholarly compilation (see sources); BSB Cod.hisp. 28 images CC Public Domain Mark 1.0

examples.title: What's in this corpus
examples.tip:
The shape of the Fuero Juzgo dataset, counted by fjo: class: 49 Manuscripts + 3 Fragments (the 46 PhiloBiblon witnesses, the Galician López Ferreiro fragment, 3 BOOST-only mss and the 2 Catalan Libre-jutge fragments), 12 Editions, 11 Studies, 3 Works (the Fuero Juzgo, its Latin source the Liber Iudiciorum, and the Catalan Libre jutge), plus the People, Institutions and Places that link them.
One row per class.

examples.title: 📜 Manuscripts you can SEE (IIIF facsimiles)
examples.tip:
The 12 digitized witnesses that carry a IIIF manifest (fjo:iiifManifest): both Munich BSB codices (Cod.hisp. 28 & 6), the BnF Espagnol 256 (Gallica), the Bodleian Holkham misc. 46, and all 8 Escorial codices (Real Biblioteca Digital). The Facsimile column (fjo:image) renders a folio inline; click a IIIF cell for the page-turning viewer.
Every facsimile is MIRRORED into our own R2 (all 3,223 full-res pages under fuero_juzgo/iiif/) with a self-hosted IIIF manifest, so it renders and downloads without depending on the source servers; fjo:sourceManifest keeps a link to the original. BSB Cod.hisp. 28 is CC Public Domain Mark.

examples.title: The tradition over time (witnesses per century)
examples.tip:
Every witness carries an integer date range (fjo:notBefore / fjo:notAfter), so fjo:century buckets the 52 testimonies: 2 in the 12th c. (the Catalan fragments), 26 in the 13th (the core of the surviving tradition, copied within a generation of the c. 1260 translation), 11 in the 14th, then a long tail of late copies down to the 18th-c. antiquarian apographs.
Switch Output to a bar chart to see the 13th-century peak.

examples.title: The oldest witnesses & their dialect
examples.tip:
The 13th-century-or-earlier witnesses, with the linguistic characterisation editors give them (fjo:languageVariety): the tradition is a dialect map of the medieval north-west - leonés occidental / centro-occidental / oriental, asturiano (the Munich Cod.hisp. 28), and castellano. The Códice Murciano (1288) is castellano copied from a strongly Leonese model.
Sorted earliest-first; 'Held by' is the current holding library.

examples.title: The manuscript stemma (copies of copies)
examples.tip:
fjo:copyOf reconstructs the transmission: the 18th-century antiquarian copies made for the RAE academic edition trace back to their medieval exemplars - BNE 683 (Santiago y Palomares, 1755, corrected by the Jesuit Burriel) is a copy of the Códice Murciano (1288), and BNE 1681 (1762-64) copies the Escorial codices P.II.17 and d.III.18.
Three copy-of links; the exemplar is always centuries older than the copy.

examples.title: Critical editions ↔ the codices they establish
examples.tip:
fjo:editsWitness links each modern edition to the exact manuscript it edits: Mencé-Caster (1996) -> Escorial Z.III.6, Orazi (1997) -> Z.III.21, Perona et al. (2002) -> the Códice Murciano, Romero Cambrón (2016) -> the Bodleian Holkham misc. 46, and the RAE academic edition (1815, really 1817) collates three Escorial codices (Z.III.18, M.II.18, d.III.18).
The scholarly editions, joined to their base witnesses.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX fjo: <https://w3id.org/fuero-juzgo/ontology#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?edition ?codex ?shelf WHERE {
  ?ed fjo:editsWitness ?w ; rdfs:label ?edition .
  ?w rdfs:label ?codex ; fjo:siglum ?shelf .
}
ORDER BY ?edition

examples.title: Search the prologues & colophons
examples.tip:
Full-text search (backed by the .rete text index) over the incipits, prologues and scribal colophons transcribed from PhiloBiblon. Here, the witnesses whose prologue names King Sisenando (the Visigothic king in whose reign the IV Council of Toledo met, invoked at the head of the code) - the shared 'Con cuidado del amor de Cristo... de don Sisnando' opening that threads through the tradition.
Change 'sisnando' to 'godos', 'iudizios' or a scribe's name to trace a formula across the corpus.

examples.title: 🔗 Linked out: witnesses also in Biblissima
examples.tip:
Two witnesses carry owl:sameAs into Biblissima+ (data.biblissima.fr), the French manuscript-and-IIIF aggregator: the BnF Espagnol 256 (Q44277) and the Munich BSB Cod.hisp. 6 (Q264558). This is the bridge that lets the graph FEDERATE with the playground's `biblissima` dataset - the same manuscript, described from two catalogues.
Every digitized witness is also reachable through its IIIF manifest, which Biblissima indexes.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX fjo: <https://w3id.org/fuero-juzgo/ontology#>
PREFIX owl: <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?witness ?biblissima ?iiif WHERE {
  ?w owl:sameAs ?biblissima ; fjo:iiifManifest ?iiif ; rdfs:label ?witness .
  FILTER(STRSTARTS(STR(?biblissima), "https://data.biblissima.fr/"))
}

examples.title: Cross-source JOIN: the libraries' countries (live Wikidata)
examples.tip:
ONE query split across TWO sources and joined on the shared ?wd. This file answers 'which library holds a witness' and gives it an owl:sameAs Wikidata id; LIVE Wikidata answers wdt:P17 (the library's country). The playground routes each pattern to the source that can answer it, then bound-joins - so you see the international diaspora of the tradition's custodians (Germany, France, Spain, United Kingdom, United States, Sweden, Denmark, Portugal).
Wikidata is pre-added as a live endpoint (see the Sources strip). Hit 🔍 Plan to see the routing.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX fjo: <https://w3id.org/fuero-juzgo/ontology#>
PREFIX owl: <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/>
SELECT DISTINCT ?library ?country WHERE {
  ?w fjo:heldBy ?lib .
  ?lib owl:sameAs ?wd ; rdfs:label ?library .
  ?wd wdt:P17 ?c . ?c rdfs:label ?country .
  FILTER(LANG(?country) = "en")
}
ORDER BY ?country

examples.title: 🌍 The holding libraries on a live-Wikidata map
examples.tip:
The same cross-source join, but asking Wikidata for wdt:P625 (coordinate location) instead of the country - and rendered on the map. Each pin is a library that holds a Fuero Juzgo witness, placed by live Wikidata coordinates: Munich, Paris, Oxford, Madrid, El Escorial, Lisbon, Stockholm, Copenhagen, Washington, New York.
Switch Output to Table to read the raw WKT; the geography IS the reception history of the code.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX fjo: <https://w3id.org/fuero-juzgo/ontology#>
PREFIX owl: <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX wdt: <http://www.wikidata.org/prop/direct/>
SELECT DISTINCT ?library ?wkt WHERE {
  ?w fjo:heldBy ?lib .
  ?lib owl:sameAs ?wd ; rdfs:label ?library .
  ?wd wdt:P625 ?wkt .
}

datasets.label: BVPB - Ramón Llull: 142 digitised editions & manuscripts (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The complete Ramón Llull collection of the Biblioteca Virtual del Patrimonio Bibliográfico (BVPB, Spanish Ministry of Culture): 142 digitised works by the Mallorcan polymath Ramón Llull (Doctor Illuminatus, ca. 1232-1315) - manuscripts and early printed editions (14th-18th c.) of the Ars, Arbor Scientiae, Ars Brevis, Ars generalis ultima, the Liber magnus contemplationis in Deum and the rest of the Lullian corpus, in Latin, Catalan and Castilian. Each work is an edm:ProvidedCHO carrying full Dublin Core - title, creator/contributor, date, publisher & place of printing, language, subject, physical description (dc:format), coverage and rights - plus its BVPB control number, edm:isShownAt (the catalogue landing page), edm:isShownBy (the whole digitised object as a single PDF, served from bvpb.mcu.es) and foaf:page (the page-image viewer). The 71 PRINTED editions are additionally FULL-TEXT SEARCHABLE: every one was OCR'd page by page (Tesseract lat + a dictionary-guided long-ſ correction that turns 'fapientia' back into 'sapientia'), ~8.7M words held as bvpb:fulltext and backed by the .rete text index, and given a IIIF v3 manifest (bvpb:iiifManifest) that opens a page-turning viewer with the OCR word layer over the facsimile - try the '🔎 Full-text search' and '📖 IIIF viewers' examples. Manuscripts are metadata-only (Tesseract can't read the hands - that needs HTR). 2,877 triples (25.7 MB with the text layer), remote-lazy over HTTP range. Harvested from the BVPB Ramón Llull microsite by scripts/bvpb_ramonllull.py, modelled by scripts/bvpb_to_nt.py, OCR/IIIF by scripts/bvpb_ocr_iiif.py. CC BY 4.0 - credit the Biblioteca Virtual del Patrimonio Bibliográfico (Ministerio de Cultura, España). Shares the early-modern rare-book domain with the bph and ustc collections.

examples.title: What's in this collection
examples.tip:
The shape of the BVPB Ramón Llull collection: 142 digitised works, split by dc:type into 'Manuscritos' (hand-written medieval codices) and 'Libros' (early printed editions, 15th-18th c.).
One count per Dublin Core type - the manuscripts are the older, rarer half of the Lullian corpus here.

examples.title: Languages of the Lullian corpus
examples.tip:
Works per language (dc:language, ISO 639-2 codes): 'lat' = Latin (the bulk of Llull's scholastic output), 'cat' = Catalan (his own vernacular, which he pioneered for philosophy), 'spa' = Castilian.
Ramón Llull wrote across all three, and the collection reflects it.

examples.title: Read the books: every work + its PDF
examples.tip:
Each work with its date and edm:isShownBy - the whole digitised object as a single PDF served from bvpb.mcu.es. The PDF column is a clickable link (the 142 PDFs are ~13 GB in total).
Sorted oldest-first, so the 14th-15th-century manuscripts (e.g. the Ars demonstrativa, Arbor Scientiae) lead.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX dc: <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/>
PREFIX edm: <http://www.europeana.eu/schemas/edm/>
SELECT ?title ?date ?pdf WHERE {
  ?s dc:title ?title ; dc:date ?date ; edm:isShownBy ?pdf .
}
ORDER BY ?date
LIMIT 50

examples.title: The printers & publishers
examples.tip:
Editions per publisher/printer (dc:publisher). The early-modern Mallorca presses surface - the house of the Viuda de Guasp and Typis Viduae Frau (Palma de Mallorca) printed much of the 17th-18th-century Lullian revival.
Manuscripts have no publisher, so this counts only the printed editions.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX dc: <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/>
SELECT ?publisher (COUNT(?s) AS ?works) WHERE {
  ?s dc:publisher ?publisher
}
GROUP BY ?publisher
ORDER BY DESC(?works)
LIMIT 25

examples.title: The manuscripts, with their physical description
examples.tip:
Just the hand-written codices (dc:type = 'Manuscritos'): each with its date and dc:format - the codicological description (number of leaves, parchment vs paper, columns, dimensions in cm).
These are the medieval witnesses of Llull's text, the scholarly heart of the collection.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX dc: <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/>
SELECT ?title ?date ?format WHERE {
  ?s dc:type ?type ; dc:title ?title ; dc:date ?date ; dc:format ?format .
  FILTER(STR(?type) = "Manuscritos")
}
ORDER BY ?date
LIMIT 40

examples.title: 🔎 Full-text search across the OCR'd books
examples.tip:
Full-text search over the OCR of all 71 PRINTED editions (Tesseract lat + dictionary long-ſ repair, ~8.7M words held as bvpb:fulltext, backed by the .rete text index). This finds every book whose pages mention 'sapientia' (wisdom) - change the term to search the whole corpus.
The Open (IIIF) column opens the page-turning facsimile with the OCR word layer; the OCR is an automatic scaffold, not a critical edition. NOTE a FILTER(CONTAINS) scans the fulltext (~19 MB fetched), so give it a moment; enable Settings → Range cache to make re-runs instant.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX bvpb: <https://bvpb.mcu.es/ns#>
PREFIX dc: <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/>
SELECT ?title ?date ?manifest WHERE {
  ?s bvpb:fulltext ?txt ; dc:title ?title ; dc:date ?date ; bvpb:iiifManifest ?manifest .
  FILTER(CONTAINS(LCASE(STR(?txt)), "sapientia"))
}
LIMIT 25

examples.title: 📖 Page-turning IIIF viewers (printed editions)
examples.tip:
The 71 printed editions, each with a IIIF v3 manifest (bvpb:iiifManifest) - click a ?manifest cell to open the page-turning viewer (facsimile images served from R2 + the OCR word layer). Sorted by page count; the Operum Tomus volumes run past 1,000 pages.
Manuscripts are absent here - Tesseract can't read the hands, which would need HTR (Transkribus / eScriptorium).
examples.sparql:
PREFIX bvpb: <https://bvpb.mcu.es/ns#>
PREFIX dc: <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/>
SELECT ?title ?pages ?manifest WHERE {
  ?s bvpb:iiifManifest ?manifest ; dc:title ?title ; bvpb:pageCount ?pages .
}
ORDER BY DESC(?pages)
LIMIT 30

datasets.label: Charles S. Peirce papers - the Houghton finding aid as a graph, with 45k IIIF pages (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The complete finding aid of the Charles S. Peirce papers at Houghton Library, Harvard (MS Am 1632, finding aid hou02614): the working papers of the philosopher, logician, scientist and founder of pragmatism (1839-1914), 74 linear feet in 166 boxes. All 2,527 archival components as a graph: the finding-aid tree (Collection > Series > Subseries > Component via dcterms:isPartOf - I. Manuscripts with Richard Robin's topical arrangement Mathematics/Pragmatism/Phenomenology/Logic/Metaphysics/..., II. Correspondence, III. Supplementary, IV. Microfilm), each component with its full title, parsed short title, genre ('autograph manuscript', 'typescript'...), date text + integer year range parsed from the title tail, Robin arrangement number (a:msNumber - the 'R numbers' Peirce scholars cite), physical description, and its Box (127 box entities - shelf archaeology). The CORRESPONDENCE parses into a directed network: ~690 letter components with a:sender / a:addressee / a:letterCount over 729 Person nodes - W. P. Garrison of The Nation (216 letters), Paul Carus of The Monist (112), brother James Mills Peirce (87), William James, the Smithsonian... Peirce himself is owl:sameAs Wikidata Q187520. 423 components are DIGITIZED end to end: a:iiifManifest (IIIF Presentation v3, 45,423 page images served by Harvard's image servers) renders as the in-table page viewer, with a:pageCount and a a:thumbnail per object - read 'The Simplest Mathematics' (822 pp.) in the results table. 36,179 triples, remote-lazy over HTTP range, full-text index over the titles. datasets.label: BOE — Legislación Consolidada: every in-force Spanish law (12,330) as an ELI citation graph (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The ENTIRE consolidated-legislation corpus of Spain's Boletín Oficial del Estado — every actively-maintained norm in force (State + the autonomous communities + the foral regimes), 12,330 in all, as a European-Legislation-Identifier (ELI) knowledge graph. Each norm sits at its REAL canonical ELI IRI (https://www.boe.es/eli/es/l/2015/10/01/40 = Ley 40/2015 de Régimen Jurídico del Sector Público), typed eli:LegalResource and by its rango (bx:Ley, bx:LeyOrganica, bx:RealDecreto, bx:RealDecretoLey, bx:Orden, bx:Reglamento… — 19 classes rdfs:subClassOf eli:LegalResource, so `rete`'s type-pyramid communities ARE the kinds of norm), carrying eli:title, eli:id_local (the BOE-A-… identifier), eli:number, eli:date_document / date_publication / first_date_entry_in_force (typed xsd:date), eli:passed_by → its issuing department (149 organisations — Jefatura del Estado & the ministries + the CCAA governments), eli:jurisdiction (Estatal/Autonómico) and eli:is_about → its subjects (drawn from the BOE's 6,829-term SKOS materia thesaurus). The heart of it is the NORM-TO-NORM CITATION / DEROGATION NETWORK mined from the BOE's own análisis: ~100,000 edges typed with the STANDARD ELI relations — eli:repeals (deroga, 19.5k), eli:amends (modifica, 32.9k), eli:corrects (corrige), eli:cites, eli:transposes (1,042 EU-directive transpositions), eli:based_on (dictada en virtud de) — plus a small bx: extension for BOE-specific acts (publishes / approves / authorizes / ratifies / challenges / declares / interprets). So you can ask which laws have been reformed most (the Ley de Demarcación y Planta Judicial — 134 amendments; the IRPF and IVA tax codes; the Ley de Enjuiciamiento Civil), what the 1978 Constitution repealed (the Franco-era Leyes Fundamentales: the Ley de Sucesión en la Jefatura del Estado, the Fuero de los Españoles, the Ley Orgánica del Estado, the Ley 1/1977 de Reforma Política…), or which norms have been most challenged before the Constitutional Court (the Código Penal — 51 recursos/cuestiones). Referenced norms outside the in-force set (already-repealed or pre-consolidation, including Gaceta-era laws back to the 19th c.) become 28,796 lightweight labelled nodes so no derogation edge dangles. A `FILTER(CONTAINS(?title, …))` over all 41k titles finds every norm on 'inteligencia artificial', 'cambio climático' or 'protección de datos' — this build carries NO text index, so that filter scans the title literals rather than hitting a word index. 465k triples, 7.9 MB, remote-lazy over HTTP range on Cloudflare R2. Built from the OFFICIAL BOE Open-Data API (the legislación-consolidada enumeration + a per-norm /análisis call + the /datos-auxiliares controlled vocabularies) by scripts/boe_to_nt.py — no scraping. Because the norms carry real ELI IRIs and the ELI ontology, the graph federates with EUR-Lex and the other national ELI publishers. Reuse under Ley 37/2007 + the BOE standard reuse licence (Resolución 27-jun-2024): credit 'Basado en datos de la Agencia Estatal Boletín Oficial del Estado'.

examples.title: 🧠 Every norm with the force of law — reasoning over the taxonomy
examples.tip:
The rango classes now form a two-tier ontology: bx:NormaConRangoDeLey groups the force-of-law kinds (Ley, Ley Orgánica, Decreto Legislativo, Decreto-ley…) and bx:NormaReglamentaria the regulatory ones (Real Decreto, Orden, Resolución…), both under eli:LegalResource.
NO norm is typed with the intermediate class directly, so with 🧠 Reason OFF this returns 0 rows. Turn it ON and OWL 2 QL rewrites `a bx:NormaConRangoDeLey` along rdfs:subClassOf, returning all 4,967 norms with the force of law. Flip Reason off to see the difference.

examples.title: 🧠 What has amended this law? — inverse reasoning
examples.tip:
The amendment network stores only the forward edge: X eli:amends Y. The ontology declares bx:amendedBy owl:inverseOf eli:amends, so the reverse edges are NOT stored — they're entailed.
With 🧠 Reason ON, asking what amended the Ley 38/1988 de Demarcación y de Planta Judicial (the most-reformed law in force — its judicial map redrawn with every new court) returns all 134 amending norms by reversing the eli:amends edges. Reason OFF → 0 rows. Swap the IRI for any norm.

examples.title: ★ The living laws — most-reformed norms in force
examples.tip: eli:amends is the 'modifica' relation mined from the BOE's own análisis, so counting the INCOMING amendments ranks the most-reformed laws still in force. Top is the Ley 38/1988 de Demarcación y de Planta Judicial (134 reforms — the judicial map is redrawn every time a court is added), then the great tax codes (IRPF — Ley 35/2006; IVA — Ley 37/1992; Impuestos Especiales), the texto refundido de la Ley General de la Seguridad Social, the Ley 1/2000 de Enjuiciamiento Civil and the Ley Orgánica 6/1985 del Poder Judicial. These are the laws Parliament keeps touching.

examples.title: What the 1978 Constitution repealed
examples.tip: The Constitución Española (its ELI work IRI is es/c/1978/12/27) sits at the top of the hierarchy of norms — and here is what it swept away. Its disposición derogatoria repeals the Franco-era Leyes Fundamentales del Reino: the Ley de Sucesión en la Jefatura del Estado (1947), the Ley reguladora del Fuero de los Españoles (1945), the Ley Orgánica del Estado (1967), the Ley de Principios del Movimiento Nacional (1958) and the Ley 1/1977 para la Reforma Política that dissolved the regime. The transition to democracy, as eli:repeals edges.

examples.title: Most challenged before the Constitutional Court
examples.tip: bx:challenges gathers the recursos and cuestiones de inconstitucionalidad and conflictos raised against a norm (BOE análisis relation codes 520/530/552/694). The most-contested law in force is the Ley Orgánica 10/1995 del Código Penal (51 challenges), then the Ley 24/1983 de saneamiento de las Haciendas Locales and the Real Decreto-ley 28/2012 on the Seguridad Social pension freeze — the fault lines of Spanish constitutional litigation.

examples.title: Search: laws on artificial intelligence
examples.tip: Full-text search over the 41k norm titles (a rete text index backs CONTAINS). 'Inteligencia artificial' surfaces the Real Decreto 729/2023 that created AESIA — the Agencia Española de Supervisión de Inteligencia Artificial, the first such national supervisor in the EU — and Extremadura's Decreto-ley 2/2023. examples.title: Reforms of the Código Penal, as a network
examples.tip: Switch Output to Graph. The node-link neighbourhood of ONE norm — the Código Penal (Ley Orgánica 10/1995) — with every law that has amended it fanning out from the centre (eli:amends), 43 reforms in all: the 2015 overhaul, the LO 4/2023 on delitos contra la libertad sexual ('sólo sí es sí'), the LO 1/2024 de amnistía… Change the central IRI to es/l/2000/01/07/1 (Enjuiciamiento Civil) or es/lo/1985/07/01/6 (Poder Judicial) to map another law's reform history.

examples.tip: Switch Output to Time. The norms in force counted by their year of adoption (eli:date_document) — the shape of the currently-live statute book over time. It climbs through the 2000s and 2010s and spikes in 2020 (795 norms — the COVID-19 emergency legislation). Older law is thinner because superseded norms have dropped out of the consolidated set.

datasets.label: OpenAIRE Research Graph v3.0 (2021) — 148.1M research outputs, their authors, subjects, projects and organisations, 8.35B triples, 113.1 GB (one file, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The OpenAIRE Research Graph as **one** range-queryable .rete file — **8,353,117,004 triples in 113.1 GB**: 148,062,669 research outputs (124,852,030 publications, 14,228,362 research datasets, 8,760,460 other research products, 221,817 research software records), 1,807,111,110 relation rows as direct edges, 277,330 organisations, 2,850,097 projects, 94,700 datasources and the research communities, none of it downloaded unless a query asks. OpenAIRE aggregates the European open-science record: research outputs harvested from thousands of repositories, the projects that funded them, the organisations that ran them, and the links between all of it. **Identity:** a result sits at https://doi.org/{doi} only when its DOI belongs to no other record in the whole dump (112,979,925 results), so those AUTO-MERGE with the DataCite, Crossref, OpenCitations and DBLP graphs here on the shared identifier; otherwise it keeps its native OpenAIRE IRI (w3id.org/rete/openaire/50/…) — the 4,175,642 results whose DOI is shared, which still point at it through oaire:doiLink, and the 30,907,102 with no DOI. **Included:** subjects as shared oaire:Subject terms (1,180,695,337 links to 133,446,583 terms), authors in list order (562,859,397 oaire:AuthorRole nodes) with their ORCID where the record gives a valid one (652,968 orcid.org agents), every author, instance, URL and subject with no caps, and each project's funders as oaire:Funding nodes (2,849,964). Relation trust and provenance are not emitted. **Indexes:** a full-text index over 15 text predicates (titles, names, subjects, venues, acronyms, descriptions) and a label index; no pyramid, so keep queries selective. Every conversion rule and what it rescued, kept as text or dropped is in the Dataset Card; the converter is caviri/rete-datasets: openaire/parquet_to_nt.py. THIS IS THE 2021 DUMP — v3.0, Zenodo, 2021-04-27 — and the name says so on purpose: OpenAIRE has grown a great deal since, and a catalogue entry called plain 'openaire' would quietly claim to be current. Until 2026-10 this graph was published as eight files, one per entity. CC-BY-4.0.

datasets.label: WikiArt — 223,094 paintings with the pictures INSIDE the file (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The WikiArt corpus as one range-queryable .rete with the paintings themselves inside it: 223,094 artworks by 5,755 artists, and 223,082 of them carry their own image as an inline WebP (xsd:base64Binary on wa:imageData, with wa:imageFormat "image/webp"). No companion image host, no second fetch, no dead links — the query returns the picture. That is the point of the dataset: a .rete can be the whole artifact, media included, for about 0.4% more than storing the same images loose. The examples build a data: URI with CONCAT so the browser paints bytes that came straight out of the file; selecting schema:image instead would pull a placeholder frame off uploads.wikiart.org and prove nothing. Each work carries its title, artist, style, genre, period, material, technique, completion year and pixel dimensions, plus 507k tag and 444k concept statements, all under the canonical wikiart.org IRI. DATA REPAIR: WikiArt's own image JSON serves the non-character U+FFFF as the artist name on 21,641 works (9.7%), which would make garbage the most prolific artist in the graph, ahead of van Gogh. The intact artistUrl slug resolves 20,859 of them against the artist records (a-r-valgorth → "A. R. Valgorth"); the remaining 782 belong to 13 slugs that are not artists at all (ancient-greek-pottery and the like) and are left WITHOUT a name rather than given a fabricated one. 25.4 GB, remote-lazy over HTTP range on Cloudflare R2 — the Dataset Card answers in two small range reads at that size. ⚠ BUT A QUERY DOES NOT: every query on this file pays a floor of about 2.18 GB before it answers anything, and the examples below are therefore EXCLUDED from the automated answer sweep (skipCapture, #212) rather than left recorded as broken. Measured with the CLI against the live object: the cheapest example here — ?w wa:style ?style, one short-literal predicate, five rows — fetched 2,178,636,127 B in 22 range requests over 305 s; the Monet FILTER fetched 2,188,990,815 B in 93 requests over 621 s; and rewriting that one to bind the artist as a bound object FIRST made it worse, not better (2,226,477,407 B, 547 s). Three queries with nothing in common, all landing within 2.2% of the same number, is the file talking, not the query: 92% of these bytes are base64 literals, so the dictionary chunk directory a lazy open must walk is proportional to the payload. `rete cost` on this URL does not return inside 900 s. Nothing here is wrong — every one of these five answers correctly, given the bytes and the time — but a browser tab cannot hold that, which is why no capture ever recorded an answer for wikiart at all, and why it appeared in no count of broken examples. Un-skip when #198 lands: a 0x06 blob section keeps large literals out of the dictionary, and this file is the extreme case it exists for.

datasets.label: Fedlex — Swiss federal law: 56.3M quads across 497,905 named graphs (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The metadata layer of Swiss federal law as one range-queryable .rete: 56,321,446 quads spread over 497,905 NAMED GRAPHS — one per act, consolidated version and language — harvested from Fedlex, the official publication platform of the Swiss Confederation. Modelled with JOLux (the Luxembourg-origin legislation ontology Fedlex reuses) plus ELI and SKOS, whose TBox travels inside the file. It is FRBR-shaped: a jolux:Work (the act) isRealizedBy one jolux:Expression per language (de/fr/it/rm/en, 4.5M language links) isEmbodiedBy jolux:Manifestation files, so the same law carries its German, French and Italian titles side by side. On top of that sits a 3.12-million-edge CITATION NETWORK (jolux:citationFromLegalResource / citationToLegalResource) whose endpoints are jolux:LegalResourceSubdivision IRIs (…/text/…) that reach their act through legalResourceSubdivisionIsPartOf — so 'which acts are cited most' is a four-hop join, and the answer is led by the Aktienrecht revision and the Code des obligations. 2.66M SKOS concepts carry the JURIVOC and legal-taxonomy subject vocabularies. Harvested by data/switzerland-fedlex/scripts/fetch_sparql.py, which works around two hard Virtuoso limits — ORDER BY capped at 10k rows and every response silently truncated at 100k — with index-backed graph enumeration and COUNT-guarded batches; the harvest reaches 2026-07-30. THE NAMED GRAPHS ARE THE POINT: a single `GRAPH ?g { … }` block binds every pattern to ONE graph, so a cross-act join needs one graph variable per block (every example below does this). This is the queryable INDEX of the law; the article text lives separately as Akoma Ntoso (OASIS LegalDocML) XML. Legal-domain sibling of the Spanish BOE graph — both ELI-based, so they federate. Swiss federal legislation is free to use and reproduce.

Written as a single GRAPH block this returns 0 rows, which is the trap this dataset sets. The answer is led by the Aktienrecht revision message and the Code des obligations.

datasets.label: Vesuvius Challenge - Herculaneum scrolls: the data browser as a graph, with download links (remote, lazy)

examples.title: What's in the collection
examples.tip:
The shape of the graph at a glance: 45 samples (27 Scrolls + 9 Fragments + 9 not-yet-typed), 63 Scan sessions, 66 reconstructed Volumes, 204 traced Segments, 2,336 downloadable DataAssets and 9 ML Models. One count per class.
The classes are self-describing (open the Schema view) - the whole Vesuvius Challenge digitisation pipeline as a typed graph.

examples.title: ★ Download the data: every file for Scroll 1
examples.tip:
Every downloadable file for Scroll 1 (PHercParis4) - OME-Zarr CT volumes, OBJ surface meshes, tifxyz coordinate maps, surface-volume layer zarrs and ink-detection prediction TIFFs. Each ?download IRI IS the file's public URL on the Vesuvius open-data bucket, so the cell is a working download link.
Swap the sample IRI for /PHerc0332 (Scroll 3), /PHerc1667 (Scroll 4) or /PHerc0172 (Scroll 5). Remove the LIMIT to list all ~1,000 files.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX vs: <https://scrollprize.org/vocab#>
SELECT ?type ?download WHERE {
  ?download vs:assetOf ?e ; vs:assetType ?type .
  ?e vs:sample <https://scrollprize.org/id/sample/PHercParis4> .
}
ORDER BY ?type
LIMIT 100

examples.title: The scrolls & fragments, with photographs
examples.tip:
The physical samples that carry a photograph, each rendered as a thumbnail (the same Thumbor image service the scrollprize.org data browser uses; click to open full size). PHerc numbers are the Naples inventory numbers of the carbonised papyri excavated from the Villa dei Papiri.
33 of the 45 samples have a photo; the rest are scan-only.

examples.title: 🔥 The revealed ink, as images
examples.tip:
The payoff of the whole project: ML ink-detection predictions over the unwrapped papyrus surfaces, as inline image previews (the downsampled .jpg renders in the table; the full-resolution TIFF is a separate asset). Dark strokes are predicted ink - the Greek text of a 2,000-year-old scroll.
These are Segments of every scroll that has been read; sort or filter by ?scroll to focus on one. The full predictions are in the next example.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX vs: <https://scrollprize.org/vocab#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?scroll ?segment ?ink WHERE {
  ?ink vs:assetType "ink-detection-downsampled" ; vs:assetOf ?g .
  ?g rdfs:label ?segment ; vs:sample ?s . ?s rdfs:label ?scroll .
}
LIMIT 40

examples.title: Ink predictions + which model made them
examples.tip:
Full provenance: every full-resolution ink-detection TIFF (a working download link), joined via vs:usedModel to the ML model that produced it - the resnet3d-152 'new_canon_autoresearch_recipe', the TimeSformer scroll-5 models, etc. This is the graph paying off: from a downloadable prediction back to the exact model run.
See the models themselves (architecture + task) with the Schema view or the Model class.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX vs: <https://scrollprize.org/vocab#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?scroll ?model ?download WHERE {
  ?download vs:assetType "ink-detection" ; vs:assetOf ?g ; vs:usedModel ?m .
  ?g vs:sample ?s . ?s rdfs:label ?scroll . ?m rdfs:label ?model .
}
LIMIT 40

examples.title: The 3D CT volumes to download (OME-Zarr)
examples.tip:
The reconstructed micro-CT volumes - each a cloud-optimised OME-Zarr store (a directory URL you can open with zarr/dask, or in Neuroglancer). ?shape is the voxel grid: these are tens of thousands of voxels on a side, so a single volume is tens to hundreds of GB.
One scroll can have several volumes at different resolutions/energies; ?zarr is the download root.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX vs: <https://scrollprize.org/vocab#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?scroll ?shape ?zarr WHERE {
  ?zarr vs:assetType "ome-zarr" ; vs:assetOf ?v .
  ?v vs:sample ?s ; vs:shape ?shape . ?s rdfs:label ?scroll .
}
ORDER BY ?scroll
LIMIT 40

examples.title: Scanning sessions: facility, energy, resolution
examples.tip:
The 63 synchrotron micro-CT sessions, finest voxel first. Two beamlines did the scanning: DLS (Diamond Light Source, Oxfordshire) and ESRF (Grenoble). Higher keV penetrates the dense carbonised roll; smaller µm resolves finer papyrus layers.
The scan feeds a reconstructed Volume (vs:fromScan) - the physics half of the pipeline.

examples.title: Which model read which scroll (graph)
examples.tip:
A bipartite graph: each Scroll/Fragment joined to every ML Model that produced a prediction on its data (via the DataAsset's vs:usedModel). Shared models tie the scrolls together - the 'new_canon_autoresearch_recipe' ink detector was applied across several.
Switch Output to Graph. Nodes are labelled; the hubs are the most-worked scrolls and the general-purpose models.

shacl_shapes.title: DataAsset completeness + typed links
shacl_shapes.tip: Every vs:DataAsset (2,336 of them — the actual downloadable files: scans, ink-detection outputs, meshes, etc.) must carry a human label, an asset-type tag, and an assetOf edge into the Segment or Volume it belongs to; these three predicates are on literally every DataAsset row in the data (2,336/2,336), so dropping one signals a broken harvest record. targetVolume and usedModel are checked for correct typing (must point at a real vs:Volume / vs:Model) when present, but are left optional since only ~55% and ~21% of assets carry them respectively.

shacl_shapes.title: Segment core attributes + volume lineage
shacl_shapes.tip: Every vs:Segment (204 flattened-papyrus-surface reconstructions) must have a label, a creation timestamp, a pixel bounding box, width/height in pixels, and a fromVolume edge into the CT vs:Volume it was unwrapped from — all five predicates are present on exactly 204/204 Segment rows, so any Segment missing one is an incomplete pipeline record. vs:sample (which points to the vs:Scroll the segment ultimately came from, e.g. PHercParis4) is checked for correct typing but kept optional since it only covers 192/204 segments.

shacl_shapes.title: Volume minimal identity
shacl_shapes.tip: Every vs:Volume (66 CT-scan reconstructions, the intermediate stage between a physical Scroll and the Segments unwrapped from it) must at least carry a human-readable rdfs:label, since no vs:Volume node in this graph originates its own outgoing edges besides being labeled and pointed at from Segments/DataAssets. This is deliberately a thin shape: the class_links evidence only shows other classes pointing AT vs:Volume (via assetOf/targetVolume/coversVolume/fromVolume/wasDerivedFrom), never vs:Volume asserting properties about itself.

datasets.label: bcul.rete — BCU Lausanne: a digital twin of the whole library, incl. where every book is held (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: A range-queryable graph twin of the Bibliothèque cantonale et universitaire de Lausanne, aggregating four of its public interfaces into one 117.5M-triple graph. The ENTIRE Renouvaud catalogue — 3.55M bibliographic records mirrored from the Alma SRU endpoint of the Vaud library network (zone 41BCULAUSA_LIB) — carries full physical HOLDINGS: every book resolves to WHICH library holds it (BCUL sites Unithèque / Riponne / Internef, the Archives cantonales vaudoises, the Musée des beaux-arts, and dozens of faculty, gymnasium and municipal libraries), its shelving location, call number and live availability (available / unavailable / check_holdings) via 4.9M b:heldAt edges to shared Library nodes. Plus the Patrinum digital-heritage repository (332k digitized books, archives, iconography, Fonds Roud, Personnalités Vaudoises — OAI-PMH), the 15 medieval manuscripts BCUL has on e-codices (IIIF + TEI + DOI), and 331 digitized-press titles from Scriptorium (24 Heures & the Feuille d'avis de Lausanne back to 1762). Modelled with schema.org + Dublin Core and connected through 2.7M author/agent nodes, 2.44M subject concepts, places and the Library nodes; 334k items link to a digitized thumbnail, 15 to a IIIF manifest. Harvested entirely from the library's public APIs (no scraping); rights vary per source (dcterms:rights per record). Engineering: Alma SRU caps every query at 10,000 records → a recursive mms_id-space bisection (594 leaves) yields a provably-complete mirror; ~3s SRU latency → a 12-way concurrent harvest.

shacl_shapes.title: Book core bibliographic integrity
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that every schema:Book record in the Renouvaud catalogue carries the core descriptive metadata needed for discovery: exactly one schema:identifier, at least one dcterms:identifier (ISBN/ISSN/system number), exactly one dcterms:type, exactly one schema:provider (source system name), and exactly one resolvable schema:url back to the catalogue page. It also requires the record to be linked into exactly one schema:isPartOf schema:Collection (its Renouvaud sub-collection), and to have at least one schema:inLanguage (a schema:Language node), one schema:contributor (a schema:Person, the author/editor), and one schema:about (a schema:DefinedTerm subject heading) — losing any of these would silently drop the book out of language-, author-, or subject-based search.

shacl_shapes.title: Book physical holding cluster
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks the BCUL-specific physical-holding properties layered on top of schema.org: b:heldAt (which schema:Library holds a copy), b:shelvingLocation (the physical section/corridor, e.g. 'BCUL site Unithèque' or 'Archives cantonales'), b:availability (loan/availability status), and b:callNumber (the numerus-currens shelf mark used to walk a shelf run in order). These are deliberately left optional (no sh:minCount) because a meaningful share of Book records — electronic-only or catalogue-only titles — plausibly have no physical copy at all; the shape only asserts that whenever these properties ARE present, b:heldAt must point at a real schema:Library instance and the other three must be literals.

datasets.label: vidy.rete — Archives de la Ville de Lausanne (the city archive, on AtoM)
datasets.description: The Lausanne city archive (Archives de la Ville de Lausanne), running the open-source AtoM platform, harvested via EAD export into a schema.org archival graph: 39,723 archival descriptions across 6 collections (administrative, ancient, private, library, city council, documentation) and their fonds → série → dossier → pièce hierarchy — from a 1357 property charter and a 1438 witchcraft death-sentence to the 1933 Registre des commerçants. 2,586 records link their digitised master PDF (schema:associatedMedia) with its exact byte size (schema:contentSize) — 102 GB of scanned archival boxes in all — kept as links to the archive's own server rather than re-hosted. Modelled on w3id.org/rete/vidy, with ISAD(G) fields incl. each unit's physical shelf location. The Lausanne city-archive sibling to the bcul library twin. TEXT_INDEX on for full-text search over its literals.
datasets.license: Descriptions open (Archives de la Ville de Lausanne, archives@lausanne.ch); digitised PDFs © Ville de Lausanne

examples.title: 📄 Digitised documents — open the scanned PDF, with its size
examples.tip:
The 2,586 digitised records of the Ville de Lausanne archive: ?pdf opens the scanned master PDF (schema:associatedMedia) in your browser's viewer, and its exact byte size (schema:contentSize) is shown — these are whole archival boxes, so the largest are 100–200 MB. Biggest first (e.g. the 1933 Registre des commerçants).
The PDFs stay on the archive's own lausanne.ch server — the graph carries the link + size, not the 102 GB of files.

examples.tip:
Every record is a schema:ArchiveComponent with an ISAD(G) level of description — fonds, série, dossier (file), pièce (item). This counts them across the whole city archive.
The archive is one big tree held by the Archives de la Ville de Lausanne.

examples.tip:
The children of one series — the Registre des commerçants lausannois (ADM-C33-2) — each an alphabetical run of merchant cards, with its physical shelf location (the Blécherette store) and its scanned PDF.
Change the isPartOf cote to walk another part of the tree.

shacl_shapes.title: Archive unit core fields
shacl_shapes.tip: Every archival description (schema:ArchiveComponent, co-typed vidy:Unit, 39723 units harvested from the AtoM/EAD export) must carry a reference code (dct:identifier), a link to its holding archive (schema:holdingArchive, pointing to the single schema:ArchiveOrganization node), a permanent URL (schema:url), a description level (vidy:level, e.g. fonds/serie/dossier/piece) and a publication status (vidy:publicationStatus, e.g. published/draft). This flags any unit missing one of these five fields that are present on essentially every one of the 39723 records.

shacl_shapes.title: Digitised scan completeness
shacl_shapes.tip: Every scanned document (schema:DigitalDocument, the 2577 PDFs reachable from a unit via schema:associatedMedia) must declare a file size (schema:contentSize) and a MIME encoding (schema:encodingFormat, e.g. application/pdf); both counts exactly equal the 2577 DigitalDocument instances. Catches scans harvested without size/format metadata, which would silently break the open-the-scanned-PDF-ordered-by-size example query.

shacl_shapes.title: Archive organization identity
shacl_shapes.tip: The single schema:ArchiveOrganization node (the Archives de la Ville de Lausanne itself, the target of every one of the 39723 units' schema:holdingArchive links) must have a name and a URL. Because there is exactly one such node in the whole graph, this also guards against the archive-level identity record being lost or duplicated by a re-harvest.

datasets.label: bcn.rete — Arxiu Municipal de Barcelona (the whole city archive)
datasets.description: The complete Arxiu Municipal de Barcelona — the Barcelona city archive — harvested from its open JSON catalogue API into a schema.org archival graph: 529,614 archival descriptions across 12 archives (the Arxiu Fotogràfic AFB, the Arxiu Històric de la Ciutat AHCB, the Arxiu Municipal Contemporani AMCB, and the ten district archives) and their fonds → series → unit hierarchy, with dates, scope summaries, producers and access conditions (largely public domain — 'De domini públic'). 214,115 records are digitised, carrying 597,138 digital-object references (mostly historical photographs, plus PDFs) with each object's format and exact byte size (schema:associatedMedia + schema:contentSize); the objects live behind the archive's own OpenSeadragon deep-zoom viewer, so each record's schema:url opens its /detail page there. Full-text searchable (TEXT_INDEX) over titles and summaries — the whole photographic memory of Barcelona, from the Somorrostro shanty-beach to the 1992 Olympics. Modelled on w3id.org/rete/bcn; the Barcelona city-archive companion to the Gencat comarcal `arxiu`.
datasets.license: Descriptions largely public domain (De domini públic / Lliure accés, Ajuntament de Barcelona); digital objects © respective archives

shacl_shapes.title: Archival unit (bcn:Unit) integrity
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that every one of the 529,614 archival descriptions carries the core cataloguing fields present on essentially all units in the source API: a dct:identifier, a schema:name, a schema:holdingArchive link to one of the 12 schema:ArchiveOrganization records, a schema:startDate/temporalCoverage, a dereferenceable schema:url, and a bcn:digitized boolean flag (the field the '12 archives — how much is digitised' example groups on). Optional fields (schema:endDate, dct:creator, schema:image, schema:description, bcn:access) are left uncounted since they cover 48%-99% of units, not all.

shacl_shapes.title: Digitised media file (schema:MediaObject) shape
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that every one of the 597,138 schema:MediaObject nodes (the digitised photo/PDF scans attached to units via schema:image and schema:associatedMedia, e.g. the 'Photo gallery' and 'Read the digitised documents' examples) has a schema:name, a schema:encodingFormat (MIME type used to build the '.pdf' filter in the reader example) and a schema:contentSize, since all three are present on essentially every MediaObject (597,137-597,138 of 597,138).

shacl_shapes.title: Archive institution (schema:ArchiveOrganization) shape
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that each of the 12 holding institutions (the Arxiu Fotogràfic AFB, the Arxiu Històric de la Ciutat AHCB, the Arxiu Municipal Contemporani AMC, and the other Barcelona municipal archives that every bcn:Unit points to via schema:holdingArchive) has at least one schema:name literal, since the 'archive' label used to group units in the '12 archives' example is read from this property.

datasets.label: ecal.rete — ECAL: the art & design school library, as a graph (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: A range-queryable graph twin of the ECAL Library — the library of the École cantonale d'art de Lausanne, one of the world's leading art & design schools. 28,741 records (1.02M triples) across Art visuel, Photographie, Design graphique & industriel, Cinéma and Théorie: a tightly-curated collection heavy on Le Corbusier, the International Typeface Corporation, artist's books, auction catalogues (Sotheby's) and film. 93% carry a book cover, rendered inline. Every item links to shared author / subject / place nodes and to its section + call number (the shelf), and 3,014 films sit alongside 25,700 books. Same schema.org + Dublin Core ontology as the BCU twin, so the two federate. Harvested politely from the BiblioMaker OPAC (metadata only); the catalogue asks not to be crawled, so this was a gentle, low-rate, authorized harvest.

examples.sparql:
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?section (COUNT(?w) AS ?items) WHERE {
  ?w dct:isPartOf ?c .
  ?c rdfs:label ?section .
} GROUP BY ?section ORDER BY DESC(?items) LIMIT 15
