shacl_shapes.title: Book required fields
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that every schema:Book (25,699 records) carries its core catalog fields: a title/name pair, a schema:identifier, a dct:type, a schema:provider string, a resolvable schema:url, and a link into its schema:Collection (the library section, e.g. "Photographie" or "Design graphique"). These property counts each equal the full Book count in the source data, so minCount 1 is used. Optional fields (call number, publisher, spatial coverage) are included as unconstrained checks so malformed values still get flagged if present.

shacl_shapes.title: DefinedTerm has a label
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that every schema:DefinedTerm (46,065 of them — the subject-heading/keyword vocabulary attached to Books and VideoObjects via schema:about) has an rdfs:label literal. The relation count (46,065) exactly matches the DefinedTerm instance count in the source data, so a labelless term would mean a broken subject heading that can't be displayed or searched.

shacl_shapes.title: Collection (library section) has a label
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that every schema:Collection (only 10 in this graph — the top-level library sections such as "Photographie", "Design graphique & industriel", "Cinema", "Theorie") has an rdfs:label, since example queries in this catalog group Books by looking up ?c rdfs:label ?section. A Collection without a label would silently disappear from any section browser or facet.

shacl_shapes.title: VideoObject subject links point to DefinedTerm
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that whenever a schema:VideoObject (3,014 films/recordings) carries a schema:about link (25,281 such links in the graph, averaging ~8 subject terms per video), the object is typed as a schema:DefinedTerm rather than a dangling or mistyped node. This is left optional (no minCount) since not every video is guaranteed to carry a subject term, but any link that does exist must resolve to a real DefinedTerm.

datasets.label: GBIF Birds — Spain & Switzerland: 50M sightings with a taxonomic zoom + map (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: Fifty MILLION georeferenced bird (Aves) occurrences — Spain 47.9M, Switzerland 2.26M, 1,104 species — from the GBIF Open Data snapshot (2026-07-01), as one 334M-triple range-queryable file (1.53 GB, remote-lazy over HTTP range). This is the SEMANTIC-ZOOM dataset: every occurrence is rdf:type its species, and each species carries a full taxonomic subClassOf chain Species ⊑ Genus ⊑ Family ⊑ Order ⊑ Aves ⊑ Chordata ⊑ Animalia — so the schema pyramid rolls the 50M sightings up into a 6-LEVEL zoom you can read WITHOUT touching the triple index (open the Schema tab): level 3 = Orders (Passeriformes 29.7M, Charadriiformes 5.1M, Accipitriformes/raptors 2.9M, Anseriformes 2.2M …), level 4 = Families (Fringillidae, Muscicapidae, Accipitridae, Laridae …), level 5 = the 1,104 species. Ask a question about birds at the Order or Family level and you never descend to a single record — the abstraction is the point. ENRICHED build: every species now also carries its COMMON NAME in up to 47 European languages (27,922 language-tagged dwc:vernacularName — French, Catalan, Basque, Welsh, Breton … all present), its IUCN Red List category (967 species; 165 flagged v:sensitive as near-threatened or worse), and precomputed occurrence stats (recordCount, estimatedIndividuals, first/last year). And it is an RDF-STAR showcase: each ADDED fact is a quoted triple annotated with its provenance — << species dwc:vernacularName '…' >> dct:source 'Catalogue of Life' ; prov:generatedAtTime '2026-07-11' — statements about statements, the natural home for who-said-it-and-when. Every occurrence also carries a GeoSPARQL POINT (map view), its country, year, basis-of-record (mostly citizen-science HUMAN_OBSERVATION — eBird & friends), source dataset and its dwc:individualCount where the observer recorded one (33.4M records). IRIs round-trip to live GBIF: occurrence = gbif.org/occurrence/<id>, species owl:sameAs gbif.org/species/<key>. Built KEYLESS from the GBIF AWS Parquet snapshot via DuckDB (scripts/gbif_birds_extract.py + gbif_birds_to_nt.py); names from the GBIF vernacular API, conservation from the IUCN Red List via Wikidata; enrichment emitted as N-Triples-star (scripts/gbif_birds_enrich_nt.py). CC BY-NC 4.0 (GBIF); cite GBIF.org. Selective queries (a species, a small area), the Schema pyramid, and every enrichment lookup are cheap over HTTP range; a full 50M-row aggregate scans the file, so lean on the pyramid for the big picture.

examples.title: ★ Semantic zoom: the taxonomic ladder of a species
examples.tip:
The whole point of this dataset. rdfs:subClassOf+ walks the Barn Swallow (Hirundo rustica) UP its taxonomic ladder: Genus Hirundo → Family Hirundinidae → Order Passeriformes → Class Aves → Phylum Chordata → Kingdom Animalia. This same chain, over all 1,104 species, is what the Schema tab rolls the 50M sightings up into — open it to see the 6-level pyramid (level 3 = Orders: Passeriformes 29.7M, raptors 2.9M …).
Ask a bird question at the Order or Family level and you never touch a single record. Swap the species key (owl:sameAs gbif.org/species/<key>) for any of the 1,104.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX dwc: <http://rs.tdwg.org/dwc/terms/>
PREFIX v: <https://w3id.org/rete/gbif/vocab#>
SELECT ?rank ?name WHERE {
  <https://w3id.org/rete/gbif/taxon/species/9515886> rdfs:subClassOf+ ?anc .
  ?anc rdfs:label ?name ; dwc:taxonRank ?rank .
}

examples.title: 🌍 A bird's common name in every European language
examples.tip:
New in this build: every species carries its common name in up to 47 European languages as a language-tagged dwc:vernacularName. This lists them all for the Barn Swallow (Hirundo rustica, gbif.org/species/9515886) — ca 'Oreneta vulgar', fr 'Hirondelle rustique', eu (Basque) 'Enara arrunt', cy (Welsh) 'gwennol', br (Breton) 'Gwennili-siminal', cs 'vlaštovka obecná' …
Swap the species key (2481912 White Stork, 2480649 Bearded Vulture) to read any of the 1,020 named species in your own language.

examples.title: ✨ RDF-star: where did this name come from?
examples.tip:
The headline of this build — provenance as RDF-star. Each name assertion is itself a QUOTED TRIPLE << species dwc:vernacularName "…" >> annotated with dct:source (which checklist it came from) and prov:generatedAtTime (when we added it). Here: every name of the Egyptian Vulture (Neophron percnopterus, IUCN Endangered) with its source — fr 'Petit vautour', ca 'Miloca', es 'Alimoche'.
This is a statement ABOUT a statement: the name has no node of its own, so the provenance lives on the quoted triple. Add `prov:wasDerivedFrom ?api` to get the live GBIF API URL each name was pulled from.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX dwc: <http://rs.tdwg.org/dwc/terms/>
PREFIX dct: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/>
PREFIX prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#>
SELECT ?name ?src ?when WHERE {
  << <https://w3id.org/rete/gbif/taxon/species/2480696> dwc:vernacularName ?name >>
     dct:source ?src ; prov:generatedAtTime ?when .
}

examples.title: 🔎 Find a bird by its Catalan name
examples.tip:
Reverse lookup: search the multilingual names instead of the scientific ones. 'oreneta' is Catalan for swallow, so this finds every swallow species recorded in Spain + Switzerland — Oreneta vulgar (Barn Swallow), de ribera (Sand Martin), cuablanca (House Martin), de cingle (Crag Martin) …
Change "oreneta" and the language tag to search another language — LANG(?n)="fr" with "mésange" for the tits, "es" with "águila" for the eagles.

examples.title: 🛡️ Threatened birds: the IUCN Red List species
examples.tip:
165 of the 1,104 species carry an IUCN Red List category worse than Least Concern (NT near-threatened → CR critically endangered → EX). This lists them with their English name, most-threatened first: the Egyptian Vulture (EN), Aquatic Warbler (VU), Balearic Shearwater (CR) … Conservation status comes from the IUCN Red List via Wikidata; each v:iucnStatus assertion carries its own RDF-star provenance.
Drop the FILTER for just CR/EN to see only the gravest cases, or map them with the next example.

examples.title: 🗺️ Map the Endangered & Critically Endangered birds
examples.tip:
Conservation crossed with geography: every occurrence of a species the IUCN lists as Endangered (EN) or Critically Endangered (CR), mapped across Spain + Switzerland — Egyptian Vulture, Balearic Shearwater, Aquatic Warbler, Steppe Eagle … Switch Output to Map. Fans out over the threatened species (each cheap and selective via v:iucnStatus), so it is LIMITed.
Swap the FILTER to ("VU") to add the vulnerable species, or to a single status for a cleaner map.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX v: <https://w3id.org/rete/gbif/vocab#>
PREFIX geo: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>
SELECT ?wkt ?st WHERE {
  ?sp v:iucnStatus ?st . FILTER(?st IN ("EN", "CR"))
  ?o a ?sp ; geo:asWKT ?wkt .
}
LIMIT 3000

examples.title: 📊 A species' record book: counts, individuals, span
examples.tip:
Per-species occurrence statistics, precomputed at build time and stored (with RDF-star provenance) so you read them without scanning the 333M records: v:recordCount (how many sightings), v:estimatedIndividuals (the summed dwc:individualCount — the 'number estimated'), and the first/last year seen. White Stork (Ciconia ciconia): 330,039 records, ~7.08M individuals counted, 1579→2026.
Each occurrence also carries its own dwc:individualCount where the observer recorded one — swap the species key for any bird.

examples.title: 🗺️ Map a species: Barn Swallow across Iberia & the Alps
examples.tip:
Every occurrence carries a GeoSPARQL POINT. This maps the first 4,000 Barn Swallow (Hirundo rustica) sightings — Switch Output to Map. Selective by species with a LIMIT, so it early-outs and stays cheap over HTTP range (it never scans the 1.2 GB file).
Swap the species key for 5231190 (House Sparrow), 2490719 (Blackbird), 2492956 (Blackcap) to map another bird.

examples.title: Every swallow species (family Hirundinidae)
examples.tip:
rdfs:subClassOf+ DOWN from a family node lists all species it contains (species ⊑ genus ⊑ family, so it's transitive) — the swallows & martins recorded in Spain + Switzerland: Barn Swallow, House Martin, Sand Martin, Crag Martin, Red-rumped Swallow …
Swap the family for /Accipitridae (hawks & eagles), /Anatidae (ducks & geese), /Laridae (gulls & terns) to browse another branch.

examples.title: A species' records: House Sparrow, with country & year
examples.tip:
The raw records for one species (House Sparrow, Passer domesticus): each ?occ IRI round-trips to its page on gbif.org/occurrence/<id>, with the country and year of the sighting. Bounded by species + LIMIT, so it's a cheap lazy read.
Most records are HUMAN_OBSERVATION — citizen-science checklists (eBird and national schemes) dominate bird data.

examples.title: 🗺️ Map the raptors: where are the Accipitridae?
examples.tip:
A taxonomy-driven map: all occurrences whose species is (transitively) in the hawk-and-eagle family Accipitridae — hitting the pyramid's Family level, then joining to points. This crosses the taxonomy INTO the geography. Heavier than a single-species map (it fans out over many species), so it's LIMITed; give it a moment on a cold cache.
This is the 'ask at the Family level, get a map' pattern — no need to name every eagle and harrier species.

examples.title: One sighting, the full record
examples.tip:
Everything the graph knows about a single occurrence — its species type, GeoSPARQL point, country, year, basis-of-record and source dataset. The subject IRI is the live GBIF occurrence page.
Swap the occurrence IRI for any ?occ you get from the other examples.

examples.title: Taxonomic richness: which genera have the most species?
examples.tip:
A pure-taxonomy question, answered over the small T-Box (the ~13k subClassOf/label triples) — NOT the 50M records, so it's cheap. Counts how many species each genus contains: Emberiza (buntings) 21, Anas (dabbling ducks) 18, Calidris (sandpipers) 18, Sylvia (typical warblers) 18 … the most speciose bird genera recorded in Spain + Switzerland.
This is the ontology talking, not the observations — the pyramid's raw material.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX dwc: <http://rs.tdwg.org/dwc/terms/>
PREFIX v: <https://w3id.org/rete/gbif/vocab#>
SELECT ?genus (COUNT(?sp) AS ?n) WHERE {
  ?sp dwc:taxonRank "species" ; rdfs:subClassOf ?g .
  ?g rdfs:label ?genus ; dwc:taxonRank "genus" .
}
GROUP BY ?genus ORDER BY DESC(?n) LIMIT 25

examples.title: 🗺️ Map the Bearded Vulture — Alps ↔ Pyrenees
examples.tip:
The Bearded Vulture (Gypaetus barbatus, gbif.org/species/2480649) — one of Europe's rarest raptors, its bone-eating lammergeier — maps beautifully across BOTH countries: a native Pyrenean stronghold in Spain and the famous Alpine reintroduction in Switzerland. Bounded to one species, so it's a cheap lazy map.
Try 2481912 (White Stork), 4352332 (Greater Flamingo), 2481047 (Peregrine Falcon) for other icons.

examples.title: 📈 White Stork sightings by year
examples.tip:
The White Stork (Ciconia ciconia) recorded per year — switch Output to Time to see the curve. Bounded to one species, and the count climbs steeply with the rise of citizen-science checklists (~52k in 2024). A window onto observer effort as much as bird numbers.
Swap the species key to chart any bird's recording history; the low current-year bar is just the year-to-date.

examples.title: How is a species recorded? (basis of record)
examples.tip:
Where the data comes from, for one species (Blue Tit, Cyanistes caeruleus): HUMAN_OBSERVATION (a birdwatcher's checklist) dwarfs PRESERVED_SPECIMEN (a museum skin), LIVING_SPECIMEN (a ringed/zoo bird) and MACHINE_OBSERVATION (a camera/acoustic sensor). Bird data is overwhelmingly citizen science.
Museum-heavy groups look very different — try an insect or a plant species in the full-taxa build if we ship one.

examples.title: 🗺️ Map a whole genus: the falcons (Falco)
examples.tip:
Taxonomy → geography at the GENUS level: every falcon (genus Falco — Kestrel, Peregrine, Hobby, Merlin, Eleonora's …) mapped in one query via rdfs:subClassOf+, no need to name each species. Fans out over several species, so it's LIMITed and a touch heavier than a single-species map.
Swap /genus/Falco for /genus/Aquila (true eagles), /genus/Larus (large gulls), /genus/Anas (dabbling ducks).

examples.title: The bird orders, by species richness
examples.tip:
Every bird Order and how many species it holds, over the T-Box only (cheap): the perching birds Passeriformes dominate with 410 species, then Charadriiformes (waders & gulls) 148, Anseriformes (wildfowl) 123 — and Psittaciformes (parrots) 60, a telltale sign of escaped/feral cage-birds now breeding in Spain (Monk & Rose-ringed Parakeets).
This is level 3 of the schema pyramid as a query; the Schema tab shows the same rollup weighted by sightings instead of species.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
PREFIX dwc: <http://rs.tdwg.org/dwc/terms/>
PREFIX v: <https://w3id.org/rete/gbif/vocab#>
SELECT ?order (COUNT(DISTINCT ?sp) AS ?n) WHERE {
  ?sp dwc:taxonRank "species" ; rdfs:subClassOf+ ?o .
  ?o dwc:taxonRank "order" ; rdfs:label ?order .
}
GROUP BY ?order ORDER BY DESC(?n)

examples.title: Genera in a family: the ducks & geese (Anatidae)
examples.tip:
One step of the taxonomy: the genera directly inside family Anatidae (wildfowl) — Aix, Anas (dabbling ducks), Anser (grey geese), Aythya (diving ducks), Branta, Mergus, Tadorna … the shape of a family at a glance.
Swap /family/Anatidae for /family/Muscicapidae (chats & flycatchers), /family/Laridae (gulls), /family/Fringillidae (finches).

examples.title: 🗺️ Flamingos in Spain (Doñana, Ebro delta, Fuente de Piedra)
examples.tip:
A species map narrowed to ONE country: Greater Flamingo (Phoenicopterus roseus) sightings in Spain only — the great saline wetlands light up (the Guadalquivir marshes at Doñana, the Ebro delta, the Fuente de Piedra lagoon). Bounded by species AND v:inCountry, so it's a cheap, targeted lazy read.
Switch the country to /country/CH for the handful of Swiss records, or drop the country line to map both.

examples.title: 🌳 The owl family tree (graph)
examples.tip:
The taxonomy rendered as a NODE-LINK graph — switch Output to Graph. rdfs:subClassOf+ gathers everything under the owl family Strigidae, then the CONSTRUCT rebuilds the tree: family → genera (Athene, Asio, Bubo, Strix, Otus …) → species. A living picture of a clade, all from the T-Box.
Swap /family/Strigidae for /order/Anseriformes (a bigger tree), /family/Accipitridae (hawks & eagles), or any taxon node.

shacl_shapes.title: Occurrence core fields
shacl_shapes.tip:
Checks that occurrence records typed under a species class (e.g. species/9515886 and species/5231190, two of the dataset's highest-volume species) carry the mandatory GBIF fields: a country via dct:spatial (schema:Country), a source dataset via void:inDataset (void:Dataset), a dwc:basisOfRecord code, and a geo:asWKT geometry literal.
These four properties are present on essentially 100% of occurrences for these species per the class_links counts, so minCount 1 is enforced; dwc:year (~99% coverage) and dwc:individualCount (~66% coverage) are included but left optional since they do not cover every occurrence.

shacl_shapes.title: Taxonomic-ladder node fields
shacl_shapes.tip:
Checks every node in the taxonomy tree (kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species — reached via sh:targetSubjectsOf dwc:taxonRank, since ranks are modeled as classes-of-classes rather than instances of one shared 'Taxon' class) carries a dwc:taxonRank code and at least one rdfs:label.
Optional properties cover the rest of the hierarchy metadata: rdfs:subClassOf links a rank to its parent rank (absent only for the root kingdom, so not required), owl:sameAs links a species to an external identifier such as Wikidata, and vocab#recordCount/firstYear/lastYear are summary statistics attached only at the species leaf level (not on higher ranks).

datasets.label: worldcup.rete — FIFA World Cup 2022: stats, player careers & multi-source predictions (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The 2022 FIFA World Cup as one queryable knowledge graph, weaving together three things you rarely see in the same place. STATS: all 64 matches (group + full knockout) with scores, penalty shootouts, ~170 goals and their scorers, 8 stadiums with coordinates, and the final standings — Argentina champions, France runners-up. PLAYER EVOLUTION: club-by-club career timelines with start/end years (linked to Wikidata) for the marquee players, so you can trace Messi from Newell's Old Boys to Inter Miami. PREDICTIONS: what different forecasters said would happen, as timestamped, source-attributed claims — FiveThirtyEight's SPI model across 6 snapshots (pre-tournament through the quarter-finals, so you can watch Argentina's title probability dip after the shock Saudi Arabia loss and climb back), plus pre-tournament bookmaker and Opta champion odds. Each prediction is an n-ary node carrying probability + source (PROV-O) + forecast date, so you can compare parties, track how the odds moved, and score who called it best against the real result. Modelled with schema.org + Dublin Core + GeoSPARQL + a small wc: vocab on w3id.org/rete. Open data (OpenFootball, FiveThirtyEight CC-BY, Wikidata CC0).
datasets.license: Open data (OpenFootball PD, 538 CC-BY, Wikidata CC0)

examples.title: 👥 A team's full squad
examples.tip:
The complete 26-man roster (from Wikipedia) — shirt number, position, club at the tournament, and date of birth. Here Argentina; swap the team IRI for any nation.
This is the FULL squad, not just the goalscorers — every dataset player links to their national team via wc:representedTeam.

examples.title: 🏟️ Clubs that sent the most players
examples.tip:
Now that every squad is in the graph, ask which clubs supplied the most World Cup players — the elite European sides dominate (Barcelona, Bayern, Man City), with the host nation's club a surprise high entry.
GROUP BY over wc:clubAtTournament across all 32/48 full squads.

examples.title: What's in this graph
examples.tip:
The shape of the WC2022 graph: 588 Predictions (538 × 6 dates + Opta + bookmaker), 162 Goals, 90 CareerStints, 64 Matches, 8 Stadiums.
One row per rdf:type. The class name comes from the IRI, not from rdfs:label — only the four wc:Outcome classes carry a label, so joining ?c rdfs:label ?kind used to drop every row (#212).

examples.title: 🏆 The Golden Boot (top scorers)
examples.tip:
Who scored most: Kylián Mbappé 8 (the actual Golden Boot), Messi 7, then Álvarez & Giroud 4. Own goals are excluded via FILTER NOT EXISTS.
Names are normalised so 'Mbappé' and 'Kylian Mbappé' count as one player.

examples.title: 📈 Argentina's title odds, snapshot by snapshot (538)
examples.tip:
The predictions payoff. FiveThirtyEight's probability that Argentina would WIN the cup, at each of 6 forecast dates: 0.085 pre-tournament → 0.047 right after the shock loss to Saudi Arabia (Nov 24) → climbing to 0.315 by the quarter-finals.
Switch Output → Time for the curve. Change the team IRI (…/team/France, /Brazil, /Morocco) to trace another run.

examples.title: 🎲 Who was the favourite? Champion odds by forecaster
examples.tip:
Different parties, side by side: the pre-tournament (Nov 20) probability each source gave for winning the whole thing. Brazil led every forecaster (book 17%, Opta 15%); Argentina — who actually won — sat 2nd around 13-14%.
This is the 'compare who predicted what' query, joined on the shared team.

examples.title: 🥅 The final, goal by goal
examples.tip:
Argentina 3-3 France (Argentina won 4-2 on penalties) — the goals in order: Messi 23'(pen), Di María 36', then Mbappé's hat-trick 80'(pen), 81', 118', with Messi's 108'.
match/064 is the final; swap it for match/063 (third place) or any group match.

examples.title: ⚽ Player evolution: Messi's club career
examples.tip:
The temporal dimension. Every club stint of Lionel Messi with start/end years — Newell's Old Boys → Barcelona (2004-2021) → PSG → Inter Miami — pulled from Wikidata (P54 + date qualifiers) and attached to the WC scorer node.
Swap the player IRI for …/player/Kylian_Mbappé, /Olivier_Giroud, /Luka_Modrić.

examples.title: 🗺️ The eight Qatar stadiums
examples.tip:
Every venue as a GeoSPARQL point — switch Output → Map to see them clustered around Doha. The Lusail Iconic Stadium (88,966) hosted the final.
Each match links to its wc:venue, so you can map where any game was played.

examples.title: 🚩 The knockout bracket
examples.tip:
Every knockout tie from Round of 16 to the Final, with the score in the label and the date. The wc:stage predicate partitions the tournament (group / round_of_16 / quarter_final / semi_final / third_place / final).
Drop the FILTER to include all 64 matches.

examples.title: 📊 The title race, snapshot by snapshot
examples.tip:
The whole tournament as a shifting leaderboard: FiveThirtyEight's champion probability for every team above 10%, at each of the 6 forecast dates. Read top to bottom and watch the story unfold — Brazil the runaway favourite (peaking at 33% on Dec 6) until Croatia knocked them out on Dec 9, and Argentina surging from off-the-list after the Saudi shock to 32% and the top.
Lower the FILTER threshold for the long tail; swap the source IRI to compare forecasters.

shacl_shapes.title: Person squad-record shape
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that every schema:Person (players, 984 of them) has a name, and that any team-affiliation properties they carry (national representedTeam, club clubAtTournament) point to real schema:SportsTeam nodes rather than literals or dangling values. birthDate/caps/position/shirtNumber are constrained to be literals when present, since not every Person row in this graph is a full squad entry (e.g. some are goal-scorers only).

shacl_shapes.title: SportsTeam roster shape
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that any label a schema:SportsTeam carries (rdfs:label — covers both the 32 national squads and the club teams referenced via clubAtTournament) is a plain literal, and that every wc:squadPlayer it lists resolves to a real schema:Person node. Not every SportsTeam is required to have squadPlayer entries, since club-side teams in this graph are only ever the object of clubAtTournament, never the subject of squadPlayer.

shacl_shapes.title: Prediction completeness shape
shacl_shapes.tip: Every wc:Prediction (588 forecast records, one per team per PROV-tracked forecasting run) must carry all six of its core fields: prov:generatedAtTime and wc:forecastDate (when it was made), prov:wasAttributedTo a real prov:Agent (which model/source made it), wc:aboutTeam a real schema:SportsTeam, wc:outcome a real wc:Outcome node, and wc:probability. minCount 1 is used on all six because the counts (588) exactly match the Prediction instance count, meaning these are mandatory fields on every prediction, not optional annotations.

shacl_shapes.title: Goal attribution shape
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that every wc:Goal (162 of the ~170 goals in the tournament, excluding a few unmatched edge cases) is attributed to exactly one real schema:SportsTeam via wc:forTeam. minCount/maxCount 1 are both used because the wc:forTeam count (162) exactly equals the Goal instance count and a goal logically belongs to a single team.

datasets.label: worldcup2026.rete — FIFA World Cup 2026: a LIVE snapshot, cross-checked vs live sources (results + player careers)
datasets.description: The 2026 FIFA World Cup (Canada · USA · Mexico; 48 teams, 12 groups, Round of 32) as a LIVE, IN-PROGRESS knowledge graph. ⚠ Snapshot: the group stage, Round of 32, Round of 16 and quarter-finals are played (100 matches) — the semi-finals (France v Spain, England v Argentina) and final are still to come, modelled as scheduled fixtures. ✓ Cross-checked against live sources (Yahoo Sports, CBS, FIFA) on 2026-07-12: the results, the four semi-finalists (France, Spain, England, Argentina) and the bracket all match — though OpenFootball's community data can carry the odd scorer-level error (it credits Lisandro rather than Lautaro Martínez for Argentina's late QF goal). It holds every played match with scores, penalty shootouts, goals and scorers (Messi & Mbappé lead the race on 8), 16 stadiums across three countries with coordinates, and club career timelines (linked to Wikidata) for the top scorers. Unlike the 2022 twin there is NO prediction layer — FiveThirtyEight is retired and no 2026 forecast time-series is available. schema.org + Dublin Core + GeoSPARQL + a wc: vocab on w3id.org/rete.

examples.title: ⚽ Player evolution: Mbappé's club career
examples.tip:
The temporal dimension, same as the 2022 twin: Kylian Mbappé's club stints with start/end years, from Wikidata (P54 + date qualifiers).
Swap the IRI for …/player/Lionel_Messi, /Erling_Haaland, /Jude_Bellingham.

examples.title: 🗺️ 16 stadiums across three countries
examples.tip:
The first tri-nation World Cup — switch Output → Map to see the venues spread from Vancouver and Seattle down to Mexico City. Each carries capacity and a GeoSPARQL point.
The Estadio Azteca and MetLife (the final's venue) are the biggest.

examples.title: 💥 Penalty shootouts (the knockout drama)
examples.tip:
Every knockout tie decided from the spot — matches carrying wc:homePenalties / wc:awayPenalties. Big names went out this way (Germany and the Netherlands both fell in the Round of 32).
The label shows the 120-minute score; the penalty columns show the shootout.

examples.title: 🥅 Goals per group stage vs knockout
examples.tip:
How the goals spread across the rounds — the 48-team group stage is high-scoring, the knockouts tighten up.
Group by wc:stage over the goals, joined through each goal's match.

shacl_shapes.title: Player core fields
shacl_shapes.tip: Every schema:Person (player) must carry a name — the card shows schema:name on all 1,513 Person instances, so it's required. birthDate/caps/position/shirtNumber/clubAtTournament/representedTeam are common (1,248 of 1,513, i.e. players with a recorded tournament appearance) but not universal — some Person rows may be staff/unlinked records — so those stay optional. representedTeam and clubAtTournament must point at a real schema:SportsTeam node (the club or national team the player is tied to).

shacl_shapes.title: Team label + roster links
shacl_shapes.tip: schema:SportsTeam covers both the 48 national teams AND the real-world clubs players belong to (~1,296 total), so rdfs:label is required (covers 1,248/1,296, i.e. essentially every team/club node) while wc:squadPlayer — the national-team roster edge to a schema:Person — is optional since it fires only for the small national-team subset, not for every club. When present, squadPlayer must point at a real Person node.

shacl_shapes.title: Goal completeness
shacl_shapes.tip: Every wc:Goal (291 of them) must record all four facts needed to make sense of it: which team it was for (wc:forTeam -> schema:SportsTeam), which match it happened in (wc:inMatch -> wc:Match), the minute it was scored (wc:minute), and who scored it (wc:scoredBy -> schema:Person) — all four relations have exactly 291 triples in the card, i.e. one each per Goal, so all are required and single-valued.

shacl_shapes.title: Match fixture fields
shacl_shapes.tip: Every wc:Match (102 of them, the whole schedule through the quarter-finals per the card) must have a label, a startDate, be linked into the wc:Tournament via dct:isPartOf, and name its awayTeam — all four counts equal 102 in the card, i.e. one each per Match, so all are required. awayTeam must resolve to a real schema:SportsTeam.

datasets.label: tracking.rete — a full match as a spatiotemporal graph (player + ball 2D positions over time)
datasets.description: A full football match as a SPATIOTEMPORAL graph: the 2D position of every player and the ball, ~5 frames/second across ~94 minutes, on a 105x68 m pitch — 2.55M triples, ~637k position rows. From Metrica Sports' open sample data (anonymised). Each position carries tr:t (seconds), tr:x, tr:y and tr:object, so you can query any object's location in any time window — the basis for a 2D movement replay (a query returns a frame; interpolate between frames to animate). The 'movement over time' at the finest grain, complementing the tournament-scale forecasts and career-scale transfers in the World Cup graphs. tr: vocab on w3id.org/rete.

examples.title: What's in this tracking graph
examples.tip:
The shape of a spatiotemporal match: 27 tracked objects (players + ball), ~28k time frames, ~637k position rows.
Each position = tr:object + tr:t (s) + tr:x + tr:y on a 105x68 m pitch.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX tr: <https://w3id.org/rete/tracking#>
SELECT ("positions" AS ?metric) (COUNT(?p) AS ?n) WHERE { ?p tr:t ?t }

examples.title: 📸 Everyone's position at one instant
examples.tip:
A single animation frame: every player and the ball at t≈300 s (5:00). A 2D replay is just this query, stepped through time and drawn on a pitch.
Widen the window or change the time to scrub.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX tr: <https://w3id.org/rete/tracking#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?obj ?x ?y WHERE {
  ?p tr:t ?t ; tr:object ?o ; tr:x ?x ; tr:y ?y .
  ?o rdfs:label ?obj .
  FILTER(?t >= 300 && ?t < 300.2)
} ORDER BY ?obj

examples.title: 🏃 One player's path over 30 seconds
examples.tip:
The trajectory of Home #10 across half a minute — the raw material of a movement trail or heatmap. Bounded by object + time window, so it's a cheap lazy read.
Swap the object IRI (…/obj/home_10) for any player or …/obj/ball.

shacl_shapes.title: Player has identity fields
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks every tr:Player instance (26 tracked bodies excluding the ball) carries exactly one rdfs:label (display name), one tr:jersey (shirt number), and one tr:team assignment. minCount 1 is used because the counts of label/jersey/team triples (26 each) exactly match the 26 Player instances, i.e. these are present on every player, not optional extras.

shacl_shapes.title: Match config is complete
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks the single tr:TrackedMatch node (the whole-game record) carries exactly one rdfs:label, tr:fps (sampling rate, ~5/sec), tr:pitchLength and tr:pitchWidth (the 105x68 m pitch dimensions), and tr:source (provenance string, Metrica Sports). All five properties have a 1:1 count against the single TrackedMatch instance, so minCount/maxCount 1 enforce that a viewer can always read pitch geometry and frame rate before rendering.

shacl_shapes.title: Position sample is well-formed
shacl_shapes.tip: The ~637,746 position-observation nodes (one per tracked body per timestamped frame) have no rdf:type of their own, so this shape targets them structurally via sh:targetSubjectsOf tr:t instead of sh:targetClass. It checks each sample carries exactly one tr:t (seconds), tr:x, tr:y coordinate, and exactly one tr:object link pointing to either a tr:Player or the tr:Ball, catching any orphan or malformed frame in the spatiotemporal trajectory data.

datasets.label: dance.rete — salsa duets as a motion knowledge graph: partner-relative steps + hand contact (CoMPAS3D, remote, lazy)
datasets.description: Partnered social DANCE as a motion knowledge graph — the 'movement over time' idea with limbs, roles and a partner. From CoMPAS3D (Rosie Lab, SFU): 9 pairs / 18 dancers across beginner, intermediate and professional skill, improvising LA-style salsa to 4 songs (with tempo), captured on a 20-camera Vicon system and fitted to SMPL-X. This graph turns 72 recorded performances and 2,920 annotated 8-count SEGMENTS into something queryable. Each segment is typed by the move(s) it contains — an OWL 2 QL subclass hierarchy straight from the CoMPAS3D glossary (RightTurn / LeftTurn ⊑ Turn ⊑ Move; CrossBodyLead / Enchufla / Copa / DileQueNo / ChangeOfDirection ⊑ Figure ⊑ Move; Lady / ManStyling ⊑ Styling) so 🧠 Reason answers 'all turns' (521), 'all figures' (1,153) or 'all moves' (3,968) from the leaf types — plus its hold (open / closed / crossed / shadow), timing and turn flags. Two DERIVED layers make it distinctive, computed from the raw motion (validated against the annotations, 0.97 agreement): the follower's position in the LEADER'S reference frame (dance:followerMeanForward / followerMeanLeft — the steps relative to the partner) and inter-dancer HAND CONTACT (dance:handContactFraction, from hand-marker proximity). The derived hand metric recovers a real proficiency signal it was never told: beginners keep hands connected 92% of the time, intermediates 72%, the professional pair only 59% — more skill means MORE open figures, throws and releases, not fewer. Dancers, pairs, skill levels and songs round out the entity graph. Modelled with schema.org (Person / MusicRecording) + PROV + OWL-Time + a dance: vocab on w3id.org/rete. Lossless companions sit beside it on R2: a wide `segments` table, the full 30 fps `frames` motion streams (leader/follower pelvis xyz + leader-frame offset + hand distance — the robot / virtual-environment export surface), and a flat `triples` table (Parquet + DuckDB). Built by data/dance-kg/scripts/{build_nt,build_parquet}.py → rete build --pyramid-algo types --card. CC-BY-NC-4.0 (non-commercial; audio rights retained by owners — no video or audio is republished, only derived motion + annotations). Tiny (531 KB) — explore freely.

examples.title: ▶ Watch a couple dance (3D + time)
examples.tip:
Each row plays that couple's ACTUAL salsa motion as an interactive 3D skeleton, right in the results — one take per pair, across all three skill levels. Drag to orbit, ⛶ to enlarge.
License-clean: the CoMPAS3D motion only (an articulated stick figure), NO SMPL-X body mesh. The glb URL in the last column is what the 3D cell renders and autoplays.

examples.title: 📊 Each couple — the numbers + the dance
examples.tip:
The DIFFERENT PARTS of each couple's dance — how many 8-count moves they do, how connected their hands stay, how far apart they dance — right next to the 3D animation of that exact take. Ordered by hand connection, so the skill gradient reads down the table (beginners tightest at the top, the professional pair loosest) while you watch each couple move.
Annotated couples only (pairs 1–5); '▶ Watch a couple dance' shows all nine.

examples.title: 🎞 Freeze-frame each move — jump the 3D to the moment
examples.tip:
We know the exact second every move happens (dance:startTime / dance:endTime), so the query builds the glb URL with a TIME FRAGMENT — …skeleton.glb#t=8.3 — and the 3D cell freezes the couple at that moment. Scroll one take's moves and see the pose the instant each one lands: the cross-body lead, the right turn, the enchufla, the dile que no.
The published clips are 16 s, so this shows the take's first ~15 s; re-bake full-length to seek the whole 2.5-minute dance.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX dance: <https://w3id.org/rete/dance#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?start ?move ?clip WHERE {
  <https://w3id.org/rete/dance/id/pair3-song1-take1> dance:hasSegment ?seg ; dance:animation ?glb .
  ?seg dance:section "Together" ; dance:startTime ?start ; dance:endTime ?end ; rdfs:label ?move .
  FILTER(?start < 15)
  BIND((?start + ?end)/2 AS ?mid)
  BIND(URI(CONCAT(STR(?glb), "#t=", STR(?mid))) AS ?clip)
} ORDER BY ?start

examples.title: What's in this dance graph
examples.tip:
The shape of the graph: 18 dancers in 9 pairs, 72 recorded salsa performances, and 2,920 annotated 8-count move segments.
Each segment is one move with its hold, timing and derived partner-relative + hand-contact metrics.

examples.title: 💃 Hand connection by skill level
examples.tip:
The headline finding, straight from the graph: the fraction of each move spent with the partners' hands in contact, averaged by the pair's proficiency. It's INVERSE — beginners hold on 92% of the time, the professional pair only 59% (pros dance more open figures, throws and releases).
Both columns are DERIVED from the raw SMPL-X motion, not annotated.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX dance: <https://w3id.org/rete/dance#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?skill (COUNT(?seg) AS ?segments) (ROUND(AVG(?hcf)*1000)/1000 AS ?handContact) (ROUND(AVG(?sep)*100)/100 AS ?separation_m) WHERE {
  ?perf dance:hasSegment ?seg ; dance:hasLeader ?l .
  ?l dance:hasSkillLevel ?sl . ?sl rdfs:label ?skill .
  ?seg dance:handContactFraction ?hcf ; dance:meanCoupleSeparation ?sep .
} GROUP BY ?skill ORDER BY DESC(?handContact)

examples.title: 🧠 Every turn in the corpus
examples.tip:
This example auto-enables the 🧠 Reason toggle. Segments are typed with the LEAF move (RightTurn / LeftTurn), never dance:Turn directly — but the OWL 2 QL move taxonomy has RightTurn ⊑ Turn ⊑ Move, so the reasoner returns all 521 turns anyway.
Swap dance:Turn for dance:Figure (1,153) or dance:Move (3,968) to widen the net.

examples.title: 🎼 One dance, move by move
examples.tip:
The paired-move timeline of a single take — Pair 3 (beginner), song 1 — as its 8-count moves in order with the hand hold each uses. This is one improvised salsa read as a sequence.
Swap the performance IRI (…/pair3-song1-take1) for any pairN-songM-takeK.

examples.title: 📍 Where the follower is, by move
examples.tip:
The partner-relative layer: the follower's mean position in the LEADER'S reference frame, per move type (forward = ahead of the leader, left = to the leader's left). Basic step keeps the follower ahead; a swap/cross-body pulls them back and across.
These offsets are computed per-frame from the SMPL-X motion, then averaged over each segment.

examples.title: ⚠️ Execution errors by skill
examples.tip:
Segments annotated as execution errors (off-beat, mixed signals, misstep, failed move) tallied by the pair's proficiency. Beginners rack up the most; the professional pair has none flagged in the annotated takes.
Errors are their own annotation track (dance:ErrorSegment), typed by the specific error kind.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX dance: <https://w3id.org/rete/dance#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?skill (COUNT(?e) AS ?errors) WHERE {
  ?perf dance:hasSegment ?e ; dance:hasLeader ?l .
  ?e a dance:ErrorSegment .
  ?l dance:hasSkillLevel/rdfs:label ?skill .
} GROUP BY ?skill ORDER BY DESC(?errors)

shacl_shapes.title: Performance has one pair, one leader, one follower
shacl_shapes.tip: Every dance:Performance must link to exactly one dance:Pair (via dance:performedBy), exactly one leader and one follower dancer (dance:hasLeader/dance:hasFollower, both typed dance:Dancer), and at least one movement segment (dance:hasSegment). Counts for hasLeader/hasFollower/performedBy are each 72, exactly matching the 72 Performance instances, so this is a 1:1 relation, not just 'usually present'.

shacl_shapes.title: Every movement segment has a full timeline record
shacl_shapes.tip: A 'segment' in this graph is any node typed as one of the four role classes dance:PairedSegment, dance:FollowerSegment, dance:LeaderSegment or dance:ErrorSegment (these four counts sum to exactly 2,920, the total segment count). This shape checks each such segment carries a label plus its startTime/endTime/duration/section exactly once -- these four predicates each fire exactly 2,920 times dataset-wide, i.e. on literally every segment, so minCount/maxCount 1 is not a guess.

shacl_shapes.title: Motion-capture metrics on named move types stay single-valued
shacl_shapes.tip: For the two move-type classes with directly evidenced schema (dance:Steps, dance:CrossBodyLead), the five motion-capture aggregates (followerMeanForward/Left, handContactFraction, meanCoupleSeparation, meanHandDistance) are present on roughly 97% of instances -- not quite universal, so they stay optional here (no minCount) -- but this shape still catches the data-quality bug of a segment somehow getting two conflicting values for the same metric (maxCount 1).

datasets.label: subtitles.rete — one film, 20 languages, over time (Tears of Steel · CC-BY)
datasets.description: Tears of Steel — the Blender Foundation's open sci-fi short — subtitled in TWENTY languages, as one temporal + multilingual knowledge graph (14,376 triples). It's the 'over time' idea applied to language. Every su:Line is a MOMENT in the film (su:start / su:end in seconds) carrying the SAME utterance in all 20 tongues as language-tagged literals: English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Dutch, Russian, Polish, Czech, Hungarian, Greek, Portuguese (BR), Danish, Indonesian, Norwegian, Japanese, Chinese (Simplified + Traditional), and right-to-left Persian & Hebrew. Each su:Cue is one language track's own timed segment (its real start/end + su:text "…"@lang), aligned to the English original by time-overlap — 1,536 cues over 76 lines. So you can scrub a timeline and watch the dialogue appear in every language at once, ask 'what's on screen at 1:05 in Japanese and Persian', diff how one line was rendered across 20 cultures, or full-text-search the dialogue (a TEXT_INDEX is baked in). Subtitles are all timed to the same audio, so the shared timeline IS the cross-language alignment. Open data: Tears of Steel (CC BY 3.0, Blender Foundation, mango.blender.org), subtitle .srt files from media.xiph.org/mango. su: vocab + schema.org + Dublin Core on w3id.org/rete.

examples.title: The 20 language tracks
examples.tip:
What's in the graph: 20 subtitle tracks for one film, each a full language version. English (en) is the pivot with 76 cues; other tongues merge or split lines slightly, so counts differ.
Each track is a su:SubtitleTrack of Tears of Steel (Blender, CC BY 3.0).

examples.title: 🌍 One line, every language
examples.tip:
The film's first spoken line — “You're a jerk, Thom.” at 0:23 — in every language at once, including right-to-left Persian & Hebrew and CJK Japanese/Chinese.
A su:Line is one MOMENT; each language hangs off it as a su:text "…"@lang literal.

examples.title: 🎬 The whole film in one language
examples.tip:
Play one language's subtitle track in order — here Japanese (ja), each su:Cue with its own start time. This is the film as a timeline of text.
Change "ja" to es, fr, ru, fa, zh-Hant … to switch language.

examples.title: ⏱ What's on screen at 1:02
examples.tip:
Freeze the film at t = 62 s (1:02) and read the line whose [su:start, su:end] interval covers that instant — "This is pretty freaky.", in six languages side by side.
It's a time-window query: change 62 to any second to scrub the whole film. Pick a second nothing is spoken and you get nothing, correctly: the film has 76 subtitle lines over 567 s and the gaps are real — this example asked for t = 65, which falls between the line ending at 63.0 and the next starting at 117.0, and shipped an empty answer for it (#212).
examples.sparql:
PREFIX su: <https://w3id.org/rete/subtitles#>
SELECT ?language ?text WHERE {
  ?line a su:Line ; su:start ?s ; su:end ?e ; su:text ?text .
  FILTER(?s <= 62 && ?e >= 62)
  BIND(LANG(?text) AS ?language)
  FILTER(?language IN ("en","es","ja","ru","fa","zh-Hans"))
} ORDER BY ?language

examples.title: 🔤 Find a word in the dialogue
examples.tip:
Every subtitle mentioning “robot”, across all 20 languages, and exactly when it's said — full-text over the dialogue (a TEXT_INDEX is baked into the .rete).
Swap 'robot' for any word, or add a dct:language filter to search one language.

examples.title: 🔀 How one line was translated
examples.tip:
Line up the opening lines of dialogue with their Spanish, French, German, Russian and Japanese translations side by side — the same utterance, five ways.
The English su:Line is the hub; each language is a su:text literal hanging off it.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX su: <https://w3id.org/rete/subtitles#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?time ?english (GROUP_CONCAT(CONCAT(?lg,"=",?tx); separator="   ·   ") AS ?translations) WHERE {
  ?line a su:Line ; su:start ?time ; rdfs:label ?english ; su:text ?tx .
  BIND(LANG(?tx) AS ?lg)
  FILTER(?lg IN ("es","fr","de","ru","ja"))
} GROUP BY ?line ?time ?english ORDER BY ?time LIMIT 12

shacl_shapes.title: Cue anchoring & language tag
shacl_shapes.tip: Every su:Cue (1,536 of them, one per language-track subtitle event) must carry a start/end time window, a sequence index, its own subtitle text, a dct:language string tag, and exactly one su:inTrack link to a su:SubtitleTrack. The optional su:line link (present on ~1,510 of 1,536 cues) ties a language-specific cue back to its canonical multilingual su:Line moment, so it is left minCount 0.

shacl_shapes.title: Line moments & multilingual text
shacl_shapes.tip: A su:Line is a single moment in the film (76 of them), identified by its own start/end/index and linked back to the film via su:ofWork -> schema:Movie. Its su:text property is intentionally left multi-valued (minCount 1, no maxCount): the same Line node carries the same utterance in roughly 20 languages as language-tagged (rdf:langString) literals, which is exactly what the '🌍 one line, every language' example query relies on.

shacl_shapes.title: SubtitleTrack completeness
shacl_shapes.tip: Each of the 20 su:SubtitleTrack nodes (one per language edition) must declare a dct:language code, a human-readable rdfs:label, a su:cueCount tally, and a su:direction (text direction, e.g. ltr/rtl) - exactly the four fields the 'the 20 language tracks' overview example query selects. Missing any of these on a track would silently break that per-language listing without failing any query.

datasets.label: mtg.rete — Magic: The Gathering: the whole card pool as a graph (34,633 cards, with images)
datasets.description: The entire Magic: The Gathering card pool as a queryable knowledge graph — 34,633 unique cards (Oracle-level concepts, from MTGJSON's AtomicCards, MIT-licensed) richly interlinked with their colors, card types, subtypes, keywords, mana, formats and named+dated sets, each carrying its Scryfall card IMAGE, full Oracle text and official rulings (76,990 of them). Card types are OWL classes (Creature, Instant, Sorcery, Land, Artifact, Enchantment, Planeswalker … rdfs:subClassOf mtg:Card) and every card rdf:type its types, so the Schema tab is a card-type zoom and the reasoner has a real TBox. Oracle text lives in a TEXT_INDEX, so you can find cards by what they DO ('draw two cards', 'destroy target creature'). Ask for red creatures with flying legal in Modern (and see the cards), every Goblin or Dragon ranked by EDHREC popularity, the colour pie, legendary planeswalkers, cards on the Reserved List, or what a set contains. This is the card-semantics layer from the semantic-MTG-engine plan (building on cmdoret/mtg_ontology): the executable rules engine is a separate deterministic system, but the cards ARE a graph — a big, fun, richly-joined one. mtg: vocab on w3id.org/rete + schema.org; card data MIT (MTGJSON), images © Wizards of the Coast served via Scryfall's CDN. Cyril Matthey-Doret's mtg_ontology is merged in as the TBox foundation — each card type is owl:equivalentClass its class in his ontology, and colours/keywords link to his concepts, so you can query the cards THROUGH his vocabulary.
datasets.license: Card data MIT (MTGJSON); images © WotC via Scryfall; ontology GPL-3.0 (cmdoret)

examples.title: How many cards of each type
examples.tip:
34,633 cards grouped by card type (Creature, Instant, Land, Artifact …). Each type is an OWL class (rdfs:subClassOf mtg:Card) — open the Schema tab to see the same breakdown as a type zoom.
Cards can have several types, so an Artifact Creature counts under both.

examples.title: 🔥 Red fliers legal in Modern
examples.tip:
A real deckbuilding query: red Creatures with the Flying keyword that are legal in the Modern format, most-played first (mtg:edhrecRank). The pictures come straight from the graph — mtg:image resolves to Scryfall's card art.
Swap color/R for /U, flying for haste, or modern for legacy / commander.

examples.title: 🔎 Cards that draw two cards
examples.tip:
Full-text over Oracle text (a TEXT_INDEX is baked into the .rete): every card whose rules text says “draw two cards”. This is finding cards by what they DO.
Change the phrase — 'destroy target creature', 'create a Treasure token', 'gain 3 life' — to search by effect.

examples.title: 🐉 The most popular Dragons
examples.tip:
Every card with the Dragon creature type, ranked by EDHREC popularity — a picture gallery of the game's dragons.
Swap subtype/dragon for /goblin, /angel, /zombie, /elf … (there are 613 creature types in the graph).

examples.title: 🎨 The colour pie
examples.tip:
How many cards fall in each of Magic's five colours (White, Blue, Black, Red, Green). Multicolour cards count under every colour they contain; colourless cards have none.
mtg:color links a card to a colour node carrying an rdfs:label.

examples.title: ⭐ The most-played cards
examples.tip:
The most popular cards in the whole game by EDHREC rank (1 = most played) — Sol Ring and friends — as a picture gallery.
Every row's picture is a mtg:image edge resolved to Scryfall's CDN; drop the ORDER BY to browse randomly.

examples.title: 🗓 The first cards ever (Alpha, 1993)
examples.tip:
Every card from Limited Edition Alpha — Magic's very first set, released 5 Aug 1993 — most-played today first. Sets are now named, dated nodes (mtg:printedIn → a Set with schema:name + mtg:releaseDate).
Swap set/LEA for any set code to browse a set as a gallery.

examples.title: 📜 Search the official rulings
examples.tip:
Full-text over 76,990 official rulings (the plan's rule-evidence layer): every ruling that mentions “the legend rule”, with the card it clarifies.
Rulings hang off cards as mtg:ruling → a Ruling with dct:date + rdfs:comment; change the phrase to search any rules concept.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX mtg: <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?card ?ruling WHERE {
  ?c schema:name ?card ; mtg:ruling ?r .
  ?r rdfs:comment ?ruling .
  FILTER(CONTAINS(LCASE(?ruling), "legend rule"))
} LIMIT 20

examples.title: 🔗 Query cards through Cyril's ontology
examples.tip:
cmdoret/mtg_ontology is merged in as the TBox: this asks for creatures via HIS class (cmdoret:Creature), reached through owl:equivalentClass back to our mtg:Creature — the two vocabularies are one graph.
Swap Creature for Instant, Land or Artifact to cross the bridge the other way.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX mtg: <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX owl: <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#>
SELECT ?image ?card WHERE {
  <https://cmdoret.net/mtg_ontology/Creature> ^owl:equivalentClass ?t .
  ?c a ?t ; schema:name ?card ; mtg:image ?image ; mtg:edhrecRank ?rank .
} ORDER BY ?rank LIMIT 24

shacl_shapes.title: Card core fields
shacl_shapes.tip: Every Card must carry a display name, an image, and a numeric mana value — these three predicates (schema:name, mtg:image, mtg:manaValue) are present on all 34,633 Oracle-level Card concepts in the dataset, so their absence signals a broken MTGJSON import. mtg:oracleText is included as an optional check since a small minority of cards (e.g. vanguards/tokens with no rules text) legitimately lack it.

shacl_shapes.title: Creature stats and links
shacl_shapes.tip: A Creature (19,072 of the 34,633 cards, e.g. Dragons, Elves, Angels) must expose power and toughness — present on ~98.5% of creatures (18,788/19,072) — and, when present, its mtg:legalIn must point to a real Format node and mtg:color to a real Color node from the cmdoret.net/mtg_ontology vocabulary, catching mis-typed or dangling links introduced during ingestion.

shacl_shapes.title: Ruling has date and comment
shacl_shapes.tip: Every Ruling (76,990 official Wizards-of-the-Coast rulings text-linked from Creature and other card types via mtg:ruling) must carry exactly one dc:date and at least one rdfs:comment — both predicates appear on every single Ruling instance (76,990/76,990), so a Ruling missing either is a truncated MTGJSON record.

datasets.label: mtg-game.rete — a live Magic game state as OWL + SPARQL (no engine)
datasets.description: The DECLARATIVE half of the semantic-MTG-engine plan, in miniature: a runtime OWL ontology (GameState, Player, Zone, ZoneMembership, CardInstance, SpellInstance, the Stack), a handful of cards modelled with their real STRUCTURED abilities (cost / condition / effect / action — the way cmdoret/mtg_ontology intends, e.g. Bonders' Enclave's “{3},{T}: draw a card, only if you control a creature with power ≥ 4”), and one concrete match — Alice vs Bob — captured as two immutable snapshots: state S1 (Alice's turn 3, main phase) and its successor S2 after she casts Lightning Bolt at Bob's Grizzly Bears (the spell now sits on the stack, a Mountain is tapped). There is NO game engine here — just OWL classes and data — yet plain SPARQL answers the plan's question families: DESCRIBE the board, VALIDATE that every card instance is in exactly one zone, decide LEGALITY (which instants Alice can actually pay for from her untapped lands), read what each card DOES from its ability structure, and diff S1→S2. Card concepts reuse the 34k-catalogue IRIs (the `mtg` dataset), so the two graphs are one entity space. mtgg: runtime vocab on w3id.org/rete, building on Cyril Matthey-Doret's mtg_ontology (mtgo: structural classes + MTG-wiki action classes). CC BY 4.0. Its companion `mtg` is the whole card pool; this is one match modelled in full. TEXT_INDEX on for full-text search over its literals.

examples.title: 🎲 What's on the battlefield (state S1)
examples.tip:
The plan's 'Describe' question, in SPARQL: every card instance on the battlefield in game state S1 and who controls it — Alice has Llanowar Elves + two Mountains, Bob has Grizzly Bears + Serra Angel.
ZoneMembership is state-scoped, so change s1 to s2 to see the board a move later.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX mtgg: <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?controller ?card WHERE {
  ?m a mtgg:ZoneMembership ; mtgg:inState <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game/s1> ; mtgg:object ?i ; mtgg:zone <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game/battlefield> .
  ?i mtgg:ofCard ?c ; mtgg:controller ?ctrl .
  ?c schema:name ?card . ?ctrl rdfs:label ?controller .
} ORDER BY ?controller ?card

examples.title: 📜 What does each card DO?
examples.tip:
Cards aren't text blobs here — each ability is a structured object (cost / condition / effect / action), the way cmdoret/mtg_ontology models them. The action links to the MTG-wiki concept (draw, add_mana …).
Bonders' Enclave shows two abilities incl. its power-≥4 condition.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX mtgg: <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game#>
PREFIX mtg: <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?card ?ability ?action WHERE {
  ?c a mtg:Card ; schema:name ?card ; mtgg:ability ?ab .
  ?ab rdfs:label ?ability ; mtgg:effect ?e . ?e mtgg:action ?action .
} ORDER BY ?card

examples.title: ✅ Which instants can Alice cast now?
examples.tip:
The plan's 'Legality' question answered WITHOUT an engine: an instant in Alice's hand whose mana value she can pay from her untapped mana sources in S1. Lightning Bolt (cost 1) is castable — she has 2 untapped Mountains.
Tap a Mountain (use s2) and re-run to watch it drop out.

examples.title: 🧪 Is the state coherent? (one zone per card)
examples.tip:
A SHACL-style coherence check as SPARQL: every card instance must be in exactly one zone in a state. This returns the OFFENDERS — an empty result means S1 is valid.
A well-formed game state should always answer nothing here.

examples.title: 🪄 On the stack: Bolt → Bears (state S2)
examples.tip:
State S2 is the successor of S1 after Alice casts Lightning Bolt at Bob's Grizzly Bears — the spell instance now sits on the Stack with its target and controller. Successor states link back with mtgg:previousState.
This is a transition captured as data, not run by an engine.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX mtgg: <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?spell ?targetCard ?controller WHERE {
  ?m mtgg:inState <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game/s2> ; mtgg:object ?sp ; mtgg:zone <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game/stack> .
  ?sp rdfs:label ?spell ; mtgg:target ?t ; mtgg:controller ?ctrl .
  ?t mtgg:ofCard ?tc . ?tc schema:name ?targetCard . ?ctrl rdfs:label ?controller .
}

examples.title: 🔁 What changed from S1 to S2
examples.tip:
Diff two snapshots: permanents that were untapped in S1 but tapped in S2 — i.e. what paying for the Bolt cost. Here it's the one Mountain Alice tapped for {R}.
Comparing states is just a join across two mtgg:inState values.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX mtgg: <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
SELECT ?card WHERE {
  ?m2 mtgg:inState <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game/s2> ; mtgg:object ?o ; mtgg:tapped true .
  ?m1 mtgg:inState <https://w3id.org/rete/mtg/game/s1> ; mtgg:object ?o ; mtgg:tapped false .
  ?o mtgg:ofCard ?c . ?c schema:name ?card .
}

shacl_shapes.title: ZoneMembership integrity
shacl_shapes.tip:
Every ZoneMembership row must anchor to exactly one GameState (mtgg:inState) and exactly one CardInstance (mtgg:object), and record which zone it sits in (mtgg:zone, e.g. Battlefield/Hand/Stack) as an IRI.
Catches orphaned zone-membership rows missing their game-state anchor, their card-instance target, or their zone - any of these being absent would make a card silently disappear from 'what's on the battlefield' or 'what's in Alice's hand' queries.

shacl_shapes.title: CardInstance ownership
shacl_shapes.tip:
A CardInstance (a specific card token in play, distinct from the static mtg:Card definition it instantiates) must declare both an owner (who started the game with it) and a controller (who currently controls it), and both must be Player IRIs.
Owner and controller are allowed to differ (e.g. a stolen or borrowed permanent), so both links are required separately - missing either breaks any query that depends on 'whose turn is it' or 'whose creature can attack'.

shacl_shapes.title: ActivatedAbility must cost and do something
shacl_shapes.tip:
An ActivatedAbility (e.g. a land's tap-for-mana ability, or a creature's activated power) must carry a human-readable rdfs:label, a mtgg:cost pointing to a Cost node (e.g. {T}: tap this permanent), and a mtgg:effect pointing to an Effect node describing what happens.
An ability missing its cost or effect is unplayable data - the declarative engine has no rule to check affordability or to resolve the ability, so this shape enforces the cost/effect structure the whole semantic-MTG-engine design depends on.

shacl_shapes.title: LifeTotal is scoped and numeric
shacl_shapes.tip:
Every LifeTotal record must be pinned to exactly one GameState via mtgg:inState and must carry exactly one integer mtgg:life value (Magic life totals normally start at 20 and move up/down).
A LifeTotal left floating without a game-state anchor, or holding a non-integer or missing life value, would make 'has a player lost yet?' or 'who is ahead on life' queries return nothing or garbage.

datasets.label: arxiu.rete — Arxius en Línia: complete Catalan archives, with scanned documents
datasets.description: Complete Catalan archives from the Generalitat de Catalunya's online archives (Arxius en Línia), harvested one whole archive at a time and merged into a single graph. Four complete archives so far — the Arxiu Nacional de Catalunya (431,776 units), the Arxiu Comarcal de l'Anoia (137,054), the Arxiu Comarcal del Baix Llobregat (53,644) and the Arxiu Històric de Tarragona (7,401) — 629,875 archival units across 507 fonds. Each archival unit carries its holding archive, fonds, reference code, dates, description AND its scanned document: non-reserved scans are shown as a downsized WebP (~180 KB, ~15% of the ~1.5 MB original) mirrored to R2 so they render inline in query results, and every unit keeps arx:originalImage → the original full-res JPEG on Gencat's own server (the source of record). Reserved documents — 56% of Tarragona, 93% of Baix Llobregat, 99% of Anoia, 73% of the ANC — keep only the link, respecting the holding archives' rights (so ~117,940 units render a WebP — photographs plus PDF documents shown by their rendered first page; the rest are metadata + the original Gencat link). The same open API holds ~1.43M image-records across ~65 archives (~1.5 TB); this graph grows archive by archive. Modelled with schema.org archival vocabulary (schema:ArchiveComponent held by an ArchiveOrganization, part of a Collection/fonds) on w3id.org/rete. Descriptions are openly reusable (Llicència oberta d'ús d'informació / Llei 37/2007, Generalitat de Catalunya, with attribution). TEXT_INDEX on for full-text search over its literals.
datasets.license: Descriptions: Llicència oberta / CC0 (Llei 37/2007); images © holding archives

examples.title: 🖼 Browse the scans: image, title, description & dates
examples.tip:
One card per digitized archival unit: the scan, its title, the archivist's description, and the covered date range — best in the Cards output (tap a photo to zoom, tap a card to page through).
The ?id column is the archive's own record identifier; the unit IRI itself names the fonds it belongs to (schema:isPartOf walks the hierarchy).

examples.title: 📍 Map the geocoded units
examples.tip:
6,531 units are geocoded: their titles name a “Terme municipal”, matched to the municipality’s Wikidata coordinates — cemetery surveys, municipal fonds … Switch Output to Map: one pin per unit, hover for the title.
Add FILTER(CONTAINS(LCASE(STR(?title)), "conca de barber")) to map just one comarca.

examples.title: 🔗 Federated: each unit's province (joins geoadmin)
examples.tip:
A TRUE cross-dataset join, live in your browser: each unit’s schema:contentLocation IRI is a district in the geoadmin world-boundaries dataset, so ?province’s label comes from a DIFFERENT .rete file than the archival unit. Press 🔍 Plan to see which source answers which pattern.
It has to be a FLAT BGP. The cross-source planner declines OPTIONAL / UNION / property paths and AGGREGATES, and falls back to running the whole query on each source and merging — which for a join means every source answers nothing. That is exactly what the (COUNT(?d) … GROUP BY ?province) version of this example did, and why it shipped an empty answer (#212). Group it after the fact, or bind one district and count on arxiu alone.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?province ?title WHERE {
  ?d schema:contentLocation ?p .
  ?d schema:name ?title .
  ?p rdfs:label ?province .
} LIMIT 50

examples.title: 🗺 Files about the Conca de Barberà
examples.tip:
Full-text place search over the titles: every unit naming the Conca de Barberà (the comarca around Montblanc, Tarragona) — cemetery surveys of Santa Coloma de Queralt, municipal records … one card per unit with its first scan.
Swap the FILTER text for any place — “priorat”, “montblanc”, “poblet” — to search another area; ?original links the archive's own master file (often a PDF).

examples.title: 🏛 The archives (and their size)
examples.tip:
The complete Catalan archives harvested so far, with how many digitised units each holds and how many have a WebP scan (the rest keep only the Gencat link — many are rights-reserved).
Each unit is a schema:ArchiveComponent held by an ArchiveOrganization.

examples.title: 🖼 Scanned documents (gallery)
examples.tip:
The scanned documents themselves — each schema:image is the downsized WebP mirrored to R2 (rendered here), ~15% the size of Gencat's original JPEG. Many are medieval charters, notarial and land-registry records.
Drop the LIMIT to browse all 3,101 scans.

examples.title: 📅 The oldest documents
examples.tip:
Units that carry a parsed start date, earliest first — the deep end of the archive (charters, cartularies).
Dates come from schema:startDate; not every unit has a machine-readable one.

examples.title: 🔎 Documents mentioning Tarragona
examples.tip:
Full-text over the descriptions (a TEXT_INDEX is built in): units whose description mentions “Tarragona” (848 of them), with their scan.
Change the word — Reus, Tortosa, cadastre … — to search the catalogue by content.

examples.title: 🔗 WebP copy + original Gencat link
examples.tip:
Every scan is kept two ways: a downsized WebP on R2 (schema:image, rendered here) and the original full-res JPEG on Gencat's own server (arx:originalImage) — the source of record always points back to the holding archive.
The reservat flag is respected: reserved images are linked, never re-hosted.

examples.title: 📄 PDF documents (rendered first page)
examples.tip:
About 3% of the documents are multi-page PDFs, not single images. Their first page is rendered to a WebP (via PyMuPDF) so they still show in the gallery; arx:originalImage links the full PDF on Gencat.
Filter by arx:contentType to separate PDFs from photographs.

shacl_shapes.title: Units link to an owning archive and a parent fonds
shacl_shapes.tip: Every arx:Unit (a scanned archival unit; the class is also typed schema:ArchiveComponent) must carry a dct:identifier, a schema:holdingArchive pointing to a schema:ArchiveOrganization, and a schema:isPartOf pointing to its parent arx:Fonds (the fonds/collection it belongs to). It also requires the internal arx:reserved access-flag and arx:contentType descriptor, since the harvest sets both on effectively all 629,875 units (629,874-629,875 have them).

shacl_shapes.title: Every fonds is named and links to its holding archive
shacl_shapes.tip: Each arx:Fonds (dual-typed schema:Collection; one of the 507 archival fonds/collections in the graph) must have a schema:name literal and a schema:holdingArchive link to the schema:ArchiveOrganization that holds it, since both relations are present on all 507 fonds in the source data.

shacl_shapes.title: Archive organizations are named
shacl_shapes.tip: The 4 schema:ArchiveOrganization nodes are the top-level archives themselves (e.g. Arxiu Nacional de Catalunya, Arxiu Comarcal de l'Anoia) that every Unit and Fonds points back to via schema:holdingArchive. This is the smallest class in the graph, so it requires a schema:name literal on all 4 - a naming gap here would silently break every downstream label or join.

datasets.label: zenodo-records.rete — every Zenodo record (7.76M) as a DataCite scholarly graph (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: Every published record on Zenodo — CERN's open research repository — as one 215M-triple range-queryable graph (2.09 GB, remote-lazy over HTTP range on Cloudflare R2). Built from the OFFICIAL Zenodo exporter dump (the site-wide records-xml snapshot: 7,759,325 records, each DataCite kernel-4.5 metadata) — essentially ALL of Zenodo's descriptive metadata: datasets, software, preprints, journal articles, images, presentations, theses… Each record sits at its CANONICAL DOI IRI (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8435696) and is typed both zen:Record and its DataCite resource class (dcite:Dataset, dcite:Software, dcite:JournalArticle, dcite:Image, dcite:Preprint …) — so the type-pyramid communities ARE the kinds of research output: JournalArticle 2.41M, Text 1.40M, Image 1.23M, Dataset 875k, Software 645k. It carries dcite:title, dcite:publisherName, dcite:publicationYear, dcite:landingPage, the license, dcterms:subject keywords, and — the connective tissue — the DataCite RELATION NETWORK mined from relatedIdentifiers: dcite:isVersionOf (every version → its concept DOI), dcite:isPartOf, dcite:cites / dcite:references / dcite:isSupplementTo, mapped as edges between DOIs so version chains and citation/derivation links are all traversable. 877,926 CREATOR nodes carry an ORCID and mint at their canonical https://orcid.org/{orcid} IRI. Because works are keyed by DOI and people by ORCID, this graph AUTO-MERGES with the DataCite / OpenAIRE / OpenCitations / ORCID / DBLP scholarly datasets on the shared identifiers — the same node, no owl:sameAs (see the scholar ontology). Built by scripts/zenodo/records_to_nt.py (Parquet → N-Triples honoring the scholar-alignment canonical-IRI policy) → rete build --pyramid-algo types --card. CC-BY 4.0 (Zenodo metadata export). Selective queries — one DOI's neighbourhood, an author's works, a keyword — are cheap over HTTP range; a full 215M-triple aggregate scans the file, so lean on the Schema pyramid for the big picture.

examples.title: What's in the graph — records by type
examples.tip:
Every Zenodo record is typed by its DataCite resource class, so this GROUP BY is the shape of the whole repository: JournalArticle 2.41M, Text 1.40M, Image 1.23M, Dataset 875k, Software 645k, Preprint 272k, Book 304k…
The Schema tab shows the same breakdown as a type pyramid, read straight from the file's pyramid section — no full scan.

examples.title: Works and their ORCID authors (the federation key)
examples.tip:
dcite:creator points at a PERSON node minted at its canonical https://orcid.org/{orcid} IRI — the exact node the ORCID, DataCite and OpenAIRE graphs use, so a union merges them for free (no owl:sameAs).
This lists works with an ORCID'd author; paste a specific orcid.org IRI to get one researcher's whole Zenodo output.

examples.title: Everything about one record
examples.tip:
One DOI, every fact — the row-per-fact view of a single Zenodo record (a CMS-physics presentation): its type(s), title, publisher, year, license, creator and the dcite:isVersionOf link to its concept DOI.
Paste any https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.… IRI to inspect another record.

examples.title: Every version of a record
examples.tip:
Zenodo mints a fresh DOI for every version of a deposit, all sharing one CONCEPT DOI; dcite:isVersionOf links each version to that concept, so this returns a deposit's full release history.
zenodo.597466 is one of the most-versioned records on Zenodo — 2,710 versions (a continuously-released dataset). Try zenodo.3628045 (1,779) or any concept DOI.

examples.title: A record's version tree, as a graph
examples.tip:
Switch Output to Graph. The concept DOI at the centre with its version DOIs fanning out along dcite:isVersionOf — one deposit's release history as a node-link star (capped at 40).
Change the central IRI to any concept DOI to map another record's versions.

examples.title: Zenodo output, year by year
examples.tip:
Switch Output to Time. Records counted by dcite:publicationYear — the growth of Zenodo, climbing steeply through the 2020s (2025 alone: 1.12M records).
This scans the whole graph, so it's the one heavy example here — the selective queries above are cheap over HTTP range.

shacl_shapes.title: Record core fields
shacl_shapes.tip: Every zenodo:Record must carry the identifying/bibliographic core that the grounded counts show on virtually all ~7.76M records: a DOI, a title, a landing page URL, a recordId, a publication year and a publisher name. isVersionOf and conceptDoi are left optional (only ~80% of records are non-root versions) but when isVersionOf is present it must point to another IRI-identified Record — that's the version-chain edge (see the reach dimension).

shacl_shapes.title: Journal article completeness
shacl_shapes.tip: Targets dcite:JournalArticle (2.42M instances, the largest single resourceType) and checks that each carries at least one creator (dc:creator) and at least one license statement (dc:license) — both grounded counts run near 2x the class size, meaning almost every article has both, just often more than one. It also requires the per-article DataCite bookkeeping fields (publicationYear, schemaVersion, updated) which are present 1:1 with the class count.

shacl_shapes.title: Agent identity fields
shacl_shapes.tip: Targets dcite:Agent (3.92M creator/contributor nodes, the ORCID federation key used by the example query joining works to authors). Requires exactly one rdfs:label and one dcite:agentName per agent (counts are 1:1 with the class size), and requires an orcid literal since the grounded orcid-triple count also matches the Agent count exactly — every Agent node carries an orcid statement in this build. affiliationName stays optional (~78% coverage).

shacl_shapes.title: Tagged creative works (Image/Text)
shacl_shapes.tip: Targets dcite:Image and dcite:Text (1.23M + 1.40M instances) — the two resourceTypes with the heaviest subject-tagging in the graph (avg 5-6 dc:subject tags per instance). Requires at least one dc:subject and one dc:creator, catching Image/Text records that were exported without any keyword tag or without any listed creator, both of which should be essentially impossible given how dense these predicates are on these classes.

datasets.label: biosyslit.rete — Zenodo Biodiversity Literature Repository: taxonomic treatments with Darwin Core taxonomy + IIIF (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The Biodiversity Literature Repository (BLR) community on Zenodo — curated by Plazi / Pensoft — as one 106M-triple range-queryable graph (1.65 GB, remote-lazy over HTTP range). 2,013,749 records, of which 688,222 are TAXONOMIC TREATMENTS (zen:TaxonomicTreatment ⊑ dcite:Text): each describes a taxon and carries the full DARWIN CORE taxonomy directly in the dwc: namespace — dwc:kingdom / dwc:phylum / dwc:class / dwc:order / dwc:family / dwc:genus, dwc:taxonRank, dwc:scientificNameAuthorship — so you can roll treatments up by family (Staphylinidae 17,101, Formicidae 15,424, Cerambycidae 12,068, Ichneumonidae, Curculionidae…), order or genus WITHOUT touching a single record. Every record sits at its canonical DOI IRI and carries dcite:title, the full treatment description text, usage stats (zen:views / zen:downloads), an IIIF manifest (zen:iiifManifest → the treatment's figures on Zenodo's IIIF server), its files (zen:hasFile → treatment.html / images with mime + byte size) and its community membership (zen:inCommunity → the biosyslit zen:Community node). The RELATION NETWORK links each treatment to its source journal article and related treatments (dcite:isPartOf / dcite:cites / dcite:isVersionOf → other DOIs). Because works are DOIs and ORCID authors mint at orcid.org, it federates with the DataCite / OpenAIRE / ORCID scholarly graph — and it is a rich subset of the sibling `zenodo-records` graph (BLR records ARE Zenodo records), kept separate for the Zenodo-native detail (IIIF, files, Darwin Core) that the bare DataCite metadata drops. Built by scripts/zenodo/biosyslit_to_nt.py → rete build --pyramid-algo types --card. CC-BY 4.0. The richest slice of Zenodo for biodiversity.

examples.title: What's in the graph — by type
examples.tip:
The BLR community is dominated by taxonomic treatments — 688,222 zen:TaxonomicTreatment, each a described taxon — the rest journal articles, figures and datasets.
The Schema tab shows the type pyramid read straight from the file.

examples.title: Treatments by Darwin Core family
examples.tip:
Every treatment carries its taxonomy directly in the Darwin Core namespace (dwc:kingdom … dwc:genus), so grouping by dwc:family rolls 688k treatments up into the beetle / ant / wasp families with no record touched: Staphylinidae (rove beetles) 17,101, Formicidae (ants) 15,424, Cerambycidae (longhorns) 12,068, Ichneumonidae, Curculionidae…
Swap dwc:family for dwc:order (Coleoptera 99k, Hymenoptera 76k…) or dwc:genus to zoom the taxonomy.

examples.title: Longhorn beetles (Cerambycidae) with their figures
examples.tip:
A selective slice — treatments in one family — with each treatment's IIIF manifest (zen:iiifManifest → its figure plates on Zenodo's IIIF server, openable in a IIIF viewer).
Change the family literal ("Formicidae", "Carabidae", "Scarabaeidae"…) or match on dwc:genus for a genus.

examples.title: A treatment and its source article + links
examples.tip:
The relation network around one treatment (Oxygonia Mannerheim, 1837): dcite:isVersionOf → its concept DOI, dcite:isPartOf → the Zootaxa article it was extracted from (10.11646/zootaxa.5353.2.3) plus the Plazi / ZooBank identifiers, dcite:cites → the works it cites.
This is what ties treatments back into the wider literature graph.

examples.title: All treatments from one journal article
examples.tip:
Switch Output to Graph. One source article (a Zootaxa paper) at the centre with every taxonomic treatment extracted from it linking in via dcite:isPartOf — how Plazi turns a taxonomic paper into machine-readable treatments.
Change the article DOI to fan out another paper's treatments.

shacl_shapes.title: Zenodo Record core metadata
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that every zen:Record (the base container class covering all 2,013,536 harvested Zenodo deposits — journal articles, images, taxonomic treatments, datasets, etc.) carries a DOI, a title, a declared resourceType, and a publicationDate. These four predicates each occur exactly once per Record in the source data, so a missing one signals a broken harvest.

shacl_shapes.title: Zenodo File asset fixity
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that every zen:File (a binary asset — PDF, image blob, etc. — attached to a Record; 1,931,695 of them) declares byteSize, checksum, fileName and mediaType, each required exactly once. This is the fixity metadata a downstream client needs to verify a downloaded file matches what Zenodo actually served.

shacl_shapes.title: Taxonomic treatment linkage
