shacl_shapes.tip: Checks the shape of a zen:TaxonomicTreatment (a Plazi-extracted description of one taxon pulled out of a journal article; 688,222 of them). dct:subject/dct:creator hold literal keyword and author strings (average ~9.5 subjects and ~3 creators per treatment, so left optional/multi-valued rather than minCount 1); dcite:isSourceOf and dcite:isPartOf are IRI links out — to the figure/image the treatment produced, and to the journal article it was extracted from — tying the taxonomic-literature graph together.

shacl_shapes.title: Image-to-file attachment
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that each dcite:Image (a figure/plate harvested from the Biodiversity Literature Repository; 780,361 of them) links via zen:hasFile to at least one zen:File carrying the actual image bytes — the ratio of hasFile triples to Image instances is ~1.02, i.e. essentially every image has its file attached, so this is required. dct:creator/dct:subject stay literal-typed and optional (multi-valued), and dcite:isPartOf is an IRI link back to the treatment or article the image illustrates.

datasets.label: gotriple.rete — GoTriple: 2.7M Social-Sciences & Humanities publications, DOI-federated (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The GoTriple metadata corpus — the EU-funded discovery platform for the Social Sciences & Humanities (gotriple.eu / TRIPLE / OPERAS) — as one 57.7M-triple range-queryable graph (832 MB, remote-lazy over HTTP range on Cloudflare R2). Built from the CC0 Zenodo dump (18185971): 6,074,813 discipline-placements that DEDUPLICATE, under rete's canonical-IRI policy, into 2,712,267 DISTINCT publications — a multi-disciplinary paper (same GoTriple id across several discipline files) and a paper indexed from several providers (same DOI) MERGE into one gtr:Document node that carries all its gtr:inDiscipline tags (so 855,688 distinct DOIs come from 2.46M DOI-bearing records, ~2.9 copies each). Each document carries a multilingual gtr:title, its GoTriple discipline(s) (a 26-term SKOS scheme: History, Sociology, Law, Psychology, Economics, Linguistics, Philosophy, Art…), authors, keywords, source provider/publisher, language, access status and its full-text URL — and, the connective tissue, gtr:knowsAbout → shared SSH-LCSH subject-authority nodes (semantics.gr, with multilingual labels) that DEDUPE across the whole corpus into a real subject graph (Education links 288k docs, Economics 229k, 'State, The' 219k…). The 855,688 documents WITH a DOI mint at their canonical https://doi.org/{doi} IRI, so this graph AUTO-MERGES with the DataCite / Zenodo / OpenAIRE / OpenCitations scholarly datasets on the shared DOI — and it brings the SSH breadth those STEM-heavy sources lack (see the scholar ontology). The go-triple.ttl ontology (gtr:) travels INSIDE the file. Built by scripts/gotriple/{jsonl_to_parquet,gotriple_to_nt}.py → rete build --no-pyramid + rete repyramid --pyramid-algo types. CC0. Selective queries — one DOI, a subject's documents, an open-access slice of one discipline — are cheap over HTTP range; a full-corpus aggregate scans the file, so lean on the Schema pyramid for the big picture.

examples.title: Rich record view — subject, source & full text
examples.tip:
A wide slice of one discipline (Sociology): each row is a publication with an SSH-LCSH subject (English label), its source repository, and TWO resolvable URLs — the DOI (?doc) and the full-text link (?fulltext). A paper repeats once per subject it is about.
Change gtr:discipline-socio to any discipline (gtr:discipline-hist, -psy, -eco…).

examples.title: Three URLs — open access: DOI + subject authority + full text
examples.tip:
Open-access Law papers, each row carrying THREE resolvable URLs: the DOI (?doc, https://doi.org/…), the linked SSH-LCSH subject authority (?subjectAuthority, semantics.gr — the closest thing to a ROR here: an external controlled-vocabulary id) and the full-text PDF (?fulltext).
GoTriple carries no organization RORs (it is SSH metadata without affiliations), but every subject IS a shared authority node.

examples.title: One publication → its subject authorities (EN labels)
examples.tip:
Everything one paper is 'about': its SSH-LCSH subject authority URIs (semantics.gr) with their English labels, plus the paper's discipline (English prefLabel from the embedded ontology) and language — five columns from one DOI, cheap over HTTP range.
Paste any https://doi.org/… IRI that GoTriple indexes.

examples.title: Publications about a subject, with full text
examples.tip:
gtr:knowsAbout links documents to a shared SSH-LCSH subject node (deduped at its semantics.gr URI across the whole corpus). This lists publications about 'Education' (sh85040989, ~288k documents) with their DOI, language and full-text link.
Swap the subject IRI — find one via its rdfs:label — to pivot the corpus by topic.

examples.title: Publications per discipline
examples.tip:
Counting gtr:inDiscipline edges, labelled by the embedded ontology's English prefLabels — History, Sociology, Environmental studies and Linguistics lead. A paper can sit in several disciplines, so these sum to more than the 2.71M distinct documents.
This scans the corpus; the Schema tab shows the type pyramid without a scan.

examples.title: A publication's subjects, as a graph
examples.tip:
Switch Output to Graph. One document at the centre with its SSH-LCSH subjects fanning out (gtr:knowsAbout), each labelled in English — how a paper is placed in the subject network.
Because the document sits at its canonical DOI IRI, this same node is where it joins the DataCite / Zenodo / OpenAIRE graphs. Change the DOI to explore another paper.

shacl_shapes.title: Document core fields
shacl_shapes.tip:
Checks that every gtr:Document (an SSH publication indexed by GoTriple) has a title, is placed in at least one gtr:Discipline via gtr:inDiscipline, and has a full-text URL — the dataset was built specifically from records that all carry a full-text link, and inDiscipline is the classification edge every one of the 6.07M documents is partitioned by.
Also checks that gtr:doi, when present, is a plain string (it is only ~69% populated, so it stays optional) and that gtr:hasAuthor / gtr:knowsAbout targets are real IRIs pointing at gtr:Author / being generic IRI-typed subject links.

shacl_shapes.title: Discipline is a scheme member
shacl_shapes.tip:
Checks that every gtr:Discipline (the ~15-way SSH classification GoTriple partitions the corpus by, e.g. discipline-socio, discipline-droit) has an English skos:prefLabel and is declared skos:inScheme the single gtr:disciplines concept scheme.
This catches disciplines that were minted as bare IRIs (e.g. from a bad harvest row) without ever being wired into the controlled vocabulary the ontology declares.

shacl_shapes.title: Subject authority URI
shacl_shapes.tip:
Checks that every gtr:Subject (a linked SSH-LCSH subject authority reached via gtr:knowsAbout, identified by its own semantics.gr IRI, e.g. http://semantics.gr/authorities/SSH-LCSH/sh85040989) is itself an IRI node, and that when it carries the gtr:subjectUri copy-of-self literal, that literal is typed xsd:anyURI.
This guards against subject authorities accidentally created as blank nodes or literals instead of dereferenceable semantics.gr IRIs, which would silently break cross-document subject joins.

shacl_shapes.title: Author has a name
shacl_shapes.tip:
Checks that every gtr:Author (an author of a GoTriple document, reached via gtr:hasAuthor) carries at least one gtr:authorName string — GoTriple author records are aggregated from a raw fullname field, so a missing name means the harvest dropped the only human-readable identifier for that person.
Name is left without a maxCount since some author records legitimately carry variant-form duplicates.

datasets.label: orcid.rete — every public ORCID profile: 25M researchers, 150M works, ONE 1.3-billion-triple file (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The ORCID Public Data File 2025 (CC0) as ONE range-queryable graph — 1,296,338,454 triples / 397M terms / 17.5 GB, the largest single .rete published, and the first built with the memory-bounded external build (rete build --memory-budget-mb 16384: the 198 GB N-Triples stream is chunked to disk, dictionaries k-way-merged, each permutation external-sorted — peak RAM stays inside the budget while the output is byte-identical to an in-RAM build). 25,048,058 researchers sit at their CANONICAL https://orcid.org/{id} IRI (orc:Researcher with given/family names, credit-name label, country) — so this graph AUTO-MERGES with zenodo-records' 877k ORCID creators and the rest of the scholarly constellation (see the scholar ontology). 149,782,968 works (orc:Work + a fine-grained type like orc:journal-article / orc:conference-paper / orc:book-chapter) carry dcterms:creator → the researcher, the title as rdfs:label, orc:publicationYear, orc:journalTitle — and 78% carry orc:doi, the join key to DataCite / OpenAIRE / OpenCitations / DBLP. 25,063,901 affiliations are reified career events — orc:Employment / orc:Education / orc:Qualification / orc:Distinction / orc:InvitedPosition / orc:Membership / orc:Service ⊑ orc:Affiliation — each with orc:affiliationOf → the person, orc:organizationName, orc:roleTitle, start/end years, and (where ORCID disambiguated the org to ROR) orc:affiliationWith → the RAW https://ror.org/{id} IRI: the ror.rete dataset answers those same nodes, so the two files JOIN cross-source in the playground. Plus 1,838,095 fundings (orc:Funding, orc:awardedTo). The orcid.ttl OWL 2 QL ontology (https://w3id.org/rete/orcid#) travels inside the file. Built by scripts/orcid/orcid_to_nt.py → scripts/orcid/build_single_rete.sh. NOTE: the external build ships no Schema pyramid yet — keep queries SELECTIVE (one person, one org's people, one work's neighbourhood); each such query reads ~30–60 MB of the 17.5 GB over HTTP range, but a whole-graph aggregate would scan the file.

examples.title: Researcher cards: Berners-Lee, Bengio & co
examples.tip:
Three single-subject probes on a 1.3-BILLION-triple file — https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1279-3709 is Tim Berners-Lee, 0000-0002-9322-3515 is Yoshua Bengio — each read fetches only the index tiles those nodes touch (~30 MB of 17.5 GB).
The iD column is the canonical orcid.org IRI itself: paste any ORCID you know into the VALUES to add a row.

examples.title: Bengio's journal articles — title, journal, year, live DOI link
examples.tip:
Works claiming dcterms:creator → https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9322-3515 (Yoshua Bengio, the deep-learning pioneer): Nature Reviews Chemistry, INFORMS Journal on Computing… — 78% of the 149.8M works carry orc:doi, and BIND(IRI(...)) turns it into a clickable https://doi.org/ link straight to the paper.
The bound creator keeps this a selective tile read, not a scan of the 150M-work sea; the Type column is the fine-grained ORCID work class (orc:journal-article).

examples.title: Who works at CERN — role, kind, since when
examples.tip:
ORCID disambiguated 19M affiliations to ROR, and this file keeps the raw https://ror.org/{id} IRI as the org node: 01ggx4157 is CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research). One bound object → its people, each with their self-declared role, the affiliation kind (orc:Employment / orc:Education …) and the start year.
Swap in any ROR id — 02s376052 is EPFL, 05a28rw58 ETH Zürich — or open the ror dataset to find one. Want newest-first? Add ORDER BY DESC(?start) — no timeout in the playground, but sorting must enumerate EVERY CERN affiliation before the LIMIT instead of stopping at 50 rows, so expect a minute or two.

examples.title: Degrees minted at McGill University
examples.tip:
Affiliations are reified career events: every orc:Education node naming "McGill University", with the degree title and its years — Yoshua Bengio's 1988–1991 PhD sits somewhere in this table among thousands of BScs, MScs and doctorates.
The exact-literal organization name is the pivot; swap in "University of Oxford" or "Universidad de Sevilla" to mint another alumni list from the 25M-researcher graph. Sorting (ORDER BY DESC(?end)) works too — it just enumerates every match before the LIMIT rather than stopping at 100.

examples.title: 🔗 Cross-source JOIN: CERN's people ⋈ its ROR org card
examples.tip:
The real federation: ONE query split across TWO files and JOINED on the shared node https://ror.org/01ggx4157 — CERN. orcid.rete (1.3B triples) answers who lists it and as what; ror.rete answers what the org IS — official name, city, country — because ORCID's disambiguation kept ROR's canonical IRIs.
The planner routes each pattern by which file answers its predicate (orc:* → orcid, ror:* → ror), so keep the org columns on ror-only predicates like ror:name. Remove the ror chip and watch those columns go unanswered.

shacl_shapes.title: Researcher identity + contribution links
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks every orcid:Researcher (an ORCID iD holder) is identified by a real IRI rather than a blank node or literal, and that any orcid:hasContribution edge it carries points to an actual orcid:Contribution node (the reified researcher-in-work link that captures role and author order, rather than a bare work-to-person edge).

shacl_shapes.title: Education-affiliation completeness
shacl_shapes.tip: Every orcid:Education record (a reified affiliation asserting where a researcher studied, one of the 7 ORCID affiliation subtypes) must resolve to exactly one owning Researcher via affiliationOf and at least one Organization via affiliationWith, matching the ontology's existential restriction on affiliationWith. Also range-checks the denormalized literal fields ORCID stores directly on the affiliation node itself: organizationName, roleTitle, startYear, endYear.

shacl_shapes.title: Journal article core fields
shacl_shapes.tip: Targets orcid:journal-article, the ORCID work-type mapped 1:1 to fabio:JournalArticle. Requires a title (rdfs:label) and at least one dcterms:creator edge resolving to a real orcid:Researcher IRI (the claiming author), and checks journalTitle is a plain string whenever present.

shacl_shapes.title: Contribution reification shape
shacl_shapes.tip: orcid:Contribution reifies one researcher's participation in one work so that co-authorship order and role survive (instead of a bare work-creator edge). Requires exactly one contributor (a Researcher) and exactly one contributionTo (a Work); when withRole is present it must point to a skos:Concept from the ContributorRole vocabulary (e.g. author/editor), not a bare string.

datasets.label: gharchive-2025-07.rete — a full month of GitHub: every public event of July 2025, 1.64 BILLION triples with RDF-star provenance (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: One full UTC month of the public GitHub event stream (GH Archive, July 2025) as ONE range-queryable graph — 1,644,492,596 triples / 334.5M terms / 17.1 GB, the LARGEST single .rete published (it passes orcid's 1.30B). ~118M events are PROV activities — gh:PushEvent / PullRequestEvent / IssuesEvent / IssueCommentEvent / WatchEvent (a star) / ForkEvent / CreateEvent / DeleteEvent / ReleaseEvent / the review events, all ⊑ prov:Activity — each carrying prov:atTime, prov:wasAssociatedWith → the actor and gh:repo → the repository, plus ~90M commits (truncated messages + author names; emails deliberately excluded), 8.5M PR nodes with adds/dels/merged-by, issues with labels, and 4.2M releases. Entities live at their REAL GitHub URLs (https://github.com/{login}, /{owner}/{repo}, /pull/{n}, /commit/{sha}) — the same bare-GitHub-URL IRIs open-pulse and oss-github-benchmark use, so repositories, users and orgs are the SAME NODES across those graphs. THE RDF-STAR LAYER IS THE POINT: GitHub events embed full repository objects, so volatile metadata becomes dated OBSERVATIONS — << ?repo gh:stars ?n >> prov:generatedAtTime ?t ; prov:wasGeneratedBy ?event (~14M embedded repo snapshots) — microsoft/vscode's star count resolves hour-by-hour from 174,029 (Jul 1, 00:33) to 175,188 (Jul 31, 23:54), and every gh:starred / gh:forked edge knows who, when, and from which event. Stable facts (schema:description, programmingLanguage, SPDX licence IRI, topics, dateCreated) sit plainly on the repo node. WHY JULY 2025: GitHub cut the public feed around Aug–Sep 2025 — stars/PRs/issues dropped ~200×, PushEvent lost its commits[] — so this is one of the last full months of the rich firehose, a preserved snapshot of GitHub's social pulse. Streamed through the memory-bounded external build ({ cat ontology; zcat 186 day-section .nt.gz } | rete build - --memory-budget-mb 16384, 42 chunks, ~4.5 h). Public GitHub timeline via gharchive.org; content © its authors. NOTE: no Schema pyramid (external-build v1) — keep queries SELECTIVE (one repo, one user, one PR): each reads ~30–330 MB of the 17 GB over HTTP range; a whole-graph aggregate would scan the file.
datasets.license: Public GitHub timeline (gharchive.org); content © its authors

examples.title: ⭐ VS Code's star count, hour by hour — RDF-star observations
examples.tip:
Every GitHub PR event embeds the repository's live metadata, so the graph holds the star count of microsoft/vscode (the VS Code editor) as ~1,900 dated OBSERVATIONS rather than one overwritten number: << repo gh:stars ?n >> prov:generatedAtTime ?t. Across July 2025 it climbs from 174,029 to 175,188.
This is the RDF-star quoted-triple syntax — the subject of prov:generatedAtTime is the star-count statement itself. Swap in any busy repo's https://github.com/{owner}/{repo} IRI to chart its month.

examples.title: Who starred PyTorch on July 22 — with full provenance
examples.tip:
Each gh:starred edge is annotated with WHEN it happened and WHICH archived event asserted it — the provenance triple pattern << ?user gh:starred ?repo >> prov:atTime ?t ; prov:wasGeneratedBy ?ev. pytorch/pytorch is the deep-learning framework's main repo.
The FILTER keeps one day of the month; drop it to see all 572 July stargazers. The ?ev IRI is the GH Archive event id — a stable citation for the observation.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX gh: <https://w3id.org/rete/gharchive#>
PREFIX prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#>
PREFIX xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#>
SELECT ?user ?t ?ev WHERE {
  << ?user gh:starred <https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch> >> prov:atTime ?t .
  << ?user gh:starred <https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch> >> prov:wasGeneratedBy ?ev .
  FILTER(?t >= "2025-07-22T00:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime && ?t < "2025-07-23T00:00:00Z"^^xsd:dateTime)
} ORDER BY ?t LIMIT 100

examples.title: Linus Torvalds' July, event by event
examples.tip:
One person's public month: all 65 events prov:wasAssociatedWith https://github.com/torvalds — kernel pushes to torvalds/linux interleaved with commits to 1590A, his guitar-pedal electronics side project.
Users sit at their real GitHub URL, so any https://github.com/{login} works here — and because the IRIs are shared, the same node carries data in the open-pulse and oss-github-benchmark graphs.

examples.title: A repository's metadata card: 🤗 transformers
examples.tip:
The stable facts observed for huggingface/transformers during July: schema:description, programmingLanguage Python, the licence as a real SPDX IRI (Apache-2.0), 21 schema:keywords topics, dateCreated — plus the RDF-star-annotated volatile counts (gh:stars/gh:forks) with their observation times.
All of it was harvested from event payloads alone — no GitHub API call was ever made. Bind any repo that had a PR or fork in July 2025 (~1.9M of them carry a snapshot).

examples.title: Home Assistant's July release train
examples.tip:
Releases are first-class nodes linked to their repo by gh:inRepo and to the archived ReleaseEvent that announced them — home-assistant/core (the smart-home platform) shipped its 2025.7 betas, the 2025.7.x patch series and the first 2025.8 beta inside the month.
Join ?ev prov:atTime for the exact publication moment; gh:tag holds the git tag string.

datasets.label: gharchive-2026-06.rete — GitHub's public timeline AFTER the cut: June 2026, 730M triples (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The most recent complete month of the public GitHub event stream (June 2026, 729,745,084 triples / 163.5M terms / 6.49 GB) — and the measured AFTER of the sibling gharchive dataset's before. Around Aug–Sep 2025 GitHub quietly reduced what the public events API exposes, and this graph preserves exactly what remains: 112.2M events, 85% of them PushEvents stripped to a skeleton (the pushed gh:ref survives; commit lists, messages and author emails are gone from the feed itself — the head/before shas GitHub still sends live in the dataset's day-level Parquet tables, not the graph), 14M branch/tag CreateEvent/DeleteEvent churn events, and a shrunken social layer: 310,744 stars month-wide, ~12× below July 2025's 3.7M — and the cut keeps DEEPENING: by late July 2026 the star stream runs ~200× low, and pytorch/pytorch records just 39 WatchEvents in this ENTIRE month versus 572 in the sibling (~15×). The ASYMMETRY of what survived is the interesting part: 1.16M PullRequestEvents arrive as bare pointers (action + number — the pull_request object is EMPTY: no title, no diff stats, no merged-by, and no embedded base/head repos, so the RDF-star star-count observation layer that defines the 2025 sibling is effectively absent here; the only embedded repo objects left are 68,891 fresh forkees, all ≤1 star), while 844k issue events KEPT their titles, labels and comment bodies, and 69,837 releases kept their tags. Same model as gharchive: PROV activities at w3id.org/rete/gharchive/event/, actors/repos/orgs at their real github.com URLs (shared nodes with gharchive, open-pulse, oss-github-benchmark — query a repo across BOTH months to see the cut with your own eyes). Built by the identical pipeline (data/github-archive/scripts/, streamed memory-bounded external build). Public GitHub timeline via gharchive.org; content © its authors. No pyramid — keep queries SELECTIVE (one repo, one user); a whole-graph aggregate scans the 6.5 GB.
datasets.license: Public GitHub timeline (gharchive.org); content © its authors

examples.title: 📉 The cut, one row per star: PyTorch's ENTIRE June 2026
examples.tip:
Every star pytorch/pytorch — one of the most-starred projects on GitHub — received in this ENTIRE month, named and timestamped. There are 39 of them. The same question on the sibling gharchive dataset (July 2025, before GitHub reduced the public feed) returns 572 — a ~15× drop for the same repo, one year apart. Nothing changed about PyTorch; what changed is how much of GitHub's social activity the public timeline still exposes. Run both to measure the cut yourself.
Why 39 ROWS and not one COUNT: a bare aggregate returns exactly one row whatever the data says, so an answer of nothing looks identical to an answer — this example used to be COUNT(*) and shipped the number 0 for months without anything noticing (tests/gate/checks/check_catalog_answers.mjs now catches that shape).
The same 39 stars also exist as RDF-star observations — << ?user gh:starred <…/pytorch/pytorch> >> prov:atTime ?t — but walking the quoted triples costs ~355 MB against 49 MB for this PROV-side phrasing of the identical fact. See the sibling dataset's first two examples for the RDF-star layer at full strength.

examples.title: Linus Torvalds' June 2026 — the GuitarPedal era
examples.tip:
The kernel's creator, one year on from the sibling dataset's July-2025 ledger: still pushing to torvalds/linux — and hacking on torvalds/GuitarPedal, the successor to his 1590A guitar-electronics side project.
Actors keep their real https://github.com/{login} IRI across both months, so the same node carries his 2025 and 2026 activity — add gharchive as a second source and one query spans the year gap.

examples.title: What a push still says: home-assistant/core's June branches
examples.tip:
Post-cut PushEvents keep the ref being pushed — so per-repo branch activity (feature branches, CI experiments like ci-uv-managed-python, the dev mainline) is still fully reconstructible, with timestamps.
What's gone from the feed is the commit list itself: no shas-with-messages, no author names. The head/before shas GitHub still sends live in this dataset's Parquet tables rather than the graph.
No ORDER BY, deliberately. home-assistant/core pushed 763 times to 170 branches this month, and a global sort has to hold every one of them in memory before LIMIT can throw them away — on this pyramid-less 6.5 GB file that is enough to exhaust a browser tab (measured: it fails). Without it the engine streams and stops at 100 — 88 MB instead of 149 MB, and it answers. Add ORDER BY DESC(?t) on a quieter repo, or in the CLI, where the memory is yours to spend.

examples.title: Issues kept their words: home-assistant/core in June
examples.tip:
The cut is asymmetric: PullRequestEvents were stripped to bare action+number pointers, but ISSUE events kept their full objects — titles, labels, comment bodies. Here is home-assistant/core's June issue stream, readable as plain text ("Matter Device response time slowdown", "Fix ESPHome UTF-8 unique id collisions" …).
The rdfs:label join is what the emptied PR nodes can't offer — compare a PR-node lookup on the same repo to see the difference.

examples.title: 🪞 This repository, watching itself grow — day by day
examples.tip:
A knowledge graph that contains its own making: caviri/rete is the repository this playground is built from, and June 2026 was a development month — first pushes on the 9th, a sprint peaking on the 20th (30 events, 9 branches opened in one day), then steady mainline pushes to the end of the month.
BIND(day(?t)) + SUM(IF(…)) pivots the raw event stream into a six-column daily progress table — swap in any https://github.com/{owner}/{repo} to chart a month of anything.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX gh: <https://w3id.org/rete/gharchive#>
PREFIX prov: <http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#>
SELECT ?day (COUNT(*) AS ?events)
       (SUM(IF(?type = gh:PushEvent, 1, 0)) AS ?pushes)
       (SUM(IF(?type = gh:CreateEvent, 1, 0)) AS ?branchesCreated)
       (SUM(IF(?type = gh:DeleteEvent, 1, 0)) AS ?branchesDeleted)
       (SUM(IF(?type = gh:PullRequestEvent, 1, 0)) AS ?prEvents)
WHERE {
  ?ev gh:repo <https://github.com/caviri/rete> ; a ?type ; prov:atTime ?t .
  BIND(day(?t) AS ?day)
} GROUP BY ?day ORDER BY ?day

examples.title: The dev story, told by branch names — a readable changelog
examples.tip:
Branch names narrate development better than most changelogs: feat/shacl-progressive-docs, feat/static-playground-console … every create, push and delete timestamped, so you watch features open, iterate and get merged away — in the very repository that renders this page.
The OPTIONALs keep rows for event types that carry no ref (PR events). Replace the repo IRI with your own to read your month back like a diary.

examples.title: 🔭 Two summers of one researcher — across BOTH datasets
examples.tip:
This one runs over TWO graphs at once — the July-2025 sibling preloads as a second source. The same person, one year apart: summer 2025 reviewing PRs on sdsc-ordes/open-pulse-graph-classifier and pushing Imaging-Plaza work; June 2026 building sdsc-ordes/open-pulse and caviri/rete — the engine this playground runs on.
BIND(year(?t))/month(?t) buckets the merged timeline so each era lands in its own rows; actors keep the same https://github.com/{login} IRI in both files, which is what makes the union just work.

datasets.label: ror.rete — the Research Organization Registry: 111k organizations, the org authority of the scholarly web (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: ROR v1.54 (CC0) — all 111,068 registered research organizations as one 1.87M-triple graph (30 MB, remote-lazy). ROR is THE open successor to GRID: virtually every scholarly dataset that disambiguates an institution points here, and each org sits at its canonical https://ror.org/{id} IRI — the exact IRIs orcid.rete's 19M ROR-disambiguated affiliations target with orc:affiliationWith, so the two files JOIN cross-source in the playground (and DataCite / OpenAIRE / EPFL-graph resolve here too). Each organization is typed ror:Organization plus its roles — ror:Education / ror:Funder / ror:Facility / ror:Government / ror:Healthcare / ror:Company / ror:Archive / ror:Nonprofit — and carries its rdfs:label + aliases, ror:countryCode / ror:countryName, ror:locationName with ror:lat / ror:long, ror:established (gYear), ror:status, ror:website and ror:wikipedia. The CROSSWALK layer is the quiet superpower: ror:grid, ror:isni, ror:wikidata and ror:fundref put the legacy GRID ids, ISNIs, Wikidata Q-ids and Crossref Funder ids in one place, so any older dataset keyed to those resolves through this file. The org HIERARCHY is here too — ror:hasParent / ror:hasChild (CNRS alone has 383 child institutes), ror:predecessor / ror:successor, ror:relatedOrganization — a real institutional family tree. The ror.ttl ontology travels inside the file; Schema pyramid included (types algo). Built by scripts/ror/ror_to_nt.py → rete build --pyramid-algo types --card. Small enough to explore freely — aggregates, maps of a country's orgs, transitive hierarchy walks are all cheap.

examples.title: Five flagship org cards: CERN, EPFL, ETH, MIT, Oxford
examples.tip:
One row per canonical https://ror.org/{id} — CERN (01ggx4157, founded 1954), EPFL, ETH Zürich, MIT and Oxford (founded 1096!) — with country, city, founding year, the live website and a clickable Wikidata entity built from the ror:wikidata crosswalk.
That crosswalk (plus ror:grid, ror:isni, ror:fundref) is what makes this 30 MB file the id-resolution hub of the scholarly datasets.

examples.title: Switzerland's research landscape, oldest first
examples.tip:
Every ROR-registered organization with ror:countryCode "CH", ordered by founding year — the University of Basel (1460) leads centuries before ETH, EPFL, CERN, Empa and PSI appear — each with its city and live website.
Change the code ("ES", "DE", "JP"…) to walk any country's registry the same way.

examples.title: Countries × organization roles
examples.tip:
The registry's world map crossed with WHAT the orgs are — ror:Education vs ror:Company vs ror:Facility vs ror:Funder — so you can see that the US leads in companies while education dominates elsewhere.
At 30 MB the whole file is cheap to aggregate, unlike its billion-triple sibling orcid.

examples.title: The CNRS family: 383 child institutes, with coordinates
examples.tip:
ROR keeps the institutional HIERARCHY: https://ror.org/02feahw73 is the CNRS (Centre national de la recherche scientifique), and ror:hasChild fans out to its 383 joint labs and institutes — each row placed with its city and lat/long across the map of France.
Try ror:hasParent from a small lab to climb the other way, or ror:predecessor to trace mergers.

examples.title: 🔗 Cross-source JOIN: who lists EPFL? (live from the 1.3B ORCID graph)
examples.tip:
The join in the other direction: ror.rete resolves https://ror.org/02s376052 to EPFL (École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, Lausanne); the 17.5 GB orcid.rete — preloaded as a second source — answers who lists that same node, in what role, since when.
The planner routes each pattern by which file answers its predicate (ror:* here, orc:* there); the bound org keeps the billion-triple side to a few range reads. Swap the ROR id to poll any institution's people.

shacl_shapes.title: Organization core fields
shacl_shapes.tip: Every ror:Organization (all 111,068 of them) must carry the identity and location literals that ROR guarantees on every record: rdfs:label/ror:name, ror:rorId, ror:countryCode/countryName, ror:locationName, ror:lat/ror:long, and ror:status. minCount 1 is used only on the properties whose predicate count in the data (111,068) exactly matches the Organization class size, i.e. properties present on literally every org; website/grid/established are left optional since their counts (108,631 / 103,674 / 94,164) fall short of full coverage.

shacl_shapes.title: Every org has an operational type
shacl_shapes.tip: ROR classifies each organization into one or more operational categories (Company, Education, Funder, Nonprofit, Healthcare, Facility, OtherOrganization, Government, Archive) in addition to the umbrella ror:Organization type. This shape checks that no org is left with ONLY the generic type: the sum of the 9 subtype counts (~128,308) tracks almost exactly the extra rdf:type triples beyond one-per-org (239,410 type triples minus 111,068 orgs = 128,342), so requiring at least one subtype tag is a real, data-grounded invariant, not a guess.

shacl_shapes.title: Parent links stay inside the org graph
shacl_shapes.tip: Only about 20% of organizations (21,987 of 111,068) declare a ror:hasParent link, so this is left fully optional (no minCount) — but wherever it does appear, the object must itself be a real ror:Organization IRI, catching any parent link that dangles outside the org set (e.g. points at a literal or an unclassified node) rather than forming a genuine org-to-org edge.

datasets.label: dblp.rete — the DBLP computer-science bibliography, with the author co-authorship graph (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The complete DBLP computer-science bibliography (dblp.org, CC0) as one 196.8M-triple range-queryable graph (2.27 GB, remote-lazy over HTTP range on Cloudflare R2). 12.74M records: 8,608,631 PUBLICATIONS (dblp:Publication + a subtype — dblp:Article 4.36M, dblp:Inproceedings/conference-paper 3.91M, dblp:Incollection, dblp:Book, dblp:Thesis 156k…) plus 4.14M dblp:PersonPage author home-pages, wired to 5.79M CREATOR nodes by 33.76M dblp:authoredBy edges — the CO-AUTHORSHIP graph (ask for an author's collaborators, ranked by shared papers). Each publication carries dblp:title, dblp:year, dblp:venue (journal/booktitle), volume/number/pages/publisher, and sits at its CANONICAL DOI IRI when it has one (7,257,488 do → https://doi.org/{doi}) else its real DBLP page https://dblp.org/rec/{key}. Authors mint at https://orcid.org/{orcid} when known (1,542,309 ORCID'd creators) else a DBLP-disambiguated name IRI (DBLP's own '… 0001' homonym suffixes keep distinct people apart). Because works are keyed by DOI and people by ORCID, this graph AUTO-MERGES with the DataCite / Zenodo / OpenAIRE / OpenCitations datasets on the DOI and with the 25M-researcher orcid.rete on the ORCID — DBLP is the COMPUTER-SCIENCE vertex of the scholarly graph, and the one that brings a dense author collaboration network. Built by scripts/dblp/dblp_to_nt.py → rete build --memory-budget-mb 6000 (bounded-RAM external build); embeds the dblp.ttl ontology, itself aligned to DBLP's own official https://dblp.org/rdf/schema#. CC0. No Schema pyramid yet (repyramid OOMs at this scale on a shared box) — keep queries SELECTIVE (one author's papers, their co-authors, a specific paper); each reads a few MB over HTTP range, while a full-corpus aggregate scans the file.

examples.title: An author's publications
examples.tip:
Everything by one researcher — here Mohamed-Slim Alouini (ORCID 0000-0003-4827-1793), one of DBLP's most prolific authors (~2,000 papers). ?p is the record's canonical IRI: its DOI (https://doi.org/…) when it has one, else its DBLP page (https://dblp.org/rec/…).
Swap the ORCID IRI for any author — or use a https://w3id.org/rete/dblp/author/{name} IRI for authors without an ORCID.

examples.title: An author's top collaborators
examples.tip:
The co-authorship network around one author: everyone who shares a publication with Alouini, ranked by how many papers they co-wrote. Al-Naffouri (206), Rezki (102), Yang (98)…
?coauthor is an https://orcid.org/… IRI when the collaborator has an ORCID (so it joins the ORCID dataset), else a DBLP name IRI. This is what makes DBLP the collaboration-graph vertex of the scholarly graph.

examples.title: An author's DOI papers (federation-ready)
examples.tip:
The same author's publications that carry a DOI — so ?p is a https://doi.org/… IRI, the exact node the DataCite / Zenodo / OpenAIRE / OpenCitations graphs use. Load one of those as a second source and these rows join straight across.
7.26M of DBLP's 8.6M publications have a DOI.

examples.title: A paper's authors, with their ORCIDs
examples.tip:
One publication's full author list. Each ?author sits at its canonical IRI — https://orcid.org/… when the author has an ORCID (1.54M of DBLP's authors do), else a DBLP-disambiguated name IRI.
Change the record IRI (a DOI https://doi.org/… or a DBLP page https://dblp.org/rec/…) to inspect any paper.

examples.title: An author's output over the years
examples.tip:
Switch Output to Time. One researcher's publication count per year — a whole career at a glance (Alouini ramps up through the 2000s). Anchored on one author, so it stays cheap over HTTP range.
Swap the author IRI for any researcher (a https://orcid.org/… or a DBLP name IRI).

examples.title: An author's co-authorship ego network, as a graph
examples.tip:
Switch Output to Graph. One author's papers and every co-author on them, as a node-link graph (capped here) — the local shape of the collaboration network.
Because authors with an ORCID sit at https://orcid.org/… and papers with a DOI at https://doi.org/…, this same neighbourhood is where DBLP stitches into the ORCID and DataCite/Zenodo graphs. Change the central author IRI to map another ego network.

shacl_shapes.title: Publication core fields
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that every dblp:Publication (the 8.6M bibliographic records: Article, Inproceedings, Book, etc.) carries its DBLP record key (e.g. 'journals/cacm/Codd70') and a title as literals, and that authoredBy/doi, when present, point to the right node kinds. recordKey and title are near-universal on a DBLP record, so they are required; doi and authoredBy are optional since many older/edited records lack a DOI or use editedBy instead.

shacl_shapes.title: Creator identity fields
shacl_shapes.tip: Checks that every dblp:Creator (author or editor, the graph's 12.74M-minus-publications 'people' side) has a human-readable creatorName literal, and that orcid (when present) and coAuthorOf (the symmetric co-authorship edge) point to IRIs rather than literals. creatorName is required because it is how DBLP names every creator node; orcid coverage is partial since only ORCID-linked authors carry it.

shacl_shapes.title: Author-signature reification integrity
shacl_shapes.tip: dblp:AuthorSignature is the reified 'one row per authorship' node that preserves author order and per-signature ORCID; this shape checks each signature links to exactly one dblp:Publication (via signaturePublication) and exactly one dblp:Creator (via signatureCreator), both as IRIs of the right class. Missing or duplicated links here would mean an authorship record that cannot be resolved back to a real paper or a real person.

shacl_shapes.title: Journal article venue/year completeness
shacl_shapes.tip: Targets dblp:Article specifically (the largest publication subtype, 4.36M records) and requires a venue (journal name) and a year literal of the right datatype, since a DBLP journal-article record is essentially never entered without both. Catches malformed Article rows that would silently drop out of venue- or year-filtered queries.

datasets.label: aifdb-open.rete — QT30: argument & conflict in BBC Question Time, as a graph (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: QT30 — the largest corpus of analysed broadcast political debate — as a queryable argument graph in the **Argument Interchange Format**. 30 episodes of the BBC's *Question Time* (2020–21), 1,478 annotated fragments, hand-analysed with Inference Anchoring Theory by **Hautli-Janisz, Kikteva, Siskou, Gorska, Becker & Reed (LREC 2022)** and published open at [corpora.aifdb.org/qt30](https://corpora.aifdb.org/qt30). The distinctive thing about AIF is that every fragment carries **two layers at once**: the *dialogue* as spoken (aif:L-node locutions with a resolved speaker, aif:TA-node transitions) and the *argument* as reconstructed (aif:I-node claims joined by scheme nodes — aif:RA-node inference, aif:CA-node conflict, aif:MA-node rephrase), stitched together by aif:YA-node illocutionary anchors (Asserting / Arguing / Disagreeing / RhetoricalQuestioning …). So you can ask both *what was argued* and *who said it, and how*. 841 speakers are resolved to schema:Person nodes — host Fiona Bruce (5,692 locutions), then the politicians and panellists (Lisa Nandy, Nadhim Zahawi, Grant Shapps, Caroline Lucas…) and studio-audience turns. Because the raw AIF edges keep the scheme-node indirection, this build also materialises one-step shortcuts over them — **aifx:supports**, **aifx:conflictsWith**, **aifx:rephrases** and **aifx:illocutes** (locution → the claim it conveys) — so 'which claims are attacked, and by how many distinct speakers' is a single pattern. The AIF TBox (aif.ttl, OWL 2 QL-safe: I/L/RA/CA/MA/YA/TA class hierarchy + property domains) travels inside the file, and TEXT_INDEX is on for full-text search over every claim. Node IRIs match AIFdb's own RDF (aifdb.org/nodes/…) so this federates with the wider Argument Web. Built by data/aifdb/scripts/{harvest,aifdb_to_nt}.py → rete build --pyramid-algo types --card --text-index. **Licence: the QT30 annotation metadata is released as open data (CC0 1.0) by its authors; the underlying material is public BBC broadcast debate.** This is the one corpus of AIFdb's 538 with a clean open-licence + public-broadcast footing — the rest (many carrying forum/Reddit usernames, most with undeclared licences) stay unpublished. Tiny (13.6 MB) — explore freely.
datasets.license: CC0-1.0 (QT30 annotation metadata; underlying material is public BBC broadcast)

examples.title: Who speaks most in Question Time
examples.tip:
Every locution (aif:L-node) is resolved to a schema:Person, so counting them ranks the voices in the room. Top is Fiona Bruce — the host who chairs Question Time — then the politicians and panellists (Lisa Nandy, Nadhim Zahawi, Grant Shapps...).
QT30 text is annotated as 'Annotator : Speaker : words', so the real speaker is the middle segment (the parsing trap is documented in data/aifdb/README.md); the long tail is studio-audience turns.

examples.title: The most contested claims
examples.tip:
A claim (aif:I-node) is attacked when a conflicting claim points at it through a CA-node — collapsed here into the aifx:conflictsWith shortcut. Joining back through aifx:illocutes to the speaker counts how many DISTINCT people pushed back on each claim.
This single pattern is the payoff of the two-layer model: it needs the argument layer (conflict) and the dialogue layer (who spoke) at once.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX aif: <http://www.arg.tech/aif#>
PREFIX aifx: <https://w3id.org/rete/aif#>
SELECT ?claim (COUNT(DISTINCT ?attacker) AS ?n) WHERE {
  ?att aifx:conflictsWith ?target .
  ?loc aifx:illocutes ?att ; aifx:speaker ?attacker .
  ?target aif:claimText ?claim .
} GROUP BY ?claim HAVING (COUNT(DISTINCT ?attacker) > 1) ORDER BY DESC(?n) LIMIT 20

examples.title: Chains of support between claims
examples.tip:
aifx:supports collapses an RA-node (inference) into a direct claim-to-claim edge: the 'from' claim is offered as a premise for the 'to' claim. Read side by side, they show the reconstructed reasoning — e.g. 'over half the deaths are in care homes' -> 'at the centre of this pandemic is the care homes in Scotland'.
Swap aifx:supports for aifx:conflictsWith or aifx:rephrases to walk the other two argument relations.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX aif: <http://www.arg.tech/aif#>
PREFIX aifx: <https://w3id.org/rete/aif#>
SELECT ?from ?to WHERE {
  ?a aifx:supports ?b .
  ?a aif:claimText ?from .
  ?b aif:claimText ?to .
} LIMIT 40

examples.title: How one politician argues
examples.tip:
The YA-node on each locution records its illocutionary force — the speech act behind the words. This profiles one speaker (here Lisa Nandy, Labour): mostly Asserting, with some RhetoricalQuestioning and AssertiveQuestioning.
Swap the speaker IRI for another panellist — .../speaker/Nadhim_Zahawi or .../speaker/Grant_Shapps — to compare rhetorical styles.

examples.title: The conflict network
examples.tip:
Switch Output to Graph. Builds a node-link diagram of claims that attack one another (aifx:conflictsWith), carrying each claim's text as its rdfs:label so the nodes are readable — the disagreement structure of the debates, drawn.
Raise the LIMIT for a denser web, or swap in aifx:supports to draw the inference structure instead.

datasets.label: plantatlas.rete — Digital Plant Atlas: archaeobotany seed/fruit & geolocated field photos, each with its picture (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The **Digital Plant Atlas** ([plantatlas.eu](https://www.plantatlas.eu/), GIA-Groningen + DAI Berlin, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 NL) — an archaeobotany reference collection of high-quality photos of plant **seeds, fruits and vegetative parts** with verified scientific names — as one 1.33M-triple range-queryable graph (10.3 MB, remote-lazy over HTTP range on Cloudflare R2). **28,595 pa:Photo**, each carrying its own **WebP picture** (schema:image + foaf:depiction → data.graphplaza.com/plantatlas/images_webp/<id>.webp — switch a column's cell type to Image and the photos render inline), plus Darwin Core taxonomy (dwc:family / dwc:genus / dwc:scientificName), pa:plantPart, pa:lengthMm / pa:widthMm, pa:appendages / pa:surface. **52,907 pa:Specimen** reference-collection records (provenance: pa:deliveryInstitution, dwc:country, taphonomy pa:processing, dwc:verbatimEventDate + a cleaned dwc:eventDate) wired to their photos by **pa:hasPhoto** — the specimen↔photo join. **3,920 pa:Locality** places (859 with WGS84 geo:lat/long + GeoSPARQL geo:asWKT — switch Output → Map to see where the 'Nature' field photos were collected). **3,551 pa:Taxon** (family/genus, genus skos:broader family). Two photo sets live here: MI_/DF_ seed-fruit reference photos (with measurements) and RC_ geolocated field photos (lat/lon lives only in the map layer). Coordinates cleaned (the 'Unknown' / −25,133 placeholders dropped, out-of-range flagged); taxa come from family+genus because the upstream scientificName is only 13% filled. TEXT_INDEX on for full-text name/locality search. Acquired by a reverse-engineered crawl of the site's Pimcore/Symfony JSON endpoints (no public API) → Parquet → data/plantatlas/scripts/build_nt.py + plantatlas-ontology.ttl → rete build --pyramid-algo types --card --text-index. Remote-lazy on Cloudflare R2.
datasets.license: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 NL (© Digital Plant Atlas — RUG & DAI; commercial use → info@plantatlas.eu)

examples.title: Wheat (Triticum) seeds & fruits, with the photo
examples.tip:
Every pa:Photo carries its picture as a WebP URL (schema:image). The 'Photo' column ends in .webp, so the playground renders it inline as a thumbnail — click to enlarge.
This pulls the reference-collection photos of the wheat genus Triticum (MI_/DF_ accessions) with their published plant part.

examples.title: Where the field ('Nature') photos were collected
examples.tip:
The RC_ 'Nature' photos are the only geolocated set — their collection place (pa:atLocality → a pa:Locality with geo:asWKT) is the sole source of lat/lon.
Switch Output → Map to plot each photo at its locality; the popup shows the species and its WebP picture.

examples.title: Top plant families by number of photos
examples.tip:
Taxon comes from dwc:family (100% filled) rather than the upstream scientificName (only 13% filled).
Poaceae (grasses — the cereals) and Fabaceae (legumes) dominate, as you'd expect of an archaeobotany seed reference collection.

examples.title: A specimen → its example photos
examples.tip:
pa:hasPhoto is the specimen↔photo join, recovered from the reference-collection detail pages: one pa:Specimen has several pa:Photo parts (florets, fruits, spikelets…).
The 'Photo' column renders each part's WebP inline — a single specimen shown from several angles/parts.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX pa: <https://w3id.org/rete/plantatlas/ontology#>
PREFIX schema: <http://schema.org/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?label ?part ?image WHERE {
  ?spec a pa:Specimen ; rdfs:label ?label ; pa:hasPhoto ?photo .
  ?photo schema:image ?image ; pa:plantPart ?part .
} LIMIT 40

examples.title: Plant parts across all photos
examples.tip:
pa:plantPart is the published archaeobotanical part label — what the reference photo actually shows.
Seed and Fruit dominate (this is a seed/fruit identification atlas), then whole plants (the geolocated field photos) and finer parts like fruitlet, floret and spikelet.

datasets.label: datacite.rete — the whole DataCite corpus + the PID Graph: 10.18B triples, 109.3M records, 613M provenance-bearing events (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The **complete DataCite Public Data Files** (2023, 2024, 2025; CC0) and both **PID Links** files as ONE range-queryable graph — **10,184,067,429 unique triples in 67.6 GB over a 1.959-billion-term dictionary**. **The records:** 109,263,993 DOI-identified research outputs, **one per DOI** (newest snapshot wins, `dcite:fromSnapshot` says which) — `dcite:Dataset`, `dcite:Text`, `dcite:PhysicalObject`, `dcite:Image`, `dcite:JournalArticle`, `dcite:Software`, `dcite:Collection`, `dcite:Preprint`, `dcite:Dissertation`, `dcite:Workflow` … (all 32 DataCite 4.6 types) — each at its canonical `https://doi.org/{doi}` IRI with title, year, publisher, resource type, citation/view counters, `dct:subject` keywords, reified creators (`dcite:AgentRole` carrying the name and affiliations the record gives, held by an `https://orcid.org/` agent when the ORCID checks out) and funders (`dcite:fundedBy` ROR / Crossref Funder ID, with the record's own funder name on its `dcite:FundingReference`). **The PID Graph:** 613,426,158 relation events (Cites, References, IsSupplementTo, IsVersionOf, IsPartOf, IsDerivedFrom, all 38 DataCite 4.6 types …), each a direct typed edge **and** one `dcite:PidRelation` per event with exactly one `dcite:assertedBy` source and `dcite:occurredAt` time. Every conversion rule (R0–R20) and what it rescued, kept as text or dropped is in the Dataset Card; a DOI pointer typed with typographic dashes names the registered DOI with `-` (R20: 136 related identifiers and 250 PID Links endpoints, checked against this dump's DOIs and Crossref's), and the text as written stays on the edge (an RDF 1.2 reifier, or the `dcite:PidRelation`); every IRI was checked by an RFC 3987 parser and the build refuses to finish if a DOI would mint two records' IRI or a single-valued property were stated twice. Works key by DOI and people by ORCID, so it auto-merges with crossref, opencitations, dblp, zenodo, openaire and orcid. `dcite:` ontology 1.3.0 travels in the file. **Full-text search** (`CONTAINS`, the playground's word search) over titles, subjects and the names of creators, affiliations, publishers and funders, from the file's text index. **No pyramid at this scale** — keep queries SELECTIVE (one DOI, one publisher, one type); each reads a few MB over HTTP range. CC0.

examples.title: Research-output cards straight from the DOI registry
examples.tip: One row per DataCite record: the DOI (clickable — it resolves to the publisher's landing page), the title, the year, who published it and what kind of thing it is. This is the bibliographic card for 109.3M outputs, one per DOI; bind ?publisher to a specific repository to browse just theirs.

examples.title: Research software, ranked by citations
examples.tip: DataCite is where software gets a DOI, and this file has 778,189 dcite:Software records. Each row carries the citation and view counters DataCite tracks, plus the keywords the depositor supplied — so you can see which research code is actually cited. Swap dcite:Software for dcite:Dataset (56.7M) or dcite:Workflow.

examples.title: The PID Graph: what a work points at, and why
examples.tip: DataCite's relation network as first-class, provenance-bearing edges: each dcite:PidRelation records the subject DOI, the relation type (References, Cites, IsSupplementTo, IsVersionOf, IsPartOf, IsDerivedFrom…), the object DOI, and WHO asserted it. Both DOIs are clickable, so you can follow the link out to the real objects. 613M of these events are in the file, one PidRelation each.

examples.title: The whole corpus by resource type
examples.tip: A GROUP BY over the full 1.47-billion-row rdf:type slice of a 10.18-billion-triple file — 30 groups back. This is the exact query the benchmark measures at 131 s inside a 4 GiB container: aggregation streams, so memory is O(groups), not O(rows). It reads a large slice over HTTP, so expect it to take a while in the browser.

examples.title: DOI pointers typed with typographic dashes, repaired (R20)
examples.tip: 136 related identifiers were typed with an en dash, a Unicode hyphen or a minus sign where the registered DOI has an ASCII hyphen; the edge now names the registered DOI, and an RDF 1.2 reifier keeps the text as DataCite has it (dcite:relatedIdentifierAsWritten). A DOI registered with its dash is left alone. The predicate is rare, so this reads a few tiles.

examples.title: Records with a word in their title (full-text index)
examples.tip: CONTAINS is answered from the file's text index (titles, subjects, and the names of creators, affiliations, publishers and funders), so only the posting lists of the word are read, not 10,184,067,429 triples. Change the word; for a name, search dcite:creatorName on the dcite:AgentRole instead.

datasets.label: epfl-graph.rete — the EPFL GraphOntology: 6.2M Wikipedia concepts linked by embedding similarity (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: EPFL’s **GraphOntology** (Apache-2.0) as one range-queryable graph — **427 million triples (6.8 GB)**: a Wikipedia-derived **concept network** modelled on SKOS. **6.2M `epfl:Concept` nodes** plus Wikipedia categories, wired by the relation network — `epfl:related` / `epfl:relatedDirected`, the category hierarchy (`epfl:broader`), anchor pages (`epfl:anchorPage`) — and above all by the **192.6M-edge embedding-similarity graph** `epfl:similarTo`, whose similarity score rides on the edge itself as **RDF-star** (`<< ?a epfl:similarTo ?b >> epfl:score ?s`). Ask it what a topic is *near* in meaning: the neighbours of *Machine learning* come back as Statistical learning theory, Artificial intelligence, Pattern recognition, Empirical risk minimization. Categories carry `epfl:referencePageUrl` — **the real Wikipedia page**, one click from any result row — and align to the OpenAlex topic taxonomy through `epfl:alignedTopic` → `https://openalex.org/T…`, so a concept query can hand off to the bibliographic graphs (openaire, crossref, opencitations) by topic. Vocabulary `epfl:` = `w3id.org/rete/epflgraph#`, aligned to SKOS / Dublin Core / schema.org, travels in the file. Built by `data/epfl-graph/scripts/parquet_to_nt.py` → streamed `rete build` from the 258M-row EPFL Parquet export. Keep queries SELECTIVE (one concept and its neighbours); each reads a few MB over HTTP range. Apache-2.0.

examples.title: What is 'Machine learning' near, in meaning?
examples.tip: The heart of this graph: 192.6M embedding-similarity edges between Wikipedia concepts. From the Machine learning node you get Statistical learning theory, Artificial intelligence, Pattern recognition, Empirical risk minimization… — semantic neighbours, not link neighbours. Each row carries the neighbour's Wikipedia page, one click away. Change the seed name to any concept.

examples.title: Concepts bridged to the OpenAlex topic taxonomy
examples.tip: Where this graph hands off to the bibliographic ones: epfl:alignedTopic maps a Wikipedia category onto an OpenAlex topic IRI (clickable — it opens the topic on openalex.org). Take a topic id from here and query openaire, crossref or opencitations for the literature under it.

examples.title: The category tree, with its Wikipedia pages
examples.tip: The concept hierarchy itself: epfl:broader walks a category to its parent, and both ends arrive with their real Wikipedia page so you can read what a node actually means. Add another epfl:broader hop — or use a property path — to climb further up the tree.

datasets.label: crossref.rete — the Crossref Public Data File (March 2026): 179.5M works with their authors, funding, licences and relations (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The **Crossref Public Data File (March 2026)** as one range-queryable graph: **179,536,192 DOI-registered works** in **8,271,040,725 statements** (66.4 GB), rebuilt in October 2026 from the original dump with a converter that counts every rescue and drop. Every work sits at `https://doi.org/{doi}`, written exactly as the DataCite and OpenAIRE graphs write it (the shared identifier rules of caviri/rete-datasets: `common/ids.py`), so the graphs join on DOIs — including the 69k DOIs with `[ ]` and the ones with `%XX` that joined nothing before. One class per Crossref type (`cx:JournalArticle` 120M, `cx:BookChapter` 24M, `cx:ProceedingsArticle` 9.6M, `cx:Component`, `cx:Dataset`, `cx:PostedContent`, … 30 in all). Titles are plain text in `rdfs:label`; the raw JATS/HTML is kept as `cx:titleMarkup` where it differs. **Contributors are nodes**: `cx:author` / `cx:editor` / `cx:translator` / `cx:chair` → one role node per list position (515M) with `cx:givenName`, `cx:familyName` or `cx:name`, `cx:position`, `cx:sequence`, the ORCID iD of THAT contributor as `cx:isHeldBy <https://orcid.org/…>` (48.4M, checksum-valid, with `cx:orcidAuthenticated`) and affiliations (`cx:affiliation`, 148.8M, 2.1M with a checked `cx:ror`). **Funding**: 35.3M `cx:Funding` nodes (`cx:funding`) with the funder name, award numbers and, for a valid Crossref Funder ID only, `cx:funder` and `cx:fundedBy` → `https://doi.org/10.13039/…`; DOI-less funders are kept by name. Also every ISSN and ISBN with its type, 123M licences (URL, content version, start), 16M typed relations (`cx:isPreprintOf`, `cx:hasReview`, `cx:isVersionOf`, …), 1.04M `cx:Update` nodes (corrections and retractions, Retraction Watch included), events, peer reviews, institutions and grant projects. **The citation edges (`cx:cites`) are a companion file, `crossref-citations.rete`**, at the same IRIs (add it as a second source). No abstracts. Built by caviri/rete-datasets: `crossref/parquet_to_nt.py` + `crossref/build_rete.sh` (`rete build --strict`, guarded, curated card with starter queries; the full tally travels as `crossref.tally.json`). NO pyramid at this scale — keep queries SELECTIVE (one work, one funder, one ORCID). CC0 1.0: Crossref metadata is facts, and the graph holds no abstracts.

examples.title: Bibliographic cards — 7 columns of metadata
examples.tip:
Every work carries its bibliographic card as typed properties — this lists 25 with all seven filled.
Work IRIs are the shared https://doi.org/… form, so any ?work opens the real paper and joins DataCite and OpenAIRE on the DOI. Titles are plain text; the raw JATS/HTML stays in cx:titleMarkup where it differs.

examples.title: Authors in list order, with the ORCID iD of THAT author
examples.tip:
Each author is a node (cx:author → role) with its list position, name parts and — when Crossref has one — the ORCID iD of that person as cx:isHeldBy <https://orcid.org/…>, checksum-checked, with Crossref's authenticated-orcid flag.
The iD is the same node orcid.rete and dblp.rete mint: add orcid as a second source to pull the author's full profile.

examples.title: NIH-funded works with their award numbers
examples.tip:
Each funder entry of a work is a cx:Funding node with the name and award numbers the publisher deposited; cx:funder points to the Crossref Funder ID only when it is a valid 10.13039/<digits> — here the National Institutes of Health, https://doi.org/10.13039/100000002.
Swap in any Funder ID (Wellcome 10.13039/100004440, ERC 10.13039/501100000781) for its funded output.

examples.title: Retractions: the notice, the retracted work and who reported it
examples.tip: Crossref's update-to and updated-by entries become cx:Update nodes — 104,676 retraction notices among 1.04M corrections, errata and new versions — with both works, the date and the source (the publisher, or Retraction Watch, whose records Crossref carries).

examples.title: Preprints and the work each one became
examples.tip: One of the 75 typed Crossref relations: cx:isPreprintOf links a posted preprint to the version of record (749k such links). Swap in cx:hasReview, cx:isVersionOf or cx:isSupplementTo to walk the others.

examples.title: Browse the built-in ontology (no pyramid needed)
examples.tip:
The Schema tab needs a build-time pyramid that this 8.27B-statement build skips — but the cx: ontology travels IN the graph, so this query IS the schema browser: its 47 classes with labels, superclasses and definitions.
Keep the OPTIONAL shape when you adapt it: the OPTIONALs seed from the classes rather than from the 170M rdfs:label literals. Swap owl:Class for owl:ObjectProperty or owl:DatatypeProperty to browse the 276 properties.

datasets.label: crossref-citations.rete — the Crossref citation graph: 1.97B cx:cites edges between DOIs (remote, lazy)
datasets.description: The **citation edges of the Crossref Public Data File (March 2026)**: **1,981,904,784 statements** (34.3 GB). **1,974,482,380 `cx:cites` edges**, one per distinct DOI a work's deposited references name (2.74B references; every DOI read through the hub's shared normaliser, written exactly as the DataCite and OpenAIRE graphs write it; the 756M references without a DOI are counted and left out). **3,637,026 references were deposited with typographic dashes** (`10.1111/j.1465‐3362…` in Wiley and AGU reference lists); their edges cite the registered DOI with `-` (1,947,433 distinct DOIs; the 35 DOIs registered WITH a dash are kept as written). Each repaired reference keeps the DOI as the publisher typed it: its own node, `<work>/reference/<k>`, is an RDF 1.2 reifier — a node that stands for the statement `<work> cx:cites <doi>` (`rdf:reifies <<( … )>>`) — carrying `cx:citedDOIAsWritten`; query it with `?r rdf:reifies << ?citing cx:cites ?cited >> ; cx:citedDOIAsWritten ?text`. Reference values that are not DOIs (148,348) are `cx:citedDOIText` on the citing work. The companion of `crossref.rete` (titles, authors, funding) at the same `https://doi.org/{doi}` IRIs: add it as a second source and one query joins a citation to its journal, year or authors (`cx:` properties). This file also holds one `rdfs:label` (and one `rdf:type`), in the declaration of `cx:citedDOIAsWritten`; the playground's cross-source join sends a pattern to every source that has its predicate and unions the rows, so a citing work's `rdfs:label` comes from `crossref.rete`. Two files because rete's external build would need ~17 GB of dictionary-merge memory for both at once. A bound cited-DOI lookup reads a few tiles; whole-graph aggregates scan the file. Built by caviri/rete-datasets: `crossref/parquet_to_nt.py emit --part citations` + `crossref/build_rete.sh` (guarded; tally `crossref-citations.tally.json`). CC0 1.0.

examples.title: Who cites the diamond-thermometry Nature paper?
examples.tip:
Kucsko et al., 'Nanometre-scale thermometry in a living cell' (Nature 2013, doi 10.1038/nature12373) — its citing works, with their journal and year joined from crossref.rete (added as a second source).
A bound cited-DOI lookup reads a handful of tiles even inside the 1.97-billion-edge cites run.
examples.sparql:
PREFIX cx: <https://w3id.org/rete/crossref#>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?citing ?journal ?year WHERE {
  ?citing cx:cites <https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12373> .
  ?citing cx:containerTitle ?journal .
  ?citing cx:issuedYear ?year .
} LIMIT 50

examples.title: How many works cite it?
examples.tip: Counts the works whose references name 10.1038/nature12373: 1,730 — exactly Crossref's own is-referenced-by-count for the paper (cx:isReferencedByCount in crossref.rete).

examples.title: Two hops down a citation chain
examples.tip:
Starts at Ghosh et al.'s JACS 2002 copper-corrole paper (doi 10.1021/ja0113697) and walks cx:cites twice: what it cites, and what those references cite in turn.
Both hops stay bound, so the chain reads a few MB — copy the pattern for deeper walks.

examples.title: Repaired edges and the DOI as the publisher typed it
examples.tip:
Wiley and AGU reference lists deposit DOIs with typographic dashes (U+2010 ‐ instead of -). R15 points the edge to the registered DOI and keeps the text as typed on an RDF 1.2 reifier of the edge — the reference's own node <work>/reference/<k>, which rdf:reifies the triple term <<( work cx:cites doi )>>.
The `<< … >>` pattern matches that triple term, so one query returns both ends of the edge and the original text.

examples.title: Reference DOI values that are not DOIs, kept as text
examples.tip: A reference value the shared DOI normaliser cannot read (spaces inside, no 10.NNNN/ prefix) is never minted as an IRI: it stays on the citing work as cx:citedDOIText, counted in the tally.
